Opening of Parliament
THURSDAY, 19 MAY 1977
Parliament was prorogued on 4 March 1977 and met again for the dispatch of business
on 19 May 1977.
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
OPENING OF PARLIAMENT
A message from His Excellency the Governor-General desiring the immediate attend-
ance of honourable members in the Council Chamber was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod.
Accordingly, Mr Speaker, accompanied by honourable members, and preceded by the
Serjeant-at-Arms, proceeded to the Council Chamber, and, after a short absence, returned.
MEMBERS SWORN
Mr Speaker administered the oath of allegiance to Mr David Russell Lange and Mr
John Howard Falloon, who then took their seats in the Chamber.
EXPIRING LAWS CONTINUANCE BILL
This Bill was read a first time pro forma.
GOVERNOR-GENERAL'S SPEECH
Mr SPEAKER: I desire to report that, when the House did attend upon His Excellency
the Governor-General this day in the Council Chamber, His Excellency was pleased to make
a speech, the text of which speech was handed to me by His Excellency, and I now lay it on
the table of the House. The text of the speech is:
HONOURABLE MEMBERS OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
It is over four years since I first addressed you in Parliament assembled. My term of
office as the representative of the Queen in our country is now drawing to a close. From the
very beginning my wife and I have been deeply sensible that the Vice-Regal Commission is
the highest honour which can be granted to a citizen of New Zealand.
On our retirement we shall take with us countless happy memories amongst which will
be the loyalty which New Zealanders have for their Queen and the friendly co-operation we
have enjoyed with all honourable members. These have demonstrated to us in a very
personal way our great heritage where the Monarchy and the elected representatives of our
people share the responsibilities of safeguarding the rights and interests of all New Zealand-
ers.
The New Zealand economic outlook is more difficult than at any time since the second
world war. Despite encouraging signs such as the halt in the rate of increase in prices and
substantial reductions in both the balance of payments and Government deficits, all three
remain at levels which are unsustainable in the longer term.
The Government sees no room for complacency. Economic policy in the next few years
must continue to aim at restrained internal demand, a reduced rate of inflation, and the
diversion of production to exporting. In particular, there can be no return to complete
freedom from income restraint in the meantime.
Nevertheless, the Government believes the private sector should be left free as far as is
practicable to operate within a normal, commercial, competitive environment. Accordingly,
the Government intends to introduce legislation to establish a wage fixing system incorporat-
ing both flexibility and restraint.
Short-term economic problems-while urgent and important in themselves—are symp-
tomatic of some underlying weaknesses within the economy. Perhaps the most startling
evidence of this is that in the decade ending in 1974 the rate of increase in our national
income per head was less than that in every other developed country. The Government is
letermined not to let the need to overcome short-term difficulties overshadow the search for
solutions to the more basic problems.
The permanence and extent of the problem suggests that fundamental changes will be
required over the next few years in most areas of the economy. Already the Government has
instituted measures such as the energy pricing policy, the promotion of industry develop-

ment plans and the stimulation of export industries to encourage the efficient use of
resources. But it is clear that further measures will be needed.
Ministers therefore attach special importance to the proper co-ordination of priorities in
all spheres of public and private planning; they recognise that the social and regional aspects
of national development require considerable attention so that planning for economic
growth and stability can be undertaken on a much broader basis than in the past.
The establishment of the New Zealand Planning Council should provide a catalyst and a
focus for co-operative endeavours by Government, local and regional authorities' and
private agencies and individuals to plan for improvements in New Zealand's economic,
social, and cultural life, with due regard for the environment. The Government will give
priority this session to the introduction of a Bill to define the status and functions of the
Planning Council.
A further major economic measure for consideration this session is the Public Finance
Bill which will contain some important new measures designed to enhance parliamentary
control over the expenditure of public money.
The severe inflation experienced over the last few years, coupled with historical cost
accounting, may have distorted investment patterns and discouraged productive investment.
Ministers are studying submissions made on the report of the Committee of Inquiry into
Inflation Accounting.
New Zealand's future prosperity will continue to depend on the vigour of its primary
industries and their ability to compete for export markets. The Government's commitment
to increasing agricultural production is evident from the successful establishment of the
livestock incentive scheme to accelerate increase in livestock numbers. The Rural Bank will
continue to be provided with adequate funds by the Government to meet the reasonable
needs of the agricultural sector, particularly for farm development.
Among other measures aimed at increasing production and efficiency the Government
will introduce a Noxious Plants Bill to improve noxious weeds administration, a Potato
Growing Industry Bill to bring the industry under a reconstituted Potato Board, and a Wool
Industry Bill to merge the Wool Board and the Wool Marketing Corporation.
While continuing to encourage the export industries based on forest resources and to
maintain a substantial afforestation programme, the Government will examine the future
contributions to the economy of this sector and its likely demands on other resources.
Legislation will be introduced this session to revise the Forest and Rural Fires Act 1955 and
to amend the Noxious Animals Act 1956.
There has been, in recent months, a substantial increase in the activity of foreign fishing
fleets in the waters around New Zealand. In a measure of far-reaching importance the
Government will propose the establishment of a 200-mile economic zone.
The proposed action does not mean that the Government has changed its aim of
reaching a multilateral agreement on all aspects of the law of the sea in a new, widely
supported treaty. The measures to be introduced will be fully in accordance with the work
done in the Law of the Sea Conference. In accordance with the decision of the South Pacific
Forum the Government will consult with the other members of the forum concerning the
date on which the measure is to be implemented.
The establishment of the economic zone will provide an opportunity to increase the
scale and value of our fishing industry. A review of the assistance necessary to achieve this is
currently under way. You will also be asked to consider further the Fisheries Amendment
Bill which is at present before a select committee. To check the reckless exploitation of
natural resources a Bill will be introduced to protect marine mammals.
The Government's policy on overseas trade recognises the urgent need to increase the
efficient production and export of a wider range and a greater value of goods especially those
with a high degree of local content. Vigorous encouragement will be given to exporters both
by the refinement of existing measures and the introduction of new measures.
Continued efforts will be made to improve and secure access arrangements for New
Zealand's primary products into its traditional markets in Western Europe, North America,
and Japan. At the same time, emphasis will be placed on the further strengthening of trade
and economic relations with countries in the Middle East, Asia, South America, the Pacific
and socialist countries.
Recognising the need for speeding up economic development in the South Pacific Island
nations with which New Zealand has traditionally had close ties, the Government will
continue to encourage New Zealand companies to establish appropriate manufacturing
ventures in these countries. Legal recognition will be given to the Pacific Forum Shipping
Line, the aims of which are to co-ordinate shipping in the region.
Despite progress in correcting the balance of payments situation, restraints on imports

by means of import control will need to be continued. Import policies aimed at holding
employment and production at reasonable levels and promoting exports will be maintained.
The Government intends to review and update commercial legislation. As a start a Bill
will be introduced to control the practice of financial advertising. In addition a uniform code
is proposed dealing with the insolvency of persons or organisations of different types thereby
providing the legal machinery to deal with a group financial collapse irrespective of the
different legal entities involved.
The Sales Tax Bill will be introduced which will alter the existing sales tax legislation
from a negative system in which all items are taxable unless specifically exempted to a system
which will positively identify the liability of goods to sales tax.
The Government will give high priority to planning for adequate energy supplies to
meet the reasonable needs of the community and to provide for economic development. In
doing so it will consider carefully how to make the best possible use of indigenous resources.
Close attention will be given to all energy conservation opportunities and to the scope for the
future development of New Zealand's renewable energy resources.
The Government will continue to promote the orderly and economic development of all
transport modes to obtain the best utilisation of resources for the benefit of the consumer.
In presenting legislation the Government will be guided by its strong belief that the
family is the firm basis of New Zealand society.
The Government will introduce a Social Security Amendment Bill validating increases
in the rates of social security benefits in accordance with the policy of adjusting benefits
every six months.
The Children and Young Persons Act 1974 has now been in operation for about two
years. In that time certain problems, mostly of a technical nature, have arisen and you will be
asked to consider a Bill to clarify the intention of the Act and to make its operation more
effective.
The law relating to divorce, separation, maintenance, and paternity will be revised and,
in line with the Government's policy, the sole ground for divorce will be the irretrievable
breakdown of the marriage. The principle embodied in last year's Matrimonial Property
Act, that on the dissolution of a marriage by divorce the matrimonial property belongs to
both parties regardless of legal title, will be extended to the distribution of a married
person's property when he or she dies.
The Government's policy of progressive law reform will be further advanced by several
Bills implementing reports of the law reform committees. It is also intended to review the
Electoral Act 1957 and the Unit Titles Act 1972.
New Zealand has one of the lowest levels of unemployment amongst OECD countries,
an achievement assisted by the extended use of Government-funded special work program-
mes. However employment growth is likely to remain at a low level during the remainder of
this year. Despite this it is expected that the average unemployment level will be only slightly
above last year's.
The special work programmes within the public sector will be continued as a major
component of the Government's policy. Greater emphasis will however be given to assisting
private employers to participate in similar schemes, thereby reflecting the Government's
objective of redeploying resources in favour of the private sector.
The tight occupational controls which the Government implemented to reduce immigra-
tion from the abnormally high levels of 1974 and 1975 have operated successfully, and the
number of immigrants has dropped to a level which is consistent with the country's ability to
absorb them. Now that this level has been reached it will be possible to relax controls slightly
so that as the need for skilled workers becomes apparent more immigrants can be granted
entry.
The temporary entry of workers from the South Pacific has already been facilitated by
the introduction of revised work permit schemes for persons from Tonga, Fiji, and Western
Samoa, and the Government expects that the use of these schemes will be of considerable
benefit to employers, to permit holders, and to the economies of the Island nations.
An Immigration Amendment Bill will be introduced with the object of increasing the
effectiveness of immigration controls and also to provide better services to immigrants and to
the general public.
You will also be asked to consider a Bill to consolidate the British Nationality and New
Zealand Citizenship Act 1948 and the Aliens Act 1948. The most important change will be to
give women equal status with men in the transmission of citizenship by descent to children of
the first generation.
New Zealanders rightly expect a reasonable standard of accommodation and the
Government will ensure to the fullest possible extent that these expectations are met. The

Government accepts as socially and economically desirable the better utilisation of existing
housing and will be reviewing all housing policies with this in mind. But this policy will need
to maintain a viable homebuilding industry.
The Government will continue to encourage home ownership savings schemes to ensure
that individuals will be able to make a worthwhile contribution towards a home of their own
choice, as well as to provide a growing source of funds as an alternative to direct State
intervention in the housing market.
The Government will pursue its policy of improving the health services by the extension
and development of preventive and community health programmes.
Parliament will be given the opportunity of considering legislation based on the
recommendations in the report of the Royal Commission of Inquiry into Contraception,
Sterilisation, and Abortion.
As foreshadowed last year a committee has been set up under the chairmanship of Sir
John Marshall to study and make recommendations on the certification, registration, and
discipline of teachers. The outcome of the report, which should be completed in July, is
likely to be of considerable importance to the professional status of teachers and
consequently will have a bearing on the welfare of the pupils in the schools.
The Government will continue to give full attention to meeting the special needs of the
Maori people. Special trade training schemes for young people will be further developed and
the Maori housing, land development, and social welfare activities will be maintained. The
active involvement of Maori owners in the control and management of their land will be
further encouraged by the transfer of Maori reserved lands to the control of incorporations
or trustees.
You will be asked to consider a major revision of the Town and Country Planning Act
1953. The Government intends to give effect to many of the recommendations of the review
committee which was set up in 1972 and, in particular, to strengthen regional planning and
relate it more directly to the Government's economic, social and development policies.
A Local Government Amendment Bill, revising and consolidating into one enactment a
substantial portion of the Municipal Corporations and Counties Acts, will be introduced.
Further Bills of this nature will be submitted by the Government until the very major task
involved in this revision of basic local government legislation is completed.
Her Majesty Queen Elizabeth II graciously indicated at the second session of this
Parliament that she was pleased to associate her name with the proposed National Trust in
commemoration of the Silver Jubilee. A Bill will be introduced this session to establish the
trust.
Honourable members, the Government will pursue New Zealand's political and
economic interests overseas with determination and will seek to promote greater co-
operation between countries.
The Prime Minister's recent talks with leaders in Australia, Britain and Europe and his
proposed visit to the United States underline the fundamental importance the Government
attaches to sustaining and developing New Zealand's relationships with the Western
community.
Of equal importance to New Zealand is its partnership with countries of Asia and the
Pacific. The Government will work for a secure and long-term economic relationship with
Japan within a framework of mutual co-operation. It will also strengthen relationships with
the ASEAN countries.
The Prime Minister's attendance at the London meeting of the Commonwealth Heads
of Government will enable contacts with a wide range of countries to be renewed.
The Government will give full support to the United Nations in its work of maintaining
peace and security. It will work with both East and West for the conclusion of a nuclear
weapon test-ban treaty. It will oppose all forms of racial discrimination and support
international endeavours to secure full human rights for all people.
The Government, consistent with its adherence to a policy of collective defence,
attaches high priority to the maintenance of armed forces adequate for New Zealand's
foreseeable needs and capable of timely expansion should the need arise. In the light of
recent changes in the global and Pacific strategic situation, and modifications in the defence
policies of our major allies, the Government is undertaking a review of defence needs in the
1980s.
Honourable members, it is now my privilege to exercise, for the last time, the
prerogative of Her Majesty The Queen in opening this third session of the thirty-eighth
Parliament. In doing so I commend all these matters to your careful consideration and I pray
that divine guidance will attend your decisions.

Motion agreed to.
CIVIL LIST AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That the Civil List Amendment
Bill be introduced. The Bill provides for the payment of an annuity to a retired Governor-
General who is domiciled in New Zealand at the time of his appointment and who continues
to reside in New Zealand on vacating his office. This situation has not arisen before, but is
likely to be the case in the future. The payment of an annuity to a retiring Governor-General
recognises his particular status in the community. The annuity will be at the same rate as that
paid to a former Prime Minister. There is also provision in the Bill for the widow of a former
Governor-General to receive an annuity equal to half that received by her husband. If the
situation should arise where a person is entitled to more than one of these annuities he or she
will receive only the higher of the annuities.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
TRADE AND INDUSTRY AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I move, That the
Trade and Industry Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill is a machinery measure of two
substantive clauses. Clause 2 inserts a new section 2A in the principal Act. The new section
provides that any right, power, discretion, or authority that may be exercised by the Minister
of Trade and Industry under the Act may also be exercised by the Minister of Overseas
Trade or the Minister of Regional Development. This amendment reflects the fact that my
department undertakes in practice statutory functions and responsibilities now under the
control of and within the respective portfolios of three Ministers. In addition, I may exercise
certain powers-for example to establish committees of inquiry and advisory committees in
relation to matters of trade and industry and to publish information gained in terms of the
Act. This amendment will simply enable my colleagues to exercise those powers in matters
administratively within their own portfolios in their own right, and provides them with
formal authority in relation to activities conducted by my department under their control.
The effect of the second amendment in clause 3 is that Part X of the Customs Act 1966,
which relates to agents and carriers, shall be deemed to form part of those provisions of the
principal Act that relate to the control of imports. This means that customs agents as
prescribed or authorised by the Comptroller of Customs under the Customs Act will be
permitted to deal with my department and the Customs Department on import licensing
matters in the same manner and under the same conditions of control as apply in other
customs matters.
Bill introduced and read a first time.

Contractual Mistakes Bill
CONTRACTUAL MISTAKES BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Contractual Mistakes
Bill be introduced. This short Bill implements the 1976 report of the Contracts and
Commercial Law Reform Committee on the effect of the mistakes on contracts. It represents
the first attempt in a common law country to codify what is readily acknowledged to be a
highly complex and fragmented area of commercial law. In essence the Bill, subject to
certain limitations, allows a party who entered into a contract on the basis, for example, of a
mistaken opinion or calculation to apply to the court for relief if the other party to the
contract knew him to be mistaken and the mistake resulted in a significantly unequal
exchange of values. The court is authorised, in effect, to grant such relief as it thinks just in
the particular circumstances.
The report of the law reform committee sets out in some detail the confusing state of the
existing law and the rigid nature of the remedies available at present to a person who enters
into a contract while relying on certain circumstances that were, in fact, mistaken. I do not
propose to canvass all the details put forward by that committee. One point that the law
reform committee did make however, was that the remedies available for mistake are drastic
and inflexible. A good example of this is a trilogy of English cases referred to by the
committee, which, although they had very similar facts, gave rise to vastly differing results
once the legal position had been established. I think perhaps the details of the cases would
best be established by those honourable members who wish to look at the report itself, which
has been available publicly since May of last year. The law reform committee's report has
met with general acceptance by a number of district law societies. Nevertheless, I propose to
move that the Bill be sent to the Statutes Revision Committee to enable interested parties to
present submissions, the hearings to be open to the news media.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I welcome this Bill. As the Minister knows, and I
know all too well, there is continually a backlog of material in departmental shelves to give
effect to the reports of various law reform committees, but it is not always easy to find
parliamentary time to deal with them. This is a relatively recent report, presented as late as
May 1976. There are many reports longer in the tooth awaiting action and I hope we will see
them before long. I must confess to some surprise that the report did not create a bigger
impact. It was one of the bolder ventures of the law reform committee-and I am bound to
say that the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee has a reputation for more
boldness than do some of the others. It may be that there were reverberations in some
academic circles that are unknown to me, but now that it has been enshrined in legislative
form I shall be interested to see the reaction throughout the country; indeed, I believe it will
attract a good deal of attention overseas, and if successful here-striking out new ground as
it does-I believe it is fairly likely to be adapted by other countries.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Contractual Mistakes
Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee, and that the proceedings of that committee
be open to accredited representatives of the news media.
Motion agreed to.
INCOME TAX (COMPENSATORY EXPORT INCENTIVE ALLOWANCE) BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I move, That the Income
Tax (Compensatory Export Incentive Allowance) Bill be introduced. This is a short tax Bill to
give effect to the Government's announcement, following the Australian devaluation of the
dollar in December 1976, that a compensatory export incentive allowance would be given to
exporters. This was to help sustain their export sales at a time of difficulty. The important
thing to note is that the Bill applies to export sales of the same type of goods that would
normally qualify for the taxation incentive for increased exports. The Bill provides for a
special deduction from taxable income of 3 percent of total qualifying export sales for both
the 1977 and 1978 income years. For the 1977 income year the 3 percent rate is calculated on
the basis of 9 percent restricted to one-third of the total export sales. This in effect gives an
effective rate of 3 percent for the full year. The restriction to one-third of export sales for the
1977 year is related to the fact that the change in exchange rates came when two-thirds of the
1977 financial year had elapsed. Manufacturers have been receiving and will continue to
receive help from the additional concessions in this difficult period after the Australian
devaluation.
The additional concession will apply not only to export sales to Australia, but to sales to
other countries. This should give manufacturers added incentives to expand their export
markets. Members should note that the concession is automatically repealed from 1 October

Yesterday we heard the Speech from the Throne. The headline in the Evening Post
summed it up pretty well when it stated "Increased unemployment likely as the nation's
earning capacity lags." A summary of the Speech from the Throne is a summary of the
National Party's blueprint for the next 12 months-lagging production, increased unemploy-
ment. What a testimonial to a Government that was so strong on promise in 1975. It has
belted the New Zealand family, particularly the single-income family, right, left, and centre.
People are fed up. It is no wonder that when those in Mangere had an opportunity to express
their views they gave the Labour member a bigger majority even than in 1972. And when we
got to Pahiatua the Labour candidate won seats that Labour had not won for 34 years.
Mr Comber: Seats?
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: Booths-because the people are fed up with the kind of
activity, and repression on the other hand, of this Government. Government members can,
if they like, cling desperately to any statistics that are wheeled up to try to give them some
kind of credibility.
Mr Elliott: How many polling booths?
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING: Whangarei will be an interesting one too. I suggest the
member for Whangarei pay a little more attention to what is happening there. He might take
some consolation from statistics, but the people are not concerned with mathematical hocus-

that will result from the deliberate actions of this Government. They are concerned with
meeting their next rent payments, and there are thousands of families in that position. They

of large fishing vessels to expand New Zealand's indigenous catching capacity. So far, 10 new
boats have come in under the scheme. Companies are waiting to bring in additional boats.

procedural matter. This morning urgency was accorded the passing of the Imprest Supply
Bill, and, in accordance with Standing Order 47, that authorises the House to set aside
normal rules as to sitting hours to proceed with the matter of the Bill, and complete

of the kind that is customary in a second reading, which may contemplate only the deferment

after they have been dealt with, return to urgency. The mattter currently before the House is

Mr McLay: The argument advanced by the member for Henderson seems to centre on
the suggestion that the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition is not in some
way a proceeding on the Bill. I draw your attention, Mr Speaker, to the fact that the Leader
of the Opposition was able to move his amendment because he moved it during the course of
a debate on the Bill, and he referred it specifically to the Bill. It is clear from page 517 of
Erskine May, and from the pages that follow, that any amendment that is moved, whether it
be in Committee of the Whole or during the debate on the Bill, during any stage of the
debate, in fact becomes a proceeding on the Bill, and therefore the argument advanced by
the member for Henderson does not hold up.
Mr SPEAKER: I have not time to refer to the authority offered me since there does
seem to be occasion to rule on this matter at once, but from what is said I am glad to gather
that it seems probable that the view set out in Erskine May supports the one I believe is
applicable in this case, and does seem to make common sense. It has been implied, in the
raising of the point suggesting that urgency has been broken, that had an amendment been
moved suggesting deferment of the Bill until this day 3 months or 6 months—and that was
called the usual amendment-that would not have amounted to a breach of urgency; but it is
also suggested that the present amendment goes further than that, is of a different nature,
and does break urgency. Therefore, a different kind of amendment or a different wording of
the amendment in some cases would, and in some would not, amount to a breach of urgency.
Not only do I feel that the view that there are different types of amendments near or far
from what was called the usual amendment that have different effects on urgency, is not
substantiated, but we find something more near an authority in Standing Order 228, which,
following the orders providing for the "deferment this day 3 months or 6 months" type of
amendment, says: "No other amendment may be moved to such question unless the same be
strictly relevant to the Bill: Provided that an amendment relating to public affairs may be
moved to the question for the second reading of an Imprest Supply Bill or the main
Appropriation Bill." The amendment before us is exactly such an amendment, and, as a
matter of common sense, it seems to me a proper interpretation of the meaning of the
expression "proceedings thereon" to say that any acceptable amendment is a proceeding on
the Bill rather than to say that one type of amendment adding "this day 3 months or 6
months" is a proceeding on the Bill, but that an amendment that goes wider, yet is still
within the definition of an amendment as set out in Standing Order 228, is not a proceeding
on the Bill. I accordingly rule that the amendment is a proceeding on the Bill and that
urgency has not been broken.

In the long run our economic problems can be overcome only by growth and expansion.
When a nation has idle productive resources as New Zealand has at present-unemployed
manpower, surplus factory capacity, idle plant equipment and contractors' equipment-it
makes economic common sense to find finance to put them to work. The best way to achieve
economic stability and to halt the rate of inflation is to increase output by putting together
the idle sources of production. Finding money to put to work and to use productively those
assets of manpower and equipment which have the capacity to produce is not inflationary.
The other day, in Auckland, the spokesman for real estate agents, Mr Molesworth, said that

meet their repayments and difficult to cope with prohibitive rates of interest. Mr Molesworth

During this Government's term nearly all its actions have been destructive to family life.
Nothing can be more destructive than the inability of the family to command decent housing.
High interest rates and prohibitive rents are creating serious problems. Nothing can be more
detrimental to the family, and in particular to the one-income family and to widows and
others with dependants, than the rapid rise in the cost of living. The Government is not
making adjustments in those areas where adjustments have been recommended. In
November last the Kennedy Good report referred to the deterioration in the standard of
living of the family and urged adjustments in a wide range of areas, but so far the
Government has taken no action. Here are areas where action was suggested: immediate
adjustments in the family benefit, free medical care for children under 5 years of age, a
review of the tax and income structures, the development of a family policy, and the
Department of Education to investigate the cost of extras for schooling for the low-income
family. Six months have elapsed since that report but, under worsening conditions for the
family, the Government has taken no action.

TUESDAY, 24 MAY 1977

ADDRESS IN REPLY
With the leave of the House, it was agreed that the speaking time allowed the member for
New Plymouth and the member for Awarua in this debate be extended.
Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth): I move, That a respectful address be presented to
His Excellency the Governor-General in reply to His Excellency's Speech.
In moving this motion I am fully aware of the responsibility which is mine and the
honour that responsibility accords my electorate, New Plymouth. In accordance with
tradition, and with the support of loyal New Zealanders, I am pleased to pay tribute to His
Excellency the Governor-General and to assure His Excellency of our continuing firm
allegiance to the Crown. Through their quiet dignity, and untiring dedication to the many
demands made upon them, Sir Denis and Lady Blundell have endeared themselves to all
sectors of society. I am sure all members of this House will join with me when I express the
thanks of the people of this country for the sacrifices Their Excellencies have so willingly
made during their term of office.
The Crown has always occupied a place near to the heart of this nation. This fact was
reinforced during the recent most successful jubilee tour of Her Majesty the Queen and
Prince Philip. That tour brought pleasure and joy to many thousands of people. During the
visit we all witnessed loyalty from one end of New Zealand to the other. This left no doubt in
my mind that the public attitude towards royalty has not slipped as suggested by the Deputy
Leader of the Opposition in the Christchurch Star of 8 March. His claim that the tour was a
"non-event" is as pathetic as it is distasteful, and his prediction that New Zealand is heading
for republican status is as far from the mainstream of public opinion as are his usual
outlandish utterances.
The state of the economy has been at the centre of New Zealand's political arena for the
past 3 or 4 years. It stands at the focal point of public concern, and it stands there because it
is the single factor that will govern the standard of living this country will enjoy in the future.
The general public is well aware that the extent of the advance, or even retreat, which is
made in the fields of health, social welfare, education, commerce, employment, and other
sectors of the community depends in the long run upon the strength of the economy. If the
economy crumbles so too does our way of life, and the plans and aspirations that we all hold
for the future become no more than dreams. For at least 2 years while in Opposition the
National Party consistently drew the attention of the people and the then Labour Govern-
ment to the problem areas. It was stated on many occasions then, and it has been stated
since, that the rebuilding of the economy will not be quick, nor will it be easy. However, it is
generally acknowledged that the present Government has the ability to recognise the
problems and has the strength to face up to them-attributes which were sadly lacking in
Government before 1975. The public is aware of this, and that is one reason why National
members occupy the Government benches today.
On taking office approximately 18 months ago the Government and New Zealand faced
four major economic problems: a massive deficit in the Budget; a huge balance of payments
deficit; a high and rapidly increasing rate of inflation; and an ominous growth in unemploy-
ment. All of these factors were and are interrelated and interwoven. Attacks upon the
balance of payments deficit can create unemployment. Measures to reduce the Budget
deficit are likely to reduce inflation but increase unemployment. Measures to reduce
unemployment can increase the size of the balance of payments deficit, the budget deficit,
and inflation. The problem is a complex one, but despite its complexity the National
Government has been prepared to take action, and the measures taken are proving
successful. For the first time since 1972 there has been a consistent slowing down in the rate
of increase in the consumer price index. This means that for the first time since 1972 we are
seeing a slowing down in the annual rate of inflation. There is no need for me to spell out the
cruelty of inflation-the effect it has on small savings, the effect it has on the family budget,
the effect it has on the viability of businesses, and on the morale of wage and salary earners.
We are all well aware of this, and it seems as if the Opposition as well is coming to
realise it. Inflation must be controlled and beaten. Since the second half of last year the
quarterly increases in prices have been reducing. They have been 3.2 percent, 2.8 percent,
and the latest figure, for the March quarter, is 2.6 percent, a quarterly figure which the
Leader of the Opposition predicted would be more than 5 percent. He was 100 percent out.
However, that is the degree of accuracy we have come to expect from him, in his rather


## p. 59 (#67) ##############################################

24 May
59
Address in Reply
childish attempts to mislead. As usual, facts prove him wrong, but I notice he tries to avoid
facts nowadays because they do not suit him. The facts show a gradual but consistent
improvement—an improvement which to date has brought the annual rate of inflation down
from the 15.7 percent it reached under Labour to 13.7 percent. Planned and deliberate
measures taken by the National Government are giving results, encouraging results which
Labour did not even dream to be possible. There is still a long way to go, but real progress is
being made.
A major factor contributing towards inflation was the massive Budget deficit we took
over at the end of 1975. During the 3 years of the last Labour Government there was a
tremendous growth in Government spending. In that 3-year period Government spending
rose from 30 percent of the gross national product to 42 percent. Big Brother was becoming
more and more important at the expense of the independence of the man in the street. In
1972 the Labour Government took over a Budget deficit of $200 million, and by the time it
was ejected from office in 1975 this had been increased to $1,200 million and was still
growing-a deficit of $400 for every man, woman and child. The money to meet such deficits
does not come out of thin air, nor does wishful thinking provide it. The deficit is borrowed. If
it is borrowed from the people of New Zealand then interest will have to be paid out of taxes
and the capital repaid out of taxes. If it is borrowed from the Reserve Bank it can be
compared to turning on the printing press. If it is borrowed from overseas it is also new
money in circulation. This is where inflationary pressure comes from. That is why we have
been working at reducing Government spending. That is why subsidies were reduced, and
that is why the deficit before borrowing for the year just ended was reduced to $500 million.
No one enjoyed making the unpleasant decisions that were necessary to achieve this result,
but they had to be made.
The Labour member for Manukau, bless him, recently suggested that we should refund
$200 million or $300 million of taxation and increase the deficit again. Let me remind him, it
was that type of thinking that created the financial mess in the first place. Next to inflation,
the massive balance of payments deficit has been the cause of greatest concern. The deficit
on overseas exchange transactions at the end of 1974 was $816 million-far higher than it had
ever been before. By the end of 1975 it had increased even further, to just under $1,000
million. After the first year of this National Government the deficit had been reduced to
under $600 million. This is a far better result than even these figures indicate, but it is more
meaningful to note that the deficit in the year ended December 1975 was equal to over 9
percent of the gross national product, and it had been reduced to just over 5 percent by the
end of 1976.
There are a number of good reasons why the deficit did not come down even more
quickly. The Government was unwilling to make drastic cuts in the volume of imports as this
would have caused serious unemployment. It should also be noted that a very large part of
the reduced deficit is made up of debt servicing charges. This is basically interest paid on
Government and private overseas debts, charges which totalled $77 million when Labour
took office in 1972, charges which had risen to $304 million by the end of 1976. But for these
enormous increases the deficit would have been reduced much further. Nor should it be
forgotten that the rise in farm investment has created a demand for substantial increases in
imports of fertiliser, farm machinery, and other farm equipment. So, too the revival of
manufactured exports has required a considerable increase in imported raw materials to
bring about the impressive expansion seen in that sector over the last 12 months. The vast
Maui project—a project which is currently having an important impact on the lives of the
people in New Plymouth electorate and in Taranaki, and which will be of benefit to the
entire country-has required a large volume of imports, which was not the case in 1975. The
remaining imports, those used for domestic consumption, have in fact significantly fallen in
volume.
Prospects for 1977 give grounds for encouragement. The New Zealand Institute of
Economic Research in its latest forecast expects the total volume of imports to have fallen
3.5 percent in the year ended March 1977. That is a far cry from the 32 percent increase in
the volume of imports seen in 1974 under the last Labour Government. Furthermore, it is
safe to predict that there will be more worth-while reductions in the balance of payments
deficit over the next 6 months. National Government policies are showing positive
results-results which the Labour Party said could not be achieved without massive
unemployment. Remember their scare tactics, involving figures of 70 000 and 80 000
unemployed. Remember the way they pointed to the very high level of unemployment in the
United States, Britain, and Australia. We in the National Party are determined that the
hardship, distress, and waste of unemployment will not be the solution. The deliberate aim


## p. 60 (#68) ##############################################

60
24 May

of policies has been to maintain a high level of employment, policies which have encouraged
increased farm investment-that means more jobs-policies which have resulted in a sharp
increase in manufactured exports. Again, this has provided more jobs-jobs for people who
would be without work today if they had to rely upon domestic consumption. We have
reduced the flow of immigrants and so maintained work opportunities for New Zealanders.
The National Government has implemented a balanced strategy-a strategy aimed at
overcoming the economic difficulties facing New Zealand. The results to date are encourag-
ing and positive. It can be seen that we as a country are making progress on the road to
economic recovery. This progress has not been made without sacrifices. These encouraging
results are due not only to the positive leadership of the Government, but also to the co-
operation of the general public-due to the fact that all sectors of the community have been
prepared to play their part. They are due to wage and salary earners, employers, farmers,
housewives, manufacturers, and rank and file union members. All have played a construc-
tive role in the drive towards achieving economic recovery. There is a small group who,
wishing to see our economy fall, have obstructed in every way they could, but they are very
much in the minority. It is a very healthy sign that, despite that destructive group, the
majority has accepted the measures taken-measures which everyone can see are equitable,
measures which ensure that the burden is shared by all sectors of society.
At this stage we can see the first rays of sunlight in our economic recovery. The rate of
inflation is dropping, the Budget deficit is being cut back, and the overseas current account
deficit is diminishing. There is a long way to go yet, but we are progressing. It is vital that this
progress should continue. We as a nation must not allow the Labour Party to try to fool us
into believing we can continue to live beyond our income. It cannot be done. We are a
country of only 3 000 000 people in a world of many hundreds of millions. There is no great
benefactor out there among those millions of people with the financial interests of New
Zealand at heart. We shall be treated according to our credit rating. No one out there is
interested in providing charity to ensure that 3 000 000 New Zealanders live beyond their
means. We shall sink or swim according to our own ability. I am confident that we shall
continue to see bold, constructive economic management from the National Government,
and continue to see the support and co-operation of the vast majority of New Zealanders.
We will achieve the goal of financial stability as a result of the honest sweat on our brows and
we as a nation will leave the Labour Party to plot the nationalisation of the means of
production, distribution, and exchange, and to dream about financial benefactors. But let
them dream. Let them dream as we work. Let them dream as we go about building export
production-production which is directly responding to Government encouragement.
Reserve Bank figures show that in the first 12 months of this National Government
manufactured exports increased by 56 percent, forestry exports by 59 percent, tourism
receipts by 22 percent, and fish exports by 47 percent-tangible increases in export
production. For the first time since 1972 we are seeing a revival of confidence in the
agricultural sector, New Zealand's most important earner of overseas exchange. It is vital to
us all that the agricultural sector be kept in peak condition, a fact which occasionally appears
to be overlooked in some major centres, but is seldom disregarded in the provincial towns
and cities. For cities like my electorate of New Plymouth, agriculture plays a major role on
their growth and well-being. We have other industries, but the real wealth of our community
depends to a very large degree upon the purchasing power of the farmers. No one should

estimated yield of fish inside the 200-mile limit for New Zealand is 200 000 tonnes, but with
New Zealand landing only 60 000 tonnes of that catch, the remaining 140 000 tonnes were
shared among the Russian, Korean, Japanese, and Taiwanese fishing fleets. These fishing
resources, while not spectacular by international standards, are nevertheless sufficiently
valuable to attract attention and even envy from several of the world's leading fishing
nations.
In addition to Japan, Russia, Korea, and Taiwan, which already have fishing fleets in
the South Pacific, New Zealand has in the last 12 months received approaches from Poland,
Yugoslavia, Bulgaria, Italy, West Germany, Spain, Norway, and Britain. The extent of this
interest indicates the value of the resource, and illustrates the need for the careful planning
and sound development that has already been put into train by this Government. In the 1976
Budget, provision was made for the importation of large fishing vessels duty-free, and that
was an important first step. Recently, an announcement was made of a central co-ordinating
station here in Wellington to monitor the activities of all foreign fishing fleets. Another 1976
budgetary provision was the substantial berthage fee for visiting foreign vessels. That was a
useful temporary measure. It may interest people to know that, at present, fisheries
research—which has never received a great deal of public notice—is running at three-and-a-
half times that of agriculture on an export-earning basis. This clearly underlines the
importance the Government attaches to the developing fishing industry. The action of the
National Government in elevating the fishing industry from its historical role as junior
partner to agriculture to a full-scale ministry, and the appointment of the member for King
Country as the first Minister of Fisheries is the greatest shot in the arm ever received by
fishing in this country. The appointment has been greeted enthusiastically by our fishing
industry. Recently, the fishermen in my electorate had the opportunity to meet the Minister.
There is a great deal of interest in fishing in Awarua, and rightly so, because the Southland
ports of Waikawa—which many of you have never heard of-Half Moon Bay, Riverton, and
Bluff export more fish by value than any other province in New Zealand. These four small
communities are very dependent on the success and the protection of inshore fishing. I
commend the Minister for his frank and pertinent discussions with my constituents during his
visit to Southland.
In my view, fishing is not unlike farming. It is a primary resource. Its harvest, surplus to
domestic requirements, is an important and substantial earner of overseas exchange.
Because of the similarities, I make the following suggestions. We should be giving very
careful thought to extending to fishing the incentives now available in the primary export
industry of farming. Young fishermen should have the same opportunities that young
farmers have through the farm ownership savings scheme. Good fishing boats cost about the
same as good farms, and the entry of young men into the industry is essential for its healthy
progress. But we should go further than that. We should give consideration also to the
3.

establishment of fishing equalisation accounts, helping the fisherman to relate his business
enterprise to a more stable scale of income. As a transitional step, finance through the Rural

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
South Africa-Sporting Contacts
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Prime Minister, Will he, before he leaves
for overseas, make a formal statement to clarify the Government's present attitude on
sporting contacts with South Africa?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): The member is directed to statements
made in the National Party's official policy prior to the election, which reads: "The National
Party strongly believes in the responsibility and autonomy of sporting and recreational
bodies. Under a National Government there will be no political interference in sport in any
form. Sporting organisations will be free to associate with any sporting groups from other
countries, regardless of race, creed, or internal politics."
Hon. W. W. Freer: Does the Prime Minister now dissociate himself with the statements
made by the former member for Pahiatua, the Deputy Leader of the Government, and the
Prime Minister's own statement earlier this year in Wanganui?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: No, he does not. Nor does he dissociate himself from the
following statement in elaboration of the Government's position, which was unanimously
agreed to by every member of the Government caucus following the return of the Deputy
Prime Minister from Africa late last year: "He, Mr Talboys, told us of the deeply held
attitude of Africans to the indignity of racial policy such as apartheid. They consider the
international campaign against sports contacts with South Africa an important part of their
efforts against the apartheid system. Mr Talboys told them that our basic policy on sports
contacts was that sporting bodies must decide for themselves who to compete with, and we
shall not depart from that. As we have said many times now, with the right to decide goes the
duty to consider the wider effects of those decisions. Our election time policy, to which we
adhere, is that we strongly believe in the responsibility and autonomy of sporting and
recreational bodies. Under a National Government there will be no political interference in
sport in any form. Sporting organisations will be free to associate with any sporting groups
from other countries regardless of race, creed, or internal politics." That statement was
unanimously agreed to by every member of the Government caucus. Because this is an
important matter, could I crave the indulgence of the House and read a statement made by
the Prime Minister of Canada at a press conference in London a few days ago. He said, “I
cannot speak for another Prime Minister, but in the negotiations which are taking place it
seems to me that he"- and he was referring to me-"is coming much closer to the Canadian
and British positions, which are not extreme positions. They are, I think, ones which the
Africans accept. We are not saying that nobody can go and play in South Africa. We are just
saying that we should not subsidise them with the taxpayers' money." As far as I can see, you
could not get a cigarette paper between that position and the position of the New Zealand
Government.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Does the Prime Minister not agree, as obviously the Canadian Prime
Minister Mr Trudeau does, that the Prime Minister is changing his ground?
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: I do not, and in support of that statement I read another
report. This is from "Morning Report", a radio programme, of 30 March 1977, reporting an
interview that took place in Brussels between one Trevor Henry, who is apparently a
reporter on that programme, and Mr Sonny Ramphal, the Commonwealth Secretary-
General. Mr Ramphal said: "I believe that there would be many of our colleagues in Africa
who would hope to see a little bit more, but a little bit more, you know, can sometimes
evolve out of just understanding what already is." And Mr Henry said, "Mr Ramphal
believes there is evidence that African leaders are getting a better understanding of New
Zealand's position." If certain people, including certain Labour members, would have a
little more regard for their country and a little less regard for Labour Party politics, that
understanding could have taken place some considerable time ago.
Hon. H. R. Lapwood: Does the Prime Minister condone the Labour Party's action in

Onerahi High School, Whangarei
2. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Education, What is the current state
of planning of the Onerahi High School in Whangarei?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): My department has recently reviewed
the educational needs of the Whangarei area. This review indicates that a secondary school
will not be needed at Onerahi within the next 5 years, and consequently no planning is being
undertaken. However, discussions with the Whangarei High Schools Board and other
controlling authorities are continuing.
Mr Marshall: Would the Minister indicate what new factors have arisen to make it
necessary for him and the department to overturn the recommendation made by his
predecessor, I think in 1974, that there should be a high school?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: It is correct that my predecessor made a recommendation, but it
was quite contrary to the normal planning procedure. He did not consult with the education
board or the teacher organisations. Consequently, that decision met with a great deal of
resistance from the board, and the organisations. Subsequently, that decision was not
continued with for the very good reason that strong objections were raised by those
organisations. There is no possibility at present of the number of children in that area
warranting another high school until 1985 at least. If anything should change in the
meantime, obviously the whole matter will be reviewed.
Mr Elliott: Would the Minister agree that given proper planning procedures such as he
mentioned earlier, and given other financial commitments in education, a secondary school
catering for about 500 to 600 pupils would be a viable proposition in some circumstances?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: There is no doubt that that would be correct, but the problem in
Whangarei is that the rolls, based on the figures known at present, show a decline in the
numbers for each of the four existing high schools, except for the Whangarei Boys' High
School. If, without any change in the present circumstances, another school for 600 pupils
was built, then obviously those schools would also suffer declining rolls.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the Minister's statement that the numbers do not warrant the
building of a new high school, but that numbers warrant the establishment of technical

Coal Production
3. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines, Has he read the article
"Men of Energy—Ian Dick” in the New Zealand Energy Journal, December 1976, reprinted
in the autumn issue of New Zealand Coal, which states that, other than new mines under
construction at Huntly, "it will not be able to open any new underground mines before 1990
which would give a production date of 1994", and how does he reconcile it with his
statements in the same issue of New Zealand Coal that, “Coal is once again a valuable fuel,
and we are expected to turn on supplies overnight. Coal in New Zealand has a bright future,
but we are going to ensure that this is a planned and orderly future...."?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines): This question implies that there is some
inconsistency between these two statements, but that is not so. When the Secretary of Mines
said that his department would not be able to open any new underground mines before 1990,
he was speaking of large modern mines of the type of Huntly west. Mr Dick had in mind the
time required to develop the expertise necessary for the operation of a fully mechanised
mine producing up to 1 000 000 tonnes of coal a year. It is expected that by the mid-1980s we
should be ready to plan the next big mine at Huntly. None of this is inconsistent with my
statement that coal in New Zealand has a bright future, but that we are going to ensure that
it is a planned and orderly future. The Government took an important step last year in
planning this future, when it allocated $750 000 to extend the coal exploration programme
from Huntly to other parts of the country. Under the scheme, exploration has started into
the lignite deposits of Southland and of Charleston near Westport, and it will be extended to
other areas in the future. If the need arises, this work could lead quite soon to the
development of new mines, particularly opencast mines, in places other than Huntly.
Hon. F. M. Colman: In view of the Minister's reply, could he indicate what new mines
are being planned for development in the very near future, other than the major type of
mine that he outlines-1 000 000 tonnes or more-for the Huntly region?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: If this was put down as a separate question—and I think it should be a
written question-I would be pleased to give the member a detailed answer, but quite
detailed work is being done in some places on the West Coast, in the Huntly area, and, as I
mentioned in my earlier answer, in the Southland area, proving what in fact could be
developed in the way of new mines.
Marilyn Waring: Would the Minister confirm that new opencast mines-the question
referred to underground mines-are being opened and developed in the Huntly area, and
that the restraints spoken of by Mr Dick are largely those of mining technology and
extraction rates, and difficulty of terrain, and that in that respect, his comments and the
Minister's are entirely compatible?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I am pleased to confirm the member's comments.
Mr T. J. Young: Could the Minister confirm that the statement from the Secretary of
Mines, that no new underground mine which would be opened before 1990 would give
production much before 1994, would not apply to coal mines in the South Island, either on
the West Coast or in Southland?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I do not think the member has quite understood the exchange that
has been going on between the member for Petone and myself. We are talking about major
underground mining developments. Mr Dick was perfectly correct when he pointed out in
the article in New Zealand Coal-and I commend the article to the member for Hutt-that
the technological problems in some of these major underground mines are very real and will
take some years to resolve. A number of small mining operations will be developed
concurrently during this period, some underground and a number opencast, but in terms of
the major development, Mr Dick's observations were sound and still stand.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Is the Minister aware that the Secretary of Mines specifically
referred to any new underground mines before 1990? I suggest to the Minister that there is a
conflict between the Minister's answers and the statement by the Secretary of Mines.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It would be an abuse of the time of the House to read the whole
article, but I invite the member for Petone to read it to see the quotation in its proper
context. I am sure that as a reasonable man he would agree that the reference was to major
underground mines.

Price Milburn
4. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Education, Can he confirm that the
publishing firm of Price Milburn, which is active in the field of educational publishing, has
been acquired by the primary teachers trade union, the NZEI, and, if so, can he give any
guarantee that in future decisions regarding the selection of standard texts in New Zealand
schools will be made without any political or financial bias?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I am informed that the New Zealand
Educational Institute has acquired an interest in the publishing firm of Price Milburn. I am
also informed that Price Milburn will carry on under its present management. Price Milburn
publish almost exclusively for the lower classes of primary schools, where anything that can
be regarded as a standard text is provided by the school publications branch of the
Department of Education. Price Milburn readers are supplementary to official texts, and
other publishers provide similar supplementary material. The choice as to which supplemen-
tary reader shall be purchased rests with the individual school. The question also asks if a
guarantee can be given that standard texts will be selected without any political or financial
bias. In so far as Price Milburn publish supplementary material only, the fact that the NZEI
has an interest in the firm will have no effect on the selection of standard texts.
Mr Malcolm: In view of the Minister's reply, which clearly sets out the position, what
precautions must be taken in future to ensure that Price Milburn does not move into other
fields of publishing; and what precautions can be taken to ensure that, in doing so, we do not
get to a stage where members of the NZEI form the selection committees, in fact, write the
books, and then arrange for their own trade union to print them?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I repeat that at present Price Milburn only supplies supplemen-
tary texts to textbooks which are published by the publications division. The other point is
that, of course, schools themselves decide what they will buy. There is no compulsion on

in educational fields. It would be over to the sense and the responsibility of the people who
use the material to judge whether or not it is suitable for the children within the system.

8. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, Can he advise the

Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I reply on behalf of the Minister of

the Government's 1975 election manifesto: (1) introduced national superannuation; (2)
increased social security benefits from 14 January 1976, 28 July 1976, and 12 January 1977;
(3) implemented improved checks on continued eligibility for social security benefits; (4) set
up the Cabinet committee on family affairs; (5) set up the advisory council for the
community welfare of disabled persons under the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act
1975; (6) paid the special Christmas payment to beneficiaries in December 1975 and
December 1976; (7) made special provision for single women over 55 years of age who
received special age benefit, which is no longer available under national superannuation; (8)
reviewed the reciprocal arrangements between New Zealand and Australia and New
Zealand and the United Kingdom so that they embrace national superannuation; and (9)
disestablished the special beneficiaries index.

because of the time factor, is the Minister aware of any promises in that general election
policy that have been broken?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: I am not aware of any.

provision to increase allowable income for widows and also to make effective the full
provisions of the disabled persons Act?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: If any have not been implemented, the answer is as soon as
possible.

election policy it is stated, "All the existing social security benefits will be continued,
including the new additional benefits." How many other policy statements have been brcken
or disowned?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: As far as I am aware, not one promise has been broken.

URGENT QUESTION
Physiotherapy Students' Bursaries
Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Health, as an urgent question, Has he read
the report in the New Zealand Herald of 24 May 1977 that physiotherapy students at the
Auckland Technical Institute are suffering severe hardship because they have not yet been
paid their bursaries normally paid before the end of the first term, and, if so, can he say how
much longer these students will have to wait?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Health): I have read the report in the
New Zealand Herald of 24 May 1977 and there is reasonable news on the answer. The report
is incorrect in two important aspects. First, it is incorrect to say that the students have not
been paid their bursaries this year. The physiotherapy students at the Auckland Technical
Institute have been paid their standard tertiary bursaries during the first term. Secondly, it is
incorrect to say that last year the supplementary bursaries under the Health Bursaries
Regulations were paid in the first term. The position is that the supplementary health
bursaries, to which I am sure they were referring, are paid in two instalments during the
year. The first 20 weeks' instalment is normally paid towards the end of May, as was the case
last year. This year's payment is now in hand and I understand cheques are at present being
posted to the technical institutes. In short, the supplementary allowances will be paid, as
they were last year, towards the end of May. They are virtually there now.

Minister that he was indeed justified in questioning, during a recent TV interview, the morality

state which he admits goes back to March 1976, he and the Government acted irresponsibly and

to many of those investors.
My motion refers to a recent TV interview in which the Prime Minister was asked
whether he or his Government admitted any responsibility for the collapse of the
Securitibank combine, and the interviewer put particular stress on the fact that Government
departments and Government agencies had been investors in the group and that this had
been specifically referred to in advertisements by the group, leaving the impression that the
enterprise was Government supported. The Prime Minister was quick with his denial of any
lega responsibility. I concede that at the outset, but he, on his own initiative, went on to say,
"but moral responsibility-that is another thing". This debate gives us a brief opportunity to
consider whether that moral responsibility existed, and if so at what level.

answered on today's Order Paper. It related to why inspectors had not been appointed under

Companies under that section, although I must add that that independence is, to a degree,
modified by the terms of subsection (4), and goes on to say that my question was misleading
because in my term of office as Minister of Justice I made no requests to the registrar. That,
o course, is perfectly true, but several discussions took place between me and him and other
alvisers at which a consensus was reached in relation to different companies. That consensus
was acted upon and there was no need for a request. It is now evident, from the Minister's
roly, that a similar discussion took place between him and his advisers in relation to
Scuritibank, the outcome of which was conveyed to the Prime Minister in March 1976 and,
pesumably, was fully considered by him and discussed between him and the Minister of
Jstice. It appears that the agreement reached was that the appearance of inspectors in the
goup's premises would aggravate a situation already known to the Government to be
srious. I must say that I am far from being wholly persuaded by this argument. A strict
sreen of security and secrecy is provided by section 9A, and despite the imperious and unco-
perative attitude of the combine's overlord I believe that some private scrutiny could have

my colleague has said, the habit over the years of being accident-prone. He is accident-prone
again on this occasion. I should tell the House that this motion is being debated at the
request of the Government and not at the request of the Opposition, even though it is an
Opposition motion. The first time that the affairs of Securitibank and its difficulties came to
the notice of the House was in November 1973 in the time of the Labour Government when
the member who moved this motion was the Minister of Justice. The Minister of Finance
then was the present Leader of the Opposition. The group approached the Reserve Bank,
foreseeing liquidity problems, and from that time until the end of 1975 it was in constant
touch with the Reserve Bank and, I have not the slightest doubt, with successive Ministers of
Finance.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: You are quite incorrect.
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: The second Minister of Finance, now the Deputy Leader of
the Opposition, says that is quite incorrect. That tells me he was not doing his job, because if
an organisation of that size is in constant touch with the Reserve Bank over its liquidity
problems, and the Minister of Finance has not made inquiries, then he is not doing his job.
The same applies to the former Minister of Finance, now the Leader of the Opposition. Late
in 1974 a very large number of financial institutions were in grave liquidity difficulties. That
was common knowledge. It was certainly known to me, and I did not get my information
from any official sources. I am certain that the Minister of Finance at that time was talking to
the Reserve Bank about the problem; if he was not, he was not doing his job.

Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON: He says he was not. Let him get up and say that is so,

Government. The shareholding of those two agencies subsisted during the Labour Govern-
ment's administration. The member uses the word "investor" in two entirely different
contexts in his motion, but appears to equate them as having the same meaning. The two
Government agencies were shareholders in Securitibank, and, as the member well knows,
the liability of any shareholder is limited to the amount still to be paid on his shares, and he is
lowest in priority in a liquidation. The other so-called investors referred to invested by
lending moneys to the companies.
The fact that the Government is not happy with the type of advertising used by
Securitibank, which made reference to its shareholders, is shown by its response. It will
introduce legislation this year to control financial advertising. One of the provisions in that
Bill, or in the associated regulations, will forbid the mentioning of the name of any
shareholder in an advertisement unless that shareholder is unconditionally guaranteeing the
company placing the advertisement. I gave instructions for the preparation of such legisla-
tion early last year after the commercial affairs division of the Registrar of Companies had
reported to me and I had reported to the Prime Minister. As members understand, it is
complex legislation, and was acknowledged as such by the member for Henderson. The
drafting is proving difficult, but it will go in this year. It is known that the Labour
Government was interested in passing such legislation as early as 1974, but apparently did
nothing about it and did not give it a high enough priority to ensure its introduction and
passage. The Labour Government had no doubt that legislation could have stopped the
advertising of which the member's notice complains.
I readily say that I discussed with the Prime Minister the precarious state of Securitibank
as it was made known to me in March 1976. That is exactly what I should have done. That is
what should have happened during the Labour Government's term when it knew of the
liquidity problems that Securitibank was having as early as 1973. It was Securitibank's
liquidity, not profitability, that was its worry. I discussed the matter on the basis of the report
that I received from the commercial affairs division early in my administration. The previous
Government knew of the inadequate staffing, particularly in the professional investigating
offices in the commercial affairs division, which the second National Government set up in
1972 to deal with this work. The Registrar decided in March 1976 not to order an inspection
of the Securitibank company, and he so informed me at that time. He was concerned that,
with the company operating as Securitibank did in the short-term money market, knowledge
that inspectors had been appointed and were at work could have brought the company down
more surely than the publication of rumours in the press. Indeed, as we all know it was the
publication in Truth that triggered off its fall. At least it would have added to the company's
troubles and decreased the chance that the group would find a way through its difficulties.
This is an inherent problem in the early use of Section 9A of the Act and will disappear
only when the commercial affairs division has a corps of inspectors adequate to make, and be
known to make, random checks on stable as well as shaky companies. That ideal situation
certainly did not exist in the Government administration when the third National Govern-
ment took over from Labour. Recognition of the registrar's problems by the National
Government is evidenced by the management audit of the commercial affairs division that is
proceeding. The audit team is to report to the Chairman of the State Services Commission
and the Secretary for Justice by the middle of next month. This collapse is of a group of
companies of orthodox structure. It did not have the peculiarities of personal ownership of

HOUSING FINANCE
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda): I move, That this House notes with deep concern: (1)
the increasing plight of the homeless families facing prohibitive and uncontrolled mortgage
interest rates for private sector finance and the hopelessly inadequate State mortgage finance;
(2) the increasing burden being shouldered by rent payers where the State sets the example of
rent hikes of up to $10 per week at a time when wages and salaries are strictly controlled, and
calls upon the Government to acknowledge that any society which accepts the family as the
basic unit of society must realistically face the fact that a home is a basic necessity for all
families.
Rents have increased by up to $10 a week each year, and there is no longer a reasonable
and fair formula based on one-sixth of income. People's earnings are desperately needed to
pay for the massive increases in the price of food, transport, power, and almost everything
else, but this has been disregarded by the Government. People have less money, and the
most important exercise appears to be the balancing of the country's books. The Govern-
ment has become one of the most rapacious landlords. One of the most serious problems
facing the country is the plight of the homeless people who face crippling mortgage interest
rates either for their first home or for refinancing. Never before in our history has a
Government adopted such a heartless policy, such a do-nothing policy-a non-housing
policy.
The Government says that the position is not serious. There is no real problem, says the
Prime Minister. He cannot see it. Earlier today we had statements from members

SOCIALISM
Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei): I move, That this House compliments the Labour Party on
finding at last, after more than 61 years of searching, its socialist philosophy and heritage

following debate at its annual conference in Christchurch, but expresses its concern as to how

step backwards", and likens his position to that of the Rt. Hon. Hugh Gaitskell who waged a
constant but losing battle against left-wing socialism in the British Labour Party in the late
1950s and early 1960s.
The Labour Party has finally made up its mind to re-embrace socialism, at least for now,
with grave reservations by its parliamentary leader, and with valiant attempts to define it in a
way that will not alarm New Zealanders. The 1978 Labour Party manifesto will have a
special preface telling us that the party believes in democratic socialism. Yet Mr O'Flynn, of
the Kapiti Labour Electorate Committee, got a standing ovation when he said that vague
words like caring and social justice were no substitute for a socialist philosophy. He also said
that it did not mean nationalisation of everything, because there were more sophisticated
methods of control-there are more sophisticated ways of dealing with socialism and of
gaining the nationalisation of everything that the Labour Party believes in. What exactly
does that mean? To my mind, it is extremely sinister. The Leader of the Opposition must be
in a real dilemma.
There is no question that the Labour Party has turned its head back to its cloth-cap days
of the 1930s. When the Leader of the Opposition was asked for his definition of socialism he
said he wished he could think of a nice trite statement, but he could not. He did not like Miss
Vicki Buck's resolution one bit. Miss Buck, the youth representative, moved at the Labour
