distribution, and exchange. What is this democratic socialism that the Labour Party has
embraced? At the conference Mr C. A. Beckett said quite plainly that socialism meant the
public ownership of the means of production, distribution, and exchange. Surely that means
State control of all private enterprise. He was supported by a prominent Auckland member
of the Labour Party, Barry Gustafson, who said, "I suggest our goal should be to destroy
capitalism, to destroy the system of private ownership." Socialism has no place in a
democracy, and the words “democratic socialism” are mumbo-jumbo.
Mr O'Brien: Democratic socialism has a place in our society.
Mr ELLIOTT: The member for Island Bay says that democratic socialism does have a

some years the Labour Party is at least prepared to be honest and admit that it does believe
in socialism. Members of the Labour Party have been saying that socialism does not
necessarily mean totalitarianism. Yet we know that, by placing the State in control of
virtually every sector of society, this will lead, as it has in the communist states, to
totalitarianism—a system that permits no rival loyalties or parties. That is the way this State
would go if the socialist Labour Party was in control of every sector of our society. That is
exactly what members opposite are planning. Where is the Labour Party in 1977? It is in
political oblivion, and likely to stay there. We knew that members of the Labour Party were
socialists. As candidates in 1975 we said up and down the country that they were socialists.
What is more, the people believed it. The member for Northern Maori nods his head and
agrees. Now members of the Labour Party confirm that they are socialists. I am happy to see
members opposite nodding their heads and agreeing, because it seems to me an amazing
admission.
In March 1976 the Whangarei branch of the Labour Party produced a newsletter. I

election. The secretary stated: “Socialism is the philosophy of life, but we have ruined the

Mr HUNT (New Lynn): Political philosophies are concerned with the question of
power. As power has been so inextricably connected with inequalities of income and wealth,
democratic socialism is a philosophy based on the removal of such inequalities. Its twin roots
are democracy and socialism. The democratic element is the recognition that people should
control their own situation, while the socialist element is the indication that, in the society in
which we live, and with the technology we use, this control must be exercised by groups in
co-operation with one another. I refer honourable members to page 1936 of the Shorter
Oxford English Dictionary, which defines "socialism" as "a theory or policy of social
organisation which advocates the ownership and control of the means of production, capital,
land, property, etc. by the community as a whole, and their administration or distribution in
the interests of all", and to Webster's Dictionary on page 2162 where "socialisation" is
described as "the process by which a human being beginning at infancy acquires the habits,
beliefs, and accumulated knowledge of his society through his education and training for
adult status". I was fascinated when the national socialist party opposite—because indeed
National Party members are just as socialist as were the members of the party of that name in

should be going. It states: "Society is not a collection of separate economic, social, cultural,

INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS
Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): I move That this House notes with concern the Prime Minister's
recent unfavourable statements regarding the Combined State Service Organisations made at
his press conference on Monday, 16 May 1977, and is not surprised that as a result of this
Government's primitive approach to industrial relations New Zealand has just suffered the
highest rate of industrial stoppages since 1951, and the second highest rate of industrial
stoppages in its history. The purport of my motion is evident to everybody, because it
concerns industrial relations, particularly as they affect the Combined State Service Organ-
isations and the Minister of State Services, who is also the Minister of Labour. The motion
points out that we have had an unprecedented rupture in industrial relations throughout the
country and that there has been a 150 percent increase in industrial disputes or worker-days
lost since the last year of the Labour Government. More than 500 000 worker-days have
been lost through labour stoppages-the highest number in our history apart from that of
1951.
I want to look at what the Minister of State Services has sent back here from Canada as
reported in tonight's Evening Post. He is coming through with a new idea for the deregistra-
tion of unions. Incidentally, we have had a spate of Ministers going overseas and sending
long-distance ideas from wherever they are. We had one from the Minister of Health when
he was 12 000 miles away about 1c on a glass of beer. Now we have one from Canada from
the Minister of State Services. His suggestion gives us a clue about industrial conditions in
New Zealand today. He suggests that, instead of being deregistered, unions should be placed
under the trusteeship of a Supreme Court judge and two other trustees, one being an
employer and the other a unionist. That statement indicates the Minister's total inability to
appreciate what industrial relations are all about. Unions in New Zealand would prefer to
have the honour of being deregistered than to have a Supreme Court judge, a representative
of the employer, and a representative of the union running their affairs-which is what the
Minister suggests. Our industrial relations will be the worst in the world if the Minister of
State Services continues to bring these crazy ideas back from overseas.
On 16 May the Prime Minister told a press conference that the leader of the Combined
State Service Organisations is stirring his members up to make them more restive. Anyone
who is acquainted with Mr Ivan Reddish must agree that he is one of the most able and
respected leaders of any trade union organisation. The saddest thing about our deteriorating
industrial relations is that the discord is not the fault of the employers or the employees. The
Government's attitude is to blame. One could believe that the industrial relations policy of
the National Party was thought out in a paddock on a backblock farm, because it has no
relationship to what is happening nowadays. It is no wonder Mr Ivan Reddish said that the
Prime Minister's comments were an insulting criticism of his leadership, and were a crude
attempt to divert the public from the fact that relations between the Government and State
unions were at an all-time low. At election time the National Party said that it had the

panacea for industrial relations—it was a question of whether we should have voluntary or

that is causing the recent high rate of stoppages in New Zealand, but the primitive approach

because it is an interesting report and backs up my comment that it is not the primitiveness of
the Government that is causing problems, but the primitiveness of certain minority groups in
the trade union movement. The Davidson report states that about 34 submissions were
presented to the commission, which inquired as to why, in 10 years, 11 undertakings owned
by 9 companies in the heavy engineering industry had been destroyed and gone out of
business.
Mr Isbey: What are you doing about it?
Mr MALCOLM: I will come to that in a minute, because that is a key point. A major
finding of the commission was that 34 sets of tactics were used by trade unionists that had
contributed to the downfall of those 11 undertakings. I shall not read the 34 tactics, because
they make a sorry list, but I shall pick out a few that have been used. The Opposition said the
Government is a union basher. This is not union bashing. These are the official findings of
the commission; they are no longer hearsay or guesswork. It found that the unions were
refusing to operate a drill press, claiming that this was the work of a labourer, but when a
labourers' union member was assigned to the job it was claimed that he had to be a member
of the boilermakers' union. There was refusal to use overhead cranes. Boilermakers claimed

the authority of supervisors, and intimidating supervisors. This is the brutality and the law of
the jungle. This is the primitiveness we should be talking about. There was interference in
the training of apprentices, and intimidation of apprentices. Where will it end? That is a

small minority-and again, I stress "a small minority"-of people in the trade union
movement who obviously do not believe that a democratically elected Government has the
right to govern in this country.

assistance. Ordinary Kiwis who are sickened by the type of report I have just read, and by
the tactics of the Opposition in this debate, should stand on their dignity and be counted.
The Government does not know when a boilermaker refuses to touch a gas cylinder, or
handle a drill punch, or says, "Get a labourers' union man", and when the labourers' union
man comes along says, "Turn him into a boilermaker so I can work alongside him." In every

by default.

One of the predictable diversionary tactics of the Government has been to claim that the
Labour Government would have followed the same course. Members opposite know, or
they ought to know-but if they do not know I am about to tell them again-that the Labour
Government would not have taken action in isolation as the National Government did, but
would have only taken such action as part of a package also involving wage and tax
considerations; but not the National Government. The first thing it did was bring the axe
down on to the backs of the necks of the families of this country. The Labour Government
would certainly not have indiscriminately slashed at the standard of living of working
families the way the National Government has done. Let me add right now that in the future
we will not hesitate to use subsidies on basic items to protect the purchasing power of the
family unit. We have already given a clear indication of our intention to revise the tax
structure so that there is a reward for real effort. It does not matter from what source that
real effort comes. People who make a contribution to the production of the country, whether
they are truck drivers or farmers, are entitled to a real reward for the contribution they
make.
I cannot help but comment here-for the benefit of the newly appointed Minister of
Fisheries, who is trying to interject-on the National Party manifesto. On this occasion I
take the 1 in. thick manifesto, the Mark II version, which states in section 20: "The taxation
system will be used to give incentives for desirable economic activity." I like that; we will
have that again from the National Party manifesto: "The taxation system will be used to give
incentives for desirable economic activity." We can only conclude that since the tax burden
on the average wage worker in this country has been increased by 27 percent since the
change of Government the one occupation it does not consider desirable is working. I cannot
help but note, on the other hand, what has happened to interest rates. We can conclude from
that that the Government thinks the one desirable occupation is moneylending. It is this
attitude which has had a disastrous effect on another aspect of family life, the aspirations of
New Zealanders to own a home. In 1975 the National Party promised the people a dynamic
new housing policy. I can still recall the member for North Shore going up and down the
country talking about this. His first move in the great spectacular, when he became the
Minister of Housing, was to freeze Housing Corporation loans for 3 months. Since then,
what has happened? The number of dwelling units has steadily declined and interest rates on
mortgages have steadily increased.
The amount of money available for mortgages has dwindled, and thousands of potential
home owners have been driven to despair. That last point is clearly underlined by the sharp
fall in building permits. In March, for example, the number of building permits fell 19
percent, compared with the number in March 1976. In April they fell 23 percent, compared
with the number in April 1976. The situation is not only bad, but it is worsening rapidly.
People can see no point in seeking a building permit if they know they have no show of
getting money at reasonable rates of interest. If the present trend in building permits was to
continue, the country would build no more than 21 000 houses this year. As it is, the
Government's target is 7000 fewer dwelling units than the peak achieved by the Labour
Government just 2 years ago. The Minister of Housing, having failed in the energy field,
seemed absolutely determined to prove that that failure was not a fluke; and I think he will
do it. Once again we have the "stop-go❞—or more properly the "go-stop"-influence taking
over in housing, with all the problems that will inevitably arise. The National Party
manifesto is now exposed as more remote from the truth than the tales of Hans Christian
Andersen. I quote from page 11 of the glossy manifesto: "National's housing policy adds up
to a totally new deal in home finance. It means in effect, that people for whom home
ownership has become a virtual impossibility over the past three years, will once again be
able to plan and save to own their own homes, confident that their efforts will not be
frustrated." It also states: "National will provide people with the finance they need." Fifty
thousand people paid $37,000 for that particular breed of the manifesto in 1975. Two
people-the Prime Minister and the president of the National Party-repudiated it in 1977.
The problem that prevails with new housing also prevails with existing homes. In the
year ended March 1975 the Housing Corporation assisted 5140 people into existing homes.
For the 11 months to 1 March 1977-and I regret that I have not got the other month,
because the figures are not yet available-only 1964 people received such aid. On top of
that, many people who are already in their own homes are being emptied out at what can
only be described as an alarming rate. The New Zealand Herald last Saturday carried details
of 15 mortgagee sales, and the problem certainly is not confined to Auckland. It is not just
confined to homes, either. Yesterday's Dominion carried a story about more than 20 of 75


## p. 100 (#108) ############################################

100
25 May
Address in Reply
low-cost sections sold or leased by the Lower Hutt City Corporation reverting to the
corporation, because it had become impossible for young people to finance themselves
further. The full housing story is one of abject failure by a Government that told the people
it would have a dynamic new housing policy. The situation must be remedied and we in the
Labour Party say, first, that the Government must accept that there is a social cost in
meeting the housing needs of people, and that as a matter of policy it must provide finance to
complement that available at reasonable rates of interest from private sources-and comple-
ment it to a level that will ensure that the building industry works to capacity. Secondly,
interest rates must be kept within the reach of the single-income family. Thirdly, there
should be greater emphasis on the variable mortgage repayment scheme, by which repay-
ment is related or adjusted to the income of the borrower. Fourthly, there should be a
mortgage refinance fund to avoid people being tossed out on the road. We had a scheme in
1975 with the Public Trust Office, and it worked very effectively. We heard a lot from the
member for North Shore at that time about how much would be needed, but none has been
forthcoming. We say, fifthly, that a land bank should be retained and developed. Sixthly,
institutions such as the trustee savings banks and building societies should be given further
flexibility in the use of their funds, to enable people to purchase existing homes.
The last proposal would require a considerable change in the Government's attitude to
the small savings institutions. At the moment, the whole area is in chaos, with the collapse of
Securitibank as one of the more obvious manifestations. There are other developments of
concern, and when a trading bank offers 14.5 percent for money for 6 months, the system has
run amok. Small savings increases have fallen away by 16 percent, in a comparison of the
April-February period 1976-77 with that of 1975-76. That is one of the signs of the failure of
the financial package produced in March 1976. Small savers are just some of the victims, but
it is worth reminding them of what the National Party promised. I turn to the thick manifesto
this time, section 20: "Savings accounts limited as to amount will be established in which
deposits of individuals will receive an interest rate at least equal to the annual rate of
inflation, thus preserving the purchasing power of a basic savings nest egg." The Govern-
ment has done exactly the opposite. Interest rates which families have to pay, such as on
mortgages on homes, have been freed, and we have true rates of up to 23 percent, but those
trying to save with the small savings institutions-for example, those who have an ordinary
account with the Post Office Savings Bank-are restrained at 3 percent. It is not too difficult
to see whom the National Party regards as its friends.
No doubt the Prime Minister, who will have an opportunity to speak shortly, will claim
that many problems associated with housing and such like will be resolved, because the
Government has taken control of the immigration system. For the year ended February
1976, permanent and long-term migration resulted in a net inflow of 8138; but for the year
ended February 1977, there was a net outflow of 17 124. That is far and away the worst loss
that this country has ever suffered since the statistics were first recorded back in 1885. Now
we have an absolutely crazy situation where the Government is scrambling to adjust the
system to bring in more people from overseas, to make up for the loss of New Zealanders
and their skill and training. At the time of the change of Government in November 1975, 30
categories of immigrants could enter New Zealand. In December of that year the new
Government suspended applications from the United Kingdom for 6 weeks. Then, in
February of the following year, it removed the freeze and reverted to the situation that had
prevailed before the change of Government. I emphasise that in February 1976 it restored
the position that had prevailed at the time it took office. In April 1976 the National
Government started to become a bit nervous, and it increased the number of categories from
30 to 120. Then, in May 1977, someone really hit the panic button and the number of
categories was again increased, to 183. Of course, no one is told what the categories are, and
if an employer wants to bring in a particular employee he cannot find out whether that
person is in one of the permitted categories. However, as there are now 183 categories, I
suppose there is a reasonably good chance.
One of the odd points about all this shuffling around, and particularly the latest
increase, is that as recently as 22 April, when the Prime Minister was talking to the Kapiti

Last night we heard a great deal from the mover and the seconder of the motion about
Government claims of having helped the farmer. It is quite true, as I said earlier, that last
year our export income increased by more than 50 percent, no thanks to the Government. It
is equally true that a considerable amount of that went to some sectors of the farming
community, but the Government did not have much to do with that. What it did have
something to do with was the costs farmers have had to face, and here the Government has
failed misreably. I have already mentioned transport, and most farmers know exactly what
that means, but that is only part of the story because, overall, farm costs went up by 17
percent last year. Indeed, in the September quarter alone they increased by 7.9 percent. The
New Zealand Institute of Economic Research predicts that this year farm incomes will fall by
about 19 percent, working on the basis that prices will remain high. If prices slump, of
course, that is quite another matter. All this is simply a matter of increasing farm costs, not
the least being the interest bill. Whatever else the Government might or might not have
done, the interest question was one over which it had absolute control. It had power to assist
the farming community, but it deliberately took the opposite course and farmers will reflect
on that. Energy is another area which is something of a shambles. Many fine words have
been uttered, and we have had two Ministers. Now we have the threat of a giant
bureaucracy. Co-ordination might be fine, but one must be forgiven for being suspicious that
this is yet another instance of nationalist centralisation. I recall that on 18 December 1975
the then Minister said he would like to develop a co-ordinated energy-use plan over the next
3 years. Nothing happened except an on-again off-again oil levy-and the Prime Minister
knows something about that; a massive hike in power charges-and everybody knows
something about that; and the tying of local fuel costs to the price of imported oil.

have had rather a hit and miss approach to our policy in relation to oil exploration and the
like." We certainly have. Now we have another Minister and another long period of policy
gestation-2½ years is suggested. Even an elephant can give birth in less time than that. I
wondered how the present Minister of Energy got the appointment. Then I dug up an old
National Party pamphlet from the last election. Under the heading "George Gair" it shows

ous are the qualities one needs to become a Minister of Energy in the present Administra-

illusion of the ad-man, the one the Prime Minister disowned, the one about which the
president of the National Party was reported in the Christchurch Star as saying, "The
document sold to the public as the National Party manifesto is not a manifesto", the one that
cost New Zealanders $37,000-we find this statement, "If it were possible to sum up the
philosophy of the National Party in one word, that word would be freedom."
Let us have a look at that freedom after 18 months of National rule. Is there freedom to
eat? Yes, if you and your family can raise the extra 23.5 percent cost of the food that the
family needs. Is there freedom to own a home? Yes, that is fine if you have a second
mortgage and can pay a true interest rate of 20 percent or more. Is there freedom to work?
Yes, if you can find a job, but the last census recorded 27 000 people who said they were
unemployed. The most recent figures showed 5665 on relief work, and we have seen tonight
that the net outflow of New Zealanders is more than 17 400. Yes, there is freedom to work if
you can find a job. Is there freedom to be educated? Yes, if a pre-school centre can be found
which can take a child in, or if you are not one of the disadvantaged people who had special
assistance classes taken away from you, or if you have not had your night classes stopped,
then you are free to be educated. What about the freedom to drive a car? Yes, if you can
afford the extra $797 that a Ford Escort will cost since the change of Government, or the
$780 more that a Honda Civic will cost, or the $34 extra that petrol costs. It did not need to
be so much because a recommendation went to the Government which could have saved the
consumer at least 6c a gallon. You have the freedom to buy a car if you can afford the 100
percent increase in the registration cost. Yes, that is another of the National Party freedoms.
But especially there is the freedom to pay your taxes. If you are a wage worker on the
average wage your taxes will have increased by just under 37 percent under this Administra-
tion. Freedom is an in word in the National Party; even the freedom to survive if you can find
your way through the financial jungle this Government has created. Yes, it is New Zealand
the way you want it—that is, National Party style.

the country, in the little walk-abouts we had, with people coming from great distances. The

Kaeo to Whangarei and back with their nurses for just a couple of minutes to see their

know our people were delighted to have her with them.

In 1975 the Labour Government said it would cut subsidies after the election, but it did
not say by how much. That was a mistake, because nobody believes Opposition members
when they now say a Labour Government would not have cut subsidies by as much as this
Government has. They have lost their opportunity and will not have another one for a
considerable number of years. The Leader of the Opposition says he might bring them back,
but I wonder whether that is wise or desirable. Within 3 weeks of taking office the National
Government doubled the price of milk, but it is still half the price of a bottle of coca cola,
and it is still the cheapest milk in the world. The taxpayer was paying $20 a head subsidy on
milk for every man, woman and child. Before it was increased, the price of milk delivered
bottled on the doorstep was less than the cost to the farmer as it came from the cow. If he
could have got it, it would have been cheaper for the farmer to feed his calves on bottled
town milk, and some farmers are doing that. I know that some are feeding their dogs on it.
The Opposition now says that is a bad thing, but sometimes even a Labour Government has
to take such action.
The Government is trying to adjust the economy to a diminution of 45 percent in our
terms of trade in a little over 3 years. Our terms of trade are the volume of imports that a
stated volume of exports will buy. Compared with the volume a little over 3 years ago the
stated volume of exports will buy just over half of the imports it bought at that time. The
Government's aim is to adjust the economy without too much pain to any section of the
community. It cannot be done without some pain, and while in Opposition I went around the
country telling the people that it had to be done. They accepted that, and they threw out a
do-nothing Government. Let me tell you about that do-nothing Government. The man who
was Minister of Finance and then the Prime Minister, but is now the Leader of the
Opposition, said on 2 February 1973—not long after becoming Minister of Finance—that the
Government was not interested in increasing its official overseas borrowing at present. "The
Minister of Finance indicated yesterday that such borrowing was not necessary because of

National Government. But they did not last long under the Labour Government. Six months
later on 2 August 1973 we read: "New Zealand in good shape to withstand currency crisis.

after the oil crisis, we had this statement: "Rowling is optimistic on market prospects. While

world markets, the Minister of Finance, Mr Rowling, is not one of the pessimists." To give
credit where credit is due, he never was one of the pessimists. He was the eternal Micawber,
always waiting for something to turn up. What turned up was the turn-up on election day.
"The Government had no intention of allowing a liquidity crisis to develop." But, by the end
of the year, it had developed.
We heard this afternoon that by the end of the year, along with many other financial
institutions, Securitibank was in trouble-less than 12 months after the Minister of Finance

Before the year was out he had devalued-but not enough. He had to devalue again the

old houses and for housing people who were inadequately housed. For the year just ended,
only 28 000 houses were built. The target was 28 000 to 30 000 so that the building industry
would not be overcommitted and there would not be pressure upwards on the prices of
houses. I think the figure was 28 300, inside the target. The outflow of 17 000 migrants
released another 5000 houses, so with 28 000 new houses and 5000 houses there are 33 000
houses available for old houses being scrapped, and New Zealanders who are inadequately
housed being better housed, against 23 000 under Labour.
That policy is working, and it is obvious that it is working because the house waiting lists
are diminishing, and State rentals and the price of houses are stabilising. Last year the price
of houses increased about 6.25 percent, much less than the rate of inflation. The Leader of
the Opposition, the Labour Party Micawber, was tonight flooding down his crocodile tears
about the plight of those who are not housed, but he was responsible for the price of sections
increasing 133 percent in 3 years, and the price of houses increasing about 90 percent in 3
years. He comes here tonight and pretends to be sorry for those people who cannot house
themselves. In 3 years he doubled the price of the same house, capable of housing the same
people. The next year under National the price was up by 6 percent because of the policies
that were in this glossy manifesto and that have been carried out. It will take several years of
stable prices before we have the value of a house and the ability of a potential owner in line.
The deposit more than doubled, because the amount of mortgage did not increase in
proportion. There was a time under the Labour Government when the value of a deposit for
a modest family home was increasing faster than the ability of any two-income couple to
save, let along a one-income couple. On top of that the mortgage more than doubled, and
with second, third, and fourth mortgages it meant that the weekly repayments were
impossible for many couples.
The problem is still there and the Government will hear about it across the floor of the
House this year, but it will not hear what caused it. I think the member for St. Kilda is the
spokesman on housing. He was the Minister of Housing, then he was sacked, and I think he
is the spokesman again. I have heard him in the House weeping and wailing for the people
who cannot house themselves, but he was responsible, with the former Minister of Finance,
for doubling the price of a house and pricing it out of reach of the ordinary New Zealander.
The Government has to work it back gradually. That was not the worst. It required twice as
much finance for the same number of housing transactions, and that meant that housing
finance was being pulled in from other productive areas in the economy, and was not
available to finance other productive enterprises. Housing costs go into the consumer price
index. They represent about 30 percent of the consumer price index. The consumer price
index goes up and inflation goes up. Inflation was 5.5 percent in 1972 under National, 10
percent the following year when the Leader of the Opposition was the Minister of Finance,
12.5 percent the following year, 15.7 percent the following year, and still going up, with
housing underneath pushing it up. If the rate of inflation goes up then wage demands go up.
At the time of the change of Government inflation was refuelling itself out of control, living
on itself.

Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
THURSDAY, 26 MAY 1977
Mr SPEAKER took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
OTAKI AND PORIRUA TRUSTS AMENDMENT BILL
Bill introduced and read a first time.
SIR GUY POWLES-CHIEF OMBUDSMAN
Rt. Hon. R. D. MULDOON (Prime Minister): I move, That this House, noting the
retirement on 5 April 1977 of Sir Guy Richardson Powles, K. B. E., C. M. G., E. D., LL. B.,
acknowledges his distinguished service to Parliament and to New Zealand as Ombudsman
from the inception of the office on 1 October 1962, and as Chief Ombudsman, again from the
inception of that office on 13 October 1975, and extends to him its best wishes for a long and
happy retirement.
Motion agreed to.
TERRITORIAL SEA AND EXCLUSIVE ECONOMIC ZONE BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs): I move, That the Territorial Sea
and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill be introduced. I am sure honourable members will
recognise that this is a Bill of major importance to New Zealand. It establishes New Zealand
jurisdiction over an economic zone that extends out to 200 miles from our coast. At the same
time it extends the territorial sea from 3 to 12 miles. The 200-mile zone has received wide
acceptance in the international community, and this has been reflected in developments at
the United Nations' Law of the Sea Conference and, as honourable members will have
noticed, in the practice of states, as many countries have now moved or are moving to
establish the 200-mile zone. New Zealand had hoped that the Law of the Sea Conference
would by now have successfully completed its work, and that we could have introduced the
Bill in accordance with the provisions of a comprehensive treaty on the law of the sea. The
Government believes that the achievement of a treaty is of first-ranking importance both to
New Zealand and to the international community. The New Zealand delegation to the
conference, which has resumed its work in New York, has been instructed to continue to
participate actively in the search for solutions to the difficulties remaining in the way of an
overall agreement. Moreover, I should point out that the Bill fully accords with the work
done at the Law of the Sea Conference, and in particular reflects the principles embodied in
the conference's revised single negotiating text. Recent developments, including 200-mile
legislation by countries whose fleets regularly fish in our waters, have firmly established the
legality of unilateral claims to jurisdiction over the resources within the 200-mile zone. The
Government has no doubt at all about the recognition of our zone by foreign fishing
countries.
The Bill provides the powers to determine the total catch that can be harvested by all
vessels, New Zealand and foreign, in the zone. It provides powers to allocate to vessels of
foreign countries the surplus over and above what can be harvested by New Zealand boats,
and powers to establish conservation measures, including closed areas, closed seasons, and
prohibited species and fishing methods. Part I of the Bill simply brings into this legislation
the territorial sea legislation that is already on the statute book. Clause 7 provides for
regulations to be made. Part II of the Bill provides for the establishment of the exclusive
economic zone. It provides for the calculation of the total allowable catch, for the calculation
of the allowable catch by foreign fishing craft, and for the apportionment of the allowable
catch to those foreign fishermen. It prohibits the operation of unlicensed fishing vessels in
the area. It sets out details about the granting of licences, and the conditions that can be
attached to those licences, which enable a declaration to be made of the areas within the
exclusive economic zone in which fishing is authorised under the licence for seasons, times
and even for particular voyages during which fishing is to be authorised. This part of the Bill
sets out the methods that can be used, and provides for the use or processing of fish that are


## p. 121 (#129) ############################################

26 May
121
Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill
taken. It provides for the training of New Zealand personnel for directions, instructions, and
other requirements given by New Zealand Government ships, and for the installation of
equipment for fixing the positions of vessels. There is a list of offences, which provide not
only for a fine of $100,000 for fishing without a licence but also for fines for those fishing in
contravention of the licence. The Bill provides for the seizure and forfeiture of a ship, and
for the application of New Zealand fisheries law. Generally, the provisions of this legislation
come into effect on the making of an Order in Council, although clause 27 provides powers
for the making of interim and transitional measures for the conservation and management of
fisheries resources beyond the territorial sea. That power would come into effect on the
passing of the legislation.
The principal effect of the Bill has, of course, been on fisheries, but it also provides for
the future introduction of regulations to control other economic uses of the zone, particu-
larly scientific research, the control of pollution, and the establishment of artificial islands
and structures. A number of these issues-especially those of scientific research and marine
pollution, where the control and responsibility should rest entirely with the coastal
State-are still under active negotiation at the Law of the Sea Conference. The relevant
articles are not yet as well settled as those relating to fisheries, and accordingly we intend to
await the outcome of these negotiations before bringing down any definitive rules for them.
Finally, as I have indicated-and it is of some importance-the Bill will not come into force
immediately, except for clause 27. One reason is that we will need to begin negotiations with
foreign fishing countries about access to the zone. International law is quite clear on the
point. We are entitled to phase out foreign fishing fleets as the capacity of the New Zealand
industry increases, but until we have the capacity to harvest the full catch we are obliged to
allow foreign fleets access to the surplus. I should also mention that there is considerable
flexibility in the matters that a coastal State may take into account in allocating its surplus
amongst foreign countries. Another, and equally important, factor bearing upon the entry
into force of the zone is the Government's desire to consult and co-ordinate with the
countries of the South Pacific. As honourable members will know, there has been consider-
able discussion at the South Pacific Forum to try to get agreement on a date for the entry into
force of 200-mile zones throughout the forum area. In moving the introduction of the Bill, I
wish to inform members that I intend to move that it should be sent to the Foreign Affairs
Committee for consideration.

PRIVATE SCHOOLS CONDITIONAL INTEGRATION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): I move, That the Private Schools
Conditional Integration Amendment Bill be introduced. The National Party's 1975 election
policy statement made it clear that the integration legislation would be reviewed to ensure
that integration would be entirely voluntary and in a form that would recognise, preserve,
and protect the special character of integrating schools. This Bill does not result from a full
review of the Private Schools Conditional Integration Act, as envisaged in that policy
statement. As I have said on several occasions, the review will be carried out when the Act
has been in operation for some time. However, my attention has been drawn by private
school authorities to aspects of the Act relating to the preservation of a school's special
character, that should be clarified. The Bill before the House in no way alters the intention
or the spirit of the principal Act. It does, however, clarify the role of the proprietor—that is,
the owner of an integrated school over the special character of the education provided by
the school. The Catholic bishops fully support the proposed amendments, and the Integra-
tion Advisory Committee also agrees to the changes. Represented on that committee are the
Interdenominational Committee of Independent Schools, the State teacher unions, and the
controlling authorities. For this reason I propose to move to the second reading stage of the
Bill, letting the Bill lie in the House for some time, and reserve the question of whether or
not a referral to the Education Committee should take place following the second reading.
As the principal Act now stands, the responsibilities of a proprietor in this particular
regard are spelt out in the interpretation section only. Thus, whilst the responsibilities are
stated, the Act confers no legal power on the proprietors to fulfil their obligations. The
amendment remedies this by stating the proprietor's responsibilities in the body of the Act,
in the form of an addition to section 3. Consequential amendments are also incorporated.
There is provision for proprietors to be consulted before any recommendation or advice
from the Integration Standing Committee is implemented, when such recommendation or
advice relates to the preservation of an integrated school's special character. The Integration
Standing Committee is also empowered to offer recommendations or advice on integration
problems to enrolment review committees, in addition to the existing bodies defined in the
Act. The Bill also introduces to the main Act clauses which make it clear that the Act and
integration agreements are binding on the Crown. Although it was intended that the Act,
and integration agreements, should be binding on the Crown, it was not specifically stated.
The proposed amendments remove any possibility of legal doubt and underline the good
faith of the Crown.
The opportunity is also taken to remedy some minor machinery defects. For example,
clauses 7 and 8 of the principal Act could be interpreted as being in conflict on the question
of when a private school is actually integrated. Clause 4 of the Bill remedies any ambiguity
and provides that the effective date as set out in the integration agreement is, in fact, the
date of integration. The principal Act was worded in such a way that school committees at
small primary integrated schools have more members than those of a comparable State
school; this was not the intention of the legislation, and the Bill brings the number of
members in line with those of State school committees. As the integration programme
proceeds it will be kept under review, and it could well be that changes in the phasing in of


## p. 126 (#134) ############################################

126
26 May
Private Schools Conditional Integration Amendment Bill
the programme might be warranted. The main Act obliges the phased programme to be
approved in the form of an Order in Council, but there is no legal authority for the present
order to be amended. The facility to vary the programme from time to time is thus
incorporated in the amendment Bill. The Bill, then, clarifies the intentions of the main Act
and should allay any concern that may be felt by the proprietors of those private schools that
are considering the implications of integration.

Marine Pollution Amendment Bill
MARINE POLLUTION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Marine Pollution
Amendment Bill be introduced. Since the Marine Pollution Act came into force in 1974
experience has shown the need for a number of small amendments to clear up some areas of
doubt, to ensure that a ship could be arrested if necessary, to clarify the Act's relationship to
the Water and Soil Conservation Act, which also deals with pollution, and to ensure that
ships' agents in New Zealand who are prosecuted under the Act are able to recover any fines
and legal costs from ships' owners. The general purpose of the Bill is to strengthen the
enforcement provisions of an Act that penalises and deters all types of marine pollution, and
controls the dumping of waste at sea. The clause dealing with agents' liabilities is to enable
New Zealand agents to pass on their liabilities under the Act to the owners of the ships. In
most cases, the ship's agent is not responsible for the pollution but is prosecuted instead of
the owner-generally a foreign shipping line-because of the difficulties involved in
prosecuting a line that has no office or place of business in this country. The Bill ensures that
in such cases the agent can recover any penalties from the owner.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): This Bill is an amendment to an Act introduced in
1974 by the previous Government, which included a number of amendments proposed by
the Opposition. At that time, the Government wanted to ensure that the owners of any ship
that came to New Zealand and offended by way of spillage could be prosecuted. The
inclusion of agents under the definition of "owner" ensured that this position could be
safeguarded, because many of the ships that have caused concern sail under flags of
convenience. The ships are foreign owned, but their agents reside in New Zealand, and
many of them expressed concern to the Government about this measure. I should like to
make certain that this provision will ensure that the owner meets the penalty if he
transgresses in any way. There must be no easing of the provisions covering pollution. It
appears that clause 4 removes the provision covering an insurance certificate issued by the
Government of the country to which the ship belongs. Presumably this is in line with clause
7, which protects the agent. While I can accept the thinking of the Government, I want to be
sure that the owners of foreign ships that come to New Zealand are not being encouraged to
ease up on safety, pollution, and spillage possibilities. Although the Act spells out that an
Agent may indemnify himself, this must be enforced by a New Zealand court. How can a
New Zealand court ensure that the agent can be indemnified? Has any thought been given to
the establishment of an indemnity fund to ensure that, if a court decides in favour of an agent
who has indemnified himself to an owner, that owner pays for any damages resulting from
spillages from his vessels? I should like the Minister to assure me that this liability can be
traced back to the person responsible, and I believe that the establishment of an indemnity
fund would be a step in the right direction.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The advice I have received from
the department is that it wishes to tighten up the provisions in the principal Act. As I said in
my introductory remarks, it has often happened that the agent, who has had nothing to do
with a spillage, has had to pay the penalty and has not been able to recoup those costs. The
main point of the Bill is to ensure that if a person agrees to be the agent for an overseas

National Housing Commission Amendment Bill
NATIONAL HOUSING COMMISSION AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): I move, That the National Housing
Commission Amendment Bill be introduced. This short Bill of two operative clauses, which
amends the National Housing Commission Act, has two functions. First, it will increase the
overall membership of the commission by two, by increasing the number of ministerial
appointments from four to six. The present commission consists of four members appointed
by the Minister of Housing, two from the Housing Corporation-the Director-General and
one Assistant Director-General-and the Secretary to the Treasury. The commission has
been in existence for almost 5 years and it is appropriate that we should now review its
structure. The Government considers that the effectiveness of the commission would be
improved by an increase in its size. The two additional members proposed will enable the
range of talent and expertise to be expanded and wider interests to be accommodated.
Secondly, clause 3 corrects the situation whereby a temporary chairman cannot be appointed
whilst the office of chairman is vacant. Under the existing provisions a temporary chairman
may be appointed only if the chairman is absent from New Zealand or if, in the Minister's
opinion, he is unable to act in his capacity as chairman.
Hon. W. A. FRASER (St. Kilda): This Bill has been in my hands only a few moments,
but on behalf of my colleagues I would say that we would have little argument with it. The
commission was established during my term as Minister. The Minister shakes his head. The
Labour Government decided to go ahead with its establishment, and it has performed a
useful role. We do not hear a great deal about it. I am a little mystified by clause 2. What will
be accomplished by increasing the number of people on the commission? Will six people be a
better bet than four? We had a good cross section with one member representing the
architectural sector, one being a retired builder, one with wide experience in finance and
land purchase, and an outstanding member of the judiciary as chairman. What type of
person does the Minister have in mind? Is he looking to other sections of the community?
Does he have in mind someone representing the homeless? If that is the general concept it
will be warmly welcomed by the Opposition, but if it is just to employ a couple of seat-
warmers the Opposition will want another look.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): It would be fair to ignore the attempt
at sarcasm by the member for St. Kilda; it adds very little to this debate. From the way the
member usually speaks about housing I thought he took it seriously, but if he talks like that
he will receive the same type of answer from me. It is proposed to increase the size of the
corporation by the two appointments. After 5 years, the commission has shaken itself down
into the role it sees for itself, of which the Government approves. The commission and the
Government agree that the commission would be strengthened if the range of talents of its
members were expanded. I have no particular person, nor a particular talent, in view at this
stage, except that there would be merit in considering an increase in the strength of the
commission in financial or home ownership interests. A woman might be a good member of
the commission. It is to the advantage of the commission and the Government to expand the
commission so that it can better fulfil its role.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
LOCAL ELECTIONS AND POLLS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Local Elections
and Polls Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a small Bill of three operative clauses.
Clauses 2 and 3 have some significance for the forthcoming local authority elections to be
held on 8 October this year. It is because of the forthcoming elections that I introduce this
matter now. Clause 2 makes it clear that any elections or polls held in conjunction with a
territorial authority's election or poll, and conducted by its returning officers, are to be
conducted by the method of voting decided on by the territorial authority. The purpose of
this is to avoid the administrative difficulties and voter confusion that would arise if a
number of elections and polls conducted at the same time by the same returning officer were
to be conducted by different methods of voting. Clauses 3 and 4 make consequential
amendments omitted last year when the principal Act was enacted. Clause 3 removes
redundant words from the nomination forms specified in the principal Act, thereby remov-
ing a possible source of confusion for returning officers when preparing nomination forms
'r this year's elections.

COUNTIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That the Counties
Amendment Bill be introduced. This also is a small Bill of two operative clauses. Clause 2
rectifies an anomaly in the principal Act. Some cases have recently been noted in which the
law, as now framed, requires the whole of an area of stopped road, which at some point in its
length touches on a river or stream, to be reserved for recreation purposes. The real
intention, however, was to make it possible for a reserve to be acquired, but only in that part
of the stopped road that actually abutted on to the waterway. Clause 2 makes this intention
clear. Clause 3 is a re-enactment of section 29 of the Counties Amendment Act 1961 with
some modifications. That section provides for the setting aside of reserves for recreation
purposes in subdivisions, other than farming subdivisions, on the banks of rivers or streams,
and in all subdivisions around lake shores and on the sea coast. The modifications are, first,
an extension of a county council's power with the consent of the Minister of Lands to grant
exemptions to the reserves requirements; secondly, a new provision that will allow the
Minister of Lands to revoke or vary exemptions he has previously granted in respect of rivers

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Container Shipping
1. Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru) asked the Minister of Transport, Is he aware of
the recent plea to the Prime Minister by Mr A. L. Friis of the New Zealand Dairy Board to
make container shipping more efficient, and, if so, what has been done about it?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I am aware of the recent plea to
the Prime Minister to make container shipping more efficient, and, as an immediate step, co-
ordinating committees have been established to keep the operation of the container
terminals at Wellington and Auckland under scrutiny. On these committees, which were set
up 3 months ago, are representatives of New Zealand Railways, terminal operators,


## p. 131 (#139) ############################################

26 May
131
Oral Answers to Questions
shipowners, and road carriers. The aim of these committees is to maximise transport
resources and to improve the flow of cargo to the hinterland supporting the terminals.
Similar committees will be set up for Lyttelton and Port Chalmers as they become necessary.
I have checked with the Ports Authority and find that the New Zealand Dairy Board will not
indicate when it intends entering the container trade, so obviously it is keeping its options
open. Therefore, I cannot understand Mr Friis's action in approaching the Prime Minister,
or the honourable gentleman's action in asking the question.
Hon. Sir Basil Arthur: As it is forecast that 80 to 90 percent of the import and export
cargo will be in containers by the end of next year, is the Minister satisfied that the
committee he has set up will be able to investigate this situation and that there will not be
bunching and container delays?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Other steps have been taken, including the establishment
of task forces by the shipowners to deal with specific items in cargo handling as they arise,
and particularly in the handling of wool and meat. Quarterly periodic reviews have been
initiated between representatives of the shipowners and other operators to facilitate the
removal of any other problems that may arise. It is difficult to ascertain now whether there
will be congestion, or how much. That depends on many factors. Containerisation was
introduced internationally, and New Zealand had to prepare very hurriedly to play its part.
We are now doing that. I can see that there may be some congestion during 1978, but after
that it appears that we will gradually come out of this problem.
Mr Walls: Does the Minister agree that the inefficiency or inability of the Ports
Authority to make decisions within a reasonable time, as evidenced by the continual delays
in arriving at a decision on the second crane at Port Chalmers, is a major cause of the
problem to which Mr Friis was referring?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I am not prepared to criticise the Ports Authority for
delays. An enormous amount of information has to be gained. Its real duty is to ascertain the
demand at different New Zealand ports. Since I have been the Minister, a number of ports'
officials have come to me and said their ports should be container ports, and the member can
see the difficulty we would get into if the Ports Authority did not take some time to make
these decisions. I cannot comment further because, as Minister of Transport, I come into the
act only when there is an appeal. I hastened to make the decision over the Bay of Plenty,
Auckland appeal, but there had been some previous delay by, I think, my predecessor;
knowing that an election was coming up, he left that one on my plate, but I made the
decision as quickly as possible.
Mr Christie: As 80 to 90 percent of the traffic out of New Zealand will be taken in
containers by 1978, creating chaotic conditions, would the Minister consider making
representations to the Shipping Corporation that it should charter a container ship that will
go into minor ports such as Napier, New Plymouth, and Nelson to relieve the congestion that
is obviously going to take place in those ports?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: I have already had discussions with the Shipping
Corporation about ships calling at secondary ports. If the ports have cargo, it is obvious that
the Shipping Corporation's ships will call; but if there is no cargo there to pick up, it is a
waste to be sending a ship in just for political reasons.
Mr Walls: Does the Minister consider that the further extended delay in reaching a
decision on the second crane for Port Chalmers, already delayed 4 weeks, is worth the $1,000
a day increase in price simply because the Ports Authority cannot write its decision, which
was made 4 weeks ago?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: It is not for me to agree or disagree that the Ports
Authority cannot write its decision. I do not know what the decision is.
Mr Christie: Does the Minister know that the port of Napier is the biggest wool selling
centre, was the third highest of the meat export ports before containerisation, and the
second highest in fruit; and would that not mean that the cargoes are there for a type of ship
that can come in to a port such as Napier and load its own containers?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: If the honourable member for Napier will give me, in
writing, the tonnage that is there to be moved, I will put the matter before the Shipping
Corporation immediately.

Garment Exports Quota
3. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, Has he

established outside the global quota as part of an agreement on apparel which is to run for a

difficulties which arise from the sudden restriction of the level of New Zealand exports
relating in particular to firm orders received by New Zealand manufacturers before the
quotas were fixed. A team of officials has already discussed this problem once with the

precise number or relate them to the orders, but there have been quite successful negotia-
tions.
Mr Lithgow: Is the Minister aware that certain orders from Australian handlers were
cancelled through slow delivery from New Zealand manufacturers well before the quotas

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: I cannot confirm that, but neither can I deny it is true.

and was continuing to rise. All of that volume of production which gave a value of about $20
million is protected.

Housing-Effect of Immigration Policy
6. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) asked the Minister of Housing, What effect has the
implementation of the Government's immigration policy had on the availability of houses
during the past 12 months?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): Under the Labour Government, New
Zealand was getting a net permanent migration gain of approximately 30 000 a year,
absorbing about one-third of all houses being built. In other words, we needed an additional
9000-odd houses each year for this reason alone. This situation has now been reversed, and
the outflow potentially frees nearly 4000 houses. The effect has been to relieve the pressure
on the building industry and to make a significant contribution in easing the housing
shortage. The relief accorded is already being reflected in the waiting lists for State rental
houses, which stood at 12 420 on 31 March 1977 compared with 14 899 12 months
previously.
Mr Talbot: Has there been any dampening down of the increase in the price of houses
during the last 12 months?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: It is my belief that the immigration policy, and the
consequent reduction in pressure on the building industry, has been largely responsible for
the very considerable decrease in the rate of increase in the price of houses during the last
year. For the 12 months to 31 March, the Government held the increase in the price of
houses to about 6 percent, compared with about 80 percent or 90 percent during the
Labour Government's 3 years.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Is the Minister aware that it is possible to have an increase in
housing demand at the same time as there is a net outflow of migrants, because age
characteristics of migrant inflows and outflows can be quite different?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I am comforted somewhat in the answer I gave earlier,
because it is very similar to an answer given by the member for Wigram in 1975 when Labour
was the Government. If the member for Petone would care to look it up, the reference is
Hansard, Volume 400, at page 3669. The member for Wigram, who was then Minister of
Statistics, said: “On the basis of 3.3 persons per dwelling-house or flat-the 75 141 would
need 22 200 dwellings, or approximately 7400 a year, to house this net gain. It should be
noted that the 7400 houses a year is the number required to house the 75 141 net gain."
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister confirm that, in addition to the 28 300 completions in
the last financial year, additions and alterations have been made to 5000 properties, thus
making an effective increase in housing stock of 33 300?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I can confirm that the volume of alterations and additions is
equivalent to the labour and materials needed for about 5000 houses.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Can I take it from the Minister's original answer that he and the
Government are proposing to solve the housing crisis by driving more people out of New
Zealand?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND: I can confirm that the Government is following its election
policy of reducing the rate of immigration, and one of the consequences of that is that it
eases the housing situation.
Hon. R. L. Bailey: Earlier, the Minister replied to a supplementary question by giving
the percentage increases in the cost of housing. Over what period did these percentages

TAKAPUNA CITY COUNCIL (RATES VALIDATION) BILL
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Regional Development): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. The Bill, as its name implies, will validate certain charges and rates.
Glenfield and Albany wards of the former County of Waitemata joined the district of the
City of Takapuna on 1 August 1974. This was pursuant to an Order in Council issued to give
effect to a final local scheme approved by the Local Government Commission. The Order in
Council divided the enlarged district into three wards known as the Takapuna, Glenfield,
and Albany Wards. Members will recall that these wards were to exist for 10 years and were
constituted for purposes of representation as well as of finance. The alteration of boundaries
occurred in the rating year beginning 1 April 1974 and before either Waitemata County
Council or Takapuna City Council had struck all the rates for the three wards for that year.
The provisions of the Counties Act 1954 on water rates and charges and separate rates for
lighting and library purposes empower a county council to make and levy such rates and
charges across a definite portion only of its district and not necessarily over the whole of it.
In contrast, the corresponding provisions in the Municipal Corporations Act 1954 authorised
the making and levying of charges and rates across the whole of the district of the
municipality but not across a defined portion of it.
By inadvertence the council proceeded to make and levy the charges on a ward basis.
Other provisions in the Municipal Corporations Act could have been used by the council to
achieve the same objectives but the Takapuna City Council did not follow the statutory
procedures required by these other provisions. As a result, water charges and lighting and
library rates for the last 3 years have been made and levied under the wrong sections of the
Municipal Corporations Act, the council having mistakenly assumed that the special
provisions relating to those charges and rates set out in the Counties Act and the Municipal
Corporations Act were the same. Therefore those charges and rates have been and are
invalid, although the obligation to pay them remains because of section 75 of the Rating Act
1967, the charges and rates not being in any case for a greater amount in the dollar than the
council was empowered to levy. The Order in Council also empowered the Takapuna City
Council, if it wished, to apply the differential rating provisions of the Counties Act for the
10 year period to either its Glenfield or Albany ward, or both. For the last 3 years, in
reliance on this authority, the council has levied a differential general rate in the Albany
ward.
Doubts have arisen as to whether the Order in Council-which was issued pursuant to
the now repealed Local Government Commission Act 1967-could confer upon the
Takapuna City Council as a municipality the power to apply to any part of its district a rating
provision reserved for counties under the Counties Act 1954. The current Local Government
Act 1974 specifically covers this situation by authorising an Order in Council to overrule the
existing statutory provisions. To remove any doubts which may exist as to the legality of the
council's levying of differential rates, the Bill would also confirm that action. The problem
which arose for the new expanded city council was a perfectly understandable one in the
circumstances, and I believe that the act of the Takapuna City Council and those members of
the previous Waitemata County Council who joined the Takapuna City Council as represen-
tatives of the Glenfield and Albany wards was one of public spiritedness in seeking to join
forces voluntarily before the Act was changed by the previous Government. In those


## p. 139 (#147) ############################################

26 May
139
Address in Reply
circumstances the House would be extending an appropriate gesture of support to the city by
setting aside its problem and clarifying the doubts that have been raised by the Act, and by
putting matters into a proper legal form.
Bill read a second time.
WAITEMATA CITY COUNCIL (FARM LAND) BILL
Mr D. M. J. JONES (Waitemata): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This
Bill validates the Waitemata City Council's farm land roll which was called into question by a
Supreme Court action in 1976. As a result of that court action the roll was not completed in
time, and the Bill validates the council's administrative actions in the meantime. The Bill will
have the effect of giving considerable rating relief to those on the farm land roll. The Local
Bills Committee made a number of amendments which I shall mention briefly. The
amendment to clause 3(1) is merely a drafting matter. There is an amendment to clause 3(5)
to extend the term of the legislation from the 1974-75 and 1975-76 rating years to 1976-77.
Clause 9 was added to ensure that the Bill expires on 31 March 1979 or on the expiry of the
farm land roll, whichever first occurs. I support the amendments made by the Local Bills
Committee and thank its members for the time they have spent in considering the Bill.
One aspect of the Waitemata City Council's submissions is of considerable interest to
the local people. On page 4 of the submissions it is stated, "My council was sorry to learn
that the Government was not prepared to enact an amendment to the Rating Act to provide
that an urban farm land roll is not required where differential rating is in force." I
respectfully suggest to the Waitemata City Council that it ascertains the opinions of the
people on the urban farm land roll before it makes such comments. I seek the indulgence of
the House to speed the Bill through all its stages, because it is urgent and I will be going
overseas shortly. I understand from the member for Henderson that he has discussed the Bill
with other members on his side of the House and that they are in agreement.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I take the opportunity of speaking briefly in
support of the Bill. No one can doubt the sorry state of the affairs of the Waitemata City
Council at present. Some of the troubles it is going through have been brought upon its own
head, but it deserves sympathy rather than blame, and assistance rather than criticism. Some
of the problems are of its own creation, some are inherited, and some are inherent in the
very nature of the institution. Someone once described a camel as a horse designed by a
committee. The Waitemata City administration is a peculiar and, I hope, unique animal, and
reflects little credit on its creators. It is neither city nor county, and the only real solution to
its problem is reorganisation into urban and suburban areas with the outer rural area
assuming a separate status. One instance of the present situation is that when land is taken
for road widening or straightening the residue of the land which was formerly on the farm
land roll ceases to be on it. Until this Bill is passed the city cannot rectify some of the
involuntary injustices which have resulted from the existing situation.
Bill read a second and a third time.

Mr LANGE (Mangere): I thank the Senior Government Whip for moving the extension
of time, and the House for agreeing to it. At the outset I acknowledge my respect for Sir
Denis Blundell as the Governor-General of New Zealand, and express my regret that the
National Government has not honoured and preserved the traditional role of Governor-
General. I record the pleasure of my constituents in Mangere at the visit of Her Majesty the
Queen to that electorate. I particularly record their pleasure at the action of the third Labour
Government, which amended the New Zealand Constitution Act and declared for all time
that New Zealand is a soverign State independent of any other country, with the free right to
legislate, and having its Queen by right of no other nation. The people of Mangere
welcomed her as their Queen.
The previous speaker seemed to have some reservations about the confidence of the
people in the Labour Party. I observe that I come into the House as the result of a by-
election held on 26 March after a man who had been a member of Parliament for 13 years
and a Minister of the Crown for 3 years resigned. I was elected in his stead by a majority of
such dimensions as to make me feel small. That was a reflection of the way in which the
people of Mangere felt, and of the confidence they placed in the Labour Party and in me. I
acknowledge the gratitude of the people of Mangere and, without being presumptuous, of
the people of the rest of New Zealand for the service that Colin Moyle gave to New Zealand
as member for Mangere and as a Minister between 1972 and 1975. His decision-which
included his wife and family-was to dedicate himself to public service. I am very new to the
game, and, from what I can see of it, even without the responsibility of a portfolio or a
principal spokesmanship, it involves a burden that makes heavy demands not only on the
member but also on his family. The people of Mangere, through me, record their gratitude
to Colin Moyle for those years of service. He has been a faithful member of the Labour
Party, and he still is.
I propose to reflect on what I regard as the three functions of one who becomes a
member of Parliament. I see the job as involving, first, a need to represent one's electorate;
secondly, the passing of legislation; and, thirdly-and for me this has a particular appeal-I
see Parliament as a talking shop where ideas are bandied about, where the Executive is held
to account for its actions; I see it as a place where the nation can be inspired, where lofty
ideals can be generated and disseminated. I see Parliament as the place that leads the
country, and moulds the country, so that it goes on to better times. I should like to speak first
of the electorate function. I am not satisfied that a member, given the existing level of
support, can adequately discharge his responsibilities within his electorate. It is not proper
that a member of Parliament should have his household turned into some sort of temporary
citizens' advice bureau. My family willingly accepts this position, and I do, because I knew
what was involved, but I believe support should be available in the electorate so that the
people can feel that they have easy contact with someone who can exercise influence and
show concern on their behalf. The demands of the capital are such that they militate against
one person's being able to discharge the electorate function and the other functions I have
spoken of.
I am proud to represent the Mangere electorate. Mangere is a good place to live in; I
have known it for years. I was born in Mangere Road, Otahuhu. We called it Mangery
Road, Oterhoo, in those days, but it is the same place. We grew up there at a time when the
electorate had at its northern end the Mangere Bridge, the old Mangere East area adjacent
to the railway line, and then those acres of Friesian town supply herds and Chinese market
gardens; and there was the Sunday afternoon trip out to the old aerodrome where the Tiger
Moths used to play. During my lifetime I have seen development there that is perhaps a
microcosm of the development of New Zealand in general. In recent years the people of
Mangere have faced the challenge of a sudden eruption of housing. The palliatives offered to
them were some gymnasiums and some community centres, but no matter what physical
structures were available to the people of Mangere they had to generate amongst themselves
that spirit of community without which no place deserves to live. They have accepted that
challenge. It is my duty as a member of Parliament to see that that spirit persists.
Sitting suspended from 5.30 p.m. to 7.30 p.m.

Mr LANGE: Before the House adjourned I was speaking of Mangere as being a good
place to live in, extolling some of its virtues. There is another side to it, a side that I believe
can be overcome by hard work within the electorate and positive action by the Government.
I believe that within the electorate we have people, within the Labour Party and without it,
who, during the election campaign, showed their determination to achieve what they set out
to do. My electorate consists basically of young families who are striving to make their
way-principally single income earners, but some who are obliged to have both parents
working so that they can achieve for themselves and their families what they consider to be
appropriate. The concern that I have is that in my electorate there are some people under
desperate stress. That stress arises from their present inability to provide sufficient for
themselves and their families to live adequately. We can, beneath a welter of political
allegation, conceal the real fact that there are people in my electorate who are bringing up
families of four children in a garage; and there are such examples throughout not only my
electorate but other areas in the city I come from. There are people under threat of losing
the homes that they struggled to obtain because they cannot obtain mortgage refinance. In
the short time since my election, I have intervened to assist two families who were under
threat of mortgagee auction sales, and in one extraordinary case I had to go late on a Sunday
night to see if I could help, and to be the bearer of the tidings to the wife of the household
that her house was being sold the following Wednesday. We can conceal the reality by the
way in which we talk, but at present we do not have appropriate Government machinery to
give relief to people who are under that sort of threat. As an electorate representative,
forgetting about my party affiliations, that surely must be the first challenge, because, unless
a family is housed and has the prospect of security, we face a poor society indeed.
I think of those in the electorate who would obtain better paid jobs if only they could get
to the place of work. My electorate has an abysmal transport service. There is some sort of
pretension that a rail service exists on the periphery of the electorate. If one could find it, if
the trains ran at the time they were needed, if there were seats in the carriages, and some
form of shelter for people to wait, then some use might be made of that system, but the
standard of rail transport in and out and on the edge of the Mangere electorate is appalling. I
come from an electorate where there are people with special learning difficulties, where
perhaps English is not the prime language-and I pay tribute to the calibre and dedication of
those members of the teaching profession who have gone to an area that has been labelled by
those who run our education system as a special area, and in that area work conscientiously
and hard. In particular I point with pride to the fact that Aorere College is a genuinely
community-based college, and that Mangere College has spread its influence throughout the
area, where teachers from both colleges spend a great deal of their time, unpaid, working
within the community. In an area that is currently part of the Otahuhu electorate, but which
on boundary change will become Mangere, Nga Tapuwae College is doing an extremely
useful community job. I think of Jean Batten Place, where for the first time a primary school
has a community officer with the special job of relating to the families whose children attend
that school. It is an area where the church is active, and where the various churches reflect
the multicultural nature of the electorate, where people are preserving in their country of
adoption the standards and customs they enjoyed in other parts, and where within their
churches they are able to show their equality whilst keeping their individual identities.
I am grateful for the work of the churches in the electorate because without it the place
would be the poorer-and I think of those people who have telephoned me. One occasion
was when a boy, who had been in the Social Welfare Department's care at Kohitere, was
discharged 7 months ago from full-time care at a cost of about $13,000 a year, and a social
worker had not been to see him since he had gone home. Within the electorate volunteers
are springing up, becoming their brothers' keepers, and I thank them. I come from an
electorate where the health needs are obvious, where there is a high incidence of ear, nose,
and throat ailments, where much preventive work is required, and where a health centre was
established, but is still without an ancillary social worker, an electorate that is part of the
South Auckland health district, which I understand was budgeted the sum of $300 for health
education last year.
I come from an electorate where people are just as inclined as people in other places to
be casual with other people's property from time to time, and occasionally, in moments of
stress, can fall into the folly of engaging in physical confrontation. I do not pretend that we
can legislate against such activity. The church has been preaching about it for more than 2000
years, and people are still prone to indulge in it, but I am convinced that the one thing that
curbs that propensity is the presence of a policeman. My electorate is in the South Auckland
police district, in which there are 300 000 people, and 23 detectives. I shall have the

distinction, after boundary changes, of representing an electorate without a police station;
