I have referred to the burdens attendant upon a member servicing an electorate, and I
propose, as perhaps many other members on both sides of the House have done, to be in a
particular place in the constituency on a Saturday morning to hear the problems and attend
to the needs of those within the electorate who seek assistance. I will be relying on my party
workers in the electorate to participate in that operation—and I assure the House that the
Labour Party in Mangere is able to take up that challenge, and does so in good heart and
with a confidence that the work will ultimately be rewarded. I shall now speak about what I
see as the second aspect of my work as a member of Parliament, and that relates broadly to
the legislative aspect of our activities. I come from the legal profession. I have been in it for a
while. It is not an easy profession to get into, and, as I discovered in Hobson in 1975, it is not
an easy profession to get out of. I do not say it is the noblest, but it is certainly streets ahead
of the church and the army. Because of that, I have had inculcated in me, I suppose, a
respect for the law which other people might not be able to share. For many years I have
been justifying the state of our law because I am the buffer between Parliament and those
who are affected by it. I simply say that I enjoy the prospect of being involved with those
who formulate the law. Now that I am no longer in the position I once held I am anxious to
say that I believe that much criticism of the law is justified. One feels grave social misgivings
about legislation that allows someone on an excess blood alcohol charge, who must have
been poured out of his car, to win the case because a sample had not been posted within the
appropriate time. How can I continue to justify to people the piecemeal approach of laws
that provide a theoretical maximum penalty of 3 months imprisonment for careless driving
causing death, a theoretical maximum penalty of 3 months imprisonment for saying
something coarse in the street, and a theoretical maximum penalty of 14 years for growing a
cannabis plant?
As legislators we must be conscious of more than just the volume of work which passes
through the House. Last year I was involved in a case under the Fugitive Offenders Act of
1881, which was described by the judge as an unburied corpse which he refused to breathe
life into. That type of rebuke is something I am now, from the other side of the fence, able to
take very seriously—although whooping with delight when the words were uttered-because
a legislator has a responsibility which transcends the partisan interest of any lawyer or
pressure group. I believe that the prime targets for legislation and intervention by the
Parliament in which I will be involved will be those areas affecting the rights of people, and I
express my disgust that we still do not give children the same rights and protections as are
afforded animals under the Animals Protection Act. It is an offence under that Act to terrify
an animal. I can find no similar provision in any statute relating to children. We have not
spelled out any form of charter of rights for people, be they children, middle aged, or
whatever, but that is one of the challenges we must face in an increasingly complex society.
I have had the distinction of working in an area of law which is remunerated at an
appalling level. Someone got the idea that I recently said that lawyers earn an average of
$70,000 a year. Some lawyers do; some burglars do too. There are people within the law who
earn one-tenth of that, and others more than that, but the area of law concerning most
people is the Police Offences Act, a statute which has its origins in medieval vagabond
legislation and is still hallowed by the seal of approval of the New Zealand Government. If a
person is charged under that legislation he is, as with any criminal offence, if he is prepared
to describe himself as an offender-just having pleaded not guilty-entitled to apply for aid
under the Offenders Legal Aid Act. His lawyer will then be remunerated at a level which,
when set in 1972, was lower than the level pertaining in 1956. There have been no
amendments since 1972. That, I submit, is a condemnation of the worth Parliament places on
the protection of the liberty of individuals, unless the idea is abroad that people must be
guilty to get themselves arrested and that therefore we need not worry unduly—and I could
mention some fairly conspicuous people who have recently been ultimately acquitted.
I want to tell more pointedly of what I feel is my ultimate role as a member of
Parliament. I can speak of my hopes about legislation, and what we hope to achieve by

fining-up the law, or what we ultimately think we can achieve by using the statute book. I
suggest that in all matters of law we are doomed to failure unless we can create a society

not the criminal law which stopped me from knocking off my trust account; it was because I

I believe that the challenge to Parliament is to speak in terms of vision, to legislate for
the proper development of the community. If anyone wants a definition of democratic
socialism and there seems to be a ready and pressing demand for such a definition-I
suggest that we do not muck around with figures or make jibes at each other but consider
whether we are prepared to create a society where people can gain the whole world and lose

in the love, the charity, and the compassion of people, because, unless we elect to take that

recidivism which currently exists. Ultimately, whichever party is the Government, if we were
to achieve social control by legislation alone, there would be the most primitive form of
totalitarianism imaginable. Our job rises far above that.
This is a country I am proud and deeply grateful to have been born in. I have had the

because there was the call home, the possibility in this well endowed land of getting away to
a place of isolation, of being with my family and those who had a part in my upbringing. All

that we would have a home. We knew we could achieve what we set out to do. The sons of

protected, we were preserved, we were given the confidence and the assurance that our

since then, to see whether this House has led the country to a new plateau of security and
achievement or whether, somewhere on that slippery slope, we might be putting the
millstones around the necks of the children in our society.

Whichever way you look at our problems, one factor is paramount: we must increase
our exports. The world does not owe us a living. The farming sector can produce the major
increase in our exports, in the long or the short term. The manufacturing sector has
responded well. Raw material exports, with added New Zealand content, have made
dramatic advances. Government assistance has been given in the form of incentives, but
there are problems, such as the Australian decision on quotas. Our future is in the land, and
with the farmers, the foresters, the fishermen, and the horticulturists. Those industries
produce between 70 and 80 percent of our overseas funds. The increase this year has been
dramatic, because of the upturn in world prices. It is well to remind ourselves that every $100
spent in this country generates $28 in demand for overseas funds. When ones realises that 76
percent, or 78 percent, or 80 percent of overseas funds come from the land, one wonders
what the social democrats have to offer. Is it their policy to bleed the goose white? Is their
policy still the same as that given during the last election campaign by their spokesman, the
previous member for Awarua, when he said, "The Labour Government is against exerting

I wonder whether the agricultural representative of the Labour Opposition thinks that

rocketing. It is interesting to recall that between 1972 and 1976 land prices escalated. The

increase; the average price of a fattening farm from $346 to $684 per hectare, an increase of
97 percent; and the average price of an arable farm from $567 to $1,704 per hectare, an
increase of about 200 percent. Why did land prices increase so greatly? It was merely

In its first year in office the former Labour Government had a record income tax
increase of 29 percent plus. In the second year it was 25 percent plus, and in the third year,
interestingly enough, it was only 7.5 percent, but that was an election year and it was the

Labour Government, Government spending increased dramatically as a percentage of the
gross national product, from 28 percent to 42 percent. Where did that increase come from?
Of course, it came from the taxpayers. The Labour Government was hell bent towards
socialism then, with control of the means of production, distribution, and exchange. I read
that in the United Kingdom, Government expenditure as a percentage of GNP has now
reached 60 percent. The National Government has reversed the trend and has knocked it
back to 38 percent. The Leader of the Opposition argues in the Dominion of 19 May that

the United Kingdom, where they have 60 percent control through the massive borrowing
from the World Bank last year for the nationalisation of their industries. Of course, the
United Kingdom has great industrial problems, and Britain, with its unemployment,
poverty, social and racial tensions, is no model for this country to follow. In 3 years of
democratic socialism we saw centralism operating in New Zealand, with compulsory control
over local bodies, hospitals, schools, transport, rivers, and coastal land—a loss of grass roots
representation, and a loss of freedom.
National undertook to restore farmers' confidence. It has changed the emphasis, with
production incentives, the livestock incentive scheme-under which 2700 applicants have
applied for an increase of more than 2 000 000 stock units as at 30 April of this year-and
with an investment of $24 million in the industry. In the 10 months to 30 April this year the
fertiliser use was 24 percent higher than 2 years ago. The dairy beef guarantee scheme has
been retained, and the bobby calf kill has been reduced by more than 160 000 animals, which
will increase our overseas funds next year—and this scheme is being continued at a higher
rate of payment. The farm ownership savings scheme has been amended, and more than
1000 applications were approved in the first financial year. Compare that record with the
farm ownership savings scheme introduced by the former Labour Government, when only
188 people took advantage of the scheme between October 1974 and March 1976 as against
the 1089 who have taken advantage of the National Government's scheme this year.
Argument about land settlement has been continuing, backwards and forwards. The

million; in 1974, $21 million; in 1975, $34 million; in 1976, $44 million; and this year $55
million-and not all that increase was caught up in inflation, because the records show that
the number being settled has increased. This year the Rural Bank has assisted 1033 young

facts are that we have no right of entry for cheese after December 1977. The uncertainty of
the Japanese market is a further problem, and the third country veterinary directive is poised
above us like the sword of Damocles. From 3 November this year all sheep heads must be
skinned and inspected with the carcass or the EEC will reject the meat. To the freezing
companies this means great cost, a cost that will finally be met by the producers. The
message I have tried to convey to this House tonight is that New Zealand depends on the
farming industry-the farmers and those who service them-and it behoves us all to
appreciate that fully.

One of the main topics in this debate has been housing. In 1935 the Labour Government
introduced the Maori Housing Act to enable our people to build their own homes with the
assistance of the Government. From then on we saw Maori people moving into homes they
are very proud of. In my electorate now, and particularly in my city, it is difficult for visitors
to determine which is a Maori home and which is a European home. This was brought about
by the policy of both Governments to allow applicants to have a house of the design of their
choice. This was made possible by the forward thinking of the officers of the Department of
Maori Affairs, and also of the Government. It was an important step forward for the social
and economic well-being of the Maori people. That is why I feel so depressed by the remarks
of the member for Awarua. I hope that the Labour Party, when it gets back on to the

live socialism—we do not just talk about it. We live it, we practise it, and we even offer it to
our European counterparts-and they need it. It is interesting that that question has been
brought up, and I shall illustrate to you the sort of socialism we practise. If the Maori people
have land for housing, they will give a section to their people. They will not demand payment
for it. This is why I am saying that the Government, be it a Labour or a National
Government, should give land to the people who require it, but should still retain the title of
that land. The applicant can pay the servicing costs.

Mr REWETI: The member for Awarua cannot seem to understand what is required.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Cannabis
1. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Health, Has he seen the statements in
the Press of 19 May by two Christchurch magistrates, when speaking from the bench, that
individually they have noted a more lenient attitude to the use of cannabis, were aware that
the community felt that the moderate use of cannabis was not a serious matter, and
remarked on the possibility of changing present laws regarding the narcotic, and has there
been any change of attitude on the part of the Minister and the Government to the use of
cannabis?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Health): I am aware of the press
statements to which the honourable member refers. There has been no change of attitude on
the part of the Minister or the Government on the use of cannabis. The Misuse of Drugs Act
1975 will come into force on 1 June. That legislation, passed under the Labour Government,


## p. 168 (#176) ############################################

168
27 May
Oral Answers to Questions
will grade maximum penalties for offences involving cannabis according to the nature of the
offence and the potency of the cannabis preparation. This is again, I suggest, a reflection of
the seriousness with which the Government still views the use and abuse of cannabis.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Does the Minister not concede that there is now a growing
understanding of the situation that possession of a very small amount of cannabis, generally
in the form of one or two cigarettes, is at most an offence that should attract a modest fine?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I understand that the Act that is coming into force does
provide for grading, but the fines seem to me to reflect a more serious view than the member
himself holds. He was in the House when the legislation was passed. As I understand it, the
classes do provide for quite serious terms of imprisonment, but for summary conviction for
possession the maximum penalties are 6 months' imprisonment or $1,000 fine or both for
class (a) controlled drugs, and 3 months' imprisonment or $500 fine or both for class (b) and
class (c) drugs. I am sure the member, having sat, I assume, on the select committee, would
have been more aware of this than I, but I do think the Government is not prepared to relax
its view that this is a serious matter.
Mr Latter: In light of the suggestion implied in the question, has the Minister read the
statement made by the Labour member for Sydenham after his return from the United
States where he saw a vastly different and harder line?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I have not seen that, but I am sure that those who have
had experience will be aware of difficulties that Governments face in assessing this problem,
and it will be kept under pretty constant review. The Minister is concerned, and I can speak
for the Government too.
Mr Kirk: Is the Minister aware that the statement I made concerning the drug problem
in the United States included the information that hard drugs were a situation that the
current Administration and other Governments overseas felt should be treated with the
utmost seriousness; but that, in fact, most major countries and Governments were looking to
a decriminalisation of marijuana.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: From my experience in select committees in previous years,
I am sure that the matter will be kept under review. But there is no certainty about soft
drugs, and that is the problem that Governments face. It is all very well to make comments
from the back benches, but we have the responsibility to administer the law, and I believe
that the Government will maintain a fairly hard line.

Container Terminal-Marsden Point
2. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister of Transport, Does he acknowledge that the situation at the Auckland and
Wellington container terminals, particularly the congestion and projected congestion as
container demand grows, makes the Marsden Point case for an international container
terminal very much stronger?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): The problem of fluctuating
congestion at the North Island container terminals would not be solved by the provision of a
third container port at Marsden Point. The problems of congestion are short term, and
current development at the two North Island terminals is expected to cope with all projected

Waitemata City Council
5. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Local Government, Has he yet received
any information which would justify his setting up a commission to take over the Waitemata
City Council, and, if not, could he specify what type of information is required by him in
view of the many specific comments that have been made about this council's activities over
the past few months?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): The answer to the first part of
the question is no. The only section of the Municipal Corporations Act under which a
commission or commissioner could be appointed is section 411, which requires as a
prerequisite that a council must wilfully or substantially refuse to perform the duties and
powers vested in it by or under that Act. I have not received any information that would
justify action under that section.
Mr Hunt: Has the Minister received any information from ratepayers or residents in the
Waitemata City Council area which gives him cause for concern about the activities of that
council?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: No.

the fact that Mr Covic resigned from the Waitemata City Council last night, does the
Minister not regard that matter as something that needs to be taken very seriously?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: This is the first I have heard of the resignation, and naturally I will
take it seriously. Perhaps this would be an appropriate time to advise the member of the
answer I intended to give in reply to question 9. Mr Colvin the mayor, wrote to me saying he
was very concerned about the situation, and he asked me to appoint some independent
person to conduct a public inquiry into the administration and as he put it-"the
procedural handling by the council and its officers of the Lincoln Road project and the
adjacent netball complex". In my reply I suggested to him that I thought an investigation by
an Ombudsman would be appropriate. I am very pleased to say that I have now received a
letter from Mr Colvin stating that the council has resolved to request the Ombudsman to
conduct an inquiry into the matters raised.

Post Office-Efficiency
11. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General, Has he read the April
1977 issue of the Katipo journal of the New Zealand Post Office Association, in which Mr
Reddish, General Secretary of the Post Office Association, states: "The effects of Govern-
ment's economic correctives are slowly but surely eroding the standard of efficiency that the
Post Office provides for its customers. Waiting lists are building up-urgent building works
are being deferred-computer applications are being delayed-training is suffering and
recruitment is inadequate. Staff ceilings are unduly restrictive and the Post Office administ-
ration continues to survive on the goodwill of its staff. Adverse criticisms are coming from
many sectors of the community and a lot of the criticism is justified. Politicians must be
prepared to go to the public and explain that the country cannot afford to maintain a decent
standard of service"; and, if so, would he confirm that the running down of the efficiency of
the Post Office is not the responsibility of the staff employed by the Post Office but is due
entirely to Government policies?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I reply on behalf of the
Postmaster-General. His answer is as follows. "I have read the article. I have considerable
respect for Mr Reddish, but I cannot accept his thesis. We are all aware that high consumer
demand has to be set against the limited resources available for every area, including the
Post Office. The Post Office simply cannot meet every demand, whether it is for phones,
buildings, computer applications or new services, but in general the efficiency of the Post
Office is at a high level. I have every confidence that the Post Office will continue to
maintain efficiency and to extend its services steadily to meet a challenging technological
future. The Post Office is a very large undertaking which provides a wide range of services
on a nationwide basis, and it will continue to do so efficiently.
Hon. F. M. Colman: What steps if any has the Government taken to mount a public
relations exercise to acquaint the customers of the Post Office that the deterioration in the
service is the result of Government restrictions and that in no way can employees be held
responsible?

175
Oral Answers to Questions
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I refuse to accept that there is a deterioration in the service.
Waiting lists have been implicit in the situation of the Post Office for many years. Indeed, as
the member knows, waiting lists fell markedly in the early 1970s but have risen steadily both
under the Labour Government and the present Government.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: No.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Waiting lists for phones were increasing steadily. If the

of the needs of such areas in Auckland. It is attempting to meet those needs, but it cannot be

Miss DEWE (Lyttelton) asked the Minister of Broadcasting, as an urgent question, In
the light of the delays which have ensued in the completion of the TV2 translator to serve the
Sumner, Redcliffs and Mount Pleasant areas of Christchurch, would the Minister advise
whether the commissioning date, which I was advised had been set back a further month to
mid-June, is now imminent, and, if so, what is the date of its commissioning and full
functioning?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I have consulted the Secretary of
the Broadcasting Corporation of New Zealand, and he confirms that the date originally
given the honourable member was mid-May, but this was set back to mid-June. The
honourable member will understand that such dates must, for technical and climatic reasons,
be taken as guidelines.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Blame it on the Labour Government.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I would if I could! Due to better progress, I am happy to
inform the honourable member and the House that the commissioning of the translator is
now expected on 1 June, and a press statement announcing this has been sent to the
honourable member.
TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL
Hon C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That the Transport
Amendment Bill be introduced. The Bill is being introduced to implement the Government's
recent decision to increase the fees payable for the registration, annual licensing, and change
of ownership of motor vehicles and trailers. The introduction of the Bill at this early stage in
the 1977 session is necessary because the licensing year runs from 1 July to 30 June the
following year. Vehicle owners must purchase the appropriate coloured stickers during the
next few weeks and display them from 1 July, when the new licensing year begins. The Bill is
brief. Clause 1 states that the Act shall come into force on the day on which it receives the
Governor-General's assent. The new fees will therefore apply to annual licences for the year
commencing 1 July 1977—that is, those purchased during the month leading up to the new
licensing year. The fees for new registrations and changes of ownership will apply from 1 July
1977, and therefore such transactions may take place at the existing rates until then. If a
vehicle transaction is made 3 weeks before 1 July the old registration or licence fee will
apply, whereas from 1 July the new rates will apply.
Mr Hunt: It just hurts the consumer.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: The honourable member should have thought about that
for 3 years when Labour was the Government, and frittered away the money. Provision is
also made to validate payments of fees at the higher rate that have been made before the Bill
becomes law. Clause 2 increases to $10 the fee payable on notification of change of
ownership of a motor vehicle. The present fee is $5. Clause 3 increases the fees payable on
registration of a new motor vehicle and for the annual licence for a motor vehicle or a trailer,
and clause 4 relates to consequential repeals. The new scale of fees is set out in the schedule
to the Bill, and is in two parts-registration fees and annual licence fees.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): This legislation is not unexpected. It was
announced some time ago, and met with widespread opposition. It is another harsh and
unjustified imposition on motorists. Opposition members are totally opposed to this
legislation, because we do not feel it is justified. We made our feelings well known when the
Minister made his announcement. The Minister and his colleagues, especially the Minister of
Finance, have an obligation to explain to owners of motor vehicles and the people generally
how they can justify the harsh increases. In round figures, the increased registration fees for
motor vehicles imposed by this legislation, including third party insurance, will now be
$39—an increase of almost 50 percent from $27. That has not been justified. The people are
entitled to a breakdown of these increases. How much is required for the costs? How much is
required for tax that will go to the Consolidated Revenue Account? The Automobile
Association made its feelings known at the time the announcement was made, and I support
its sentiments. No fair-minded person objects to paying a fair licensing fee or change of
ownership fee-that is understood-but to have an imposition inflicted upon them without
justification is something that the Automobile Association, representing the motorist, and
Opposition members will not accept without question and argument. How can the 100
percent increase in change of ownership be justified other than as another tax on the owners
and users of motor vehicles? We strongly oppose this. If the Minister and his colleagues

that salaries and wages, as a share of private income, have moved from 57 percent to 65
percent in the same 10-year period that this annual fee was not adjusted. The adjustment of
an annual licensing fee from $10 to $20, a 100 percent increase, compares with a movement
in consumer prices during that period of 122 percent. In terms of adjustments relative to
prices, it is not moving as fast as it could otherwise do. The other items, referred to by the
member for Northern Maori, which make up the $39.30 include several fees to which I
believe even Labour Opposition members would not object. Do they or do they not agree
that the accident compensation levy should meet the cost of accident compensation? There is
silence. The answer must surely be yes. This component is moving from $11.35 to $14.20. Do
they agree that the third party indemnity surcharge should be adjusted so it can clear the
outstanding legal commitments inherited by the insurance industry on the termination of the
old third party system and the introduction of accident compensation? Again there is silence.
They must agree. This fee has increased to $5, in the hope-and I believe it is a confident
hope that that level will finally clear up this item. The label fee is increased from 5c to 10c.
Have they any great objection to that? No. Costs of paper have gone up by more than that in
the 10-year period.
It is all entirely necessary and justifiable, and brought about in no small measure by the

consumer price index to rise by over 40 percent during its period of office, yet chose to freeze
a large number of Government charges, and imagined that the people were not paying. But
the people were paying in the form of tax. The member for Northern Maori reminds us that
the return from this adjustment in licence fees is about $24 million in a full year. I ask the

case the Home Office purported to revoke a TV licence obtained at the old rate because new
rates had come into force. The Government will not interfere with or revoke licences at
present in force. As I have said about three times this morning, the Bill provides for new fees
from 1 July. Therefore there is no—
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: For any fees from 1 July?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: Yes. The Bill comes into force on 1 July, but the old

Hon. A. J. Faulkner: If I buy a new car on 29 June I pay the old fees?

of days. That is why that provision is there.
Mr Prebble: It is retrospective.
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN: It is not retrospective at all; can the member not

Government charges that have not been altered in the last 10 years. I should like Opposition
members to look at the general wage rates of 10 years ago and compare them with the cost of
registering a vehicle. They will see that this is not the imposition they have been trying to
make it out to be. At least we are facing up to facts; the Labour Government did not. We are
facing facts in the interests of all New Zealanders. We are trying to control the inflation that
the Labour Government left us to deal with.

NOTICE OF MOTION
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I give notice that next sitting day I
shall move, "That the Transport Amendment Bill be passed through all its remaining stages
on Tuesday, 31 May 1977."
Mr HUNT (New Lynn): A point of order, Mr Speaker. The Acting Prime Minister has
given notice of a motion to pass a Bill through all its stages on Tuesday next. From my
recollection, that is the next sitting day of Parliament. Is it the Government's intention not
only to move and pass the motion but also to pass the Bill on that same day? Should there
not be one day's delay between the giving of the notice and its actual setting down on the
Order Paper? On Tuesday's Order Paper will appear "Orders of the Day" at 2.30 p.m., and
the leave of the House would have to be taken to proceed to Government notices of motion
because, in fact, if there were objection taken, you would proceed straight to the Address in
Reply debate.
Mr SPEAKER: In the course of formal business, notices of motion are normally taken
before the Order of the Day is proceeded to. There is certainly no obligation, and I can recall
no instance of the House proceeding at 2.30 p.m. straight to the Address in Reply debate or
legislation, in the absence of very strong reason. Notice of intention to move has been given
in accordance with the Standing Orders, and, if the House decides to adopt the motion, that
would seem to clarify the matter.
Mr Hunt: It would be the same day?
Mr SPEAKER: It would be. My impression is that it has happened often enough in the
past, not as a regular proceeding, but on occasions when there has been urgency. We have
not had the reason, but it is near the end of the month after which, I imagine, this legislation
comes into effect. The notice is in order.
SHOP TRADING HOURS BILL
Mr LUXTON (Piako): I am directed by the Labour Committee to present the report of
the committee on the Shop Trading Hours Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be
allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. The committee
has had the Bill before it for some time. It received 56 submissions and heard all 30 parties
wishing to appear before it. I am happy to report that last Wednesday the Bill was
deliberated on, and the Government Printing Office has co-operated so that the clean Bill


## p. 191 (#199) ############################################

27 May
191
Shop Trading Hours Bill
will be available once the Bill has been tabled. I know that it has attracted widespread
interest. It would be fair to say that many parties affected by the Bill as it was originally
written objected to it. We feel that we have accommodated many of their wishes, and the
form in which the Bill will be reported back to the House will certainly meet with many of
their requests. I shall detail some of the main amendments that the committee agreed to.
Clause 1: the Act will now be cited as the Shop Trading Hours Act 1977, not 1976. Clause 2:
slight changes in the interpretation were necessary. Clause 3: the Act not to apply to hotel
restaurants; this has been deleted.
The new clause 4A is the equivalent of the previous clause 12 and sets up the Shop
Trading Hours Commission, which will now comprise a commissioner, a barrister and
solicitor of 7 years' practice, and two members. This is a big change from the original Bill.
Clause 4B sets out how the commission is to exercise its powers-except for applications by
individual shops, when the commissioner alone may make the decision. In other cases the
decision of the commission shall be made by two or more members. Clause 4C deals with the
remuneration of commission members, and clause 4D deals with administrative and secreta-
rial services. Clause 4E is the equivalent of the previous clause 16 and relates to the annual
report of the commission. The one change to this clause is that in its report the commission
will no longer make recommendations on the approved and special case list. That function
will come under a special clause related to those clauses. Clause 5, which deals with
approved and special goods, has been deleted and a number of clauses inserted. The new
clause is changed to bring it more in line with the existing legislation. On the direction of the
Minister, the commission will call for and consider submissions from the public on changes to
the list. It will then make recommendations, and no Order in Council altering the list should
be made except on the recommendation of the commission. Clause 5A provides that where
the commission has not been directed by the Minister to call for general submissions on the
list, but wishes to recommend that any individual item should be placed on the list, it may so
recommend. If, however, in the opinion of the commission there may be any serious
objection to the proposal it must not recommend unless it has advertised its intention and
has considered all objections received within 1 month.
Clause 6, which deals with the opening of shops, has been amended by deleting the
proviso and adding the words "the day after New Year's Day" to subclause (1). Clause 6A
deals with public holidays, and provides for the transferral of certain public holidays which
fall on a Saturday and a Sunday to the following Monday and Tuesday. If a shop has
authority to open on a Saturday or a Sunday and the public holidays fall on those days, the
exemption will apply to the transferred holiday and not to the Saturday or Sunday. Clauses
12 and 16 of the original Bill have been deleted and replaced by clauses 4A to 4E. Clause
16 (a) deals with the authority for extended opening and replaces clauses 17 (1) and 18, and
provides for the application for extended hours of both individual shops and areas of shops.
As introduced, the Bill provided for individual, group, and area applications, and also for
applications from local authorities. The provision for local authority applications has been
deleted. Clause 17, dealing with applications, has been deleted and replaced by a very
similar clause. Clause 18, dealing with district and group applications, has been deleted.
Clause 19 has been deleted and a new clause inserted providing for the list of persons or
organisations who can appear and be heard at the hearing of an application to include,
specifically, industrial unions of employers and workers, the regional planning authority,
and the Secretary of Labour.
Subclauses (3) and (4) of clause 19 have been re-worded to indicate their intent more
clearly. Subclauses (5) and (6) are concerned with the criteria which the commission shall
have regard to. I emphasise that these criteria have been considerably expanded in
comparison with the original Bill. I believe there will be little, if any, increase in applications
pertaining to weekend trading. Subclause (7) of clause 19 is equivalent to original subclause
(6), and adds the industrial union of workers concerned and the regional planning authority
to the list of those who can apply for a cancellation of an order. Other small amendments will
be dealt with by other speakers. I do not believe that the Bill will materially change the
present lifestyle of New Zealanders, but it will legalise much of what is happening
throughout New Zealand today and much of what has been accepted in so many places. It
will make it possible for the Department of Labour to police the legislation, which it found
great difficulty in doing under the previous legislation. I am sure that this will be of
tremendous assistance and is well worth while. I support the Bill.

crux of the matter. Saturday trading is only a minor part of the Bill, and the crux of this part
is the criteria laid down in the Bill, and how they compare with those in the existing Act. We
have to consider how they have been changed in the amended Bill.
Dr Wall: What objectionable portions have been removed?
Mr BRILL: To start with, local authorities cannot commence area applications. The
status of the commission has been upgraded from the former requirement of a solicitor with
3 years' practice to the usual provision of a solicitor with 7 years' practice. The commission is
to consist of three members which will make it a stronger tribunal than that provided under
the Shops and Offices Act. Most importantly, the criteria have been substantially extended
to restore the proposition that the interests of the public are a paramount consideration. In
the 1955 Act the public interest is considered to be paramount, but the Bill as it came into
the House did not put the public interest as paramount. The amendment restores that
position; the interests of the public are to be an overriding consideration, and there are to be
sub-criteria to determine how these will be fixed by the authority. That goes a lot further
than the present law. I should like the member for Grey Lynn, or any other Labour member,
to spend 5 minutes explaining rationally and logically to the House how this amended Bill
will extend Saturday trading over and above the present law. He can use his other 5 minutes
for the meaningless mouthings we have heard from Labour members until now. He should
tell us what he finds objectionable. Instead of argument, we have been hearing wild emotive
statements that have nothing to do with what is before the House. Members opposite have
talked about life style, and rising prices. That might arise in terms of Saturday trading, but
this Bill does not extend Saturday trading.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Isn't that important?
Mr BRILL: Certainly it is important, but the member for Petone fails to appreciate that
this Bill does not extend weekend trading. If he believes it does, he should tell us how it
does. Opposition members are slithering around this point and are refusing to face up to it.
We have not been able to get anyone to tell us how this Bill as amended will introduce more
widespread Saturday trading. I shall let the next Opposition speaker elucidate that central
point-the only important point in this debate.

presume there is no objection to that course being followed?

SUSPENSION OF STANDING ORDERS-TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I move, That the Standing Orders be
so far suspended as to enable the Transport Amendment Bill to be proceeded with forthwith,
and passed through all its remaining stages during the present sitting of the House. I am sorry
that this is required. I had hoped that we could take the normal business and then proceed to
the Government notice of motion. The purpose of the motion is to pass the Transport
Amendment Bill through its remaining stages. There is an element of urgency, inasmuch as
people are about to relicense vehicles and, as honourable members know, it is desirable that
the amendment should be in operation. That point was canvassed on Friday when the Bill
was introduced.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): The motion is quite unacceptable to the
Opposition and will be opposed. We can see no real need for it. The Minister in charge of the
House has said that it is necessary to get the Bill through, because registration is about to
begin. That is an undeniable fact, but is no occasion for taking the unusual step of
suspending the Standing Orders of the House. The difficulty could have been overcome
quite simply by calling the House together a little earlier. The Government was well aware of
the problem. For reasons of its own, it has decided to double the relicensing fee. The merits
of that will be gone into at considerable length and depth before the matter is finally
disposed of, but I do not want to do so now. If, whether for a good or a bad reason, the
Government decided on that course of action, it could have arranged its activities accord-
ingly and called the House together in ample time for the necessary legislation to be passed
in the ordinary course of events, without suspending the Standing Orders.
I suppose this action must have been taken in recent years, or at some time in the past.
In my 17 years in the House I cannot recall its ever having been done when I was present,
although I could be wrong. But certainly it is, while not unprecedented, a very rare event
and should not be done lightly, nor unless the soundest possible reason is advanced in its
support. As I say, this action could have been avoided by the Government, and the reason
advanced for it is totally unacceptable to us. I suspect, however, that while that is the
ostensible reason the real reason is that the Government is trying to avoid being embarrassed
by the constitutional difficulty in which it finds itself. The most significant clause in the Bill is
clause 3, which is an enlightening if not an informative one.
Rt. Hon. B. E. Talboys: A point of order, Mr Speaker. What is being debated is whether
or not the Standing Orders should be suspended, not the provisions of the Bill. The Bill will
be under discussion after we have disposed of this motion.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: It is absolutely essential that the member who is speaking should be

Bill, but discussing the constitutional issues involved in some clauses of the Bill.

Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: I am obliged, Mr Speaker. That is exactly the course I propose
to follow. As I was saying, the significant clause for the purpose of this debate is clause 3. I
described it as enlightening, but uninformative. It is enlightening because, I suggest, it
discloses the true reason for the motion that is before us, and not the ostensible one
suggested by the Minister. It is a turgid piece of drafting, and would not be there but for a
particular event-which I suggest is well known to members of the Government-that
occurred in England in 1976 and gave rise to a case that attracted some notoriety—the case
of Congreve v. The Home Office. I suggest that it is because of that case that we find clause 3
incorporated in the Bill. It arose out of a move made in England-it seems to me executively
by the Home Office—to increase the amount of the television licence fee. It was announced
that this would come into effect on 1 April 1975. In that way the case is coincident with the
present situation; the licensing fee was to be doubled, and in this case the present
registration fee is to be doubled.
In the earlier case, no legislation was then in force to authorise the increase, and as the
announcement was made some time before 1 April it allowed several people to relicense
their sets at the lower rate then prevailing. After 1 April the Home Office demanded from
those people a further payment amounting to the extra that would have been due if the
relicensing had taken place after 1 April. It was held that the Home Office was not entitled
to make that demand and that the payment was invalid. The judgment of the Court of
Appeal, expressed through Lord Denning, Master of the Rolls, included this statement:
"There is yet another reason for holding that demands for £6 be unlawful. They were made
contrary to the Bill of Rights. They were an attempt to levy money for the use of the Crown
without the authority of this Parliament, and that is quite enough to damn them”—and he
cited authority. That is what the Government is trying to do today-to give the appearance
of authorising itself to make demands from the public without the legislative authority to do
So.
We understand that it has been possible—and I have no doubt that it has been possible
this year to relicense a motor vehicle before the month of June, when the normal
relicensing period begins. It is common for people to send in applications by post,
particularly if they are going away, and to have their vehicles relicensed before 1 June. I ask
the Government whether that has been done this year and, if so, at what rate the payment
has been received. I have before me a copy of the current registration application form to be
filled in by those who wish to relicense their vehicles as from tomorrow. I do not have, but I
hope to have within a moment or two, one of the old forms. I do not know what the old form
has printed on the bottom of it, but every form I have seen that has been printed by the
Government Printing Office has a code number at the bottom, which clearly discloses the
number of forms printed, the date upon which they were either printed or authorised, and
the year. On the form I have the only code printed is "87310A-76MCT”. What that means I
do not know, and whether the figures "76" indicate that the form was printed in 1976 I do
not know, but it is unusual to find a form printed by the Government Printing Office without
a code number disclosing the date of printing.
If payment has been made at the prevailing lower rate of $5, what is the Government's

Governments must seek parliamentary authority to give their legislation proper legal force.
Has this sort of thing been done before? Yes, it has been done many times before, and I shall
give two very well known examples. In 1974 it was necessary for Parliament, because of the
problems met by the Cornish group of companies in the inflationary conditions of that day,
to change the law in one sitting of Parliament, that changed law to have effect immediately,
otherwise a great number of investors would have been worse off. The National Party in
Opposition approved the necessary change in the order of business of the House on that
occasion. Again, in Labour's time in Government in 1975, and for the same reason-the
runaway inflation the Labour Government had promoted-the Perpetual Trustees Company
and all its investors got into great difficulty, and the Labour Government proposed a certain
motion that would accord the passage of the Trustee Companies Management Bill through
all its stages in one day. The present Leader of the Opposition, in Hansard, Volume 400, at
page 3555 is reported as having moved, "That urgency be accorded the passing through all its
stages of the Bill about to be introduced." The Bill with which the present motion is
concerned was introduced on Friday, not at a moment's notice but with some days' notice;
the Opposition has had the opportunity to see what it is all about. The Leader of the
Opposition, having moved that motion in 1975, said, “I should say in explanation that the
Minister of Justice has spoken earlier this evening with the Leader of the Opposition. The
Bill relates to the protection of trustee investments, and because of the nature of that
protection it is necessary that the Bill pass through all its stages at this sitting." So the
National Party in Opposition, and as a responsible Opposition, agreed and did not delay the
work of the House; the Trustee Companies Management Bill went through, and the people
who had dealings with, and whose money was invested with, the Perpetual Trustees
Company were protected. We have not had similar responsible action from the Labour
Opposition today.

TRANSPORT AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a second time. The decision to increase annual licensing fees, registration fees, and change of
ownership fees has been made by the Government as part of the recent review of
Government fees and charges. The review was intended to take account of upward
movements in the costs of providing Government services generally, and was begun early
last year. There is no need for me to remind the House of the increase in costs of the Ministry
of Transport, and other departments in my portfolio. The scales of fees, prescribed in the
first schedule and in section 18(7) of the Transport Act 1962, were last reviewed 10 years
ago in 1967-and have not been adjusted since. The increase of 100 percent is similar in
scale to rises in costs to the community as a whole, and refleched in the movement of the
consumer price index over the last 10 years. In other words, the increase in fees is in line with
the movement in the consumer price index over the last 10 years. When talking about motor
vehicle fees some people are confused about which fee is which. Vehicles are registered only
once, when they are new. After that they are licensed every year, and I emphasise the word
"licensed". The Bill increases the change of ownership fee, the registration fee, and the
annual licence fee for all classes of vehicle. However, the amount payable by owners of
vehicles already on the road when they relicense their vehicles next month will go up by less
than 100 percent, since some components of the full licensing fee are not being changed.
The relicensing fee is made up of an annual licensing fee, an accident compensation
levy, a third party indemnity surcharge, and a label fee. The Bill provides for a 100 percent
increase in the annual licence fee only. I emphasise this point; the accident compensation
levy and the label fee will stay the same, and on Thursday, 26 May, an amendment to the
Motor Vehicles Indemnity Surcharge Regulations was gazetted, providing for the indemnity
surcharge portion to go up by 50 percent. This latter increase has been necessary to cope
with outstanding claims under what we called the old third party insurance scheme, and is a
small portion of the full relicensing fee. In the case of a private car the increase is from $3.30
to $5 a vehicle. There has been no change in the classification of vehicles in the schedule to
the Act. The only change is in the scale of fees, and the increase has been applied uniformly
across the board. I should like to make it clear that although the relicensing of an average
family saloon will rise from a total of $27.60 to $39.30 per annum this increase is a small
proportion of the yearly running costs of such a vehicle travelling an average distance of, say,
16 000 kilometres a year. As we all know, the cost of providing facilities for all classses of
motorists places increasing pressure on limited Government funds every year. As I said
when I introduced the Bill, it is intended that the new fees will apply to registrations and
changes of ownership after the new licensing year begins on 1 July 1977, and to the
relicensing of vehicles for that year. The relicensing fees will actually be paid, as they always
are, before 1 July, when display of the new coloured windscreen sticker becomes obligatory.
During the last 18 months the Government has looked very closely at Government
expenditure. To the best of its ability it has tried to bring each section of Government
expenditure into line. As I have already said, the costs of the Ministry of Transport have
greatly increased, and one has only to stop for a moment to realise the increased costs of
policing the Transport Act, including increases in the cost of motor cycles and other motor
vehicles. Three weeks ago, in my absence, the Acting Minister of Transport announced the
Government's intention. The Bill was introduced on Friday so that the Opposition and the
people generally might know what it was about. We are here now to put it through all stages
so that the people may get on with relicensing their motor vehicles from 1 June, as usual.
Someone asked earlier, and it may be raised in this debate, about those who have already


## p. 220 (#228) ############################################

220
31 May

paid their fees. That situation will be validated by clause 3, and no doubt it will be explained
during the Committee stage.

this for the Minister of Justice, but I realise that he is not a lawyer. However, I suggest he
looks at this book, which states on page 49: "The Bill of Rights in 1688”—that is going back
far enough even for the Minister-"accordingly settled the matter for the future as regards
both direct and indirect taxation by declaring that 'Levying money for or to the use of the
Crown by pretence of prerogative without grant of Parliament for longer time or in any other
same manner than the same is or shall be granted is illegal.'" There is no doubt about it; it is
illegal. That is what is being attempted in this Bill. The book quotes a recent English
case-Wilts United Dairies (1923). In that case the Attorney-General sought to recover
£15,000 from Wilts United Dairies. "The Court of Appeal unanimously reversed this
decision, on the grounds that the charge was ultra vires being a levy of money for the use of
the Crown without the authority of Parliament." The law on the question is very clear. There
are other cases. The Congreve case again establishes the matter without any doubt. Lord
Denning, Master of the Rolls-and I would think that the Minister of Justice has heard of
him-said: "There is yet another reason for holding the demands for £6 to be unlawful. They
were made contrary to the Bill of Rights. They were an attempt to levy money for use of the
Crown without the authority of Parliament. That is quite enough to dam them."
If there is any confusion on the part of the Government as to whether the Bill of Rights
applies in New Zealand, I would have thought that it would be warned by what the Chief
Justice said last year to the Prime Minister, when he attempted to change an Act of
Parliament by a press announcement. Our Prime Minister has made the law books-he is in
the New Zealand Law Reports 1976, Volume II. The words of the Chief Justice last year
apply to the Bill before us. The Chief Justice, Sir Richard Wild, said: "The pretended power
of suspending of laws or execution of laws by regal authority without the consent of
Parliament is illegal. . . It is a graphic illustration of the depth of our legal heritage and the
strength of our constitutional law that a statute passed by an English Parliament nearly 3
centuries ago to extirpate the abuses of the Stuart kings should be available on the other side
of the world to a citizen of this country which was then virtually unknown in Europe, and on
which an Englishman was not to set foot for another 100 years. Yet it is not disputed that the
Bill of Rights is part of our law." There is no doubt in my mind that what has been done on
the instruction of the Minister-the collection of money without the authority of
Parliament is illegal.
Clause 3, which contains the retrospective provision, is somewhat obscure. I doubt that,
in fact, it will correct the legal position. Despite the passing of this Bill, I believe that what is
wrong today may well be declared to be illegal by the Supreme Court on the basis of the
Congreve case. Why is this retrospective clause included? The Government must have
decided that it would collect money illegally, otherwise the clause would not have been
needed. In other words, we have the incredible situation, not of an accidental breaking of

has taken place since the fee was last increased; and it is in line with the increases in wages.

Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): The member for Henderson pointed out that members on this
side of the House raise two very important principles in opposition to this Bill. One is the
manner in which it is written and by which an increased licence fee will be imposed, and the
other is the amount of taxation involved. Government members are avoiding a very
important constitutional issue in the manner in which this increase is being imposed. Let me
tell the member for Lyttelton that the Bill of Rights is the cornerstone of the parliamentary
system. She is showing disrespect to Parliament when she says this matter is of no
consideration whatsoever. The Bill of Rights gave to the elected representatives of the
people the power to decide whether taxation should be levied. It took from the king and
from the Executive the power to enforce such taxation without the authority of the
Legislature. The Legislature is the freely elected members of the public. The Bill of Rights is
important for safeguarding the liberties of the individual. We injure our parliamentary
system when we allow legislation to be passed in this form, because it gives the Executive or


## p. 244 (#252) ############################################

244
31 May
Transport Amendment Bill
Cabinet a power to which it is not entitled. It is completely wrong that restrospective
legislation in this form should be passed.
Members on this side of the House have referred to the Congreve case. That is, of
course, only restating a number of soundly based principles of constitutional law upheld by
the court in the interests of Parliament against the Executive. I hope that Government
members will be zealous of the rights of Parliament when they go into the lobbies. This
legislation offends the constitutional rights of the public and the freedom of the individual. I
go back to a case already stated by my colleague the member for Auckland Central, the
Attorney-General v. Wilts United Dairies, in 1921. That case refers not only to taxation, but
also to any collection of revenue whatsoever. It has been pointed out tonight that the Bill
before us is an income-gathering measure. The statement made by the judge in that case is
relevant: "If an officer of the Executive seeks to justify a charge upon the subject made for
the use of the Crown (which includes all the purposes of the public revenue), he must show,
in clear terms, that Parliament has authorised the particular charge. The intention of the
Legislature is to be inferred from the language used, and the grant of powers may, though
not expressed, have to be implied as necessarily arising from the words of a statute; but in
view of the historic struggle of the Legislature to secure for itself the sole power to levy
money upon the subject, its complete success in that struggle, the elaborate means adopted
by the Representative House to control the amount, the conditions and the purposes of the
levy, the circumstances would be remarkable indeed which would induce the court to believe
that the Legislature had sacrificed all the well known checks and precautions, and, not in
express words, but merely by implication, had entrustef a Minister of the Crown with
undefined and unlimited powers of imposing charges upon the subject for purposes
connected with his department." That is a most important constitutional principle. It is a
decision of the court upholding the rights of Parliament against the Executive. Parliament
has a responsibility for the liberty of the subjects that it represents to see that the Executive
does not take to itself power to tax in a way which is against the constitution.
I refer now to a case in Chancery known as Bowles v. the Bank of England, in which
Justice Parker in 1913 said: "Does a resolution of the Committee of the House of Commons
for Ways and Means, either alone or when adopted by the House, authorise the Crown to
levy on the subject an income tax assented to by such resolution but not yet imposed by Act
of Parliament?" I stop there to remind the House that on Friday we resolved to give the Bill
a first reading. This decision relates to that point. "Apart from the effect of certain
provisions contained in the statutes relating to the collection of income tax, to which I shall
presently refer, this question can, in my opinion, only be answered in the negative. By the
statute 1 W. & M., usually known as the Bill of Rights, it was finally settled that there could
be no taxation in this country except under authority of an Act of Parliament. The Bill of
Rights still remains unrepealed, and no practice or custom, however prolonged, or however
acquiesed in on the part of the subject"—in other words, whether the subject has already
paid his licence in full by the measure that will take effect tomorrow, even if he has acquiesed
-"can be relied on by the Crown as justifying any infringment of its provisions. It follows
that, with regard to the powers of the Crown to levy taxation, no resolution, either of the
Committee for Ways and Means or of the House itself, has any legal effect whatever. Such
resolutions are necessitated by a parliamentary procedure adopted with a view to the
protection of the subject against the hasty imposition of taxes, and it would be strange to find
them relied on as justifying the Crown in levying a tax before such tax is actually imposed by
Act of Parliament." Those are sound constitutional principles of which the House should
take notice.
I am interested to hear the cry coming from some members of the Executive casting
doubt on the wisdom of the court's decision in this matter. We, as members of the House,
have a responsibility to uphold the traditions of the House. We have a priceless heritage in
that the Bill of Rights is part of the foundation and the cornerstone of our parliamentary
system, as it is of the House of Commons. I ask members to weigh this matter carefully
before voting on the second reading of the Bill. We might grant the Government power to
alter the licence fees or to impose taxation it if were done in a constitutional manner, but I
suggest that this is unconstitutional. It does not matter that the subject has already agreed to
pay the extra fees. The people who have paid the fees have been charged illegally. It would
be unfair if those people had an advantage over the rest of the people. There is only one way
the Government can get itself out of this impasse, and that is to delay the passing of this
measure for 12 months; and the Government should give that serious consideration. This
will be an unpopular Bill to introduce 12 months hence because that will be only a few

Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport): I move, That this Bill be now read
a third time.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): I wish to report some of the
events in the Committee stage, and to emphasise, as the Opposition did then, that this Bill
was seen as a tax measure and nothing else. Constitutional issues were raised to show that, as
a tax measure, this was being improperly handled, and that its clauses-notably clause
3-contained some most unusual elements, particularly in relation to the role of the
Governor-General, his signature, and the time at which the Bill should become law. Those
elements will be canvassed in more detail by one of my colleagues. I want to refer to the
statement I made in the Committee stage, and the replies that came from the Minister. I
drew his attention to the fact that he had indicated when the Bill was introduced that extra
revenue amounting to about $24 million would accrue from its proposals. I drew his
attention to the fact that if, in the estimates of his department for 1976-77, we attributed half
the administration costs allowed to the expense of administering road transport, and added
to that the sum allowed for road transport itself, $17.4 million, we still had a sum that was
less than the increase in these charges. It came to only $23.2 million, compared with the
extra $24 million he said he was getting out of these new charges. He came back with the


## p. 259 (#267) ############################################

31 May
259
Transport Amendment Bill
very lame excuse that when the Wanganui computer is in operation the provision for salaries
will have to go up by about 10 percent. When we look at the item for salaries under the
general heading "Personnel", the total for general administration is $3.3 million; so that
gives us $1.65 million if we attribute half to road transport. The total item for road transport
salaries is $11.8 million. In other words, it comes to a total of $1.4 million extra if there is a
10 percent increase in the salaries in these two items. Therefore, to cover the extra $1.4
million required for salaries, the Government proposes to take $24 million in extra charges.
That was the contribution the Minister of Transport was able to make to justify the increase
being loaded on to the motoring public.
That clearly underlines the Opposition's contentions that the proposals in the Bill are
for additional taxation, that they are punitive, that they are very much greater than is
justified, and that, as the funds from the extra charges are to be paid directly into the
Consolidated Revenue Account, Government members should have given some explanation
of why the extra money is to be taken and where it is to be used. However, we were given no
answers to those questions. All we were given was a knowing look and the comment, "Oh,
well, you know it is going into the Consolidated Revenue Account." It was left to the
Opposition to make the case that the Government's proposal is unconstitutional and
contemptuous of the safeguards claimed by the Government but ignored by it in practice.
The Bill of Rights, the very basis of our parliamentary system since 1688, is being ignored by
the Government for the second time in just over a year. I do not wish to develop that theme
because, as I said, one of my colleagues will be doing so at some length. I wish merely to
emphasise that, to cover extra charges which by reference to last year's estimates appear to
be no greater than $1.4 million, the Government is taking $24 million in extra revenue. The
Minister of Transport said, "Oh, but we are moving to keep charges in line with costs." I do
not know whether it is the Government's principles or its arithmetic that is wrong, but no
evidence of the latter was presented in the Committee stage.
Mr LANGE (Mangere): During the Committee stage the challenge to the legislation
was twofold, as the Deputy Leader of the Opposition stated. The first aspect related to
seeking answers as to whether the legislation was intended to increase charges or to fix new
rates of taxation. The Committee was referred to clause 2, which provides for an increase in
the fee for registering motor vehicle ownership changes. That clause proposes that the fee
should be doubled from $5 to $10. During the Committee stage it was stated that the
proposed change is the first for 10 years. In fact, 10 years ago the fee for registering a change
of motor vehicle ownership was 10s., or $1, and the proposal in clause 2 represents an
increase of 1000 percent on the fee of 10 years ago.
The aspect of the legislation that exercised the Committee most was the time at which
the new fees would come into effect. There is a clear division in the Bill as to when certain
changes shall take place. The first set of changes will take place on dates certain, and in
taxation measures dates certain are consistent with our theory of government, in which the
onus on the citizen is made clear and the obligations that must be obeyed are strictly stated,
so that there can therefore be no confusion. A date certain is stated in clause 1(2), and
provides that the change of ownership fee doubles on 1 July 1977. The Committee was
concerned about the confusion in subclauses (2) and (3) of clause 3. It was observed that
there was no confusion in clause 3(4). Subclause (4) states that the existing fee for registering
a motor vehicle should remain until 1 July 1977. Again, the effect of the legislation is stated
with precision in respect of the annual licence fee payable for a motor vehicle for the year
ended 30 June 1977. It was particularly over subclause (2) that the confusion arose, and it
was contended in the Committee that in fact there was no need for this legislation because
there is in existence the first schedule of the Transport Act 1972, Part II of which fixes annual
licence fees. The question was raised as to whether it was the intention of the Minister of
Transport, through the Postmaster-General, to make a refund to any persons who have paid
the new fees demanded of them for the 1977-78 year above those which are currently set out
in the law. No answer was forthcoming, and the contention made in the Committee stage
was quite simple: we have the benefit of the existing law, which is clear, and it is improper
for any Government to demand, by way of duty, tax, or impost, anything that is not provided
in the law or for which legislative sanction is not available. It was pointed out in the
Committee stage that legislative sanction is not available in this Bill until it is passed. The
Opposition records its strong objection to the principle whereby Parliament is called upon to
validate what is an unlawful act on the part of the bureaucracy in demanding a tax. It is an
unlawful act. It was so contended in the Committee stage, and an answer was not given as to
whether the Post Office had been in order in demanding the new fees.

law, and with the language of the Bill couched in terms that seek to validate that. That was
the exception taken in the Committee stage. That is what is wrong with the legislation, quite
apart from the tax aspect. It is a practice which, having started, must now cease. This Bill
should not be passed.

OTAKI AND PORIRUA TRUSTS AMENDMENT BILL
Mr BRILL (Kapiti): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This is a private
Bill promoted by the Otaki and Porirua Trusts Board, which is a board established by its own
Act in 1943, as amended by the 1946 amendment. The principal objective of the board is to
apply its income to the provision of scholarships for post-primary education, giving prefer-
ence in particular to the members of the Ngatiraukawa, Ngatiawa, and Ngatitoa tribes in the
Wellington area. The board owns 535 acres of land at Otaki as a consequence of various
grants made by the Crown and the Church over the years. Until 1971 the bulk of the land was
leased to farmers. Since the amendment passed by the House in 1969, the board itself has
farmed the area under 50:50 sharemilking agreements, and those farming operations have
resulted in a substantial increase in the board's income. This increase has enabled a steady
programme of farm improvement and modernisation to be carried out, and has thereby
made available more money for scholarships. A comparison may be drawn between the 1972
year, when the number of scholarships was 76, and the 1977 year, when the number of
scholarships increased to 139. It can thus be seen that the change from leasing to sharemilk-
ing arrangements has been a substantial success. The efficiency of the sharemilking opera-
tions has largely been achieved by the leasing of other land for essential run-off purposes.
The purpose of the Bill is to enable the board to farm other land that it may acquire in the
future.
Bill read a second time.

High Commissioner's Office, London
1. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Foreign Affairs, Can he
explain why the New Zealand High Commissioner and the diplomatic staff stationed in

important day to day responsibilities. Consequently, I see nothing unusual about a decision
to send officials from Wellington to help that post prepare for a major international
conference.

own office set up for it, and part of the duties of those who have gone to London is to get that
office into working order.

2. Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei) asked the Minister of Education, Does the Department of

Public Companies-Return on Shareholders' Funds
3. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, What
return on shareholders' funds does his department consider reasonable for public
companies, and does the department accept shareholders' funds as being the amount shown
in the accounts of a particular company or does it have some other measure?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): In matters of price
control the Secretary of Trade and Industry exercises an independent statutory discretion.
However, in determining the prices of goods and services pursuant to the Commerce Act
1975 the secretary does not employ a uniform rate of return on shareholders' funds but sets a
rate in each case which he considers appropriate having regard to the considerations
required by section 98 of the Act to be observed by him. The rate will normally bear some
relationship to the previous earning rate of the company and the return of any other public
companies engaged in similar activities. The quantum of shareholders' funds shown in the
accounts is subject to reduction on account of circumstances such as the revaluation of
assets, assets employed outside the company, and assets not attributable to goods and
services subject to price control under the Act.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: What action does the department take when there has been a
major increase in return on shareholders' funds?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: In the case of Watties, about which company the
honourable gentleman has been making press statements, the revaluation is ignored or not
taken into account by the secretary in setting the prices of the products sold by that
company.
Mr Comber: Do tens of thousands of New Zealanders, including people on national
superannuation, invest some of their savings in the companies that are the subject of this
question? What would the effect be if those people did not receive a reasonable return on
their investment? Would it have a detrimental effect on job opportunities in the companies
concerned?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes it would have a detrimental effect on the very
large number of growers who have contracts of a horticultural or seed-growing nature with
Watties, and also it would have a detrimental effect on the very large number of staff which
that firm employs.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: If we deduct from shareholders' funds the revaluation of land and
buildings, will the Minister acknowledge that there has been a major upward movement in
the return on shareholders' funds in Watties Industries?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: I would not be prepared to do that, because it has
been the practice of the secretary to treat every individual case on its merits and to set the
proper quantum of margin for each company. It has certainly done so with this company,
which is very much in the public eye. In the case of Watties the same administration is being
carried out today by the Secretary of Trade and Industry as he carried out following the
introduction of the Stabilisation of Prices Regulations 1974, regulations that the member for
Manukau and his colleague the member for Mt. Albert brought into the House.
Mr Brill: Will the Minister confirm that in fixing the prices for category A goods the
practice of the secretary of the Commerce Commission has been to look at the actual value
of shareholders' funds and not the book value, and therefore the fluctuations in the book
value would not affect his assessment of the return on shareholders' funds?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, at actual value and historical value. Certainly
the revaluation of assets is deducted by the secretary in arriving at the profit which should
accrue to a company.
Hon. W. W. Freer: In view of the Minister's statement that exactly the same procedures
were being employed today as in the past, why has he varied the procedure so that an
investigation into a company's application for an increase is no longer heard by the
Commerce Commission in public?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: When the Commerce Act was amended last year
there was very little opposition by the Labour Party. The balance sheet of the company is
