Immigration Policies-National Party Manifesto
4. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Immigration, Can he advise the House
which policies on immigration included in the 1975 National Party manifesto have been
implemented so far?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): The National Party's election manifesto
contained several proposals for action on immigration policy, all but one of which have
already been implemented. First, for instance, we reduced the pressure on the economy
previously created by highly excessive immigration intakes. More recently we have increased
the size of our occupational lists so that it will be easier to recruit all the skilled migrants we
need while still keeping down the pressures which immigration exerts on the economy. The
work permit scheme has been revised and extended, and legislation has been passed which
enables the Minister of Immigration to order the deportation of persons who are convicted
of an offence committed within 2 years of arrival, for which the court has power to impose
imprisonment. Bona fide non-working visitors may enter New Zealand with a minimum of
immigration formalities for periods not exceeding 12 months. Special arrangements have
been made for visitors from the South Pacific. In addition, the Government has decided on a
number of policy changes which will streamline procedures and provide a better service.
Details of these changes will be announced in the near future. The only matter in the
manifesto which has not yet been implemented is the proposal that the residential qualifica-
tion for citizenship for non-British subjects be reduced from 5 years to 3 years. Provision for
this has been made in this year's legislative programme by the Minister of Internal Affairs.
Mr Malcolm: Have the changes which have been implemented as a result of that policy
made it easier for the Minister and for the department to administer a logical, sound, and
humane immigration policy?
Hon. T. F. GILL: There are still some gaps in what might be considered necessary, but
the machinery and procedures we have now are a vast improvement on anything we have
had before in this country.
Hon. F. M. Colman: To what extent has the policy outlined by the Minister as having
been implemented been responsible for the net outflow of 17 500 people from New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The questioner is under a slight misapprehension. We were talking
about immigration, not emigration. The Government does not put up any barriers—and as
Minister of Immigration nor do I-with the intention of stopping emigration by New
Zealand people who have a desire to emigrate. I presume that the member is referring to the
fact that 999 000 people came to New Zealand last year and 1 017 000 left, so there was a net
outflow of 17 000. Last year the outflow amounted to 10 000 New Zealanders; the year
before it was 9000. There have always been outflows in large numbers, as the statistics show
to anybody who cares to look at them. The member should address his question to the
overseas countries which attract immigrants from New Zealand. We have no emigration
policy.
Mr Talbot: What effect has the Government's successful immigration policy had on the
economy? Has it taken the heat off house prices and other costs?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Although the subject of the question does not fall within my
responsibility, I can say that the immigration policy has taken pressure off housing, health,

Deficit before Borrowing
6. Mr LUXTON (Piako): asked the Minister of Finance, Can he inform the House what
the deficit before borrowing was when expressed as a percentage of the net Government
expenditure for the 1972-73 financial year, the 1975-76 financial year, and the 1976-77
financial year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance): I reply on behalf of the
Minister of Finance. In 1972-73 the net Government expenditure was $2,219 million, and
revenue was $2,013 million, leaving a deficit of $206 million, or 9.3 percent. In 1975-76 the
net expenditure was $4,385.9 million, and revenue was $3,384.2 million, leaving a deficit of
$1,001.7 million, or 22.8 percent. In 1976-77 the net expenditure was $4,506 million, and
revenue was $3,999.9 million, leaving a deficit of $506.1 million, or 11.2 percent. In short,

WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Transferred on date shown
Securitibank Collapse
1. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Justice, Did the Prime
Minister confide in him in March 1976, that (as reported in the TV2 programme "Perspec-


## p. 268 (#276) ############################################

268
1 June
Questions and Replies
tives" on 3 May and in the New Zealand Herald of 4 May) he knew then the Securitibank
combine was financially shaky and that for more than a year before the collapse came he was
aware that professional people were advising against investing in it, and were there not
sufficient indications of instability before the crash to warrant his adopting the practice
followed by the Labour Administration in similar circumstances and appointing inspectors
under section 9A of the Companies Act 1955 to look into the affairs of one or more of the
associated companies and report to him?
Hon. D. S. THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, (1) I informed the Prime Minister
in March 1976 of the position of Securitibank in the light of advice I had received from the
commercial affairs division of my department. What the Prime Minister said during the TV2
"Perspective" broadcast on 3 May 1977 was as follows: "I know to my certain knowledge
that many professional people in Auckland were recommending clients and customers not to
invest in Securitibank for some considerable time before the collapse came. And I mean a
matter of a year or two, not just a few months. I knew that the company was in difficulty as
early as March of last year, but not at that time that any collapse was inevitable."; and (2)
Parliament has vested in the Registrar of Companies power to appoint inspectors under
section 9A of the Companies Act, and, as I understand it, the registrar could not be directed
by the political government to carry out any particular inspection. I consider the autonomy
thus given to the registrar to be wise and proper in the circumstances. Indeed, I am told that
no request to act under section 9A was made by the honourable member as Minister of
Justice, and his question therefore gives an altogether misleading impression. The registrar
decided in March 1976 not to order an inspection of the Securitibank companies under
section 9A, and he so informed me at the time. He was concerned that, with a company
operating as Securitibank did in the short-term money market, knowledge that inspectors
had been appointed and were at work could have brought the company down more surely
than the publication of rumours in the press. At the least it would have added to the
company's troubles and decreased the chance that the group would find a way through its
difficulties. This is an inherent problem in the early use of section 9A, and will disappear only
when we have a corps of inspectors adequate to make, and be known to make, random
checks on stable as well as shaky companies. That ideal situation certainly did not exist in
March 1976.

Coal Production
4. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines, Has he read the article
"Men of Energy-Ian Dick" in the New Zealand Energy Journal, December 1976, reprinted
in the autumn issue of New Zealand Coal, which states that, other than new mines under
construction at Huntly, "it will not be able to open any new underground mines before 1990
which would give a production date of 1994", and how does he reconcile it with his
statements in the same issue of New Zealand Coal that, "Coal is once again a valuable fuel,
and we are expected to turn on supplies overnight. Coal in New Zealand has a bright future,
but we are going to ensure that this is a planned and orderly future. . . ."?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, This question implies that there is some
inconsistency between these two statements, but that is not so. When the Secretary of Mines
said that his department would not be able to open any new underground mines before 1990,
he was speaking of large modern mines of the type of Huntly West. Mr Dick had in mind the
time required to develop the expertise necessary for the operation of a fully mechanised
mine producing up to 1 000 000 tonnes of coal a year. It is expected that by the mid 1980s we
should be ready to plan the next big mine at Huntly. None of this is inconsistent with my
statement that coal in New Zealand has a bright future, but that we are going to ensure that
it is a planned and orderly future. The Government took an important step last year in
planning this future, when it allocated $750,000 to extend the coal exploration programme
from Huntly to other parts of the country. Under the scheme, exploration has started into
the lignite deposits of Southland and of Charleston near Westport, and it will be extended to
other areas in the future. If the need arises, this work could lead quite soon to the
development of new mines, particularly opencast mines, in places other than Huntly.
(25/5/77)
Price Milburn
5. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Education, Can he confirm that the
publishing firm of Price Milburn, which is active in the field of educational publishing, has
been acquired by the primary teachers trade union, the NZEI, and, if so, can he give any
guarantee that in future decisions regarding the selection of standard texts in New Zealand
schools will be made without any political or financial bias?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education) replied, I am informed that the New
Zealand Educational Institute has acquired an interest in the publishing firm of Price
Milburn. I am also informed that Price Milburn will carry on under its present management.
Price Milburn publish almost exclusively for the lower classes of primary schools, where
anything that can be regarded as a standard text is provided by the school publications
branch of the Department of Education. Price Milburn readers are supplementary to official
texts and other publishers provide similar supplementary material. The choice as to which
supplementary reader shall be purchased rests with the individual school. The question also
asks if a guarantee can be given that standard texts will be selected without any political or
financial bias. In so far as Price Milburn publish supplementary material only, the fact that
the NZEI has an interest in the firm will have no effect on the selection of standard texts.

Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn): For the purpose of discussing ministerial replies to questions, I
move, That the House do now adjourn. I wish to refer to question 2, in which the member for
Mt. Albert asked the Prime Minister, “Will he, before he leaves for overseas, make a formal
statement to clarify the Government's present attitude on sporting contacts with South
Africa?" This was a sincere question asked on behalf of the Labour Party, which wanted to
prevent any further problems occurring at the Commonwealth Heads of Government
conference in London. The Prime Minister replied as follows: “The member is directed to
statements made in the National Party's official policy prior to the election, which reads:
'The National Party strongly believes in the responsibility and autonomy of sporting and
recreational bodies. Under a National Government there will be no political interference in
sport in any form. Sporting organisations will be free to associate with any sporting groups
from other countries, regardless of race, creed, or internal politics.'" This sounds all right as
far as it goes, but one could ask whether it was from the expurgated or unexpurgated version
of the National Party's election policy.
Let us look at statements made since the election. The Rt. Hon. Sir Keith Holyoake,
the Governor-General designate, when he was Minister of State visited the United Nations.
He spoke with the chairman of the special committee on apartheid, and met other officials.
When he came back to New Zealand he said that the Government would actively discourage
sporting bodies from going to South Africa. That was reported in the Waikato Times of 16
October 1976. Compare that statement with the Prime Minister's reply last week to the
question asked by the member for Mt. Albert. Then we come to the Deputy Prime Minister.
He visited Africa towards the end of last year and told the Africans that he would do what he
could to dissuade people from having further sporting associations with South Africa. This
was reported in the press on 10 November 1976. Recently the excellent rugby writer, T. P.
McLean, wrote in the New Zealand Herald that he had had a letter from Dr Abraham
Ordia, who had said that he had received a letter from the Prime Minister of New Zealand
and that as a result of that letter he would have recommended the lifting of the boycott
against New Zealand, but since he had received the letter conflicting statements emanating
from New Zealand had made him have another look at the position, and it had become
completely impossible for him to believe that what was said in the Prime Minister's letter was
correct.

should again demonstrate its effrontery by asking any question at all about sport when, as a
Government, it so vandalised the magnificence of sport and betrayed the sovereignty of New
Zealand and New Zealanders in its three brief years in office. That the Labour Government
did so in blatant repudiation of its pre-election policy on which so many of its members
campaigned in 1972 must surely place it in a position of complete disentitlement as the so-
called current champion of freedom. It was a party that earned the total alienation of the
sportsmen of New Zealand, first by its betrayal of the independence of sportsmen and then
by double standards in moral matters, for which the Labour Government became notorious
and by which it illuminated its arrogant contempt for the basic freedom of New Zealanders.
Today Opposition members scale the heights of rhetoric on a topic that has already led to
their downfall. The tortuous path of their morality is littered with their inconsistencies, their
appeasements, their surrenders, their manoeuvres, and their disavowals. If there is one thing
in which they are earnest—and in which their aspirations are fervent indeed—it is the frail
hope that the National Government might emulate them, and surrender to the same kind of
coercion and introduce the same kind of manipulation of sport as they did.
Labour began to use sport, I think quite deliberately, as one of its political tools when,
quite without pretensions of morality, it was seized by the tactic by which it thought it could
reinforce its designs against Taiwan and its romance with Communist China. It was then that
New Zealanders stood aghast as visas were withheld, for the first time in New Zealand's

history, from Taiwanese boy scouts, Taiwanese swimmers, and Taiwanese table tennis

Question 4 deals with coal and energy. Undoubtedly, some major steps have been
taken in the energy field in the last few weeks, with the combination of the departments of
mines, electricity, and energy resources. The Minister of Energy Resources has concentrated
on the future of coal, and the need to plan its use. At the moment the State coal mining
enterprise accounts for about 70 percent of all coal mined, and this percentage is increasing
as coal mining becomes more attractive as the price of oil increases relative to the price of
coal. At present, as most members know, the State coal mines are fully committed to
supplying existing consumers. Most of us know that the coal suppliers in our local towns are
hard pressed to keep up with the present demand. This implies that, if we have to divert coal
into other areas as a result of increased oil prices, the domestic consumer must suffer.
The use of coal is considered in terms of the lifetime of the operation rather than on a
demand basis. Consequently, a small generation project such as a thermal power station
would create a demand for 25 to 30 years. New Zealand Steel requires at least 20 000 000
to 40 000 000 tonnes over the next 30 to 50 years, and the cement industry requires about
25 000 000 tonnes over a 40 to 50 year period. If we are to convert more of our energy users
to coal we will require a change in the application of research now, because it will take 13
years to bring extra coalfields into production. Furthermore, the Ministry of Energy
Resources estimates that New Zealand has coal resources of possibly twice or three times
what has already been discovered, and that it would take about $35 million to assess those
resources if we had the manpower and skills available. About 30 percent of those resources
would have to be eliminated because of their location, not only on productive land that
cannot be disturbed, but also in urban areas. Because of the rapidly increasing demand,
proposals are afoot to bring private and State coal production into closer co-ordination. The
Ministry of Energy Resources is working on this at the moment. The first priority is to
discover the country's coal reserves; resources are being diverted to this and also to
considering the environmental implications of mining that coal. This will add greatly to the
cost of production of all qualities of coal, and will have to be considered when planning
energy resources over the next few years.

Companies was against action. The reason is very clear. If inspectors had been sent in, it
would have meant that notice of the difficulties would have been sprung on members of the
public and there would have been a collapse. The member opposite knows it far better than I
do; this is not my particular field of skill. It is important for the House and those not aware of
the details to know that this question is misleading. The Labour Administration had an
opportunity to move, but it did not.

Labour Party Conference-Democratic Socialism
Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel): I move, That this House notes how the Labour Party at its
annual conference tangled with its socialist heritage and philosophy and appeared to settle for
the new term "democratic socialism" as the ultimate; and that the House further notes that
later, after delegates were told that objectives were to destroy capitalism (which includes of
course home ownership), a resolution calling for the old Marxist creed was carried—a step
which the party leader later described as "a bloody great step backwards". What a shambles
that conference must have been. Do members opposite consider that that was really a step
backwards? Was it not really an admission of the truth of what the Labour Party stands for?
Was the conference not an admission of what the Labour Party stands for? This has been
going on all the time, particularly when we consider statements made by various members
and try to understand the philosophy of the Labour Party. Its philosophy or objectives have
always been the same-democratic socialism, nationalisation, or State control. They are all
the same, although the colour of the shirt may be different.
The records, as reported in Hansard, Volume 244, show that in April 1936 the former
member for Riccarton asked the then Prime Minister, "Is it the intention of the Government
to put into operation all the measures which have for their objectives the socialisation of the
means of production, distribution, and exchange which, it is understood, is the declared
policy of the Labour Party?" The then Prime Minister, Mr Savage, replied, "It is the
intention of the Government to carry out its policy as stated to the electors." Two or three
other former members of the Labour Party have made similar statements. The former
member for Manurewa, Mr Amos, stated at Taupo that people had been in the habit of
owning their own property, and that it was time they were educated otherwise. He said he
did not believe in home ownership and that he did not believe in private ownership. The
former members for Hamilton East and Taupo have made similar statements in the House,
and have said that they do not believe in ownership of land and that it should be owned by
the State. The member for Wanganui, who is still in the House, said in 1974, "Land surely
belongs ultimately to all of us. Each of us at best are only temporary stewards." He was
speaking about a suggestion mooted by an English group to nationalise all freehold
which would then be let out on 50-year or 99-year leases. He is another democratic socialist.
None of these people believes in private ownership; they all believe in State control. The
member for Grey Lynn, bench mate of the member for Wanganui, has said that the Labour
Party has not done enough in the past to bring the mainstream of the economy into public
ownership. It does not matter whether it is the Labour Party in Parliament, or the
Communist Party, which at every election tries to get into Parliament, or the Socialist Unity
Party, which stands behind it-they all have the same philosophy and outlook, and all
support democratic socialism. The only difference is that at its conference the Labour Party
openly admitted it. It must have been an awful blow to the Social Credit Party, because for
the last 2 or 3 years we have seen a growing courtship between the Social Credit Party and
property,

Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury): I move, That this House commend the Government

inflationary spiral, and congratulates the Minister of Finance on the third successive reduction

Labour Government, and further notes that the latest consumer price index figure for the quarter
ended March 1977 of 2.6 percent was almost half the 5 percent increase predicted for this period
by the Leader of the Opposition, a one-time Minister of Finance in this country. In the short
time since the session commenced we have heard a lot of high words from Opposition
members about their concern for people. In 1975 the people of New Zealand voted for
realism in the economy. They knew full well that the family life spoken of so proudly by the

strong and sound? It amazes me to hear members talking about the Third World. They are

cost of living increased by 40 percent-that was the legacy of socialism, democratic

3 years to tidy up the mess. Already, at the end of the March quarter of 1977, we have seen

4.1 percent. It increased in the next two quarters, but since then it has been coming down
dramatically. The National Government pledged itself to a reduction in that rate of inflation.
The rate may increase temporarily from time to time, but under National's economic policies

restored to private industry so that jobs will be available, and local production will be
encouraged. The recent reduction in the rate of inflation can be attributed to good economic
management, the tightening of monetary conditions, a sharp reduction in the deficit before
borrowing, and the rate of increase in wages. We have had the sound policy that the people
have been looking for. Look at some of the policies that have assisted in achieving an

export receipts minus import payments-for the year ending June 1977 is expected to be in

help the farmers-were increased from $18 million to $28.5 million, much more than 50

to meet. I wonder if the member for South Canterbury wants credit for that? If he does, he
will pay a much higher interest. By all means let us have a look at the record of this
Government compared with some others.

Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone): I move, That this House notes with alarm that after 18

problems that the Government should be grappling with. All we have had is indecision and
drifting. There have been two Ministers, but still no energy policy has been produced, and
the Government intends to throw that vital question over to the public, hoping people will
come up with some ideas. I have no quarrel with that. I welcome the public's being involved
in an energy policy.

proposition made by the Clutha Action Committee-comprising environmental groups
concerned with the power scheme for the Clutha River—that it should be involved in the

meaningless words from Government members. They will involve the people if they think
things are going right for the Government, but if there is to be a difficult decision the
Government's decision is absolute. How serious is the Government about involving the
people in its energy policy? The formation of an energy policy is drifting, and is in limbo.

decision.

I turn now to the nationalisation of the greater Wellington region. Before doing so I
make it clear that I do not use the word "region" in a local authority sense, because no such
region exists. In last year's Address in Reply debate I pointed out that the Labour

implementing that clear consensus.
The status and development of the Wellington area gives rise to continuing cause for
concern. Much has been made of the need to stimulate regions such as the West Coast,

figure from Wellington City to cover the four employment districts which make up the
Wellington area, employment in the surveyed industries fell by 3984 over 12 months, a drop
of 2.9 percent, and the greatest fall in New Zealand. During the same period employment

To date in this debate we have had a lot of conjecture on two topics in particular, and I
should like to point most of my remarks this evening in their direction. The first is housing,

second principle was the goal of individual home ownership, and a third was the employment
of resources to the best advantage. Overriding each of these three principles was the
principle of stability, so that the demands placed on housing avoided excessive peaks and
hollows. Adequate housing is not measured solely by permits and completions, as the
Opposition would have us believe. The important economic element is demand. We have a
low birth rate. We have a net migration loss which, on a ratio of 3.57 persons per dwelling,
has freed 4760 homes for purchase. We may not like the figures, but they are realistic. The
alternative is the large number of new and unsold homes—the cry of our master builder
friends in 1974.

Auckland Master Builders' housing group, Mr Williams, said in the New Zealand Herald of

rises. Naturally, these will cause increases, but it is interesting to note that in the years 1972-

for the higher end of the market, the average area of new units has increased, and at the
same time tighter market and price restraints during 1976 have slowed the rate of increase in
building costs. In March Mr Williams said there was no money available in the private
mortgage market, that there was little or no growth in savings deposits, and suggested that
interest rates for second mortgages were about 18 percent. He poured scorn on the fact that
new mortgage guarantees operated where interest rates were no more than 10 percent on

members, to the April 1977 Reserve Bank Bulletin, page 133, where the latest figures are
those for December 1976. They show that the average interest rate for new mortgages
registered is 10.04 percent. They show that, of a total of $96.2 million in newly registered
mortgages in December, $58 million were at less than 10.5 percent, which included $5
million at less than 5 percent.
Mr Williams complains in the same breath of high interest rates and of little growth in
savings deposits. He surely cannot fail to realise that he can borrow only savings. It is a
classical chicken-and-egg position. We cannot attract savings without realistic interest rates
to offer to depositors, and we cannot lend at less than the borrowing rate plus the bank fee. I
return to the December figures in the Reserve Bank Bulletin, which show, for the year ended

Deputy Leader of the Opposition said: "Most of the major economies nevertheless chose the

cally, we have been living in a fool's paradise. In relation to our gross national product prices

prices of exports in relation to our gross national product are falling. No longer are we living
in the 1960s, when we could tighten the belt and then release it. Now we are in a new ball

only are we spending millions of dollars we have not yet earned, but we do not know what we
are importing, from whom we are importing, when we are committed to pay for the goods,
nor even how much we are committed to pay. This area is overdue for supervision, and until
we discipline ourselves the trade gap will not be rectified. It is apparent that, while increased
markets and increased prices may go some of the way, it is sensible to cut our cloth properly
and to reduce imports-perhaps even to stop them, in some goods. I know that this is heresy
when one thinks of international agreements such as GATT, but I would ask the House
whether the Australians, the Japanese, or the member countries of the EEC have any
conscience when those agreements work to their advantage, but not to ours.
The point I want to make very clearly is that a good trader must be able to buy wisely, as
well as to sell; in fact, that is his essential ability. That is the first lesson to learn if we are ever
to become the great trading nation that we, perhaps fondly, imagine ourselves to be. So it is
obvious that industrial exports are vital, at least in the short term; if that is so, the role of the
unions is also vital. I ask the House tonight: what have the unions ever done to promote
exporting for New Zealand? Perhaps this is their greatest challenge-the role they can take
on in the future, the contribution they can make to New Zealand. If they do that, we will all
be proud of them. But not only the unions are involved. The size of New Zealand's trade
deficit tells us all clearly that we must reduce our spending, and perhaps even our standard of
living.
Is there an even greater problem? Let us ask ourselves that. Has our top-heavy society,
overloaded by welfare, the give-aways we all subscribe to, and non-productive services, no
longer got the earning capacity to continue? How big a burden can a social welfare State
carry? Are we leaning too much on the taxpayer? He is the only source, whether he be the
wage earner, the salary earner, the self-employed, the professional man, or the company. If
we want to pay out more, we must tax more; it is as simple as that. I believe that the only real
answer is productivity, and a wage system based on productivity and not on automatic
indexation. Until we adopt a system along those lines we will not solve the real problem of
inflation. That is what it is all about. I quote again a statement made by F. P. Walsh in 1948:
"We must not lose sight of the fact that the forces that brought about the chaotic conditions
of boom and slump after the last war are present in the New Zealand economy today. The
only solution to our problem is increased production. I must stress again the point that if we
are to have higher standards of living we must have more goods and services. Our movement
is no longer just fighting for wages. We want to increase actual standards of living. To do this
we must increase production. Real standards come from production, not from the printing of
a note issue." That was F. P. Walsh in 1948. So production is what all New Zealanders
should be thinking about.
But hand in hand with that increase in production, which we all want and which I hope
we can all achieve, we must consider taxation, because taxation at too high a level, whether
it be company tax or personal tax, is a positive disincentive to New Zealand's future. It
encourages industrial discontent in itself, and it discourages investment-there is no point in
investing if you do not have the money to back up that investment. In the long run fewer jobs
will be created. Perhaps more important is this question: is the principle of pushing for more
exports to gain more Government income to pay more handouts really what we want? Is a
welfare State possible, if the demands are too high and the contributions limited? I remind
members that the more dependants we create, whether they be students or superannuitants,

the fewer contributors we will have; not that we should deny the aged-no way at all; not
that we should deny the handicapped; not that we should deny our youth their fair due. But I

socialist system, which the Labour Party has adopted in strength recently, they have lost the

of life-capitalism pays for socialism. Socialism can never pay for itself. I go further and say

and some managements would rather die than sit down at a works council meeting. They
probably will die, in an economic sense.
Who, then, pays the piper? The Prime Minister has often said that there is no such thing
as a free lunch, it is the consumer who pays. The Government's responsibility is the
protection of the public. But I believe our Governments have overdone the protection.
There are decades of Government measures that control individual development in New
Zealand. We have the 40-hour trading measure, which not only restricts people to working
40 hours a week but states that you cannot open your shop and sell the guy down the road a
toothbrush, and if you sell a toothbrush you cannot sell toothpaste. We have import
licensing, which controls many items but does not control the importation of alcohol. There
are other sides to licensing-the service stations, the duty free shops, and the taxis. The
Government licenses these businesses. You name it, we license it. I wonder where we will
end up? Town planning has done nothing but add extra costs when people want to build
themselves a home. We have health regulations, and I suppose one could say that these
measures have a good effect and were made with good intentions, but I wonder what their
overall result is. Today, transport is in a mess, and my sympathy goes to the Minister who is
trying to sort out air, road, railway, and shipping transport. The Ports Authority, for
instance, would be better off playing marbles. Price controls, introduced by the Labour
Government, have now turned into vicious profit control. Today many companies show
returns of under 5 percent on their shareholders' funds. A person can earn more in a savings
bank. That is a positive disincentive to the future. That is another problem the National
Government must solve, and it will.
We must think very seriously about what we should do for the future. I believe there
should be a two-pronged attack. First, we must return freedom and competition to the
business people without the stupid bureaucratic restrictions that have been put on them.
Secondly, we must have common sense and co-operation between union and management so
that they share their knowledge by talking to each other, because it is their responsibility,
not the Government's, to plan for the future. I have said before, and I shall say again, that
even in a world of automation the person who pushes the button is the most important asset

54 percent. How could a young couple save for a house in those circumstances? Under the


## p. 312 (#320) ############################################

312
1 June
Address in Reply
National Government section prices went up 9.3 percent in 1 year. There was a 27 percent
per annum increase in house prices in the Labour Government's 3 years in office. Under
National it was 6.4 percent. The National Government is having a series of achievements in
housing, and I should like to go through some of them. As the Minister of Housing told me
in answer to a question recently, there has been a satisfactory move right through the
Government's list of housing promises. There is one point that the Minister did not make,
but which I should like to make now. National built over 800 pensioner units last year.
Labour built 618 in 1974, and 700 in 1975. I should also like to refer to the number of houses
started each month: in January 1976, 1500 houses were started; in January 1977, 1500 were
started. Stability, a rare word under the Labour Government, is returning to the building
industry. In February 1976, 2200 houses were started; in February 1977, 2400 were started.
For March 1976 and March 1977, the figures were 2300 and 2600 respectively. That gives a
total of 6000 starts in 1976, and 6500 in 1977. If we look at the number of permits issued, we
see for the first time a graph of commencements and permits that starts to represent a graph
of real stability in the building industry. The real success of the Government's housing policy
can be seen in the number of houses available for occupation. This must be related to the
Government's immigration policy because, although the Labour Government built 31 000
houses in 1974, it also allowed a net inflow of immigrants of 33 576. That meant that the
number of houses available to New Zealanders was about 22 000. Last year, 28 300 were
built, and because of the Government's immigration policy, 33 100 were available for New
Zealanders to occupy.
I should like to pay tribute to the Minister of Immigration, and his division, for the way
in which he has settled down the very unsettled immigration policy inherited from the
previous Administration. He has achieved stability, and that has enabled the administration
of a humane and realistic policy. On the news tonight there was an item that I think is worthy
of mention. The Maguires have arrived in New Zealand. The Government's intention was
not to make their arrival time public, because it believed that the family deserved some
privacy. However, word got out and the news media were there to greet them. I think I
speak on behalf of all New Zealanders when I say to the Maguires, "Welcome. You will find
yourselves in a country with a great deal of love and a great deal of acceptance of people
from other cultures." That is a good example of the humanity that has been exhibited by the
Minister of Immigration. As the member for Eden, handling a lot of immigration problems,
I find the same humanity, care, and concern exercised daily with every representation I
make to the Minister. That care and concern are what this country is all about. This country
is more about care and concern for others than it is about the divisive tactics and the false
idols of the Labour Party, which seeks to re-achieve the Government benches by division, by
emphasising class differences, by emphasising race differences, and by driving wedges
between a society which in its very heart wants to work and live together.

Ministry of Energy Resources Consultation with PSA
2. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Minister of Energy Resources, Would he inform
the House, following his announcement of the merger of the New Zealand Electricity
Department, the Mines Department, and the Ministry of Energy Resources, what was done
to ensure the best public and industrial relations, and what consultation, if any, took place
between him and the 8000 or so affected employees or their representative, the Public
Service Association?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): When the decision was made to form
a single energy department which the Government has now decided to call the Ministry of
Energy I immediately saw the permanent heads of the three departments directly concerned
and informed them of the decision. I also sent telegrams to over 100 people responsible for
important activities including production, distribution, retail sale, and union representation.
These actions were taken before the announcement was made to the press, radio, and
television. I discussed the decision with the media representatives immediately after the
release of my press statement. The discussions leading up to the decision did include a
number of senior departmental officials, including the heads of the three departments
directly concerned, but did not include officials from unions representing the employees in
the three departments affected by the Government's decision. Their members' salaries and
conditions of service will remain unchanged. They were employees of Government depart-
ments before the decision and they will still be employees of a Government department
when the decision is implemented shortly. There will be no need for changes in union
representation, and the existing channels of communication and negotiation can be
continued and developed in the same ways as hitherto.

Computers-Filing Systems Benefits
9. Mr ALLEN (Tauranga) asked the Prime Minister, Has any evidence been presented
to him tending to show that information filed with a computer is any more liable to illegal
access than information in other filing systems, and what are the benefits of computer
filings?

information filed within the computer is any more liable to illegal access than information in
other filing systems. On the contrary, the security built into computer systems, and the
restrictions placed on access to information on the computer, are far more stringent than
ordinarily apply to manual systems. Some of the benefits of computer filing are of course
quicker access to more accurate up-to-date information; specific data can be extracted
quickly; and statistical and management information, which would not normally be readily
available, can be provided.

EVIDENCE AMENDMENT BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Evidence Amendment Bill. The committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
This Bill was introduced in August last, and at the request of the select committee was held
over for consideration during the recess. The committee received 17 submissions, the
majority of which were in support of the Bill's principal intent—that is, to afford some
protection to a complainant giving evidence at a hearing on a charge of rape. All submissions
offered criticism and in some cases quite considerable criticism of the way in which the
original Bill sought to achieve that end. The committee has accepted the basic principle of


## p. 323 (#331) ############################################

2 June
323
Evidence Amendment Bill
the Bill, but recommends a change in the method by which its purpose should be achieved.
The Bill will insert a new section 23A in the Evidence Act 1908. The effect of this will be
to require that in any criminal proceeding in which a person is charged with a rape offence,
or is to be sentenced for a rape offence, no evidence should be given and no questions put to
a witness relating to either the sexual experience of the complainant—that is, the woman
who alleges she has been raped-with any person other than the accused, or the reputation
of the complainant in sexual matters, except with the permission of the trial judge. The new
section sets out the circumstances under which the judge would grant such permission.
Basically he must be satisfied that the evidence to be given, or the question to be put, is of
such direct relevance either to the facts in issue in the proceeding or to the issue of the
appropriate sentence to be imposed that to exclude it would be contrary to the interests of
justice. The new section 23A goes on to provide that where the judge has given permission
for evidence of this nature to be placed before the court it shall not be necessary to obtain
further permission to produce evidence in rebuttal of those matters. The section also makes
special provision for the situation that arises where a person is charged as a party to an
offence of rape. The committee also believes that it is necessary to provide some general
guidelines in the section as to the procedure to be followed where a request for leave to
produce such evidence is made. This is done in the proposed subsection (6) of section 23A.
It is further proposed that the Act should come into force one month from the date on
which it receives the Governor-General's assent, but that in any case in respect of which an
information has been laid before that date the case should be dealt with under the previously
existing rules of evidence. In its original form the Bill also proposed to insert a section 23B
into the Evidence Act, which would have afforded a person accused of rape some protection
when cross-examined about his character. This proposal was almost unanimously rejected by
those who made submissions to the select committee, the view being that sufficient
protection was already available under the existing law. Accordingly, the committee
recommends that that proposed section should be deleted from the Bill.
On behalf of the committee I should like to express thanks to those persons and
organisations who made submissions, particularly the New Zealand Law Society and the
Criminal Law Reform Committee, which gave support to the concept of the Bill, although
both in turn offered considerable comment and criticism on the Bill's original form. I should
also like to record the committee's appreciation of the assistance given to it by the officials of
the Department of Justice, Mrs Lowe and Mr David, and also the drafting assistance given
by Mr McVeagh, the parliamentary counsel. I understand that at a later stage the Minister of
Justice will be giving formal indication of his intention to adopt the Bill as a Government
measure. Having delivered the committee's formal report, I would like, as the member who
introduced the Bill, to express my appreciation also to those people who assisted the
committee. I believe that they and the select committee have helped to produce a fair and
practical piece of law reform. I should also like to thank the Minister of Justice for his
continuing support in my initial research, and for his support and the support of my
colleagues in the introduction of this private member's Bill. Although a similar measure
including similar amendments was introduced and passed as a private member's Bill in the
United Kingdom, I fully appreciate the New Zealand parliamentary convention that prefers
that such a Bill, if it is to be passed at all, should be passed as a Government measure.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I should like, with absolutely no denigration
whatsoever to the member for Birkenhead, to tell the House that the only part of the private
member's Bill he introduced that remains unchanged is the long title. Having said that, I
want to say that the member is entitled to every credit and congratulation for the
achievement that has resulted from his earnest endeavour in bringing forward a meritorious
Bill, which even if changed textually to a very great degree remains unchanged in the
objective it sought to attain. It is unusual for a private member to succeed in legislating, even
if he is helped over some of the procedural hurdles by having the Bill adopted by the
Government and given official sponsorship. To attain that, success depends on three main
aspects: first, the choice of topic, and this is undoubtedly important; secondly, the perti-
nancy of the member concerned; and, thirdly, the coincidence of timing. I suppose you could
call that an element of luck, and no doubt there is some aspect of luck associated in hitting
the jackpot, if I may so call it, as has happened on this occasion.
The timing that prompted the honourable member to introduce this measure was the
notorious Morgan case in England not so very long ago. That was horrific enough in its facts
and aroused a good deal of public uproar, but only a brief examination was required to show
that it broke little if any new ground of legal principle. However, the outcry was sufficient to
11


## p. 324 (#332) ############################################

2 June
Evidence Amendment Bill
prompt the British Government to set up a commission of inquiry under the chairmanship of
Mrs Justice Heilbron. Very shortly after it had embarked on its inquiries the commission was
able to dispose of any problem that arose directly out of the effects of the Morgan case, and
passed on to wider issues. The result of this was the Sexual Offences Bill, later introduced
into Parliament. Many other law reform organisations were prompted to give attention to
the same problem and most of them took the point of their departure from the Heilbron
committee report. They were mostly united in deciding that the inquiry had been too hasty
and too superficial in its studies and remedies, no doubt because of the need to allay the
public alarm that had resulted from the Morgan case.
Amongst the spate of further reports that we ourselves considered in New Zealand were
the report of the Victorian Law Reform Commissioner, a single individual, Mr Smith, whose
report was, in my judgment, the best and most penetrating of them all; the report of the
Tasmanian Law Reform Committee; the South Australian special report on rape and other
sexual offences; and the Evidence Amendment Act that was ultimately passed in that
jurisdiction. It should be noted that quite a number of those inquiries were entitled,
"evidence amendment", or "an inquiry into the crime of rape", but were as to rape and
other sexual offences. That leads me to proffer my own initial reaction to the Morgan
incident, which was that originally I preferred the wider context of rape and sexual offence,
and this was reinforced by the knowledge that our own Criminal Law Reform Committee
was working on such topics at the time of the Morgan case. This included, and for my part
certainly ought to have included, a consideration of the important question of rape in a
matrimonial setting. At present, apart from isolated exceptions of women who are legally
separated from their husbands, it is not possible, whatever may be the circumstances, for the
crime of rape to be committed by a husband on a wife. In fact, there are some matrimonial
rapes-and I know the member for Raglan strongly supports this view. Although it is by no
means easy to frame a legal prescription or a set of legal requirements that would
appropriately deal with such a situation, it is one that ought to be given thought at an early
date. We commissioned a special report from our own Criminal Law Reform Committee on
this subject and I commend its members for what they did. It was done promptly, under
considerable pressure, and with admirable results. I do not think the occasion calls for me to
say any more about the merits of the problem, and I await further debate, with this forecast
—that the discussion will be equally divided between emotional generalities and a meticul-
ous and detailed examination of the legal consequences of the language currently incorpo-
rated in the Bill. When I say that, I mean not only the words and phrases, but even the
punctuation marks.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I confirm what the member for
Birkenhead, the author of the Bill, has told the House-that the Government will be very
glad to adopt his Bill as a Government measure. I shall send the appropriate letter to the
Clerk of the House as soon as we have been able to find a precedent for its wording. It is very
rarely that an honourable member succeeds in introducing a private member's Bill and
bringing it to the stage where the Government of the day agrees to sponsor it through its
remaining stages.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: It has found great attractiveness in the House of Commons.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: There is a great attractiveness, and I think all of us on the
select committee were attracted to the practice of the House of Commons where, when an
honourable and learned member decides it is time to suggest an amendment to the criminal
law, he does get more opportunity than we have here to take it right through. However, it
has been our practice, on the rare occasions when this happens, for the Government of the
day to give its imprimatur to the measure. We will be doing that. We had the great
advantage, as indicated by the member for Henderson, of not being the first in this field. So
often in law reform we take pleasure in being the first in the common law jurisdictions to
make changes, as we did in the mistakes in contract recently. In this case, we had the
advantage of seeing what other jurisdictions had done in their relevant statutory provisions.
It is not an easy subject, because one must not prejudice a just trial of the accused; yet, at the
same time, everybody wants to limit as much as possible the embarrassment to the
complainant, who is an essential part of the proceedings. I believe the Bill will be widely
welcomed, not merely by women, but by everybody who wants to see justice done in our
courts-but not at the expense of victims of rape. I join with others in thanking the Criminal
Law Reform Committee-which, of course, is chaired by the Solicitor-General, and which is
distinguished by the tremendous amount of work it does-and also officers of the Depart-
ment of Justice. I congratulate the member for Birkenhead on his resounding success.

Insurance Law Reform Bill
INSURANCE LAW REFORM BILL
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Insurance Law Reform Bill. Th. committee recommends
that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table.
The Bill was based on a report of the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee. It
was introduced at the end of the last parliamentary session, and referred to the select
committee for consideration. It received 13 submissions, and, with the exception of those
from various individuals, companies, and organisations within the insurance industry, the
Bill was generally, and in some cases enthusiastically, supported by those who made
submissions-notably, Federated Farmers, the Consumer Institute, and the New Zealand
Law Society. The opposition from insurance interests centred on three of the five reforms
proposed in the Bill. It is appropriate that I should explain briefly each of those reforms, the
reasons for the opposition to them, and the committee's recommendations in respect of each
of them.
At present, if an insured makes an error in completing an insurance policy, whether that
error be innocent or deliberate and whether it be material or immaterial, the insurer can
theoretically use that error to avoid liability under a life policy. Clause 4 of the Bill proposes
to limit the grounds on which the insurer can use such a misstatement to avoid a policy to
such misstatements as are first, material, and, secondly, made either fraudulently or within 3
years immediately preceding the death of the insured. Under clause 6 of the Bill, materiality
is defined as that which would have "influenced the judgment of a prudent insurer in fixing
the premium, or in determining whether he would have taken or continued the risk on
substantially the same terms". Two principal arguments were argued against this clause. It
was suggested, first, that it would enable a person to benefit from his or her own fraud. It
was the opinion of the committee that this contention resulted from a misunderstanding of
the words “material” and “fraudulent”. As I indicated, “material” is defined in the Bill, and
the committee recommends the addition of a further subclause to define "fraud" as well.
This should overcome the apparent misunderstanding of those who opposed the clause on
this ground.
Further, it was suggested that the very existence of this provision would encourage
people to believe that they could get away with making fraudulent misstatements in an
insurance proposal. The terms of the Bill make it quite clear that that would not be the case,
but even if it were so the committee is not satisfied as to the logic of this objection. Secondly,
most insurance proposals and policies at present provide that for the purpose of negotiating
an insurance policy the insurance company's agent, even though he may be employed and
paid by the company, is deemed to be the agent of the insured. Thus, a person who is
proposing for an insurance policy could, for example, be legally responsible for the fact that
the company's agent, either deliberately or inadvertently, omitted relevant information from
the proposal. The law reform committee considered that this "legal fiction" created by the
insurance companies was unfair and should be abolished, and this is done in clause 10. It was
argued before the committee that this reform was unfair, in that it could make an insurance
company liable for any action or alleged action of any employee of the company. The
committee recommends that clause 10(1) of the Bill be redrafted so that it applies only to the
actions of a representative of the company who is actively involved in the negotiation of an
insurance policy. The select committee was also of the opinion that this rule should not apply
to anyone who acts in the capacity of an insurance broker. That view had also been taken by
the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee; but, like that committee, we were
unable to arrive at an acceptable definition of the term "broker". In any event, we believe
that the provisions of clause 10(3) of the bill are sufficient to exclude any genuine broker.
The third provision that provoked considerable opposition was that which makes the
provisions of the Bill retrospective, to cover all life policies entered into before the Act
comes into force. Separate provision is made in respect of other types of policy that operate
on an annual basis, and insurance interests argued that even if the reforms contained in the
Bill were to be applied to all future policies it was unfair to bind them retrospectively in
respect of policies which might have been entered into many years ago. On the other hand, it
should be noted that the New Zealand Law Society, which normally makes a strong
objection at least in principle to retrospective legislation, took no exception to this particular
clause, and the law reform committee had unanimously recommended that the provisions of
the Bill should be made retrospective. The select committee takes the view that if Parliament
has determined that the present law is unfair and should be changed it would be wrong to
apply the old law to policies that had been entered into perhaps 12 months ago, but which
might not become the subject of a dispute for, say, 30 years. The Bill makes two other


## p. 326 (#334) ############################################

326
2 June
Insurance Law Reform Bill
reforms to insurance law. First, it provides for an adjustment of moneys where there has
been an error of age in a life insurance proposal. Secondly, it provides that the arbitration
clause found in most insurance policies is not binding on an insured, and that all court actions
arising out of an insurance policy shall be determined before a judge alone.
At the commencement of this report I noted that the sole opposition to the law reform
committee's report came from various insurance interests. In rejecting each one of the
objections the committee would not want it to be inferred that any of the insurers who raised
the objections would themselves take advantage of the somewhat questionable practices that
will be abolished by the Bill. On the contrary, we were assured by those insurance
companies and we accept that they follow as a matter of policy most of the provisions of
the Bill, in any event. On that basis alone we concluded that no reputable insurance
company has anything to fear from the provisions of this Bill.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): This is a very good example of how law reform
reports should be translated into legislation. I would that all the reports that have been made
had secured the same fate that has befallen this one. This is a fairly recent report, presented
to me in July and then welcomed by me in general terms. Unhappily, there are many much
older reports gathering moss on departmental or parliamentary counsel shelves, not due to
any lack of interest by those people in them but simply owing to the inability of successive
Governments to find parliamentary time for them, which is not an easy thing to do. In a non-
partisan sense, I wish the present Administration well in its endeavours to find an approp-
riate amount of time for these things.
Hon. David Thomson: The member will be gratified.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY: Good. As usual, the report was accompanied by a draft Bill,
and I want to take this opportunity of saying briefly a word or two to dispel the notion that all
Parliament does and all the Statutes Revision Committee does when a Bill or a report is
referred to them is to act to it as a rubber stamp and simply endorse the Bill as prepared by
the very learned and energetic members of the law reform committee who do half of our
work for us by preparing the Bill. That is not the entire work. It is the responsibility of
parliamentary counsel to consider its draftsmanship and of parliament to exercise its proper
role by giving full consideration to the legislation before passing it.
As the member for Birkenhead has said, the Statutes Revision Committee received 13
detailed and intensively argued submissions, which reflected very sharply opposing points of
view. In large part, the arguments contained in them had already been canvassed and
considered by the Contracts and Commercial Law Reform Committee, but they were again
reviewed by us and I am bound to say that some changes were made. Fortunately we were
able to have the proposals that we sought to have added to the draft Bill of the committee
reconsidered-and I say "fortunately" because none of the law reform committees meets on
a regular or scheduled basis. They come together whenever the other commitments of the
members—and these are heavy-permit them to do so. It so happened that, I think during
the week we concluded our preliminary considerations, the committee did meet and the
parliamentary counsel who assisted us and who was a member of that committee was able to
have a further discussion with the committee. Perhaps I might say as an aside that the
proposal has been made on more than one occasion that when law revision Bills emanating
from a committee of that nature are being considered by the Statutes Revision Committee it
would be appropriate for a member of that law reform committee, presumably the chairman,
to be in attendance to discuss the recommendations made by the committee, what led it to
the recommendations, and whether or not we should prudently embark on any further
changes. I have ruled against that, not just because it would be a breach of our Standing
Orders to have a "stranger" present during our deliberations, but also because I think it
would be an invasion of our proper legislative and parliamentary responsibilities. However, I
shall say no more on that aspect.
I wish to deal with only one other point, and that is to say that I do not agree with one
recommendation of the committee-clearly only a majority recommendation-incorporated
in the Bill. That recommendation is referred to in paragraph 20 of the law reform
committee's report, which reads as follows: "The committee remains of the view that it is
desirable for there to be a degree of uniformity concerning arbitration clauses, but recog-
nises that many insurers believe disputes between an insurer and an insured will not fairly be
resolved if determined by a jury. Although some members do not fully endorse this view, we
consider that it would be reasonable for the provision in the draft Bill that arbitration clauses


## p. 327 (#335) ############################################

2 June
327
Insurance Law Reform Bill
shall not bind the insured to be amended to provide that resultant claims between the
insured and the insurer are to be heard before a magistrate or, if in the Supreme Court,
before a judge alone." It seems that the elimination of the jury was to be regarded as a kind
of quid pro quo for the withdrawal of arbitration rights that are found almost universally in
insurance policies. I think that belief is based on two fallacies. The first is related to the
experience of insurance companies with civil litigation arising out of personal accident
claims. It is undeniably true that the knowledge that a defendant in such a claim was insured
was prejudicial to the interests of the defendant and of the insurance company that stood
behind him. For that reason there was a rigid rule that the fact that a defendant was insured
must never be mentioned, and any breach of that rule resulted in a mistrial and the whole
proceedings being re-opened.
I believe there is absolutely no certainty that this attitude flows over to a claim against
an insurance company itself, and whatever prejudice there may have been that a jury could
be affected by the knowledge that a man suffering injuries as a result of a motorcar accident
or, more importantly, an industrial accident had an insurance company behind him, has no
real relevance to other proceedings. By virtue of the fact that insurance is compulsory in
motor car accidents and, indeed, in industrial accidents, it was largely a fiction that one was
precluded from telling the jury explicitly that a man was insured, and it was common
knowledge to juries that a verdict that they gave against a defendant would not be met by the
individual but by some insurance company. I think it is simply a kind of article of faith that
insurance companies have that they are discriminated against by a jury, and it is just
unreasoned and unreasonable prejudice that maintains that attitude in a claim against an
insurance company itself. I think that argument in support of eliminating juries can be
disposed of.
The other is that most disputed claims arising out of a rejection of a liability by an
insurance company on a claim against it turn not on points of law but on the facts at issue in
the case. This is traditionally within the province of a jury and I see no reason for departing
from our historical view that questions of fact should properly come before a jury rather than
go to a judge. I must disagree with this recommendation of the committee and I shall oppose
it at later stages of proceedings.

practised in the courts in accident claims and the like-that once it has become known to the
jury that the defendant is insured, it will be far more inclined to grant a larger sum to a
plaintiff as a consequence. That has become so much ingrained as the viewpoint of the
profession that it has now become a provision of law that the jury shall not be told and shall
not be permitted to discover that one or other of the parties is working through an insurance

LEGISLATURE AMENDMENT BILL
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): I move, That the Legislature
Amendment Bill be introduced. The purpose of the Bill is to remove some of the doubts and
anomalies that have existed, and to facilitate the conduct of the business of the House. The
Bill has two primary objectives: to give statutory sanction to the practice of carrying business
over from one session to the next-which is a practice of doubtful legality, as has been
pointed out on a number of occasions—and to enable select committees to function as select
committees between the dissolution of one Parliament and the meeting of the next.
Provision is also made for newly elected members who have not been sworn to take part in
those select committees without being in breach of the law.
Mr Hunt: That vindicates the point made by the member for Porirua last year that Mr
Speaker ruled out.
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS: We are removing any doubt. I do not think there is any
doubt in terms of the practice of the House, but there can be doubt in terms of the law; and
the Bill will set the matter right.
Rt. Hon. W. E. ROWLING (Leader of the Opposition): There can be very little quarrel
with the Bill. The practice of carrying legislation forward was introduced a few years ago,
and has proved eminently satisfactory. The old practice of legislation dying at the end of a
session was not a good one, because a great deal of time was wasted when the legislation was
reintroduced the following year. Any doubts on the legality of the process that we have
adopted for the last few years should be set aside by this legislation. The legality of newly
elected members participating in select committees has been doubtful, and this legislation
will clear that up. Those doubts could have been overcome to a large extent by calling
Parliament together at a much earlier date. Under the Labour Government there was no
difficulty, because the first work of Parliament was carried out by Parliament, and not by
select committees. The newly constituted Parliament was called together at an early date,
the members were sworn, and Parliament carried out all its duties with complete legality. I
am concerned that this legislation is giving the present Administration a further out for the
late calling together of Parliament, not just in the post-election year but throughout its term.
I do not think anybody will be particularly happy about that, because it inevitably leads to an
end-of-session rush, too much government by Cabinet, and an uneven work load on all

Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): We seem to be
getting into a fantastic position. The Acting Prime Minister has said that there is no hurry for
this legislation. It is not a matter for the Executive or for Cabinet. The member for Porirua

see and study. The Bill will have a second reading, and if at that stage it is considered
necessary or desirable for the Bill to be considered by a select committee it will be so
referred. When I first came into the House just over 19 years ago many Bills were
introduced, read a second time, and then referred to a select committee-and that procedure
proved very satisfactory. In those days, as now, the select committees had a great deal of
work before them at the beginning of a session, and it was appropriate for a Bill to be
introduced and left on the table for a month before being read a second time. If it was then
felt desirable to send the Bill to a select committee-and at that stage much of the committee
work would already have been completed,—that is what happened.
I am amazed at the attitude of the member for Henderson. I well remember a Bill for
which he was responsible as Minister of Justice, the Motor Vehicle Dealers Bill, which ran
around the traps for more than a year before being placed on the table of the House. Copies
were distributed throughout the trade and the industry, and many interested people
approached members of the then Opposition asking about the Bill. On the first occasion I
was approached I said, "What on earth are you talking about? What Bill?". After some
months we learned that a large Bill had been circulating around the traps for a year. We do
not intend to follow that procedure with this Bill. We intend to introduce the Bill, and at that
point it will be laid on the table and made available for all to see. The large piece of
legislation the member for Henderson allowed to float around for a year was a good
measure.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: And constitutional too.
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: Yes, it was constitutional when it finally came into

committee, but it was found that it did not require a great deal of consideration by the

industry, because that is its only hope. As the member for Pahiatua, I pay tribute to Sir Keith

an attitude that is desirable everywhere.
Eketahuna is a town with real problems. Its maternity home has been closed. Towns
like Pahiatua, Woodville, and Dannevirke are starting new indigenous industries with a
great future. Then there are places like Takapau and Norsewood. The people felled the bush
that stretched from Norsewood to Eketahuna. Conservationists would say "What a shame”,
and it is a shame, but those people would have had nothing to eat had they not built that road
through the 70-mile bush. The same strength and independence apparent in those early years
lives on in the electorate. Travelling from Waipukurau out to the coastline one comes across
Porangahau, which is very dear to my heart and where I worked for a year. Our Minister of
Agriculture has a farm there. There is no race relations problem for the Maoris and pakehas
living in that district. They know how to treat each other; they argue and they play hard; they
are good people.
My aims for my electorate are probably very obvious to this House. They are to improve
the co-operation and understanding between town and country-between town and country
and the cities-because we are interdependent, and the more we push against each other the
less chance we have of developing nationhood. I believe New Zealand is coming of age and
we are recognising each other's problems, but it is extremely important to remember that
each one of us plays his or her role and at the bottom of it all is the person who has to initiate
so much of this country's wealth-the farmer, and those who work with him on his farm.
Naturally, as a farmer, I intend to spend a little time talking about farmers. It is important
that we build up our agricultural production.
In my electorate we have several industries processing that production. When we talk
about the glamour industries of meat and wool, the important dairy industry is often
forgotten. In my electorate are 85 000 dairy cows, and our dairy farmers, despite the
problem of access to world markets, have shown their confidence in the future of this
industry by stretching their pockets and investing $6.5 million in a new plant near Pahiatua.
The future of New Zealand must be to build up a balanced industry which can compete with
the outside world. Import substitution is not the answer for this country. Last year the
Government introduced the "State of the Livestock Industry" report, largely to try to
convince New Zealanders that agriculture had a potential for the future, and probably to
convince the farmers also that there was some potential for them if the Government wanted
more production. That report showed a potential for 23 000 000 extra stock units by 1984,
and at present prices those stock units would earn New Zealand between $500 million and
$600 million extra each year.
Also important is the chance to provide jobs for people. It is one thing to have ideals,
but one has to have methods for achieving these ideals. If we can increase stock units and
work very hard processing them and selling them overseas, then at 2000 stock units a man,
which is the permissible figure, we can provide 12 000 extra jobs in country areas. It is said
