that four times the number of people are needed in the towns to service those stock units,
and so we are talking about 48 000 people in the towns. In other words, 60 000 extra jobs will
be provided. That is the contribution the Government can make to this country's future if we
set about it.
One of the important things that has been done in the last year, and which many farmers
have wanted but of which they have been rather suspicious, is the introduction of smoothing
schemes for meat and wool. Perhaps we have been prepared to ride with the rough and the
smooth and probably we have become known as whingers because some people have said
"we want" when the prices have been bad but have taken less interest in price smoothing
when the prices have been good. That has been a big mistake, because when prices have
been bad the farming industry has had to appeal to the Government for aid to maintain the
agricultural industry. It has not been entirely the farmers' fault because the rest of the
community has passed on its costs to the farmers, and unfortunately it still does so.
However, the smoothing schemes will provide the opportunity for the flow of money to go
from the farms and to the farms, into the service industries, and in to the community. We
will not see the situation which developed in 1973, when everyone wanted more real wages
when we had not produced a greater volume of exports. Everyone said it was a boom. It was
a boom in prices, but it was not a boom in production. One message should be made clear,
and that is we have to invest to produce growth.
I also want to emphasise the social importance of rural life. I have spoken a little about
the jobs that are potentially there. I have spoken a little about the friendliness of people.
There are some narrow-minded people, too, as there are in any community, but if you get
into trouble people come round to help you just as they do in the towns and cities-the
difference is that you are not anonymous. It is socially important that a work force is
maintained in rural areas. I am not talking about holiday homes where people go to see the
scenery, but somewhere where people can work and do their thing. It is just as important for
people from the rural areas to go into the cities so that we can try to understand each other.
One of the real problems in rural areas—and I am sure members have heard this many
times is the problem of communication. Here I should like to tell a short story about one of
my constituents. One day she took three people along a narrow, winding, and metalled
country road. She had three minor accidents going along that road, ending up in the ditch
each time. Those three people from the town arrived at her house and had afternoon tea and
they were afraid to get back into the car. That woman has lived with that situation all her life.
That farm produces $100,000 worth of overseas funds each year. Is that what these people
deserve? They have to leave the trailer at the end of the road because it is not safe to take a
truck or a trailer along it. We are trying to increase our efficiency and we must put our
resources into the rural areas to encourage people from the cities who, perhaps, through an
unfortunate or fortunate situation, might marry a farmer and go and live in the backblocks.
When they do so they find that their children suffer because they have to travel along the
narrow winding roads. We should spare a thought for the people who live at the end of the
metalled road. Our young people, whether they be from town or country, city or village, are
vital to the future of New Zealand. I have great faith in them to surmount their present
problems. They are under more pressure than many people recognise, but not many have
nothing to eat. That is because the people who came before us have solved that problem. We
owe a lot to them, but we have more pressures to contend with-the pressure of education,
of drugs, and of marriage, as well as of freedom. It sounds funny to have a pressure of
freedom, but sometimes, if you are working very hard on a job and you have to stay working
to keep yourself, then freedom is not important. We have to get used to living in an affluent
society, compared with people in other countries. Members might say it is relative, and there
are problems in cities and towns. Of course there are, but people have enough to eat. Our
real problem is teaching young people how to live with the advantages we have. They should
look positively at the problems and not involve the State in all their problems. I believe that
they can respond to such situations. I believe there should be a career structure in farming,
because without young people on the farms we will not see a future in this country. We will
have a return to the peasant situation which exists in some other countries. We have to have
young people. I am proud of the Government's policy to settle more young farmers this year
than in many other years. We have 1180 farm cadets under Federated Farmers' farm cadet
scheme founded by the Government. We settled 1035 new young farmers this year through
the Rural Bank. I am pleased that the Government has at last opened up the Department of
Lands and Survey settlement blocks because I do not believe the State should own land. The
State has an obligation to develop land and then settle it as quickly as possible. It takes great

Sex education is a problem not only in our schools, but also in society as a whole.

The problems in the freezing industry have prevented farm production from increasing
at a faster rate than it has. Industrial relations must concern the House and the public more
than any other subject. I know that industrial accidents account for more days lost than do
industrial problems, but in the freezing industry we do have real problems, because when the
grass is short and the stock is ready the stock must be killed. Employers and employees,
management and farmers, must adopt a different attitude if this important industry is to be
kept viable. Over 1 000 000 tonnes of meat are processed each year, so the industry has
grown tremendously since 1880, when it started.
To build for the future, unions, farmers, and management must look at new methods. A
new process, a pelting machine, has been introduced into the freezing industry, but workers
in Christchurch and Masterton will not use it because they say there will be redundancies.
There will be redundancies, but with the introduction of the new hygiene regulations those
people will be gainfully employed. I believe that if we do not take a good look at this industry

the last few years, and it is time for more communication between all parties. Under one roof
we have 12 unions, meat inspectors, company management, and the Meat Producers Board
all trying to do their jobs. I believe that employers and unions should look over to the other
side of the fence, and try to come to some agreement to avoid a repetition of what happened
at Whakatu last week when stock was sent home dying. I am pleased that the parties have
agreed that it will not happen again, because sometimes individual rights are not as
important as an animal that is dying of starvation.
The family unit is one of the most vital aspects of our society, and I believe that to
strengthen our society we must build on the family unit. Some women's organisations tend to
downgrade the role of mother, and many women do not like signing "housewife" on a census
form. I believe women should have equal job opportunity with men, but I also believe that

should not be geared to the need for women to work. I do not blame the Government; it is
our own attitude that demands that television set. Many women have to work, but I think the
taxation structure and the family benefit system should be improved to help the problems of
mothers with young children. I know that means spending money, but it should be done.

Last night my colleague the member for Hutt spoke about the flooding in the Hutt
Valley and Wellington as a result of the terrible storm on 20 December. I join with him in the
remarks that he made, the concern that he expressed, and the tributes that he paid to the
many people, not only in the Hutt Valley and Wellington, but throughout New Zealand,
who rose magnificently to help the people in their hour of need. I thank the Government for
the assistance that was eventually granted to those people. We should have a more
permanent form of assistance in such cases. My colleague the member for Hutt mentioned a
non-interest fund that could be made available to people in need. I believe we could go
beyond that. We have the Earthquake and War Damage Fund, but this does not provide the
necessary assistance at a time of personal crisis and hardship. When people are heavily
burdened with several mortgages and then face a catastrophe of this nature, even a very low
interest loan-a futher charge on their property-can be just too much. I hope the
Government will see the logic of setting up a special fund from which immediate grants could
be made available. Some property is uninsurable, and that became evident in the December
flooding in the Hutt Valley and Wellington. The board of control of the lottery fund
administers a large amount of money. The fund is in a fairly healthy state at present. I
commend to the Minister of Internal Affairs for his consideration the thought of setting up a
special fund with that lottery money, which the public would be willing to see devoted to
such a cause.
I now turn my attention to immigration. If ever the wheel has turned full circle it has on
immigration. Now the chickens are coming home to roost. Eighteeen months ago the
National Party made special play and propaganda out of immigration. It played on the fears
and prejudices of the people. Migrants were made the scapegoat of every imaginable ill and
shortcoming, and it was done for party political purposes; nothing more, nothing less. The
Labour Government introduced an effective immigration policy. During the election
campaign the National Party had a policy setting a target of a 5000 maximum annual gain
from immigration. In November and December 1975 there was a net gain of about 8000. It
was very close to the target the National Party had set itself, and within a few months of the
election the figure was down to a 5849 net gain. So all this really stemmed from the policies
of the previous Labour Government. We had the policies, and they were working and
producing the desired effect. But the National Government could not operate the proce-
dures that we left behind. We set employment categories that would have been monitored
continually, and when shortages showed up in any category people could have been brought
in from overseas to fill the gap. The National Party, however, was so taken in by its own
propaganda that it closed its mind and did not operate those controls. What do we see today,
18 months after the election? We find there is a net outflow of 70 418 people, of whom 17 124
have left New Zealand permanently. This is the biggest loss in our history. It far exceeds the
10 000 and 11 000 respectively who left the country in 1967 and 1968. It is worth recalling that
the present Minister of Finance, the Prime Minister, was in charge of New Zealand's
economy then. Under the Labour Government New Zealand was a desirable place to live in.
That can be confirmed by having regard to the pressures exerted by would-be migrants.
The present Prime Minister had a lot to say before and during the election campaign
about immigration and the cost of migrants. He put the figure at about $11,000 a migrant,
and came up with a figure that ran into many hundreds of millions of dollars as the cost of
bringing migrants here. It is reliably estimated that by the age of 18 each young person has
cost the country $38,000 for education, welfare, health, and training. Using the figure for the
net outflow of migrants one finds that the cost has been $670 million, which was the figure
mentioned in this debate by the Leader of the Opposition. That is what the National
Government's immigration policy is costing New Zealand. Members opposite bring out the
argument that they are taking the pressure off housing by stemming the flow of migrants and
driving thousands of New Zealanders away. The facts do not bear out that contention. The
figures for permanent long-term departures and arrivals in 1976 indicate that almost as many
families with immediate housing needs entered the country as left. The net outflow of
migrants includes 15 912 in the 20 to 24 age group. That age group constitutes 30 percent of
the total, and they are unlikely to be vacating homes, so the Government's argument means
nothing. Where are all the people who are leaving New Zealand going? In the 10 months
from April 1976 to January of this year 11 376 people migrated from Australia to New
Zealand, but 21 946 left New Zealand permanently to settle in Australia. Between New
Zealand and Australia we have an open-door policy, and the effectiveness of that policy is
the balance in the economic position in both countries.
Almost every year in recent years the permanent outflow has balanced the permanent

inflow, but in the last 12 months the situation has gone seriously out of balance. Who are

The theme of my address is production and industry. Recently, at the Labour Party
conference, the Leader of the Opposition sounded off and stated: "The man at the work
bench should have a more positive voice in the management of his industry." That statement
shows how little the Leader of the Opposition and the rest of his party know about the
management process. The statement indicates that workers should be a part of management
and decision-making in their respective industries, with none of the capital risks involved.
The Leader of the Opposition has told us that that will be a major part of the 1978 Labour
manifesto. That fits in with the socialistic thinking of members opposite. To be effective and
viable, industry demands a wide range of expertise in areas such as cost projection,
expansion programmes, sales promotion, and marketing, as well as from individual lathe
operators, fork-lift operators, and packers, who are also experts in their fields. For a
business to make headway, there must be harmony and a free flow of communication
between those inside the factory and on the shop floor and those who have responsibility to
the shareholders for the success of the operation. For the benefit of our new socialist party
on the other side, shareholders are the small people of New Zealand who invest their savings
and their confidence in companies, whether they be New Zealand based or overseas.
Watties is a company which involves in some way one in every ninety New Zealanders.
There are 7000 employees and 26 000 shareholders. That makes a total of 33 000, much
larger than the membership of the average union. Yet people accuse Watties of making too
much profit. Watties is about as typically New Zealand as roast lamb and green peas, yet
housewives and Labour M. P.s are trying to knock the company down. In most companies,
there is close communication between the work bench and management, and most of the
staff understand company plans and developments. This understanding is normally achieved
through the house journal and the monthly meeting. Presumably the Leader of the
Opposition has been influenced by union diatribes and seldom-supported complaints that
management does not understand the work force. I believe that there are unions that do not
want the work force to understand management. Think of what the boilermakers did to
Fletcher Bernard Smith, and how they held up the Bank of New Zealand site development.
It is obvious that the Leader of the Opposition does not understand New Zealand industry.
In most cases, management has come from the shop floor or some junior capacity in the
accounting business. The late Sir James Wattie, for example, started canning peaches in his
garage. There is already a high proportion of worker participation in management, but the
Leader of the Opposition says there is not. He is out of touch. If he accepts that there should
be worker contact in management and wishes to push that aim further, he should be honest
enough to do something about it. Let him inform the workers in the 1978 Labour Party
manifesto that if they want a bigger share they must put their money where their mouths are;
the workers must dig into their pocket and into the union's strike funds. Instead of those
funds being used for strikes they should be used to buy shares in industry.

On the subject of overseas trade, last month, following a week in Canberra at the Inter-

with various members of the staff to agents and wholesalers of New Zealand products, and
followed those products through to the retailers. In all cases, whether they were paddles or

Government's tax incentive, to be competitive. But the most important aspect is the capacity
to deliver on time. We are closer to Eastern Australia and a market of 9 000 000

language-than any other country; yet time and again our deliveries are late, or are even
cancelled through being too late altogether. I lay much of the blame for that on internal New

strikes-in fact, on anything that slows down production and causes us to miss the markets
overseas and I throw it right at the feet of militant union leaders and Labour Party

problems which are so vital to our marketing and to those people marketing on our behalf in
Australia. One week in Sydney convinced me that we have the opportunity to produce and
market our way out of much of our overseas debt. Yet we see very little team work, and
neither the socialists nor the unions, supported by the Labour Party, do very much to help.

I turn now to crime in industry. Late last year I expressed my concern about the security
of weekend and all-night petrol stations, and little has happened in the meantime to allay
that concern for the safety of all-night attendants. The price of petrol has certainly not
remained static over the past 4 years. No one can deny that there is now a significant increase

with modern standards in all cases. There is now a need to update security methods

policies on businesses that still use the old system of putting the tin box under the bed. The

cash dairy in many cases, invites crime because the proprietor's security methods are not
updated. If we look at the future of crime in New Zealand, I have no doubt that industrial
crime will be the direction taken by the modern criminal. Computers hold a vast quantity of
vital information for industry, time consuming data for commercial banks, and vital records
for Governments. It would be just so much easier for a criminal to hold a company to ransom
because of computer tapes in his possession. Can New Zealand industry honestly say it is
geared to prevent such an embarrassing burglary? Unfortunately, because New Zealand is
not security conscious, be it in the home or throughout industry, this makes us a ripe target
for hardened imported criminals. We have much need to firm up on security.

since my introduction to Parliament and its law-making system a year ago. My real concern is
that the language of the laws passed in the House can no longer be understood by the
ordinary citizen. The whole of my working life has been spent in the communications
business. As a journalist, I was trained to write simple, graphic English. In more recent
years, my work as a communications consultant has been to help people in organisations to

working always for clearer understanding between people, I find myself today as part of a
law-making body that speaks a language of its own—a language which is incomprehensible
to the private citizen. We define and qualify our terms; we compile clauses and phrases in a
heap of words which, by their very weight, we hope will allow nothing to escape.
I quote an example from the Trade and Industry Amendment Bill: "Minister of
Overseas Trade and Minister of Regional Development may exercise powers of
Minister-2A. Any right, power, discretion, or authority that may be exercised by the
Minister of Trade and Industry under this Act may also be exercised, at any time in his own
name, by the Minister of Overseas Trade or the Minister of Regional Development
severally; and where any such right, power, discretion, or authority is so exercised by the
Minister of Overseas Trade or the Minister of Regional Development, all the provisions of
this Act that would apply in respect thereof if that right, power, discretion, or authority had
been exercised by the Minister . . ."", and so on.
Mr Elliott: Here endeth the lesson.
Mr LAMBERT: Yes, that is enough of that lesson. Lawyers know what it means most of
the time; my fellow parliamentarians might have a broad idea of what the legislation is
about; but I have strong reason to doubt that even we, the law-makers fully understand the
laws that we are passing. In many cases, the intent of the law is buried beneath an
overburden of qualifications which effectively camouflages its real meaning and main
principles.
Our New Zealand laws today are what I would call "mouse-trap" legislation. They are
drafted to block every conceivable bolthole. We forget that with every eventuality we try to
cover, we provide more phrases and words that can be interpreted in new and different ways.
The process is self-defeating. In spite of our efforts to cover every interpretation, we still find
it necessary to pass amending legislation to stop more leaks in this over-canvassed ship of
legislation. It is the basic right of every citizen to have full access to the laws that govern him,
and to be able to understand what they mean. If to be ignorant is no defence in the breaking
of the law, how do we justify laws that the citizen cannot comprehend without a lawyer to
translate for him?
The concern I express is not just my own. The Evening Post of 24 May reported that Mr
Justice Speight had hit out at what he called "the increasingly complex legislation" coming
from Parliament. The Supreme Court was considering an appeal against the blood alcohol
provisions of the Transport Act 1962. This legislation is so bad that police and traffic officers
have publicly admitted that they have almost given up trying to enforce the drinking-driving
law a law you can drive a beer tanker through. Later in the same case the Judge shook his
head and said, "Oh, dear, this legislation is not fit for human consumption."
An editorial in the Evening Post of 26 May stated: "The measure of Parliament's worth
is not the quantity of new legislation it can pass in a working session, but the quality of the
laws which the people must endure." After discussing the case that so provoked Mr Justice
Speight, the editorial continued: "Life is increasingly complex, and our lawmakers should be
going out of their way to simplify the bureaucratic tangle in which we find ourselves rather
than looking upon each new session as a challenge to even greater legislative heights." In an
address to the National Press Club early in May, the former Chief Ombudsman, Sir Guy
Powles, commented on the complex legislation of today and said, "The old saw that
ignorance of the law is no excuse is no longer justified." Professor Geoffrey Palmer, of
Victoria University's law faculty, went to considerable lengths in the Listener of 28 May to
criticise both the quality and quantity of the laws we are passing in this House. He said: "Not
only do we have too many statutes, but they are also too detailed."
Mr T. J. Young: You do pass far too many.
Mr LAMBERT: And you passed plenty, too. “In New Zealand, the approach to
legislative drafting has increasingly been to spell out everything that can be spelt out. The
prolixity of our statutes makes them incomprehensible to the laymen and often to lawyers." I
do not agree with every criticism of the parliamentary system contained in Professor
Palmer's article, but he is one man who, with his wealth of overseas experience, is
particularly well qualified to compare New Zealand legislation with the nature of the law in
other English-speaking countries. I also find that my lawyer friends among the back-
benchers in the House share this concern about the complexity of the law.
With criticism from so many quarters, let us look very closely at the nature of the
problem to see if legislation has always been so difficult to understand, and to compare the
legislative expression of this country with that of other countries in an endeavour to see what
can be done to improve it. The barrage of words that communicates the will of Parliament in


## p. 359 (#367) ############################################

359

New Zealand seems to have begun in earnest after World War II. In 1931, all the statutes of
this country could be accommodated in eight volumes. Today, it is reasonably accurate to
say that the weight of words and legislation governing the citizens of New Zealand is roughly
equal to the entire federal legislation and annotations of the United States of America.
For simplicity of language, let us turn to the Crimes Act 1893. I quote a simple
example-that of robbery and extortion. I believe that any person can understand this law:
"Robbery is theft accompanied with violence or threats of violence to any person or property
used to extort the property stolen or to prevent or overcome resistance to its being stolen.
Every person is liable to imprisonment with hard labour for life and according to his age to
be flogged or whipped once, twice, or thrice who (1) robs any person at the time of or
immediately before, or immediately after such robbery wounds, beats, or strikes, or uses any
personal violence to any person . . ." and so on. That is very simple to understand, and
anyone who could not understand it deserved to be flogged or whipped once, twice, or
thrice. I believe that even the most dull-witted criminal in these enlightened days--and even
Opposition members present tonight-could understand the meaning of those words.
From a comparison of yesterday's law with that of today, let us turn to the laws of other
English-speaking countries. We find that New Zealand outstrips them all in the complexity
of its legal jargon. As an example, I should like to compare the accident compensation
legislation of New Zealand with its Australian counterpart, which is the National Rehabilita-
tion and Compensation Bill 1977. I shall take the sections defining relevant earnings from
both statutes. I quote first from section 104 of the New Zealand Act: "Subject to sections 117
and 118 of this Act and to the provisions of this section, for the purpose of determining the
amount of any earnings related compensation payable during or after the period of short
term incapacity (as defined in section 2 (1) of this Act) to an earner who suffers personal
injury by accident..." and so on. Even if I was reading it slowly, members would still not be
able to understand what it is all about, because it goes on like that for six pages. Its
Australian counterpart takes just 15 lines in the preliminary definition to cover the same
matter of relevant earnings. We can also look at disqualification through murder. Our New
Zealand legislation takes a full page to cover this. I shall not read it out.
Mr Prebble: Oh, go on, read it.
Mr LAMBERT: I shall read out the three lines in the Australian legislation, which
states: "A benefit is not payable under this Act to a person by reason of the death of another
person if the first person has been convicted of the murder of that other person." The New
Zealand legislation takes a full page to do the same thing. The problem in this country is that
Parliament will not be content with establishing the principles of law and leaving its
administration to the courts. Instead, we in this House try to assume the combined
responsibility of both making and interpreting the law, with the result that we produce
legislation that is a maze of clauses of qualifications in which every lawyer can wander quite
happily looking for technical loopholes for a defence. We produce legislation in which
restricting clauses assume equal significance with major clauses, so that one breach of a
technical nature throws the whole law into question. When lawyers have succeeded in
making an ass of the law, we then pass more amendments. The Almighty was able to
regulate the whole field of human conduct with 10 short commandments that any man can
understand, and in the 4000 years of human history that have since elapsed He has not found
it necessary to pass any amendments.
Instead of passing more and more legislation, should this House not consider pruning
the forest of laws we have? A Law Reform Commission has been established in Britain to
weed out extinct legislation, while here in New Zealand we just keep on passing more and
more laws. I do not lay any blame on that overworked team of 10 parliamentary counsel, the
people who burn the midnight oil to keep up with the sheer volume of legislation passed by
the House, and I do not blame this National Administration, because it is only following
precedent. The real problems are simply that our parliamentary counsel are producing
quantity rather than quality, that we are obsessed with details at the expense of basic
principles, and that we have become completely deafened by our own verbosity.
How do we simplify the law, and escape from the toils and tangles of the most complex
legislation in the British Commonwealth? I suggest that, for a start, we get back to the main
principles of law making. If the intention of the law is expressed in straightforward terms, it
becomes obvious to everybody. When attempts are made to sidestep its provisions, any court
can say, "Don't try to come at that; you know what the law means." Let us in this House
concentrate on the principles, and leave the administration to the courts. Let us have more
trust in the good sense and discretion of our judges and magistrates.


## p. 360 (#368) ############################################

360
2 June
Address in Reply
Then let us set up a commission to review and prune the whole fabric of our law and to
repeal everything that has no relevance to the present. One of the first tasks of such a
commission would be to codify our legislation under different headings, because at present
the citizen has to find where the law is before he can find out what it is or what it says.
American federal legislation is printed in volumes under separate headings, such as public
health and welfare, laws relating to the environment, commerce, and so on. Our own system
of lumping the whole lot together is not even adequately indexed. If it becomes necessary to
pass amending legislation, could we not first repeal the inadequate sections of the old
legislation, and replace them in full? The present system we have of referring back to the
original legislation, and replacing certain words and phrases, is like carrying coals to
Newcastle. I know that Mr D. A. S. Ward, a former counsel in the Law Drafting Office and
Compiler of Statutes, supports what I say.
If we cannot express our laws in simpler language-and heaven knows why we
cannot could we not insert a simple explanatory paragraph before each section of the
legislation? The object would be to simplify matters by telling the man in the street what it
means to him in everyday language. I have no doubt that we would have to increase the
overworked staff of law draftsmen, but we could consider appointing professional journalists
or copywriters who can write concise English for drafting the explanatory notes.
Before we pass new legislation, let us ask ourselves, "Is this legislation really neces-
sary?" For every commission we set up we pass a new Act to authorise and regulate its
activities. If we set up a commission to spring-clean and revitalise our legislation, please do
not let us pass a new Act to tell it what to do. Let us just tell it to get on with the job. Before
we pass new laws, let us ask ourselves, "What does this law set out to do? What is it really all
about?", and then we should leave the details to the courts that administer our laws. If we do
not show understanding and discernment in our debates in this Chamber we are not
legislating; we are just rubber-stamping legislation that is put before us.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: That's what is happening.
Mr LAMBERT: And it happened under the previous Government, too. I am not so
naive that I question the need to express our laws in the most explicit language possible, but I
do not see why explicit language must be so circumlocutory as to baffle the undertanding of
the ordinary citizen.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Income Tax on Weekly Wage
1. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Finance, What percentage
of his income did a married man with three children, earning the average ordinary-time
weekly wage, pay in tax in April 1967, and in October 1976, and what was the marginal tax
rate in April 1967 and October 1976?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): For a married man with three
children the tax paid on the average ordinary-time weekly wage in April 1967 would have
been $3.11, or 8.3 percent. In October 1976, allowing for the young family rebate, the tax
would have been $17.86, or 16.3 percent. In April 1967 his marginal tax rate, including social
security income tax, would have been 22.5 percent. In October 1976 it would have been 39.5
percent. I should note that comparisons of tax rates alone between the two dates are
misleading. The most important difference since April 1967 to October 1976 is the increase
of 15 percent in the real take-home pay in October 1976.
Hon. R. O. Douglas: The Minister said that the average tax, including the young family
rebate, was 16.3 percent. Why did he not use the marginal rate as it affected the young man
who can claim the young family rebate? In this case, is it not 54c in the dollar, and not the 39c
the Minister quoted?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I cannot understand the member. I said that allowing for the
young family rebate the October 1976 figure was $17.86, or 16.3 percent. I will repeat the
next two sentences of my original answer. In April 1967 his marginal tax rate, including
social security income tax, would have been 22.5 percent. In October 1976 it would have
been 39.5 percent. The member is confusing things. If the member wishes, and the House
permits, I would be prepared to read the total calculations for the 1967 and 1976 years. I feel
that would be overdoing it, and if the member would like to put down a written question I
would be happy to supply the details.
Mr Luxton: The Minister said that the real take-home pay had increased by 15 percent
between 1967 and 1976. Is he able to confirm that the female work force received a greater

Social Welfare-Domestic Purposes Benefit
2. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, Since the closer
scrutiny of domestic purposes benefits introduced in April 1976, how many cases have been
detected of benefits being paid to persons not entitled to them; how many persons have

married.

3. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Justice, Has he noted that

need to provide legal services to those who otherwise might not be able to afford such a
service. I am anxious to extend those facilities, but before doing so I consider that there must
be a thorough and comprehensive study of the adequacy of existing services, and examina-
tion of alternative means of providing those services to ensure that the funds that can be
made available are being used to the best advantage.

percent respectively over the previous year. There can be no fixed or useful relationship
between overseas earnings or tax income.

variables are not taken into account. The member is well aware of the key variables in costs
and expenditure and tax concessions, which make any comparison invalid.

1975, and asks for 1976. Is there any significance in this?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I was trusting the good sense of the House to note the point
and simply arguing, as I was taught at school, that comparisons are odious and very difficult
to validate. Anyone wanting to take anything from statistics in an economic sense would
have to take a decade and assess the variables that went into the figures before making any
comparison. I am surprised at this question from a former Minister of Finance.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: When the Minister refers to the odious comparisons, does he recall

Living Standard of Average Family Man
7. Mr LANGE (Mangere) asked the Minister of Finance, What is the Government's
estimate of the increase in gross income that will enable a family man on the average
ordinary-time weekly wage of $109.75, with a non-working wife and a child under 5 years, to
maintain his standard of living if there is a 15 percent inflation of consumer prices, and what
further increase would be necessary if he was to improve his standard by 5 percent?
Mr Birch: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I do not want to interfere with the member
asking his first question, but Standing Order 87(b) makes it improper to ask questions
containing expressions of opinion or hypothetical matter. Questions phrased in this way have
been challenged previously, and I draw the question to your attention because it asks what
the Government's estimate of the increase in gross income is if certain circumstances arise. It
continues, "and what further increase would be necessary if he was to improve his standard
by 5 percent." Asking a question in that way opens a wide field of discussion. The Chair has
ruled that questions that in the first instance request reasonable information, but then go on
and ask what the position would be if this or that happened, which is asked in the tail of this
question, are outside the Standing Orders because the question is hypothetical. I ask you to
rule that the question is out of order. I believe it is well within the member's capacity to
redraft it in order to obtain the information he wants.
Mr Lange: In my submission there is nothing hypothetical about the question. I can
appreciate the anxiety of the Government not to answer it.
MR SPEAKER: Order! I should explain that the insertion of debating points and jabs in
the course of discussion of a point of order is not customary. One should attempt simply to
deal with the logic of the point raised. The debating matter can be used on another occasion.
Mr Lange: I apologise to you, Mr Speaker. In my submission it is not hypothetical
because the basis of calculation is set out. It is a matter of increasing the net rate by 5
percent, and then by a very simple process extrapolating the gross rate having regard to the


## p. 368 (#376) ############################################

368
3 June
Oral Answers to Questions
tax rates. That is no different from asking a question, such as was asked recently, if certain
drainage schemes are completed will assurances be given that floods will not occur? That is
apparently a perfectly appropriate question. It was not objected to on the ground that it
involved a hypothesis. In my submission this question involves no hypothesis.
Hon. G. F. Gair: I have been in the House long enough to have heard this point argued
on a number of occasions. One reason for the House steadfastly persisting in its tradition of
resisting the hypothetical is that it makes too wide a range of questions available-questions
that quite frankly are not related to reality. It would be possible for one to pepper a Minister
with hundreds of questions preceded by "if", and in each case he would be required, if the
House changed its tradition, to give speculative answers or answers built on assumptions.
We have a healthy tradition in this matter, that where we are dealing with things the
Government is involved in or responsible for-and these can be specifically identified-the
member asking the question can properly call upon the Minister to relate his answer to
something that is known, or should be known, because it is not based on pure hypothesis.
However, in this case I am glad the matter has been raised because I had doubts about it. It is
the first question this session that has come into this category, and if we change the rules I
think we will change the character of question time.
Mr Prebble: The first part of the question is a question of fact, and the facts asked for
are available in tables held by Government departments. There are tables that estimate the
ordinary weekly wage and the purchasing power of that wage. That is what is asked. The
question also asks what is the buying power of a family with a certain amount of money,
which has been specified as $109.75. The Government has those tables too. Then the
member asks what further increase would be necessary if the man were to improve his
standard by 5 percent. That is very easily calculated; it is not a guess. The Minister is asked
to provide the answer from the tables he has available in his department. I cannot see
anything hypothetical in that question.
Mr SPEAKER: This is a difficult and borderline matter. First, let me make it clear that
the question of whether a matter is hypothetical has no relationship with whether the
question seeks or involves an expression of opinion. "Hypothesis" has been defined as “A
supposition made as a basis for reasoning, or a supposition used as a starting point for
investigation." Normally, if there is a conditional clause-such a clause as usually begins
with the word "if"-that at once makes the matter hypothetical. It can and has been argued
that if the conditional clause simply relates to a matter of arithmetic where there is a firm
computable reply, then the matter is not of the type that is normally described as
hypothetical. The mere fact in this case that the two "if" clauses are at the end instead of at
the beginning of the question does not alter the position. Although I do so with much
hesitancy, I shall on this occasion, particularly as it is the member's first question, give the
member the benefit of a very considerable doubt and say that because there could be a firm
arithmetical computation here I shall let the question pass as non-hypothetical, but I do not
want this to be regarded as a precedent.
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): The question as asked, in
relation to the average ordinary-time male wage in October 1976, is wrongly stated. The
average wage was in fact $119.99, not $109.75 as quoted. I should also note that the average
weekly male wage including overtime was at that time $129.20. For a man actually on
$109.75, the estimates requested are $32.04 or 29.2 percent, and a further $9.84 or 6.9
percent respectively.

Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): An application for closure of the
Masterton gas undertaking was received by the Gas Council on 1 December 1976. Approval
in principle to the closure of the undertaking on a date to be confirmed was given on 21
December. The borough council, to that stage, had indicated only a tentative date of 30 June
1977 for closure, and the Gas Council did not have before it definite proposals for
compensation to consumers or plans for changing consumers over to alternative energy
supply. Subsequently, the borough council has submitted proposals for closure on 30 June
1977, which include the Wairarapa Electric Power Board changing some consumers over to
LPG. The Government has agreed to discuss with the power board the terms of a local Bill
to enable the power board to trade in LPG. The Gas Council, before approving a closure
date, has to satisfy itself that reasonable provision is made for gas consumers to be changed
over to an alternative source of energy, such as electricity or LPG, and I have recently
written to the borough council on this point. Throughout this period the member for
Wairarapa has been a helpful liaison in ensuring that the local position was made clear to me,
and I have, of course, kept him posted on my proposals on this matter.
Hon. F. M. Colman: Can the Minister justify taking more than 5 or 6 months and
keeping the consumers of gas who want to remain on gas in a state of uncertainty, forcing

installing heating and cooking appliances?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The honourable member does not seem to appreciate where the real
responsibilities lie in the matter. There has been some exchange of correspondence, which
included a letter from me to the borough council dated 27 May. In that letter I made it clear
to the borough council that it now needed to submit to me, and to the Gas Council, its advice
on what was a practical date by which the council can guarantee that all remaining gas
consumers will be assured of some alternative form of energy supply. This is a local matter
requiring agreement between the power board and the borough council, and we are awaiting
advice on that agreement. The power board wanted to trade in LPG. It told the council this,
and it told the Government this, but it has no legislative authority to do so. I have told the
power board that Government will co-operate in a transitional arrangement to enable the
board to do this for the Masterton changeover.
Hon. E. S. F. Holland: Can the Minister confirm that the 800, which the member for
Petone indicated said they would change over, in fact answered a question as to whether they
would be interested in retaining gas?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: We have sought a clear indication of local opinion, and, obviously, it
is not unanimous. Another factor is that not all the consumers have the same requirement
for gas. One or two large industrial consumers take the greatest portion of the gas produced.
I believe that the Masterton consumers would be more concerned to see that the right final

GOVERNMENT LIFE INSURANCE AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister in Charge of the Government Life Insurance Office): I
move, That the Government Life Insurance Amendment Bill be introduced. This Bill is
designed to amend three sections of the Government Life Insurance Act 1953 to facilitate
the operations of the Government Life Insurance Office. Under the provisions of the 1953
Act the office has been restricted in its mortgage lending activities to freehold titles and
certain types of Crown leases.
Clause 1 is the short title. Clause 2 will allow lending on first mortgage on any type of
leasehold land approved as a trustee security, and will permit lending on strata titles and on
undivided shares of freehold supported by long-term leases. This system of home ownership
has become increasingly popular in recent years, but because of the restrictions under the
1953 Act the Government Life Insurance Office has been unable to consider mortgage loans
on land tenure of this nature. Clause 3 removes the restrictions in section 29(4) on granting
options of more than 6 months to purchase or lease land or buildings. As part of the
investment policy of the office a number of commercial and industrial buildings have been
acquired and leased on a long-term basis to selected tenants. In negotiating such arrange-
ments with the prospective lessee the office has been unable to grant a right of purchase,
which is sometimes a prior requirement for favourable lending. Clause 4 amends section 31
to allow the commissioner to finance the purchase of motorcars by employees and canvassing
agents whose duties necessitate their use. The present subsection requires the commissioner
to purchase the motorcar first before disposal on terms, and the object of the amendment is
to provide greater flexibility in the provision of motorcars to those employees eligible. The
restrictions on terms of finance are unaltered. For example, they must be on such terms and
conditions as the Minister of Finance from time to time directs.
Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition): The Opposition would like to
probe the reasons behind clause 2. If this is purely to make it possible to lend money on such
things as strata titles, not much exception will be taken. We recognise there are changing
patterns of housing development and that the formal requirements on lenders have, in some
cases, made it impossible for them to lend money on perfectly sound housing propositions
just because of the nature of the title of the proposition. A few developments in recent times
have also been doubtful. We think of some city properties and the leasing arrangements
attached to them. We will require a little more explanation from the Minister before we can
accept with cheerfulness the wording set out in the Bill. I refer specifically to some recent
actions of the Government Life Insurance Office in investing in shares which did not turn out
too well, and the use that was subsequently made by the company in which it had invested of
the fact that the insurance office had invested. Before I develop those aspects I should like
the Minister to indicate precisely the purpose of the extension, what kind of leases, who will
be assisted, how much of the office's funds will be made available for that purpose, and so
on.

material published in the National Business Review recently in which there was an account of
the Securitibank collapse. The chairman, Mr Rutherford, is quoted as saying that at the
eleventh hour, to use his words, just before the collapse, an approach was made to the Prime
Minister to inquire whether the Government agencies which are shareholders in the various

operation, whether by making loans and increasing their shareholding, or whatever. The

tion to that a proposal which in the end collapsed. We know that the Government Life
Insurance Office is, but is not, a Government department. It has a statutory independence, it
has its own Act, and is not quite the same as a Government department. One has always
been told that the commissioner has complete independence in the disposal and investment
of the funds at his command. That story seems to contradict the belief one has always had
that the government life commissioner acts according to his own likes in determining the

insurance company will build it and lease it to the person concerned for a certain number of
years, with a right to purchase at the end of that period. I repeat, that is current commercial
practice. This Bill will merely give the Government Life Insurance Office the opportunity to
provide a service that other insurance companies and lending organisations can provide.
The member for Auckland Central asked whether the move is an attempt to make it
possible to increase interest rates. That is very definitely not so. He also asked about the
percentage of money loaned on houses. The Government Life Insurance Office has about 16
percent of its investments in housing, to a value of more than $14 million at the moment. The
member for Auckland Central also said that, as a member of the investment board, I should
be able to comment on the collapse of Securitibank. I can say that I was kept informed about
the operations of that company.
Mr Prebble: How many meetings did you attend?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The last Minister in Charge of the Government Life Insurance
Office to attend a meeting of the investment board was the late Sir Walter Nash, who
attended one meeting. I repeat that I have been kept well informed on the Securitibank
affair from the time it was first investigated. As was pointed out by the Minister of Justice,
the Securitibank collapse commenced during the term of the former Labour Government,

Bill introduced and read a first time.
BROADCASTING AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Minister of Broadcasting): I move, That the Broadcasting
Amendment Bill be introduced. This is a minor amendment to Part IX-the part concerned
with finance of the Broadcasting Act 1976. It deals with the capital structure of the
Broadcasting Corporation. This amendment springs from the heavy loan indebtedness of the
corporation, which followed the rapid expansion of broadcasting services after 1972.
Between 1973 and 1977, $38.9 million was borrowed from the National Development Loans
Account by, first, the New Zealand Broadcasting Corporation, then the Broadcasting
Council, and finally and to a limited extent the Broadcasting Corporation of New Zealand.
Clause 1 declares the capital of the Broadcasting Corporation of New Zealand to be $38.9
million. In effect, that is the total amount of the Crown's advances to the BCNZ and its
predecessors up to 31 March 1977. That capital is appropriately vested in the Crown.
Members will note that the capital of the BCNZ has not, until now, been fixed by statute. By
doing this, the amendment will provide for increases in the capital of the BCNZ to be made
by Order in Council, for the BCNZ to set aside reserves, and for the BCNZ to declare
dividends. Members will be well aware that development programmes will require any
surplus that is available for some time to come, but I am hopeful that the time will come
when the BCNZ makes profits, and I have made provision for dividends to cover that
eventuality.


## p. 375 (#383) ############################################

3 June
375
Broadcasting Amendment Bill
יון
The step the Government has taken, to transform the BCNZ's loan to equity
capital-the step requiring this amendment—is designed to relieve the BCNZ of an interest
burden of $4 million per annum at the present time. It is designed to give the BCNZ the
capacity to undertake its own development programmes on a reasonable basis, and to
provide for the goal of financial viability, so assisting the corporation to maintain its
independence the independence upon which we all place so much importance. I crave the
indulgence of the House in indicating that, in effect, this was the Jarden plan. I wish to make
that clear. The late Ron Jarden took office as chairman of the Broadcasting Council on 1
July 1976, and he bent his great talents and boundless energy to analysing the broadcasting
system's financial problems. They were very real. In November 1976 he asked for interim
relief-for emergency measures, in effect-to tide broadcasting over its cash shortage. By
February 1977 he had worked out, and put forward just 2 days before his death, this proposal
for the financial restructuring of broadcasting—a proposal designed to take up the overbear-
ing loan indebtedness and interest repayments, and provide for the goal of financial viability.
Its acceptance by the Government is a tribute to Ron Jarden, to his capacity and determina-
tion, and, I believe, to his insight and common sense.
For my part, on the first occasion since February that broadcasting has been before the
House, I wish to pay tribute to Ron Jarden. As Minister, I am still coming to terms with his
loss, which I believe was a monumental one for broadcasting and for the country. I have
already set out what he meant to me in the Listener, but I should like to reinforce that, quite
briefly, by quoting a sentence from one of his colleagues in the corporation who, moved as I
was, wrote to me after Ron's death: "I am no longer a young man-far from it--but I do not
think in the course of my longish life anyone has ever made a more profound impression
upon me." That was true for many of us. It was certainly true for me, and so, as I move this
amendment to the 1976 Broadcasting Act, I recall this fine man and ask the House to
remember his part in assisting New Zealand broadcasting. I would also take this opportunity
to welcome Ian Cross as chairman of the corporation-an appointment that, I believe, has
been widely and warmly welcomed in the community. I am sure he will undertake this
important task with all the skill at his command and in the best traditions of his predecessors.

FISHERIES AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I am directed by the Lands and Agriculture
Committee to present the report of the committee on the Fisheries Amendment Bill. The
committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as amended. I move, That the
report do lie upon the table. The committee received 12 written submissions, 9 of which were
heard over the 2 days it received evidence. It then took a further 2 days to deliberate on the
submissions. I shall touch briefly on some of the more important amendments the committee
wrote into the Bill as reported back. First, it extended the definition of “fisherman" to make
allowance not only for individual applicants for licences but for groups of persons or
companies also to be included. This was partly to try to accommodate the submission made
by the New Zealand Maori Council. The revised definition also draws a distinction between
applicants for continuous and seasonal controlled fishery licences. In section 103A a new
clause has been inserted to allow the Fisheries Licensing Authority to co-opt a fourth
member. This person would be co-opted for either local or specialised knowledge about a
particular fishery and would be co-opted for consideration of that particular controlled
fishery. He would have all the rights and powers of a member, except that he would be non-
voting.
Section 119 has been extended so that incidental catch or by-catch is to be exempted
from the provision that all fishing shall be controlled. This is purely a machinery clause in

one sense, to allow for the logical development of the fishery. In section 120 a new paragraph
has been added to provide for an applicant who is not personally going to fish to give the
names and qualifications of the masters who will have command or charge of the boat or
boats intended to be used. This provision will allow an applicant to apply on behalf of a
company for licences for a number of boats. The committee recommended that section 122
be extended to include, among the matters the Fisheries Licensing Authority is to have
regard to in determining an application for a licence, the desirability of giving preference to
fishermen from a community within the area of the controlled fishery. This was put in
particularly to allow small coastal communities to obtain licences for fishing in traditional
areas. The New Zealand Maori Council's submissions stressed the need for such a provision
to protect fishing areas and species traditionally fished by our Maori people, and the
committee believes that the suggested amendment will meet that objective. A new subsec-
tion has been added to section 125 to provide, if conditions have not changed, for continuous
controlled fishing licences to be renewed without a further hearing. This will speed up the
machinery provision. A new subsection has been added to section 126 to allow temporary
masters to operate a licence if the designated master is unable, because of sickness or some
other reason, to take charge. Section 128 has been amended to provide not only that licences
and boat authorities shall not be transferable but that no goodwill shall attach to them. It will
be an offence to enter into any transaction that contravenes the provision in any way. This is
to ensure that there is no trafficking in or sale of licences. The intention of the committee is
that licences will have no goodwill value whatsoever.
There have been some minor amendments to the appeal provisions to make the
machinery run more smoothly. A new subsection has been added to section 145 to ensure
that the regulations made under this part of the Act—that is, the amending Act-shall have
precedence over regulations made under Part I and Part II of the Act, except that nothing
shall derogate from any provision that relates to Maori fishing rights in Part I and Part II.
The final amendment I shall deal with relates to section 146, which has been amended to
provide that the Governor-General can amend the second schedule by adding fisheries, and
the Governor-General in Council must be satisfied before doing so that the Fishing Industry
Board has been consulted. The committee worked very well on the Bill. There was total co-
operation among all members. It is a complex piece of legislation designed to preserve fish
stocks of controlled species which have been designated in the second schedule. I believe it is
a good Bill.

ROCK LOBSTER REGULATIONS 1969—AMENDMENT NO. 8
Mr McLAY (Birkenhead): I am directed by the Statutes Revision Committee to present
the report of the committee on the Rock Lobster Regulations 1969-Amendment No. 8,
which was passed in 1976. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. In December 1976, in
my capacity as chairman of the select committee, I received a request from Mr Alex Frame,
Lecturer in Law at Victoria University of Wellington, that Amendment No. 8 be referred to
the Statutes Revision Committee pursuant to Standing Order 378. The amendment had been
promulgated on 29 November 1976. Standing Order 378 requires the Statutes Revision
Committee to consider any regulation within the meaning of, or published pursuant to, the
Regulations Act 1936 which may be referred to it with a view to determining whether the
special attention of the House should be drawn to the regulation on any of the following
grounds: first, that it trespasses unduly on personal rights and liberties; secondly, that it
appears to make some unusual or unexpected use of powers conferred by the statute under
which it was made; or, thirdly, that for any special reason its form or purport calls for
elucidation. The Standing Order also gives the committee power to require any Government
department concerned to submit a memorandum or depute a witness for the purpose of
explaining any regulation that may be under consideration, or to report to the House or to
the Government from time to time.
Mr Frame was acting on behalf of a group of fishermen who, it was claimed, had, until
the promulgation of the regulation, earned the whole or a substantial part of their livelihood
by diving for rock lobster under the terms of licences issued to them pursuant to the
Commercial Fishing Regulations. The regulation complained of, in addition to specifying a
closed season for rock lobster in the Chatham Islands between 1 March and 30 April each
year, places an absolute prohibition on the taking of rock lobster by diving or hand picking.
Mr Frame argued that this total prohibition could, amongst other things, be regarded as an
"undue trespass on the personal rights and liberties" of those who had previously earned the
whole or a substantial part of their income by these means; and, further, that the regulations
could be construed as an unusual or unexpected use of the powers conferred by the
empowering statute-the Fisheries Act 1908. He also argued that the regulation might be
ultra vires. It was decided that it was appropriate to accede to Mr Frame's request and the


## p. 391 (#399) ############################################

3 June
391
Rock Lobster Regulations 1969-Amendment No. 8
regulation was accordingly referred to the committee, which later received submissions from
Mr Frame on behalf of the divers, and also from the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.
It is clear to the committee that the particular regulation was intended to prevent rock
lobster being taken during the period of moult, which is a significant phase in the rock
lobster breeding cycle; and to protect the quality of rock lobsters taken for export.
Furthermore, it was clear that over the years the ministry had encountered considerable
difficulty in policing the activities of divers. None the less, the committee is satisfied that
such protection could have been achieved by something less than a total ban on commercial
diving for rock lobster. Specifically, it is of the view that the same protection for breeding-
stock could have been achieved by removing the total ban and imposing instead a closed
season for a specified period of the year-that is, when the rock lobsters are in moult.
Subsequent discussions between the committee and the Ministry confirmed that such an
approach would be acceptable. It appears that the appropriate period for a closed season
would be from 1 March to 15 May in each year-except for the Chatham Islands, where the
season is already closed from 1 March to 30 April. Accordingly, the committee recommends
that the regulation be either revoked or amended so as to impose a partial ban.
Because the committee is satisfied that the regulation went further than was necessary
to provide for the protection of breeding-stock, and because it is also satisfied that at the
same time it denied persons the right to earn their living-or a part of their living-by
means they had previously pursued, it is of the opinion that, in that respect, the regulation
does trespass unduly on personal rights and liberties. It is not intended to detail in this report
every circumstance in which rights and liberties might be adversely affected, even if it were
possible to provide an exhaustive list. It is sufficient to observe that the committee takes the
view that in certain circumstances a regulation that prevents a person earning the whole or a
part of his or her living could well be such an undue trespass. It is, of course, axiomatic that
most laws in some way limit freedom of action. The committee found it necessary to consider
whether the limitations imposed on the divers were excessively great in relation to their
personal income, or inequitably applied in relation to other sectors of the fishing industry.
Furthermore, in determining the matter the committee was anxious to take into account
questions of natural justice and to look very carefully at the reasons for the amendment. It
does not, however, take the view that the promulgation of the amendment was an unusual or
unexpected use of the powers conferred by the Fisheries Act, particularly since section
25(1)(c) of that Act does authorise the making of regulations that impose a total prohibition
on the taking of fish. The committee has concluded that Standing Order 378 does not permit
a detailed inquiry into Mr Frame's suggestion that the regulation might be ultra vires. None
the less, so far as the matter was relevant, it did appear that prima facie the regulation was
within the scope of the empowering statute.
Perhaps I can now speak briefly to the report and add a personal comment to it,
particularly on the procedure whereby these matters come before the Statutes Revision
Committee. While the House is in recess the power to decide whether a particular regulation
should be referred to the committee for review pursuant to Standing Order 378 is vested, at
least in the first instance, in the chairman of that committee; that is by Standing Order 379. It
is, therefore, appropriate for me to observe that I regard the power of referral and also the
power of review that is vested in the committee as both being of a limited nature. Certainly
they are powers that have been used sparingly in the past, and, in my opinion, should
continue to be used sparingly if they are to be regarded as effective.

Orders, a trespass upon the personal rights and liberties of some citizens. It is worth recalling
what happened. A complete ban was placed on the taking of rock lobster by diving. The
committee heard evidence from a number of divers, and it was a complete shock to them to

expensive fishing boat, to make a living-not a particularly good living. I was disturbed, and
I think all members of the committee were disturbed, at the fact that, although it was not
ultra vires, the department concerned was prepared, by regulation, to take away the

duty of Parliament. We are suggesting that an arbitrary use of power, even though legal,

Rock Lobster Regulations 1969—Amendment No. 8
members who are confused about the provisions of Standing Order 378, it allows the Statutes
Revision Committee to review Bills of a technical and legal character. That is the normal
procedure of the Statutes Revision Committee when it is hearing submissions. The second
part of the Standing Order allows the Statutes Revision Committee to review regulations,
and as the chairman, the member for Birkenhead, has said that right has been very rarely
used. One of the purposes that it can be used for is to see whether there has been, or is likely
to have been, a prima facie infringement of the rights of the individual. It is important that
this right to review statutory regulations be preserved, particularly in the case of regulations
where the public generally does not have the same rights as it does with Bills presented to the
House, which can be widely debated.
As the member for Birkenhead said, the committee heard not only the representatives
of the fishermen, but also the department. The department advanced two reasons for the
introduction of the prohibition. One was that it would further protect rock lobster stock, and
the second was that it would reduce the risk of exporting rock lobster with pink flesh. It also
emphasised that it would make it easier to ensure that the numerous illegal acts that had
been taking place were stopped. The committee had to determine whether the limitation
imposed on divers was excessively severe in relation to their personal incomes, and was
unfair in relation to the position of other fishermen. The committee decided that in that
limited field the answer was yes. This was despite the fact that the prohibition had been
supported by the Fishing Industry Board and other bodies representative of fishermen. The
committee accepted the difficulties of the department in enforcing provisions regulating
scuba divers. It also accepted the difficulties in successfully prosecuting persons for taking
soft shell crayfish. Such activities were already illegal. I agree with the member for Auckland
Central on one point only. The power that is vested in the Statutes Revision Committee to
consider not only Bills but also statutory regulations is a very important one indeed. I am
very pleased that members of the public have taken the opportunity to have this statutory
regulation reviewed.

Hon. J. B. BOLGER (Minister of Fisheries): I commend the chairman of the Statutes
Revision Committee for taking the initiative in hearing the case put forward by Mr Frame
and others. The member who preceded me has, in his traditional manner, endeavoured to
create bogymen, and to create fear and distrust. The Statutes Revision Committee followed
the normal constitutional procedures that are properly laid down, and which have been

brought in last year to protect rock lobster stocks in New Zealand from overexploitation.
One method of achieving this would be to ban commercial diving for crayfish. I remind the
House that, concurrent with that, commercial diving with air has been banned, and the
committee's report does not suggest that that should be reinstated.
There will always be argument on how best we can preserve our valuable rock lobster
stocks, and other species. In recent months I have been through the fishing industry, and
have met fishermen up and down New Zealand, including the Chatham Islands, and I find a
clear division of opinion on this issue. There is no unanimity. The ministry, endeavouring to
get a common position from the industry, went to the major organisations from which it
seeks advice: the Fishing Industry Board, the Fishermen's Association, and the seafood
processors. They all agreed that the ban should be introduced. There was no suggestion of
railroading this measure through the House or by regulation. I want to make it perfectly
clear that there was wide consultation within the industry. Even though the normal
procedure of consultation was pursued, the recommendation was made that this unduly
infringed on some of the rights of individuals. Therefore the Statutes Revision Committee
decided that the measure should be reported back to the House in this manner. As the value
of the species grows, it will be much more difficult to protect it from overexploitation. Even
within recent days members will have read in the newspapers of a huge haul of illegal

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Maori Council-Appointment of Member for Wairarapa
1. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Maori Affairs, Has he seen
the report in the Evening Post of 31 May regarding the opposition to the appointment of his
colleague the member for Wairarapa to the New Zealand Maori Council, and, if so, would
he indicate under what statutory provision the appointment was made, and assure the House
that the council is not "Government controlled"?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Maori Affairs): Yes, I have seen the report. The
member for Wairarapa has told me that he resigned his position on the Ikaroa District
Council when he became a member of Parliament, and thus he is no longer a member of the
New Zealand Maori Council. However, because of his long-standing interest the Maori
Council has asked him to be an ex-officio member. The Government has had nothing to do
with that.
Hon. M. Rata: Are there any provisions for ex-officio members, and is it his intention to
introduce retrospective legislation to validate the action of the Maori Council?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: I have not checked whether there are any regulations, but the
council rules itself. No legislation is proposed.
Mr Couch: If the Maori members of the Opposition had taken the same interest as I
have in the past, would they have become ex-officio members of the Maori Council?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: That would be over to the Maori Council.
Mr Prebble: As a statutory body such as the New Zealand Maori Council, which nas no
provision for ex-officio members, has a National member serving on it, will the Minister
advise the council that it should follow the law, and also advise the member for Wairarapa
that he should resign, because he no longer has the support of his district council?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Under section 17 of the Maori Welfare Act 1962, members of the
New Zealand Maori Council are appointed by the district councils. Each district council
holds a meeting in May of any year, at which the committees are elected and three members
are appointed to the New Zealand Maori Council. There is no other statutory provision for
the appointment of members, and the council has asked the member for Wairarapa to
remain as an ex-officio member so that it can benefit from his wide experience.
Mr Prebble: Does section 17 effectively mean that the member for Wairarapa is serving
illegally on the council; and, if so, can the Minister indicate the legal provision under which
the member for Wairarapa is serving on the council?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: The legislation under which the Maori Council was set up does
not prohibit ex-officio members if the council wishes to appoint them.

National Superannuation
4. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, What is the date
for the next review of wages as they affect the rate of national superannuation, and when will
the benefit be increased accordingly?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): The rate of national superannuation
is related to the latest average ordinary-time weekly wage as disclosed by the half-yearly
survey of salaries and wages conducted by the Department of Labour in April and October
each year. The most recent survey was carried out in April, and the rates of national
superannuation will be adjusted as soon as the results are known, which is expected to be
early in July.
Mr Hunt: In view of the recent record increase in the consumer price index of last
quarter, will the Minister take account of that when he fixes the allowances that superannuit-
ants will receive?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: Superannuation is based on the average ordinary-time weekly
wage. Before the introduction of national superannuation, beneficiaries were fully compen-
sated for increases in the consumer price index, but now they are associated with the average
ordinary-time weekly wage. From August next year national superannuation will be
increased to 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister confirm the press item released following his
meeting with the Beneficiaries Association last May that "National superannuitants will be
given a rise in June to compensate for the increase in the cost of living."?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: I explained to a deputation of beneficiaries that a survey was
being carried out at that time by the Department of Labour and that I expected an
announcement would be made relating to the average ordinary-time weekly wage towards


## p. 399 (#407) ############################################

7 June
399
Oral Answers to Questions
the end of June or early in July. It was reported that it would be towards the end of June, but
as I said in my original answer, the rates of national superannuation will be adjusted as soon
as the results of the April survey are known. This is expected to be early in July.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: As wages are running behind the consumer price index, and have
not been adjusted, does the Minister intend adjusting national superannuation to give
beneficiaries the full increase?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: When national superannuation is fully implemented and
beneficiaries are receiving 80 percent of the average ordinary-time weekly wage, they will
then receive an amount equal to or greater than about 40 percent of the work force, and it is
assessed that at that time beneficiaries will receive an amount that is more generous than
they have received in the past and that will make them financially independent-something
they have not enjoyed before.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister indicate the date when the proposed increase
in national superannuation will be paid?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: As I said in my original reply, the most recent survey by the
Department of Labour was carried out in April, and the rates of national superannuation
will be adjusted as soon as the results of that survey are known, which is expected to be early
in July.
Mr Wellington: What reaction has the Minister had from superannuitants to the present
level of payment?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: The reaction generally has been good.
Hon. Michael Connelly: Will the Minister confirm that if the payment is to be effective
from the date the Minister announces the change, that will involve a change in Government
policy?
Hon. H. J. WALKER: No. This is in line with the Government's announced policy.
