Tax Increase as Percentage of GNP
5. Mr MacDONELL (Dunedin Central) asked the Minister of Finance, What was the
total increase in taxation collected in the March 1977 financial year, compared with that
collected in the March 1976 financial year; and what percentage of the gross national product
does the increase represent?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Acting
Minister of Finance. Total taxation receipts increased by $659.6 million, or 20.7 percent, in
the March 1977 financial year compared with increases of $320 million, or 11.2 percent, in
the March 1976 financial year. The 1976-77 increase represents 5.3 percent of gross national
product, a rather meaningless comparison since the increase depends on increased incomes.
Mr MacDonell: As this massive increase took place during savage cuts in Government
services and declining family incomes, what impost can taxpayers expect this financial year
when the Government claims that the economy is improving?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I am sure members will appreciate the politics in the question, which
was full of subjective judgments as to the answer, and I am quite sure the member will
appreciate the value of the answer. I am not in a position to give a foretaste of the economic
situation following the Budget, but, when the member for Dunedin Central talked about
savage imposts, that presumed that the position was worse than it had been. To the contrary,
it was generally better. Tax on private incomes shown as a percentage change over previous
years was up 27.1 percent in 1974, and that was the first year of the third Labour
Government. In the second year it was up 25.7 percent on the previous year, and in the third
year, 1976, it was up 9.1 percent. This year it is up 19 percent, which is lower than all but one
of the previous 3 years. An interesting note is that 1976 was an abnormal year. In that year
tax on private incomes increased by 9.1 percent over the previous year, while private income
before tax increased by 16.8 percent. However, that was the year in which the Labour
Government went to the polls, so it was an abnormal year.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Local Authority Borrowing
9. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Finance, Can he explain why only
$15.23 million, or 6.37 percent, of the $239 million borrowed by local authorities during
1976-77 came from private investors?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Acting
Minister of Finance. The $15.23 million invested in local authority loans by private investors
during the 1976-77 financial year is more than double the amount invested by private
investors during the 1975-76 financial year. It is also 75 percent more than was raised from
the same source in the 1974-75 financial year. During 1976-77 the Government took a
number of steps to increase investment in local authority loans. These included the setting of
realistic rates of interest. It is apparent from the increased investment by private investors
that the measures taken have been effective, although an even higher rate of private
investment would be desirable.
Mr Hunt: As last year the Minister announced increases in the maximum interest rates
ranging from 6.5 percent to 9.5 percent, or more than a 40 percent increase, can he explain
why only 6.37 percent last year came from private investors?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Obviously, this has something to do with the state of private
investment in local body securities inherited by this Government from the previous Govern-
ment, and it has taken some time to repair the position, as I will explain by the following
figures: in 1972-73, when the second National Government passed its healthy economic
position over to the Labour Government, private investment in local authority loans was
12.75 percent; in 1973-74, the first year of the Labour Government, it fell to 11.61 percent;
in 1974-75 it fell to 5.55 percent; in 1975-76, the last year of the third Labour Government, it
was down to 3.68 percent; and it has now been brought up to 6.38 percent in the first year of
the third National Government.
Mr Hunt: How much has the increased interest rate of more than 40 percent in 1 year,
from 6.5 percent to 9.5 percent, cost the ratepayers in any one rate authority district?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: As the local authorities would not have had the money otherwise, the
question is a nonsense.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Notwithstanding the savage increase in the interest rate that the
Minister has confessed to, and taking into account his dissatisfaction with the private
investment lift to 6.37 percent, will the Minister increase interest rates further in order to
encourage more private investment in local authority loans?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The honourable member will know that, unless there are savings,
there cannot be people who can borrow. I am sure the honourable member appreciates that
his question was loaded, and he is going to get the reply his question deserves. While the
country requires people who will lend money to local authorities, there must be a position in
which people are encouraged to save. People cannot be encouraged to save unless the return
on savings is fairly competitive with returns that can be achieved in other ways. The previous
Labour Government sought to freeze interest rates and hide its head from the facts, allowing
the position to deteriorate so that local body loans in the year 1975-76 were met by private
investment to the measure of only 3.68 percent, which was between one-third and one-
quarter of the position it inherited, and it managed to achieve this deterioration in three
short years.
Mr Prebble: As the Auckland Regional Authority, which is now allowing 9.5 percent
interest on loans, is not getting the money it needs from either private or any other sources,
can the Minister indicate what help will be given to authorities such as the ARA, which do
not have enough loan finance even at 9.5 percent interest?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The Auckland Regional Authority, along with many other local
authorities, has been helped very considerably by the Government through the National
Provident Fund. The way in which local body capital works were permitted to grow in 1974
and 1975 bore no relationship to the ability of the community, or the local authorities, to
finance the works, and was the cause of the need for the new National Government to
establish very strict priorities in the allocation of funds between competing local authorities'
capital works. The local authorities themselves now appreciate that they had been encour-
aged to accept a falsely optimistic situation in 1975, because in that year the then Labour
Government permitted the consumption of almost all the National Provident Fund reserves
to sustain a rate of capital activity that could not continue after those reserves had been
spent.

Oral Answers to Questions
Farms-Prices for Fattening Units
10. Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth) asked the Minister in Charge of the Valuation
Department, What was the average price per farm for freehold fattening units sold on the
open market in 1972, 1975, and 1976?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG (Minister in Charge of the Valuation Department): The average
prices for freehold fattening farms sold on the open market were: 1972, $64,264; 1975,
$132,291; and 1976, $147,649.
Mr Friedlander: Can the Minister express the annual average percentage increase that
took place between 1972 and 1975, and can he also give the percentage increase for those
farms in 1976?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: In 1973, the price increased by 29.81 percent over the previous
year, in 1974, by almost 50 percent, and in 1975 by 6.32 percent, an average of 28.4 percent
increase each year during the term of the previous Government, which compares with an
11.61 percent increase in 1976.
Hon. M. Rata: In view of the obvious burden this places on the efficiency of the nation's
agricultural output is it the Government's intention to introduce land price control?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: No, it is not the Government's intention to introduce land price
control. However, it is the Government's intention to ensure that those involved in farming
have confidence in its future, which is already indicated by the increase in stock numbers and
production under the National Government.
Mr Bruce Barclay: I am not sure whether I heard the figures correctly. Did the Minister
say that the percentage increase in farm prices during the last year of the Labour Govern-
ment was less than it was this year, under the National Government?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: That is correct, but during the 3 year period, the average annual
increase in prices for those types of farms was 28.4 percent, which was beyond the ability of a
young farmer to save to purchase his own property.
Mr Falloon: How many fattening farms were sold during the years 1972 to 1976?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: In the first effective year of the Labour Government, 774 fattening
farms were sold. In 1974, 518 were sold, and in 1975, 254. In the first year of the National
Government, 335 fattening farms were sold.
Mr Hunt: As the Minister's original answer revealed that for the first year of the
National Government there was an 11 percent increase in the price, which represents 33
percent on a 3-year basis, could he please tell his research unit to ask more effective
questions?
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

I had hoped he would mention something that I personally am devoted to, the Maruia
Declaration. The Maruia Declaration contains six points. The first is that native forests,
wherever they remain, must have recognition and protection in law. The second point is that
the wholesale burning of indigenous forests and wildlife has no place in a civilised country;
and the third is that the logging of virgin forests should be phased out by 1978. There are
three other points that I shall not read, but I know that people who adhere to those views are
supporting the declaration in a big way. Recently, Professor Knelman said that someone has
to be an unrelenting advocate of the environment, and it is unfortunate that there is no such
advocate on the Opposition benches. As I have frequently said, I am concerned about the
environment, and although much has been done much still remains to be done. I was pleased
at the recent decision to establish a science reserve at the Kopuatai Peat Dome area. This
area is south of Auckland, in the Hauraki Plains. It has been under study since 1973, but it
took the National Government to decide what to do with the land. I am pleased that some
action has been taken in some of our native forests, but I am concerned to learn that
kahikatea is scarcer than kauri, and that the brown teal is threatened. There is still much for
the National Government to do.
One point debated at length by the member for Auckland Central was people voting
with their feet. This intrigued me, because I remember a Minhinnick cartoon at Ruakura. It
hung on the wall there, and was dated 1960, and members will recall that that was the time of
the second Labour Government. The cartoon showed Walter Nash sitting behind a bench,
with Nordmeyer standing beside him. In front of them stood the late and great C. P.
McMeekin. Underneath was the caption, with Mr Nash speaking, "Brain drain, Dr
McMeekin? But we haven't been asked yet.” I do not know how much of a reflection that is
upon those two leaders of that time, but I thought that perhaps there was something we
should look at in terms of 1960. It is interesting to find that the only answer that the Minister
of Immigration had at that time to any question on the lack of action to encourage New
Zealanders to stay was this: Mr Hackett said, "They are merely paying extended visits
overseas for business reasons, tourism, and study, or for working holidays." I am sure we
would have had howls of derision from Opposition members today had I read that out first as
a reason for people leaving New Zealand. Opposition members are talking about this brain
drain, and the manpower we are losing. In 1959-60, about 13 500 people left the country.
They are now talking of the 17 000 who left in 1976. Expressed as a percentage of the
working population, which is what we are talking about, the percentage of people leaving in
1960 was higher than it is today. Is there any answer to that statistic from members opposite?

I want to speak about two or three matters concerning health and the state of the health
service. I am surprised that the member for Hamilton East did not mention the Government

withheld, and is causing serious concern to the nursing profession. In 1972, the National
Government pledged itself to achieve the change-over from hospital-based training prog-
rammes to those based on technical institutes in a minimum of 10 to 12 years. In 1977, the
New Zealand Nurses Association set out a policy that the transfer should be achieved by
1981. What are the figures to date? First, technical institute students today number 463,
whereas hospital-based nurses number 7893. The Government should act now. The space
and facilities are available, but delay may mean that provision for the courses may not exist
after 1978. Before the member for Hamilton East asks why the previous Labour Govern-
ment did not do something about the matter, I say that the time to act is now and that the
mistakes made in the past do not justify mistakes being made in the future.

I shall spend most of my time this afternoon talking about mental health, a matter far
too seldom debated in this Chamber. I commend TV2 for its telethon activities, and I hope
they will be supported by every New Zealander. Any concept of health must be based on an
understanding of the unity of man. We need to work towards developing a health service
that takes account of man and his physical, psychological, and social being. We should also
accept the interdependence and interaction of mind and body, and at all times preserve the
dignity of man and the quality of family and community life.
I want to talk about child psychiatry in New Zealand. Full psychiatric facilities exist only
in Dunedin and Auckland and, as child psychiatry clinics are now under the control of
hospital boards, no unified plan exists for development at a national level. Planning
machinery varies and is largely dependent on the knowledge of members of the hospital
psychiatric advisory committee of each board. In most hospital board areas, the need to
establish child psychiatric departments is accorded a low priority when compared with other
demands. Unlike adult psychiatry, which has achieved adequate facilities in many areas,
child psychiatry basically lacks adequate facilities, and suffers from a serious lack of trained
people at the medical level. This point is made by Professor Basil James, the head of the
department of psychological medicine at Otago University, in a report in the Dominion of 25
May 1977.
Mr A. G. Frazer, a psychiatrist with the Department of Social Welfare, in a paper
entitled "Psychiatric Needs of Disturbed Social Welfare Children and Adolescents, and
Consultative Psychiatric Practices in Social Welfare Institutions" in 1976, points to two
significant areas in which child psychiatric services could be improved, and I endorse his
remarks. He stresses the need for adequate back-up services. Back-up services are the
alternatives that support a given setting; for example, an in-patient unit would provide a
back-up service for a day hospital clinic, which in turn would back up facilities for the out-
patient clinic. There are also alternative staff resources-for example, adult psychiatrists,
paediatricians, and general practitioners with skills in treating children-which can provide a
reasonable back-up service where child psychiatric services do not exist.
Secondly, there is a need for a progression of services. It is often not possible for one
setting to provide for all the mental health needs at one time. There is a need to develop a
sequence of interlocking services which bring the child and the family to their optimum level
of functioning. An example of this progression of services would be full-time hospitalisation,
partial hospitalisation, day patients care, out-patient treatment, and graduated school
arrangements. Dr W. Warren, in the Australian and New Zealand Journal of Psychiatry
(193) 7, at page 303, October 1973, states: "An in-patient unit for adoloscents requires
associated out-patient facilities, to sort out patients for admission, to follow them up after
discharge, and to treat others outside hospital. Such a clinic for adolescents, as in the case of
children, needs, apart from the services of the psychiatrists, adequate help from an
experienced social worker and a psychologist; ideally it should be placed separately from
clinics for adults and those for younger children.”.
This is the background to what I want to say now about the conditions at the Lake Alice
Hospital adolescent unit, which we cannot be too proud of and which must be improved in
the future. The unit is housed in an old building which has been adapted for children. It does
not give the appearance of being a supportive environment for severely disturbed children. It
is staffed by a psychiatrist, Dr Selwyn Leeks, employed by the Palmerston North Hospital
Board; a psychotherapist employed full time-Mrs Priscilla Leeks; three other therapists,
who do eight part-time sessions; and 8 nurses rostered to care for 46 children.
A major problem appears to be the chronic shortage of trained nurses. Mrs Leeks, in an
article in the New Zealand Herald on 12 December 1976, stated "The nursing staff are so
busy on administrative work they do not have time to get on with the nursing." Dr Leeks
complained to the Labour Party caucus committee of the low quality of the existing nursing
staff. In particular, the nurses lack the skills needed to deal with the children. Nurses are
rostered to the unit from the general staff pool, and most do not have paediatric training.
Those staff with paediatric training are psychopaedic nurses, and their skills are related to
the care of mentally sub-normal children. Of course, in this unit there are children who are
sub-normal, but there are others with IQs of over 140. The Manawatu Evening Standard of
23 April 1977 carried a report from the chief architect of the Wanganui Education Board,
stating that the facilities were very poor and that: "They are using an overcrowded villa and a

prefab. classroom for up to 40 to 50 children." It is noteworthy that there is not a primary
school in New Zealand that is forced to operate with that sort of building with so many
children. Plans for a new school building have been prepared for a number of years, but
Department of Health procrastination has prevented any progress being made until this
year, when the Acting Minister of Health gave approval for tenders to be called. Mr
Dearsby, the chairman of the Wanganui Education Board, said: "It was clear beyond doubt
that, had the Department of Education been responsible for providing the money, the

The unit was opened in 1972 with 12 beds, and now caters for 46 disturbed children-36
boys and 10 girls aged between 8 and 15—which makes it the largest residential unit in New
Zealand. It takes patients on a national basis. One-fifth of the children are psychotic, one-
third are neurotic, and the rest are behaviourally disturbed, according to a statement made
by Dr Leeks in the Auckland Star on 15 December 1976. The majority of the children are in
the unit because of family problems, expulsion from schools, and what are referred to as
"character disorders."
The Labour Party human rights caucus committee has come up with five recommenda-
tions, and I hope that the Minister of Health will be able to comment on these. First,
investigations should be undertaken into the general staffing shortages at Lake Alice
Hospital, particularly as they relate to the adolescent unit. Secondly, the feeling of isolation
from the main stream of psychiatry expressed by various staff members and the neglect in
terms of financial assistance, staff allocations, and community support, should be remedied.
Thirdly, a general investigation of the use of ECT in psychiatric treatment, particularly in
children, should be carried out, with special emphasis on the rights of psychiatric
patients and I emphasise that and shall develop it shortly. Fourthly, child psychiatry
services in New Zealand need improvements in the facilities provided, in specialist staff, and
in the adoption of a teamwork approach to the child and the family. Fifthly, the present
siting of the adolescent unit at Lake Alice Hospital is undesirable, and a special centre with
adequate physical facilities and properly trained staff needs to be established to cater for the
growing number of children needing such psychiatric services.
There have been two inquiries recently into allegations relating to Lake Alice. One was a
commission of inquiry into the case of a Niuean boy, conducted by Mr W. G. Mitchell S.M.
of Auckland. In this case it was found that there was no express authority for ECT, either
from the family or from officers of the Department of Social Welfare, and that there was a
lack of dialogue between members of the medical profession and social workers concerning
the medical condition and treatment of children in the department's care. Mr Mitchell
concluded: first, that the use of ECT in the boy's case was warranted in terms of accepted
medical practice in psychiatric hospitals in New Zealand; and, secondly, that the use of ECT
with or without anaesthetic on children was a matter for the medical profession to decide.
That, of course, is at variance with the report of the investigation by the then
Ombudsman, Sir Guy Powles, into a complaint against the Department of Health and the
Department of Social Welfare. He concluded: first, that due to a defective medical
certificate the boy's status was that of an informal, not a formal, patient, and that the
hospital did not have the legal authority to detain the boy against his wishes or those of his
parents; and, secondly, that the Children and Young Persons Act does not authorise the
detention of a young person in a psychiatric hospital when he is either in social welfare
custody, or under supervision or guardianship, without recourse to the formal committal
procedures of the Mental Health Act, and that the boy's continued detention was therefore
seen to be unlawful.
After that investigation and report, of course, I made a statement about a document
that was presented to me by a Mr C. C. Jackson, who is a very qualified social worker in the
Department of Education, and I have noted that since I made that statement not one fact I
gave has been disputed. I have heard a comment that perhaps I might have made the
statement without sticking to the facts, but since the statement was made not one fact has
come to light that would negate any of the comments I made. As a result of the
Ombudsman's inquiries, as a result of the visual inspection the human rights caucus
committee made at Lake Alice, and as a result of allegations made by Mr Jackson, which
have not been categorically denied point by point, I believe there is a need to review the
administration of ECT in all Department of Health institutions.
I suggest that three things should be done immediately: first, the use of unmodified ECT
as a mode of treatment for children and young persons detained in psychiatric hospitals

The last point raised by the member for Wairarapa was the attitude of the OECD to
New Zealand's policies, but one finds that production and Government expenditure is rising
and inflation is falling in the leading Western countries, the United States, Germany, and
Japan. Interest rates are falling, and generally there is business confidence and investment,
in comparison with the economic position of New Zealand today. The only activities that are
booming in New Zealand are debt collections, repossessions, evictions, price increases, and
unemployment.
I pay my respects to our retiring Governor-General, Sir Denis Blundell, who, as well as

I now wish to speak about the social environment, and to refer to the disastrous and
accelerating deterioration in the quality of family life. I want also to deal with the report on
the domestic purposes benefit, and to show that it has failed to identify the real reasons for
breakdowns in marriages and the rise in illegitimacy. Those who drafted that report have
failed to reach the correct conclusions. We are experiencing today a disastrous and
accelerating deterioration in the quality of family and community life, and this is taking
place under a Government that said it was concerned about the family.
We all remember that during the 1975 general election campaign the Prime Minister and
other spokesmen on behalf of the present Government expressed lofty sentiments and high
ideals on social matters, no more so than in the field of family life. The National Party's
policy stated: "This National Government believes that the family is the basic unit of our
society, and that all social welfare policies should encourage and be compatible with good,
strong family life. To this end, under National a committee will be set up to deal exclusively
with matters affecting family life. . ."--and, of course, the chairman of that committee was
to be the Minister of Social Welfare. Now, 18 months after the election, that promise has a
very hollow ring. In that time, the National Government has demonstrated a callous
disregard for the family and for the need for policies to promote the unity and well-being of
the family. Instead of producing policies and taking initiatives in matters of the greatest
social and family need-such as helping to remove the causes of family tension and
disintegration, and building an environment within the community where family life can
flourish the Government has done the reverse. It has ignored all advice about family
needs, especially the needs of the low-income, one-income family.
It has been quick, however, to provide for those in the least need with its superannua-
tion scheme, while ignoring the plight of the low-income families with dependants. Many
former age beneficiaries who were compulsorily transferred to national superannuation have
already lost concessions, and more will do so as further stages of the scheme are
implemented until ultimately, when the scheme is fully in operation, tens of thousands of age
beneficiaries will be worse off. On the other hand, 80 000 businessmen, professional men,
executives, company directors, and others in full-time employment, who formerly could not
qualify for the age benefit or for universal superannuation, have already received substantial
national superannuation payments. For example, a married couple receives an extra $76,
and a single person an extra $46, a week.
Last month the Minister of Social Welfare addressed a meeting at Levin and was quoted
as having referred in these terms to the questions put to him: “They were predictable, and
reflected some of the fears people had because of irresponsible claims by the Opposition."
Certainly, the Opposition has drawn pensioners' attention to the manner in which the
Government has failed to honour its election pledges, and it has shown them how in the long
run, if there is no change in the Government's policy, many of them will be worse off. I
should like to tell the people of Levin that I shall be addressing a public meeting in Levin
later this month, and I shall deal with the Minister and expose the way in which the

Government has exploited them and all New Zealanders.
The income tax adjustment for low-income families with dependants applied to some
wage earners but not to others. In many cases it penalised the one-income family relative to
the two-income family, and it did nothing at all for the one-income family with dependent
children. Its effect was to help some families by offsetting the increased income tax that was
payable by all on the increased wages they received to compensate them for the increased
cost of living.
The Government has so far refused to carry out the policies it promised on the
provisions of the Disabled Persons Community Welfare Act. Apart from appointing the
council and continuing the Labour Government's policy on short-stay facilities, the Govern-
ment has done nothing to honour its pledge. On the other hand, it has not hesitated to use
the taxes paid by the parents of the disabled, and in some cases paid by the disabled
themselves if they are working, to help finance national superannuation for people who are
already receiving an annual income of $20,000, $30,000, or more.
Mr Talbot: Who supplied you with that?
Hon. MICHAEL CONNELLY: Everyone knows that that is so. Government members
will not deny it, because they know they are handing out about $2,500 a year, to single
national superannuitants with an income of $20,000 or $30,000 a year, or, if they are
married, about $4,000 a year extra; and they are taxing the parents of the disabled, and in
some cases the disabled themselves, to enable them to make those payments. The Govern-
ment has failed to act on the recommendations of its own council of social services, yet it
immediately adopted the recommendation made by the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review
Committee of a cut in the domestic purposes benefit payable to new applicants. Some people
would say that the real role of the Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee was not to
find out the causes of the breakdown of marriages and increased illegitimacy, but to save the
Government money. The order of reference and the report were not really directed at
identifying the causes of the breakdown of marriages, of family life, and of human
relationships. Instead, the order of reference could be said to have directed attention away
from the causes of the breakdown of marriages, towards what it was thought should happen
after the breakdown of a marriage, or following a deterioration in the standards of conduct
in human relationships; it could also be said that attention was directed towards whether the
final breakdown was caused by the domestic purposes benefit. That is why I believe that the
committee's report lacks depth and has failed to tackle the real issues.
Although the Minister was quick to announce a reduction in the domestic purposes
benefit for new beneficiaries-including a greater reduction for unmarried mothers than the
committee recommended-in a press release he announced few specific decisions on other
recommendations in the report. These could have assisted in preventing the final collapse of
a marriage or in the social and economic rehabilitation of those affected. For example: there
were no recommendations on conciliation services under the Domestic Proceedings Act;
there was nothing about increased marriage guidance support; there was nothing about the
increased allowable income and changed abatement provisions recommended by the report;
there were no guidelines on what constitutes a de facto marriage; there was nothing about
the use of voluntary social services; there was nothing about providing more adequate
facilities for confidential interviews, or simplified procedures for former beneficiaries who
re-apply. The key recommendations that the Government sidestepped covered job training,
retraining, upgrading of skills for women, vocational guidance, job opportunities, and child
care to assist mothers to return to work.
The overall tenor of the report gives the impression of establishing a link between the
domestic purposes benefit and the breakdown of marriages, between that benefit and the
increasing illegitimacy, between that benefit and single girls who do not make their children
available for adoption, and between that benefit and the failure to marry or remarry. For
many years there has been a significant increase in the number of divorces and separations,
and in illegitimacy. The committee alleged that children's welfare was its primary concern,
yet it failed to pursue the causes of the circumstances that are leading to the breakdown of
marriages, and the increasing number of ex-nuptial births. Indeed, it summarily dismissed
these aspects in one little comment, stating: "There was no way of assessing what were the
main causes of recent startling increases in the number of people receiving this benefit. The
problem of social standards in particular was referred to in many submissions, but there were
many other possible, even probable, causes on the significance of what different organisa-
tions adopted different views."
The committee then asserted that the generosity of the benefit, the more extensive

Address in Reply
In considering the opening of Parliament and the Address in Reply debate, we think of
the pending retirement of Their Excellencies, Sir Denis and Lady Blundell. I trust that they
will have many years of happy life together in their retirement. They have made an indelible
mark on the people, and Sir Denis has upheld the office in the highest possible tradition. I
know that I speak also for those within my electorate when I say that Sir Denis and Lady
Blundell will be missed, particularly by the many friends they have made during their term in
office.
The Speech from the Throne was a clear outline of the difficulties facing New Zealand
today, but no difficulty could equal the two major disasters that threatened New Zealand in
1975. I hasten to add that both were averted on 29 November of that year. One of the
threatened disasters was the rapid escalation of inflation; the other was the rapidly growing
fund of the New Zealand superannuation scheme, which within a very few years would have
provided the Labour Government with the capacity to control the means of manufacturing,
distribution, and exchange. Since the recent Labour Party conference in Christchurch the
word "socialism" has been bandied about frequently. The House and the country have very
clear ideas about the policies of the former Labour Government, and most realise how that
Administration intended to promote socialism throughout the country. Let us consider the
simple facts. The Labour Party's basic philosophy is socialism, as was made very clear at its
conference in Christchurch. As a result of Labour's ineptitude when in Government, the
country is experiencing many difficulties today-largely because the former Government's
leaders refused to deal with the problems when they arose or to take any firm and decisive
action.
Immigration is very important, and I am glad that the Minister of Health, who is also the
Minister of Immigration, has just spoken at length on that subject and refuted many of the
wild and misleading statements that have been made in the last year or so. I for one should
like to know whether the Leader of the Opposition would like to stop New Zealanders
travelling overseas. Perhaps he has been advised by some members of the Socialist Unity
Party that he should follow the Soviet line and not permit people to leave the country. I do
not know whether he has that at the back of his mind, but I know that he and his colleagues
are continually harping on the fact that many New Zealanders travel.
While dealing with the subject of immigration, we should all reflect on the fact that in
the three short years of the former Labour Government's term almost 90 000 additional
people came to New Zealand through immigration. That figure represents a tremendous
increase when one considers the fact that over the previous 20 years the average net
immigration gain was about 5000. It must also be remembered—and when in Opposition we
constantly reminded the Labour Government of the fact that a house is required for every
3.2 persons coming into the country. Therefore, as a result of that uncontrolled immigration,
there was a massive demand for housing and all the servicing industries, which led to an
unbelievable increase in the cost of housing and put an unprecedented strain on the
workers the people that members of the Labour Opposition claim to be so concerned
about. They were not very concerned about the workers when they were in office, as is made
clear when we consider that in 1972 the price of an average house was $16,000, whereas 3
years later, in 1975 it was $32,000. As a result, the average worker had to try to find an
additional $16,000 mortgage to be able to acquire a home. The excessive capital demand that
resulted could not possibly be sustained by our overseas earnings, and I believe the position
was clearly understood by members of the former Labour Government. At least we shall
give them credit for being able to understand that one point, even though we know and they
know that they did nothing about it.
The capital expenditure required for each immigrant amounts to $11,000. It seems that
some people, and particularly members of the Labour Opposition, fondly imagine that when
90 000 additional immigrants come in over a period of 3 years, or 30 000 enter the country in
1 year, those 90 000 or 30 000 a year-will contribute to the country's production and
increase productivity. However, that is not so. The statistics show clearly that only one in
three immigrants is a member of the work force, and the other two are dependants-either
children requiring education or older people who, in addition to housing, require health and
social services. It is very evident that Labour Party members gave no consideration to the
excessive demands on the very limited resources available.
Among many sections of rapid development, our telephone services were put under
tremendous strain; this was exacerbated by the Labour Government's refusal to take action
when the statistics showing uncontrolled immigration emerged in 1973. Nothing was done,
because the Labour Government had embarked on a policy, which has since become

Christchurch Central said something about this recently. Historically, and correctly, primary
products have been marketed by the producers through the various producer boards, and
this should continue. One is concerned when a company such as Devco, which markets New
Zealand lamb in the United States, complains that it is unable to buy sufficient quantities of
the right quality lamb. Markets must be supplied with the correct type of animal, or product,
when the market is available. It is obvious that there is some difficulty in obtaining total
unanimity between the Meat Producers Board and the export companies. They must get
together and devise a scheme that ensures that the farmer receives a premium for producing
the animals that the market wants. We must overcome this problem, but unfortunately the
time in which to overcome it is short.
It is becoming increasingly more expensive to produce animals and to process them. I


## p. 436 (#444) ############################################

436
7 June
Address in Reply
am concerned that modern processing techniques-and I refer to the mechanical pelting
machine, which has the capacity and potential to reduce significantly the cost of
processing-are not yet used commercially because of arguments between employers and
employees. I support the thoughts of some farmers that it verges on being criminal that a
machine that can significantly reduce costs is lying idle because of arguments about how it
should be introduced. We cannot allow this to continue much longer; the companies and the
employees will have to resolve their problem quickly. Costs are difficult to combat when
people are working together, but they are impossible when they are not.
I shall now touch on the expansion of the fishing industry. When the Government
introduced the Territorial Sea and Exclusive Economic Zone Bill last week, it spelt out the
intention to manage New Zealand's resources for the benefit of New Zealand. The Bill will
allow for the next stage in the development of the indigenous fishing industry, which the
Government intends to bring about as quickly as is possible. It has started happening. In
1975, exports totalled $26 million, and in 1976 they increased to $38 million. In the first 3
months of this year export volume is up by 45 percent, and the value of exports is up by $14
million, or a massive 62 percent. The development of the industry is progressing, and the
Government intends to maintain this momentum. The 200-mile zone legislation will deter-
mine the total allowable catch that can be harvested within the declared zone for both New
Zealand and foreign boats. This will be done by collating research data and arriving at the
appropriate figure. It is then up to New Zealand, through its Minister of Fisheries, to
determine what percentage of the catch can be harvested by its fishing industry, which will
have the first call on the harvest; what is left over will be allocated to the foreign fishing
boats.
It is clear that some species of fish will remain for a long time, despite the catching
efforts of foreign boats. The objective must be to expand our own catching effort to the stage
at which we phase out the foreign fishing boats. That must be the objective, and it is my
objective. During the interim we have to allocate some of the surplus catch to other
countries, and it will be allocated by species and area to ensure that New Zealand fishermen
are protected from unfair or unwarranted competition. This will entail great detail, and very
careful negotiations with the countries-and there are many-that want to fish here. All
factors will be taken into consideration, including the economic relationships between New
Zealand and each country involved.
Concern has been expressed by the fishermen and their organisations that they may be
sold out, and their interest may be overlooked as New Zealand endeavours to reach trading
arrangements. I reiterate that there is no intention, and never will be under a National
Government, to sell out the New Zealand fishing industry. The fishermen's position will be
protected. When the Government negotiates for the surplus it will take into account
everything relevant to New Zealand. It is clear that we have a long way to go in the
development of the fishing industry. It is at present very small.
The figures show that we catch about one-thousandth of the world's catch. We do not
have, as some people believe, a very large quantity of fish. We have a very large area of
water, but the quantity of fish within that water is not substantial by international standards.
We have to make the best of what is there, and that is what the Government intends to do.
For that reason the Government has allowed the industry to import large fishing vessels duty
free, making them cheaper than if they had been constructed in New Zealand. The
Government has instructed the Rural Bank and the Development Finance Corporation to
channel more money into the development of the industry-both the harvesting and the
processing sides. This type of co-operation is necessary, and it will continue. Concurrent
with that we must protect the valuable in-shore fisheries around New Zealand. Last week the
Government brought back to the House a Bill to give protection to rock lobsters, paua,
scallops, and other shellfish by licensing that industry so that it will not be exploited or
overfished, and will continue to yield an abundance to New Zealand and her fishermen for as
far into the future as we care to see.
The third stage in the development of the fishing industry is an expansion in our efforts
to farm fish. We now farm mussels, oysters, and one or two other species. We are
investigating the farming of salmon in the South Island. After completing the development
phase, it is logical that we should look at some of the advantages New Zealand can expect
from the farming of fish.

"New Zealand the way you want it." Any impartial observer of the New Zealand scene,
while he might raise one or two questions, would have to admit that, under the policies that

As you know, Mr Speaker, I, with a number of fellow members of Parliament, travelled

the United Kingdom. The Dairy Trade Federation had its annual meeting when I was there,

British decision to import 120 000 tonnes of New Zealand butter the present mountain of
250 000 tonnes would be nearly half the size.”

travelled through that part of France. This was said, at a luncheon we attended, by the most
important leaders of that region's dairy industry. W hen one thinks about it, it was a natural
response by the French and by the dairy producers in the EEC, because they see the United
Kingdom as a substantial market for their dairy produce. Already, in a relatively short time,
they have been sending more and more butter to the United Kingdom. For instance, in 1972
EEC members exported to Britain 37.4 percent of the total quantity of butter that went to
that country. Three years later that figure had risen to 74.4 percent. It dropped back again
slightly in 1976, but it is still hovering around 70 percent.
Individual countries have been substantial beneficiaries of the common agricultural
policy, particularly in dairy exporting. Again, I quote the difference in exports to Britain
between 1972 and 1975. The Dutch, for instance, sent 99 000 tonnes more to Britain in 1975
than they did in 1972, the Germans 55 000 tonnes more, and the French 35 500 tonnes more;
from those three countries alone an extra export of 190 500 tonnes. When considered in the
light of New Zealand's present quota of 120 000 tonnes, the extent of the increased sales

It is clear that New Zealand's problems of continuing access will not be solved by our
continual thumping of the table, demanding our rights because we have been supplying that
market for more than a century. I noticed that this is something that the Australians are
doing, and I cut out an extract from the Dominion, dated 2 July, headed "Fraser berates
EEC". We have to remember that as a country we are in an extremely weak position,

50 percent of the intervention price paid to EEC farmers. It is not a question of arguing
efficiency as opposed to inefficiency. The point is that they do not want our dairy produce,
nor do they need it, because our total exports are less than 1 percent of the EEC's total
consumption of dairy products.
We have to convince the EEC that it is to its advantage to give us continued access for
our produce. We have to convince it in such a way that it can see the advantage as a
community, even though there my be a short-term detriment to some of its producers, and
this will be no easy task. I believe we can deal with this problem in two ways. We can put
forward our case from a general point of view, and then we can put it forward specifically
when we talk to individual countries. It may well be that the specific approach to one country
is different from the approach to another, and that the arguments are different, one from the
other. As to the general case, we should stop talking about the case for individual
commodities. That point was emphasised when we were in Germany, in discussions with
Herr Wischnewski, the State Secretary to Chancellor Schmidt.
There is a good deal of resentment within the EEC against any external producer whose
access to the market has the effect of worsening its problems. Western Europe has a major
problem with the overproduction of butter, in particular, and it is important for New
Zealand to recognise this when developing its case. The first thing we have to do is make
more contacts with the political decision-makers, because our problems will be solved

Strasbourg as a parliamentary delegation and had detailed discussions with the agricultural

Parliament visit New Zealand to see how we operate, and to develop the close contacts that
have been built up and are likely to be built up. It was encouraging to us to find that some of
the European parliamentary members of the agricultural committee wanted much closer
contact between New Zealand and the EEC. That was an idea they put forward, and one
which I am sure will be taken up by the New Zealand Government.
The second thing we should do in putting forward our general case is to emphasise what

Last year it was necessary to introduce curbs on expenditure, with the aim of reducing
the increase that might have been expected in Government expenditure, particularly in the
areas where the Government inherited substantial deficits. Looking back, many people
appreciate that those restraints had to be imposed on education. As one of the largest

proper economic measures, it is possible to improve the quality of education. The curbs were
given many names; "cuts" and "slashes", "returns to the 1930s", and other emotional
emphases were placed on what was done. The increase in education expenditure was 17
percent that was not a cut. What the Government did was to curb the increase in the rate of
expenditure.
The imposition of a modification in the position of teachers in the day relief scheme
caused a great deal of worry. The teachers made the restoration of the original scheme their
first priority. I told them that, if they could find the $2.4 million elsewhere, I would be
prepared to accept any sensible alternative. None was forthcoming. They did, however,
make it their first priority for any new expenditure in education this year. I accepted that,
and have announced that the day relief scheme as modified last year will be restored to the
same as it was previously. The $2.4 million is now no longer available for qualitative
increases in those fields. I made this clear to the teaching profession, and it is understood. It
was not a restoration at the expense of any present financial commitment, nor was it not a
decision to substitute more spending on day relief than on some other area of educational
expenditure; it was an additional $2.4 million made available for expenditure on education in
the 1977-78 year.
I shall now briefly review one or two other matters that occurred during the year to put
the record to date into context, so that it may be examined in the light of the Budget which
will be coming down in a few weeks' time. Grants are one of the most important parts of the
fabric of education. This year, for the first time, we were able to advise controlling
authorities of their rates of grants for next year before the current year was over. Previously,
and going back for many years, grants have been announced as late as September. I have
here the record of the Labour Government, and it is hardly worth while comparing it, but
the general expenses grants for secondary education show that the increases were 4 percent
in 1973, 7.5 percent in 1974, and 8.6 percent in 1975-and that was not announced until
September 1975, with the year three-quarters gone.
Our record stands up very well. The increase last year was 12.5 percent, announced in
August, about the same time as heretofore. In December 1976, however, I was able to
announce a 15 percent increase for the current year, so that education boards knew ahead of
time what would be available for them. This has been of great assistance to education
generally, and has enabled good, sound, financial practices to be instituted. Another change
this year has been in continuous staffing. This system was successfuly introduced with the co-
operation of the New Zealand Educational Institute and education boards. We had some
teething troubles. We knew we would have them, but we have successfully introduced a
scheme, and I hope that by next year all the bugs will have been taken out. Nine hundred
additional permanent positions were created in primary education, thus effectively reducing
the student-teacher ratio from 1:35 to 1:31. Another important milestone has been reached
in the integration programme. For the first time we have made a remarkable decision-that
the amounts of money set aside for the next 5 years will be announced now, obviously in
1976 terms, so that the programme will be known by all those involved in integration. The
amount rises by varying amounts from the $1 million provided last year, until by 1981-82
there is provision for more than $17 million expenditure on integration. This means that a
programme can be carried forward in the certain knowledge that provision has been made
for it.

and of Government itself.

modern governments to regulate and control every aspect of life has never been greater, and
it continues to increase. Governments are increasingly assuming the god-like stance that they
can do and are entitled to do anything. New technology, particularly that of the computer, is
increasing enormously the present and potential power of governments and the bureaucracy
in relation to the individual. Perhaps the salient new fact of modern times is an unpre-
cedented growth in the size and power of bureaucracies and in the power of government over
people. The Deputy Leader of the Opposition, who is trying to interject, should know all
about it, because at no time in our history have the evils of which I speak proliferated more
rapidly, and no more powerful advocate for their introduction than he has existed in the long
and troubled history of the political system we have inherited. The member sits like some
fizzed-out relic of a past age.

Mr MINOGUE: It has been well said that we now have the position where governments

## p. 446 (#454) ############################################

446
7 June
Address in Reply
sustained. I repeat that these concerns are alive in all Western countries, nowhere more so
than in those which have inherited the Westminster forms and traditions of Government. It
is noteworthy also that the German Parliament has only recently completed a review, which
extended over 3 years, designed to ensure that the vital role of that parliament as a
democratic institution is effectively maintained and not eroded by the bureaucratic and other
trends of which I have spoken.
It is also relevant to observe that, in response to plain evidence of trends in the
computer field, the European Commission is urging upon all Western European states the
need to enact basic legislation to protect the individual, and to place limits upon the resultant
enormous increase in the powers of governments, so great is the potential danger to
traditionally democratic societies presented by computer technology. Of course, this tech-
nology also has advantages, but it is nevertheless seen by the European Commission as a
threat that needs to be minimised, and one that contains the potential for abuse that must be
restrained in both the public and private sectors. The key elements in the European
Commission's recommendations are the individual's right to know what is held about him or
her in any computer system, and the individual's right to correct false or misleading
information. In the public sector, there is concern that information should be used only for
the purpose for which it is gathered, otherwise through linkages of various systems the
powers of the State, through its possession and control and use of information, may reach
levels unacceptable in any society that wishes to sustain democratic principles and practices
in government.
It is a matter of comment that in the United Kingdom Parliament, from which this
Parliament originates, a Bill at present before the House of Commons is designed to remove
anomalies and dangers associated with section (2) of the Official Secrets Act, an Act which
was passed in 1911 and concerns public access to information about the affairs and conduct
of the Government. The totally negative catch-all provisions of that section are seen, after 66
years, as outworn, indeed, as dangerous. Of course, we have the identical legislation in New
Zealand. Section 6 of the New Zealand Official Secrets Act is a duplication of section 2 of
the United Kingdom Act. It would be extraordinary if after 66 years, it was not found
necessary to review and examine the appropriateness of such legislation in the radically
changed conditions of today. I urge upon the House the need to manifest the same concerns
as are currently abroad, not only in the United Kingdom but in Canada, Australia, Europe,
and the USA. The Bill now before the United Kingdom Parliament should be recognised as
providing the basis for similar New Zealand legislation. After all, we inherited the laws
concerned from the United Kingdom. If the country from which we inherited them believes
review to be necessary, we should pay heed to that.
The specific question is whether section 6 of the Official Secrets Act in this country is in
need of replacement. Plainly, it is, and, if we accept that in a democratic society people are
entitled to be reasonably well informed about the affairs and conduct of the Government,
then replaced it must be. I remind the House of the comments on this legislation made by Sir
Guy Powles. As I recollect, he remarked that it is legislation designed to protect democracy,
but that it is in fact being turned against the democracy it was designed to protect. The draft
United Kingdom Bill is notable in that it covers, not merely the question of the right of
access to information, but the individual citizen's right to privacy as well, which is why it is
called the Freedom of Information and Privacy Bill. I intend to circulate a copy of this Bill to
all members, and at an appropriate time to suggest that it should provide the basis for a
bipartisan inquiry into the need for similar legislation in New Zealand, which would be
necessary as a result of repealing the pernicious provisions of section 6. Of course, problems
are involved. There are precedents apart from the United Kingdom Act. The United States,
Canada, Australia, Sweden, Norway, and other countries have been involved in legislation
of this kind.

WEDNESDAY, 8 JUNE 1977

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Unemployment Assistance
1. Mr ISBEY (Grey Lynn) asked the Minister of Labour, In view of the fact that of
those registered unemployed under the age of 20, only 30 percent are estimated to be on
special relief work, what measures does he plan to take to assist the 70 percent for whom
nothing is being done?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): The member for Grey Lynn is
not correct when he states that nothing is being done to assist 70 percent of those registered
unemployed under the age of 20. For example, of 2224 placements made by the department
during April this year 1108, or about 50 percent, were of persons under 20. Before allocating
people to special Government work the department makes every endeavour to place them in
normal employment. Currently, most of those who are unemployed have been registered for
less than 4 weeks.
Mr Isbey: What percentage of the unemployed under the age of 20 have left New
Zealand to find work?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I can speak with no certainty on this because the statistics are
not available, but I would imagine that no person would register as unemployed if he wanted
to leave for another country.
Mr Bell: What proportion of the registered unemployed is under 20 years of age?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: The breakdown of the registered unemployed by age groups
at 29 April shows that 2464 out of 4385 were under 20. I do not have the percentage figure.
Mr Lambert: Would the Minister confirm that most of the young people under 20 or in
their early twenties who leave the country are taking the opportunity for world travel while
they can rather than travelling overseas for jobs?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: That must be a matter of opinion, because people are not
asked why they are travelling overseas, as I understand it. My observation is that most young
New Zealanders who travel overseas, do so to see other countries, but with the idea of
returning to New Zealand.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

over the previous year. In the 3 years, 1973 to 1975, the average annual increase was 26
percent.

basis, those comparisons are valid, because I think the size of the units is not strictly
comparable? Could he give us the figures on an acre or hectare basis?
Hon. V. S. YOUNG: In 1972 the average area in those types of farms was 10 ha, in 1973
it was 10 ha, in 1974 it was 9 ha, in 1975 it was 13 ha, and 1976 it was 14 ha. The average price
per hectare over those years was $3,222 in 1972, increasing to $3,686 in 1973, to $5,487 in
1974, decreasing slightly to $4,875 in 1975, and decreasing again in 1976 to $4,555.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Would the Minister explain on the fall in the years 1975 and 1976 on
a per hectare basis when the earlier information clearly indicated a rise in the value of the

Local Body Loans Authorisations
3. Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central) asked the Minister of Finance, Why has the
authorisation of local body loans in the last quarter of the 1976-77 year fallen so substantially
compared with the same quarter of the 1975 and 1976 years?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): My impression is that the
reduction in loan authorisations for 1976-77 springs from the fact that local authorities, in
common with other sectors, have exercised restraint in planning loan works. This is
confirmed by the fact that local authorities submitted 433 applications in that year, a 33
percent reduction on 1975-76.
Mr Prebble: Is the small number of applications also a reflection of the fact that local
bodies feel their ratepayers cannot afford to pay the high interest charges of approximately
9.5 percent?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I do not think it relates to that. I think it relates to the fact
that loan works are very expensive at the best of times. We have had an excessive amount of
loan work in previous years, much more than in 1976-77, and we are coming back to a
normal arrangement. Local authorities have managed to raise large sums of money in 1976-
77 for loan work, which suggests that they have some confidence that their ratepayers can
cover the charge.
Mr Prebble: Is the small proportion of loan money that has been raised a reflection of
the fact that the high interest policy of the Government is not working?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I said local authorities had been able to raise the largest
amount of loan money in any of the recent years-$238.9 million. This is the highest amount
raised in any one year by local authorities, which suggests some confidence in their capacity
to cover the loan.
Mr Wellington: Can the Minister confirm that, as an example of what he just
mentioned, the Manukau City Council, one of the largest local authorities in the country,
succeeded in raising more than $3 million last year from the private sector?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I cannot give the exact figure, but I know that local
authorities have made a successful effort to cover as much loan money as possible.
Mr Hunt: Referring to the $3 million loan of the Manukau City Council, can the
Minister confirm that the interest rate for such loans is likely to be 40 percent or more higher
than any equivalent loan the year before, and that this will be a greatly increased burden for
the ratepayers?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: That is outside the range of the question. I cannot give that
answer.

Taxation Receipts Estimate
5. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition), on behalf of Mr
MARSHALL (Wanganui), asked the Minister of Finance, What were the estimated receipts
given in the Budget for direct and indirect tax for the financial year 1976-77; what were the
actual amounts received; and how does he explain the difference?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): Estimated tax receipts given in
the 1976 Budget for the 1976-77 financial year were: direct tax, $2.659 billion; indirect tax,
including highways tax, $0.921 billion; and total tax, $3.580 billion. The audited public
account, published in a supplement to the New Zealand Gazette of 26 May, shows actual
receipts in 1976-77 to have been: direct tax, $2.894 billion; indirect tax, including highways
tax, $0.951 billion; and total tax, $3.845 billion. The increase in receipts from direct taxes is
accounted for almost entirely by income tax, as a result of growth in money incomes,
particularly salaries and wages.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Was the mistake in the estimate made by Treasury, or by the
Government in assessing its own ability to cope with the problems of inflation?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: I am sure the member knows that the Minister and the
Treasury take responsibility together. The ultimate responsibility falls on the Minister. The
growth in money incomes, which is the justification, was substantially higher than was
expected when the Budget was prepared.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Can the Minister give the figure on which the inflation estimate was
based, as compared with what actually eventuated?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: No, I cannot. I was not responsible for preparing it. At a
time of high inflation, and in terms of the former Minister's own record, the increase of 8.8
percent was not undue. The indirect taxation increase was 3 percent, which is well within
normal estimates.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: How far was the increase in indirect taxes, such as customs duties and
sales tax, the result of the Government's failure to grapple with the problem of import
levels?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: It is extremely difficult to follow what the honourable
member is getting at. He should know that any estimate is an estimate. The indirect taxation
provided for a reasonable amount. The 3 percent variation was perfectly reasonable, as the
member knows. I am sure he was distressed when incomes went up, but the increase in
incomes helped cover the amount of inflation suffered last year.

UPPER HUTT CITY (REPRESENTATION AND FINANCIAL UNIFICATION) BILL
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I am directed by the Local Bills Committee to
present the report of the committee on the Upper Hutt City (Representation and Financial
Unification) Bill. The committee recommends that the Bill be allowed to proceed as
amended. I move, That the report do lie upon the table. In speaking briefly to the report I
point out to honourable members and those interested that the Bill has been amended
substantially by the deletion of clauses 3 to 7 inclusive. Clause 3, one of the main operative
clauses, provided for the merger of the two urban wards, thereby reducing the number of
wards from three to two, comprising a rural ward, being what is known as the old Rimutaka
rural ward, and an urban ward, being the old Rimutaka urban and Upper Hutt City wards.
This move by the Upper Hutt City Council was opposed by a local ratepayers' association,
although I think it is fair to point out that some of the comments made may have been
misdirected in that they referred to the general provisions of the legislation and not to the
specific question of the Bill before us.
I shall quote briefly from the report of the Department of Internal Affairs because I
think it sums up the basic objection members of the committee on both sides found to the
particular clause: "There is objection to the provisions of the Bill which unite into one urban
ward the two presently existing urban wards. The principal grounds for objecting were that
this set aside a determination of the Local Government Commission that the three wards
should exist for 10 years, which was arrived at after considering objections to the provisional
scheme. It was suggested to the committee that the inclusion of this provision in the scheme
and its application for 10 years were virtually the conditions under which the contract uniting
the portions of Hutt County with the borough of Upper Hutt was allowed to proceed without
a poll. It is true that the commission inserted those provisions only to satisfy objectors to the
provisional scheme, and by so doing a poll on the scheme may have been averted. It is also
true that the commission had doubts on continuing the wards for 10 years when it referred to
'the feeling that by 1977 it will be time to redraw the ward boundaries of the city'." It was an


## p. 455 (#463) ############################################

8 June
Upper Hutt City (Representation and Financial Unification) Bill
455
argument that we found overwhelming, and it was one of the reasons for the changes made
by the select committee.
Another operative clause, clause 7, would have empowered the city to vary representa-
tion on the council pursuant to the provisions of section 53 of the principal Act by enabling
electors of the rural ward also to elect councillors to represent the urban ward, notwithstand-
ing the provisions to the contrary in section 54(2) of the principal Act, and by providing that
the rural ward representative must hold qualification from within the rural ward, notwith-
standing the provisions to the contrary in section 55 of the Act. I think the House would
agree that this went far beyond the general powers of the Municipal Corporations Act, and
in the opinion of members of the select committee it would have established a very
dangerous precedent. However, the committee worked through the problems and, I believe,
came up with a fairly satisfactory compromise. We entered the discussions in a spirit of co-
operation, and we certainly drew into our discussions the local member of Parliament, the
member for Heretaunga.
I think we have helped the situation as it applies to Upper Hutt City by providing, in the
proposed new clause 4, for a reduction in the number of councillors, to meet, at least in part,
the objects of the Upper Hutt City Council. This provides that, with effect from this year's
local body elections, ward representation shall be as follows: Rimutaka rural ward, one;
Rimutaka urban ward, three; and Upper Hutt City ward, eight. I also point out that a local
authority has the power to vary the numbers of its councillors by its own Act. That authority
is given in terms of section 23 of the Municipal Corporations Act, although it is also pertinent
to point out that the powers given under that legislation are superseded by the powers of the
specific Order in Council setting up the Upper Hutt City Council as we know it now. The
select committee was anxious not to negate the tenor of the Order in Council, which
provided for the merger of the ridings of the Hutt County Council and the Upper Hutt City
Council, and I believe that aim has been achieved.

Home Ownership
Mr BIRCH (Franklin): I move, That this House welcomes the lead given by the Minister
of Housing in pointing the way to home ownership for those seeking their first homes through the
use of the tax exemptions available under the new home ownership savings accounts introduced
by the National Government and supports the move to make advice more readily available by
the establishment of a pilot home guidance bureau in Auckland, and notes the Minister's
determination to assist in home ownership all those ready to make worth-while contributions of
their own to overcome the doubling of house and section prices under the disastrous 3 years of
the last Labour Government. This motion is moved to underline the crystal-clear differences
between the housing policies under a National Government and the chaos created under 3
years of Labour Government. Extraordinarily enough, it was the member for Manukau
who, as the Labour spokesman on consumer affairs, has now had the temerity to criticise
National policies when it was in his time as Minister of Housing that most of the problems
were created.
Mr Isbey: Who wrote that?
Mr BIRCH: That does not need to be written by anyone because it is well known.
However, as the public sometimes has a relatively short memory, it is useful from time to
time to set out the bare facts about the housing problems that have arisen- and I stress that
most of the problems we face today arose under the former Labour Administration. The first
point to remember is that during those 3 years of the last Labour Government a net
migration gain of 87 000 people required between 26 000 and 27 000 houses and an
investment of almost $600 million to house immigrant families alone. No wonder there was a
housing shortage. The second fact I remind the House of is that the house price index rose by
82.08 percent and the section price index rose by 162 percent during those 3 years. If we
reduce that to dollars and cents, an average house costing $13,700 in December 1972 rose to
$25,600 by December 1975. The Minister of Finance in the Labour Government shakes his
head, but it was during his time and as the result of his policies that the increases took
place—an increase of nearly $12,000 in house values in 3 years, or $4,000 a year, which was
more than any family was able to save and much more than some families were earning at the
beginning of 1972. That is the crux of the present housing problem. Even worse, an average
section which in December 1972 cost $3,785 had risen by December 1975 to $9,100, an
increase of over $5,300 in only 3 years under a Labour Government. That rapid increase in

Mr Birch: That's right.
Hon. R. O DOUGLAS: Well, let us look at the real cause of the increase in prices. The
problem began back in 1967 when the present Prime Minister used the building industry as
his whipping boy. Thousands of qualified building staff were driven overseas while housing
completions were reduced to about 22 000 a year, although demand was for 30 000 houses.
In 1972, when the day of reckoning drew close, the National Government boosted the
money supply by 28 percent in its inflationary election-bribe Budget. Secondly, it increased
the finance available from the Housing Corporation without in any way increasing the
productive capacity of the industry. Those two measures taken in the dying stages of 1972
created a large gap between the number of permits issued and the number of completions in
the housing industry during 1972-73. Secondly, they resulted in the major increase in prices
that occurred in 1973-74 and 1974-75. It was, in fact, left to the Labour Government to bring
speculators under rein and house prices back to a 5 percent annual increase in 1975. The
National Government's housing policy is a disaster, and 10 areas can be identified easily.
Disaster area No. 1 is the Government's failure to hold housing costs. The real cost of
housing is the cost per week of buying one's own home. In 1975 a married man with three
children, and who earned the average wage, could expect to borrow sufficient from the
Housing Corporation on a one-mortgage basis to buy his own home. Today that is not
possible. In 1975 the weekly repayments for the average wage earner amounted to $25 a
week. Today the average wage earner can expect to pay between $60 and $75 a week. The
repayment costs of a mortgage-that is principal and interest-under the Labour Govern-
ment in 1975 amounted to $40,000 over the period of the mortgage. Repayment costs to the
average wage earner now amount to $100,000 over a 30-year mortgage period. That is the
true cost of the National Government's housing policy.
Disaster area No. 2 is the availability of housing finance. First, I am thinking of the
availability of housing finance from the Housing Corporation. It has gone down and down.
Loans for new houses are down by 20 percent; loans for the purchase of existing homes are
down by 41 percent; loans for refinancing are down by 63 percent; family benefit capitalisa-
tion loans are down by 63 percent. Low income supplement loans are down by 56 percent,
and total urban loans are down by 32 percent. Private sector loans—and this was the area
that was to receive a great boost from a National Government—are virtually unavailable
unless one is prepared to pay 18 percent. Recently, the Northern Building Society-the
largest of its kind, with over 180 000 members-stated that its loans had to be cut back by 25
percent and that new shareholders had been advised that there was a waiting list of at least 4
years. The AMP Society has suspended all applications for loan finance because the
company is unable to meet demands. Disaster area No. 3 is the failure of the Government to
hold section prices. Housing Corporation section prices have increased from $1,000 to
$3,000 as a result of the deliberate action of the National Government, which abolished the
section remittance scheme introduced by the Labour Government. Private section prices are
up. Major builders in Auckland and elsewhere have increased their prices about $2,000 as a
result of the suspension of the private loans scheme. Section prices in Napier have increased
in the last 6 months by $1,700, or at a 3-yearly rate of $10,200. In New Plymouth, section
prices are up by 31 percent for the 6 months to December 1976, or by 62 percent a year. In
Gisborne, section prices have increased by 23 percent in 6 months to December 1976, or by
46 percent over a year.
The fourth disaster area in the National Government's housing policy is its failure to
provide section finance. Private section and Housing Corporation section finance schemes
were abolished by the National Government with the result that young couples are unable to
buy their own homes. The fifth disaster area is that of rents. During the 18 months of this
Government, Housing Corporation rents have increased by as much as 130 percent in some
cases. Today, a man earning $120 a week and with a child under five, and whose wage
increases from $120 to $140, would find that this National Government will take at least $18
of that $20 increase from him in increased rent and taxation, yet the Minister of Housing
suggests that young couples can save $12,000 in 3 years. The sixth disaster area is the whole
arena of refinance. There is at least one forced house sale a day, the highest rate since a
National Government was last in power. This is just the tip of the iceberg, because most
people get out of their own volition before being taken to court, but their situation is just as
wasteful and just as tragic as those who have a forced sale. Disaster area No. 7 is the state of
the building industry. If the present trend continues-and production is down 20 percent in
the last 2 months-overall production in the next 12 months is likely to be 21 000 to 22 000
units, with the inevitable result that production will once again fall well behind demand. I
