Economic Crisis
Mr WELLINGTON (Manurewa): I move, That this House notes with interest the
economic analysis of Mr J. V. White in the Dominion of 27 May in which he concludes,
"somehow the message has to be got across that we have been living beyond our income for
several years and that this is a situation which could not have been allowed to continue”, and
commends the Minister of Finance on the sound, realistic, and constructive approach to the
nation's most severe post-war economic crisis, which, after the relatively brief period of 18
months, has succeeded in halting the worst economic trends, thus giving the people increased
confidence in New Zealand's future as reflected in the results of the 30 April Heylen poll.
I want to focus on the two main themes of the motion. The first is that New Zealand is in
the grip of the most severe post-war economic crisis, and the second is that the third National
Government has succeeded in halting the worst trends so that it is possible today to speak of
a recovery. The country has taken a step back from the brink; and the extent of the disaster
the country faced can be indicated by two statements made by Professor Brownlie at the end
of the 1974-75 financial year. I remind the House and the country of these, the first of which
states: "The Government's economic policy"-referring to the former Labour Government,
of which the member for New Lynn, who is trying to interject, was a member-“is still based
largely on a policy of borrow and hope." Professor Brownlie's second statement was: "Here
we are at the end of 1974-75, not quite in bankruptcy, but getting very close to it."
The extent of the recovery can be verified by facts. When a Government member was
referring to Treasury projections last night I was very interested to hear the Labour member
for Wanganui say, "That's another Treasury projection." His comment is another cliché
from the slag heap of socialism, because it illustrates the frivolous disregard of members
opposite for specialised financial expertise, and characterises the Labour Opposition's
refusal to face the realities of economic life. What are the facts? Fact No. 1 is the rate of
inflation, which at the end of 1975 was running at 15.7 percent. However, in the last quarter
the increase was 2.6 percent, which is the lowest in 3 years. Fact No. 2 is the Government's
deficit before borrowing, which, if the Labour Government had continued in office, was
estimated would reach a record of $1,400 million by March 1976. Labour members opposite
might care to know that such a deficit was a major cause of the inflationary tendencies.
This Government has taken the necessary steps to restore some equilibrium. The result
is already showing through, as the Government's deficit before borrowing is now $506
million; in other words, that unparallelled deficit has been halved. How has that been done?
By doing those sorts of things that have aroused members opposite because they did not
have the fortitude to face up to their responsibilities. We have debated the increases in
transport and Post Office charges, but let me say that no Government likes having to
implement tough policies. However, the National Government will not shirk its respon-
sibilities.

"Muldoon Economic Miracle"
Mr COURTNEY (Nelson): I move, That this House notes with alarm the record 16
percent increase in inflation recorded in the consumer price index for the 1977 March year; and
the record high interest rates now required from home buyers; and the record increase of $532.7
million in income tax, half of which was collected by mistake; and the record outward
migration flow of almost 17 500 for the 1977 March year; and the 23 percent rise in food prices
in the 15 months since the election; and the drop of over 5000 from Labour's peaks in the
number of houses completed in the latest year are being described as the "Muldoon economic
miracle", and speculates exactly how bad the figures would be before being described as “the
Muldoon economic disaster". I gave notice of this motion last week to bring into focus a
statement made by the president of the National Party about the "Muldoon economic
miracle". What kind of economic miracle have we witnessed during the past 17 months of
the National Government? Could it have been some sort of miracle in which the Prime
Minister changed wine into water and that wine or water, or whatever it was, left a very
bitter taste in people's mouths? Could it have been the miracle of the loaves and fishes? The
price of a loaf of bread has increased from 18c to 32c while fish prices have gone up by over
30 percent since this Government took office. Could the miracle perhaps have been in the
immigration-cum-emigration policy of the Government, because net emigration now stands
at close to 17 500? These people have used a variety of means to leave New Zealand, but not
the miracle of walking across water.
I intend to talk about unemployment, the taxation system, the iniquitous raising of
Government charges, the vicious slashing of subsidies, and, if I have time—and an extension
of time may be necessary-our balance of payments, but I want to talk particularly about
inflation and the cost of living. This irrational National Government talks a great deal about
freedoms, but the people will remember this Government most for the freedom they have of
paying higher prices for their groceries while having no say whatsoever in the matter. This
Government removed from the Commerce Act the provision whereby consumer groups had
the right to make representations to and to sit in on price hearings. This Government also
abolished the MRP scheme and put nothing in its place. It has caused record inflation, as
witnessed by the 16 percent increase in the consumer price index, which I found on page 2 of
the latest Abstract of Statistics.
When the going gets tough, as it is at present, families put off buying new cars and
television sets and spend more of their income on food. During May, food prices rose by a
staggering 2.5 percent. If at the beginning of the month you spent $30 a week on your food
bill, at the end of the month you would have needed $30.75 to buy the same quantity of
goods. Just as the taximeter keeps on ticking over, regular as clockwork, food prices keep
ticking over at the rate of 2c a day. Food prices have risen by 26.7 percent since the
National Government came to power; and this is an area in which the Government has most
control-food, vegetables, meat, poultry, and so on. In the area that comprises over half the
food bill and excludes fruit and vegetables, meat, fish, and poultry, we have seen a massive
increase of 35.7 percent. What kind of an economic miracle is that? The president of the
National Party has been shooting his mouth off about an economic miracle. That is absolute
rubbish.
One of the freedoms dear to New Zealanders is that of owning the roof over their heads.
In the last day or two members opposite have made great play on the fact that in the time of
the third Labour Government house prices rose by 83 percent, but those very smug members
did not go on to say that during their 17 months in office so far the true cost of housing has
doubled. Typical loan repayments have doubled, which consequently doubles the cost of a
housing loan. I am, of course, assuming that the opportunity is there to buy a home; or,
under this Government, is it a privilege to own one's own home? Despite the $17,000 quoted
by the Minister of Housing in the House yesterday, statistics I obtained from the Housing
Corporation indicate that the average Housing Corporation loan to purchase a house
decreased from $14,700 in March 1976 to $13,700 in March 1977, and that in the same period
house prices rose, on average, by $2,500. This gap is widening day by day and week by week.
Some people are paying over 20 percent for second mortgage finance.
The National Government claims credit for reducing inflation, but an exercise in the
booklet Incomes and Prices, put out by the Prime Minister's Department at the taxpayers'
expense, highlights the factors contributing to inflation. If the same exercise were done
today, I suspect that half the inflation in the last financial year of the third Labour
Government would have been caused directly by the increase in import prices, over which
the Government can have no control whatsoever. In the first year of this irrational National
Government, less than one-third of the inflation was caused by import price increases. This

CHATEAU COMPANIES BILL
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That the Chateau Companies
Bill be introduced. I hope that the House will agree to my following the precedent set by the
member for Henderson when he introduced a not dissimilar Bill in 1975, by allowing me to
introduce the measure pro forma, and make one speech to the second reading.
Bill introduced and read a first time.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I move, That this Bill be now read a
second time. My first duty in introducing this legislation is one of reassurance. Insuperable
difficulties have arisen which cause the Government to believe that the best opportunity to
keep open the hotels known as "Chateau Commodore" at Blenheim and Christchurch can
only be accomplished by the passage of this legislation through all its stages tonight. No
fewer than 10 adjournments of the court proceedings at Christchurch about the three
Chateau properties have been granted. The legal difficulties involved, together with many
rumours of possible sales that have not so far eventuated, have caused discomfort to staff,
trade suppliers, customers, and travel agencies.
The Bill deals with much of that uncertainty without in any way interfering with the
proceedings before the court. Therefore, before coming to the detailed reasons for this Bill,
I want the people who fill any of the roles I have just mentioned in relation to the Chateau
properties to be reassured that the Government in its efforts has their interests as much in
mind as those of the many people who are the unsecured or secured creditors of the three
Chateau companies. The proposed action has been suggested by all the major parties, and
represents the one example in any of the companies dealing with Securitibank in which
considerable savings might be made for the benefit of all concerned, and in which it is now
clear that the law cannot adequately respond.
The Bill is a salvage operation, like certain other Acts that have been passed in the last
few years. However, it is quite different in character from these earlier Acts. What it does, in
essence, is to enable the Chateau hotels to be sold as going concerns with a clear title to the
land, leaving the legal arguments and court proceedings to go ahead against the proceeds of
the sale in exactly the same way as if those proceeds were the land. No rights, or supposed
rights, are affected-they are simply transferred from a maze of encumbered titles to a trust
fund. It appears that nothing short of legislation can achieve this.
There are three Chateau hotels, each owned by a different company. Those at Blenheim
and Christchurch are operating as accommodation hotels, while that at Timaru operates as a
dining and entertainment facility. The main shareholder in each company is, or has been, Mr


## p. 474 (#482) ############################################

474
8 June
Chateau Companies Bill
H. P. Holt, whose activities in cattle syndication have for some time been under investiga-
tion by both the police and the commercial affairs division of the Justice Department. Two
cattle syndication companies, in which he was associated with Mr J. Williams, have been
ordered to be wound up on the petition of the Registrar of Companies. A third such
company is expected to follow suit when the registrar's petition is heard later this month.
Each hotel was built, or partly constructed, by H. P. Holt, Ltd, another of Mr Holt's
companies. There is grave doubt as to whether the usual standard of building contract
documentation ever existed, and it seems that a simple "charge-up" operation left a loose
situation between the building and owning companies. That, the Government believes, is a
basic cause of the present court proceedings.
Neither the hotel companies nor H. P. Holt Ltd could finance the buildings, and moneys
were advanced, or obligations incurred to Merbank Corporation Ltd, now in liquidation;
Safe Custody Nominees Ltd, now in liquidation—both companies are purportedly secured
by mortgage and/or debenture; subcontractors of H. P. Holt Ltd, whose claims are protected
by registered and unregistered liens; and unsecured creditors of goods and services who have
no security, and a few other mortgages; the only substantial one being for a sum of over
$400,000 on the property at Timaru in favour of Perpetual Trustees. The financial position,
in summary, appears to be that there is more than $10.5 million claimed in respect of the
hotels, the greatest proportion of which is claimed by Securitibank companies which, of
course, were using publicly subscribed funds.
In late 1975 H. P. Holt Ltd, the builder, petitioned the court to wind up the three hotel
companies. The petitions were adjourned, and remain so, but a provisional liquidator was
appointed by a judge to preserve the existing position. Petitions to wind up the building
company have also been adjourned. The validity and priority of Merbank's mortgages and
securities are under challenge, and doubt exists as to the priority of the Safe Custody
Nominees Ltd mortgage as well. The lien claims of subcontractors depend on establishing
rights under the contract to each hotel and a balance owing under the contract to cover this.
The Blenheim and Christchurch hotel sites comprise the titles listed in the schedule to the
Bill, and there is very little coincidence as to the securities registered on individual titles, or
even of the priority of such charges. A claim that Merbank was in a joint venture with the
Chateau companies in building hotels could, under the provisions of the Wages and
Contractors Liens Act, result in the liens of the subcontractors being required to be first paid
from any repayment of the contractor's mortgage. The position is completely confused, and
as each new claim is made the court has adjourned the claim and all preceding claims.
At the time that the provisional liquidator was appointed, Merbank, which was then not
in liquidation, appointed a receiver for the three hotels in terms of its debentures. The
receiver therefore took over the management and control of the hotels, and the provisional
liquidator appointed by the court has very few effective functions available to him. The
receiver has been running the three businesses for 18 months, and they have become
established operating units in their communities. Both the receiver and the provisional
liquidator have been looking for buyers for the hotels, as all parties see their sale as the only
practical way to keep the hotels open while the complex court proceedings are resolved.
Clearly, the hotels are better sold as going concerns than as closed down bricks and mortar,
and the nature of the hotel and tourist trade is such that a going concern is worth a great deal
more than closed-down premises.
It seems desirable, in view of the loss by accruing interest, inflation, and the enforced
tying-up of capital, that this be accomplished at the earliest possible date but without "fire
sale" haste. That cannot be done until someone is able to sign a tranfer giving good title to
the land, and is able to sell the chattels and fittings of the hotels to the same purchaser
unencumbered. It appears likely, even if we waited until the court was able to sort out this
most complicated series of actions, that we might still find that one person was able to deal
with the land or a part thereof, and the buildings or a part thereof, while another or others
were entitled to deal with the equipment, plant, or furniture. There could be no guarantee
that those persons could agree on a sale and division of proceeds.
In late February this year, in an attempt to assist the parties, the Registrar of Companies
met with solicitors and various parties in an effort to get a formal agreement that the hotels
could be sold and that the litigation could then proceed in respect of the proceeds for sale.
All parties agreed that this was a good idea, but it has not proved possible to get a consent in
a form to which all could agree, and, in particular, agree to strip lien holders of their rights
by asking them to discharge their liens. Indeed, it is not clear that the court could sanction
such an arrangement and continue the existing proceedings as if the hotels had not been sold.


## p. 475 (#483) ############################################

8 June
475
Chateau Companies Bill
I have twice met delegations led by Mr Brian McClelland Q.C.; who acts for the provisional
liquidator, and the Government has given very full consideration to the problems. Mr
McClelland's proposal, which the Government intends to accept, is that the Government
intervene and by Act vest, free of encumbrances, the real and personal properties that
constitute the operating hotels at Blenheim and Christchurch in one trustee upon a trust for
sale. With a large outside mortgage to Perpetual Trustees, it is not necessary to vest the
property at Timaru free of encumbrance, as no challenge could be raised to the validity of
the Perpetual Trustees mortgage and that company's right could not in any way be affected.
The Bill, therefore, vests in Mr Kenneth James Jensen, a senior partner in Gilfillan,
Morris and Company, all the assets of all three hotel companies, and, except for the title to
the land at Timaru, with those assets being freed from all encumbrances but with fencing
covenants, local body rights, easements, and caveats fully protected. The intent is that Mr
Jensen will be better able to continue the hotel operations at Blenheim and Christchurch and
to investigate and, one hopes, continue the business at Timaru. It is certain that, if the legal
problems associated with the titles and encumbrances on other assets are not removed, the
hotels would close and the assets would then be sold on a "bricks and mortar" basis by the
particular person entitled to sell the particular asset or piece of land. In addition, such a sale
would not be possible until the court had resolved many complex legal points. If the hotels
had been put into mothballs, the losses to subcontractors, contributories in the Safe Custody
Nominees Ltd mortgage, and to commercial bill holders through the Securitibank mortgages
and debentures would have been very substantially higher. In addition, this Bill should result
in trade creditors agreeing to continue to supply the hotels believing that they will stay open,
and it should result in all bookings to the hotels, particularly by tour operators, being
properly secured.
It is necessary that the Bill proceed through all its stages tonight so that there can be no
uncertainty in the minds of any of the people associated with the hotels-those who have
bookings, those who supply it, those who work for it, and, not least, those who are owed
money. As the House has been previously informed, the Registrar of Companies is
conducting a full investigation of the Securitibank group. The links of that group with the
Holt-Williams companies in Christchurch also concern the Government greatly. The regis-
trar has for some time been conducting an inquiry into those companies, including the
Chateau companies. This Bill should not in any way be thought a criticism of the court
process or of the gentlemen-the provisional liquidator, Mr Restall, and the receiver, Mr
Beattie-whose efforts have kept the hotels open. But their efforts to find buyers have been
frustrated by the fact that, even if a buyer had been found for a goodly proportion of the
funds put into the hotels, neither of them, nor both of them acting together, could have sold
the hotels with clear title. Both gentlemen have offered their closest co-operation with Mr
Jensen, who will act as a trustee from 7.30 tonight. The Government hopes that this Bill will
result in the continued operation of the businesses concerned until a proper sale is negotiated
by the trustee. The Bill will also stop these properties being sold at "bargain basement"
prices, while allowing all the parties to continue the existing proceedings before the court or
to commence such new proceedings as may be proper.
I now turn to the clauses of the Bill. The substantive provisions of the Bill are contained
in clauses 3, 4, 5, 7, 12, and 13. Clause 3 applies the Bill to the three companies-Chateau
Commodore (Blenheim) Ltd, Chateau Hotels Ltd, and Chateau Commodore (Timaru) Ltd,
and under clause 4 a trustee is to be appointed to administer the assets of those companies.
Subclause (2) of clause 3 appoints Mr K. J. Jensen of Christchurch as the first trustee, while
subclause (3) provides for the appointment of different or additional trustees. Clause 5 vests
the assets of each company in the trustee. In the case of the Christchurch and Blenheim
hotels, the trustee takes the land free of encumbrance except for easements such as rights of
way and sewer easements, fencing covenants, and local body restrictions. In the case of the
Timaru business the trustee takes subject to all encumbrances. As I mentioned earlier, the
different circumstances of the Timaru company require different treatment. In respect of
chattels and other personal property, the trustee takes free of all encumbrances.
The duties of the trustee, set out in clause 7, are to take possession of the assets for the
benefit of creditors, to protect and preserve and manage those assets, to sell them, and to
hold the proceeds on trust to be applied in accordance with clauses 12 and 13. After payment
of the expenses of the trustee and certain preferential payments, clause 12 requires the
balance to be held for the secured creditors, with any balance going to unsecured creditors
and the companies. Clause 13 spells out the rights of secured creditors. Instead of rights
against the property of the companies, the creditors will have rights against that part of the


## p. 476 (#484) ############################################

476
8 June
Chateau Companies Bill
trust fund that represents the former security. The court is empowered to determine the
respective values of the realised assets. The court is required to determine the validity,
value, and priority of the various securities as if this Act had not been passed. In short, the
legal disputes will be resolved on the situation that existed before this Act. An omnibus
savings provision is contained in clause 24. The remaining clauses are of a machinery nature.
As is usual in legislation of this kind, the Bill is deemed to have come into force at 7.30
this evening. Clause 6 vests in the trustee the liquor licences under which the three premises
are operated. Without this provision the businesses would have to close at least temporarily,
and the whole purpose of the exercise could well be lost. Clause 8 applies particularly to the
Timaru business. It enables the trustee to look at the situation there, and decide whether to
allow the mortgagee to take over or to carry on the business himself. If the mortgagee enters
into possession, any balance on a sale must be paid to the trustee. Clauses 9 and 10 give the
trustee the usual powers to enable him to carry into effect the intention of the Act, while
clause 11 enables him to seek additional powers from the court. Clause 14 casts a duty on
those carrying on the companies or the businesses to surrender to the trustee all relevant
books and property.
Clause 15 protects the trustee for all acts done by him so long as he acts in good faith.
Clause 16 allows the trustee to recoup the expenses of administering the assets. Clause 17
provides for the discharge of the trustee. Clause 18 requires the trustee to report from time
to time to the Minister of Justice on the affairs of the businesses taken over and his
administration of the assets. Clause 19 is an offence provision. Clause 20 requires the trustee
to report to the Solicitor-General any offence against this Act or any breach of trust. Clauses
21 and 22 make the usual provision for the advance of money to enable the trustee to fulfil
his functions. Clause 23 varies the application of the Companies Act to the three companies.
The effect of the clause is that the companies, during the time the Act applies to them, will
not have to keep accounts or make returns, nor will any receiver be required to make any
reports. I thank honourable members for their courtesy.

What we have tonight is a little different from the legislation that preceded it, and which
I had the responsibility to introduce. Examples are the Cornish and the Perpetual Trustees

liquidity. In both those cases, members on both sides of the House were at pains to credit the
sincerity and integrity of those involved, and to say that there was certainly no moral

know. The Minister may be able to give an assurance on this later, but I sincerely trust that is
the case here, too.
This is called the Chateau Companies Bill but, as disclosed by the Minister, many of the

me if this is the last legislation we are likely to see that is related to that collapse, and if it is

moment of registration. The position is different with the lien, and it may depend not only on
the moment of notification or, as it were, registration, but also on the date of completion of
the work involved and the capacity of the lienor to assert the right of the claim he makes, all
to be encompassed within the lien period involved. There may be some difficulty in
determining where priorities lie between the various claims, on the one hand based on a land
transfer mortgage, and on the other under the contractors' liens Act. It may be that the
Minister can enlighten us a little more about that, although I believe this is an aspect that will
ultimately have to be determined by the proceedings currently before the court, or perhaps
by other proceedings yet to be instituted. As the Minister said, the title has to be transferred
from a maze of encumbered titles to a trust fund. I believe this will be a problem that will
confront the Supreme Court for some considerable time.

reason that a clear title was not available to the receiver or the liquidator was the
complicated nature of the liens, the mortgages, and the caveats. In Christchurch, there are 6
land titles involved in the property which we know as the Chateau Commodore, and on
those 6 titles there are 84 liens, 4 caveats and 7 mortgages, all of which are under challenge
through the courts. It would be impossible for any liquidator or receiver to resolve those and
to be able to sell with a clear title.
The hotel in Christchurch is unique. I do not think that would be disputed by any
member who attended the State banquet at the Chateau Commodore at the end of the
Queen's visit. Each hotel is elaborately unique, but that is no reason to close them down. If
the hotels are trading profitably, they must be given a chance to continue as going concerns
and to be made available for sale as going concerns. Most of those in Christchurch who have
been following the saga of the rise and fall of the Holt empire are aware of the value of these
hotels to Christchurch, Blenheim, and Timaru. They are very imaginative in design, and a
great tragedy will ensue if their affairs are not sorted out-and we know that they are
extremely involved. They are so confused and complicated that it is possible that the courts
may take anything up to 2 years to resolve them. In the meantime, what is the receiver for
the debenture holder to do, and what is the provisional liquidator to do? They cannot sit and
twiddle their thumbs and allow these valuable properties to deteriorate, which is what
would happen if this Bill was not passed. The hotels have been catering for tourists and
dinner guests sirfce the date of the wind-up order, and have been continuing to provide the
services for which they were built. Current debts are being paid as they are incurred, but the
receiver is under pressure. If any major supplier decided to stop providing goods and
services to the hotels, all the other suppliers might decide to do the same and, as a result, the
hotels would close. The receiver and the provisional liquidator would be faced with even
greater losses than those they are potentially faced with at present. The hotels have an
established clientele and a goodwill value based on the fact that they are trading and have a
reputation. If we allow them to be closed down, we are left with buildings that have no value
other than as shells. That would be a tragedy for the tourist and hotel industries, and for
Canterbury and Marlborough.
The encumbrances on the land are multiple, and the Court has an unenviable task in
trying to sort them out. Any lawyer in the House would shudder at the prospect. The Bill is
protective legislation, providing for the trustee to take the main asset. It is almost like a
whirlwind, lifting out of the middle of the whole legal argument the one property which is
there. It will remove it and protect it, and place it on one side away from the litigation, the
arguments, and the wrangles about the priorities of the registered charges and which has the
rights first-the mortgages, the liens, or the caveats. The protection of the buildings and the
land will enable the trustee, Mr Jensen-who is a highly reputable chartered accountant in
Christchurch, and who has previously been appointed liquidator of several companies-to
deal with a clear title. It will in no way hurt any other people who have prior claims. The Bill
completely protects all the registered mortgages, claims, liens, rights, responsibilities, and
charges. It allows the court to deal freely with those and to state priorities, but it enables the
buildings and the land to be removed from litigation so as to enable some cash to be
resurrected and some salvage operation to be made for the protection of the creditors, both
secured and unsecured. This will be a tremendous relief to many people in Canterbury.
There will be even greater relief when all these affairs are sorted out, but the knowledge that
the Bill is being passed through the House tonight will be of immense value to those who
have struggled so valiantly with the affairs of this group and who have tried, so far without
success, to salvage something for the creditors and to make some progress in the winding-up
of the companies.

Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): I thank the honourable members who
have taken part in this debate, and I particularly thank my counterpart the member for
Henderson for his sympathetic response. I do not suppose that he felt any better in 1974 and
1975 than I do now. I shall deal first with the remarks made by the member for Timaru. As
he noted, I did refer to clause 8 which applies to the Timaru complex and enables the trustee
to decide whether to allow the mortgagees-in this case Perpetual Trustees-to take over or
carry on the business themselves. If the mortgagees take possession any balance after a sale
must be paid to the trustee. Perpetual Trustees clearly hold the first mortgage, and I am sure
the honourable member would agree that the discretion must be left to the trustee.
I turn now to the points raised by the member for Henderson. He asked if there would
be any more of this kind of legislation, and my response must be the same as his was in 1975.
I believe this is the last one; and there is certainly no indication at the moment of any similar
circumstances requiring legislative interference. The honourable member then asked
whether separate sales were possible. The answer is yes, but the money must be paid into
one trust fund, as set out in the Bill, and the court will decide on the proper division.
I do not wish to pursue the question of who might buy the hotels, or what price they
might pay, because I believe that should properly be left to the trustee. Our main concern
must be to keep the hotels operating and provide, by this legislation, clear title so that the
public interest, which we have identified as the continued operation of the hotels, is best
served.
The member for Henderson then referred to the relationship with Securitibank, and
wondered whether Securitibank was not in a similar position in the Government's mind. I
have already published widely the fact that the documentation of that group's affairs was
found to be quite clear, in sharp contradistinction to those we are dealing with tonight. As
the House knows, the Government, at the request of the management and other interested
parties, asked the Company Law Advisory Committee to investigate Securitibank's affairs.
The Company Law Advisory Committee unanimously declined to recommend the use of the
Companies Special Investigations Act 1958. In other words, the existing law was found to be
adequate in dealing with the affairs of Securitibank.
The member for Henderson then referred to the priorities, and asked what would
happen if there was conflict between encumbrances under the Land Transfer Act and liens
under the Wages Protection and Contractors Liens Act. These matters can be settled only in
court; and that is where they will be settled. He then asked whether benefit would derive for
Securitibank or its public from the mortgages, and the answer is for itself and its contributory
mortgages-but as Securitibank is insolvent its creditors will receive any cash that there
might be.
The Leader of the Opposition quoted remarks made by the present Prime Minister on
the Perpetual Trustees legislation. He must understand quite clearly that in 1975 the
Chateau companies were already in receivership, so any remarks made then about Perpetual
Trustees would possibly apply to the Chateau companies as well. The failure of these
companies resulted from uncontrolled costs of the building operation, and probably also
from the high costs of financing the capital involved. The companies went into receivership
almost from the inception of their trading, and trading has certainly not been a factor in their
failure.
The Leader of the Opposition was also concerned about clause 11 and the additional
powers that may be conferred on the trustee by the court. It is not possible for me to say
what those powers might be. This is a precautionary measure, and the granting of such

ADDRESS IN REPLY
Interrupted debate on the question, That a respectful Address be presented to His

Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): Yesterday's adjournment interrupted my comments
about the need to revise section 6 of the Official Secrets Act. It is the negative catch-all
section that governs access to information about the activities of the Government and its
departments. Strict interpretation of that section would result in such absurdities as its being
an offence for a cleaning lady to reveal publicly the number of aspidistras in a particular
Government building. That could be the culmination of strict application of the section. Of
course, it is not so applied, and we hope it never would be, but it does indicate the nature of
the catch-all provision involved. Section 6 has become quite inappropriate to the circum-
stances of today, and this is not surprising, because the basic enactment came into being 66
years ago. Yesterday I referred to the current commitment of the United Kingdom
Government to review the corresponding section in the United Kingdom Official Secrets
Act; and suggested that, since the United Kingdom and the New Zealand sections were
identical, and the workings of government in both countries are similar, there is something
to be said for using United Kingdom guidelines. Such a guideline may be found in the
proposed United Kingdom Freedom of Information and Privacy Bill, a copy of which has
now been forwarded to each member of the House for his or her information. Sensibly, the
United Kingdom legislation attempts to reconcile the right to know with the individual's
right to privacy.
I trust that I have said sufficient to indicate that despite the legitimate preoccupation of
the House with matters concerning the economy there are other matters demanding
attention if the democratic nature of our political institutions is to be assured. Significantly,
as I have previously said, the need for positive action along the lines suggested has been


## p. 486 (#494) ############################################

486
8 June
Address in Reply
recognised and acted upon in other Western countries, notably Canada, the United States,
Australia, the United Kingdom, Norway, and Sweden.
Sadly enough, it is all too easy to be over-simplistic about what is required; all too easy
to pick up a precedent from abroad and say that this will do for New Zealand, and to imagine
that this, in itself, will solve the problems with which we are involved. That approach is naive
and simplistic. I hope we can avoid it, and thereby avoid the futilities that have attended its
adoption. At least, I hope we can embark upon discussions on reform in a responsible and
bipartisan spirit, encouraged by the fact that we are involved with legislation that was
formulated 66 years ago and, through the process of time alone, is in need of review. It has
been overtaken by changes of the kind that I referred to yesterday. It is legislation that in the
conditions of today, to paraphrase the words of the former Chief Ombudsman, "threatens
the democracy it was ostensibly designed to protect". I hope that in good time we will reach
some responsible solution.
The history of other countries is relevant to any attempt to remedy the state of affairs
posed by section 6 of the Official Secrets Act. The history of the United States Freedom of
Information Act, the record of the inquiry that preceded it, the record of the inquiry that was
held on the amendment needed after 6 years of operation, are all revealing of the
frustrations and the barriers that are placed in the way of reform of this kind. They are
inevitably placed by those with a vested interest in the status quo-and they are usually
found associated with the larger bureaucracies apart from anything else. The catch-all
secrecy, of course, acts as a cloak for their incompetence—and in the eyes of some people
that is a valuable cloak to have.
I refer to the sad history of events in Australia, which provided a lesson of what not to
do. The Whitlam Government was committed to reform similar legislation in Australia, and
it seems incredible that to achieve that purpose it set up a committee of bureaucrats, a
committee of people attached to the Government itself, to suggest how they should reform
the procedures according to which they worked. Predictably, after 2 years, that committee
produced recommendations that made a bad situation worse. The House should note, as I
have, the efforts of the former Minister of Justice to achieve some progress in this country. I
understand that he was instrumental in establishing an inter-departmental committee for this
purpose. In fact, as a result, a small working party of officials met only once and no decisions
have emerged even to this day. That is the kind of thing we can expect by attempting reform
of this kind per medium of an inter-departmental committee. The experience elsewhere
suggests that is an abortive reform procedure. The history of the Swedish legislation shows
that there are those in that democracy who, notwithstanding the passage of such an Act, are
ever ready to frustrate its true intent and purpose.
The events in the United Kingdom that superseded the commitment to review the
United Kingdom Official Secrets Act concerned an alleged secret involvement of the United
Kingdom Government in the Biafran war. They led to a court hearing, in which a judge was
obliged to pass severe strictures on section 6, but the history of those proceedings and the
history of the conduct of the court case and subsequent events make sad reading to all
concerned with the positive aspects of reform. They show how easily the positive aspects can
be bogged down in futile debate and argument, futile time-serving and time-wasting, and
partisan dispute. The record of debates in the Canadian Parliament and subsequent
committee hearings tell us the same things.
As a result of my inquiries, I am persuaded, first, that section 6 of the Official Secrets
Act must be replaced if New Zealand is to maintain even a pretence of being an effective
democracy. I am persuaded further that there is need for considerable care and responsibil-
ity for thorough investigation and inquiry into the legislation to repalce section 6. Thirdly, I
am persuaded that the House and some committee of Parliament-not an inter-
departmental committee-are the proper vehicles for proposed reform. A Freedom of
Information Act along the lines of the United Kingdom measure is not a cure-all for
anything. It does not, in itself, provide a guarantee of continuing democracy, but it does set
us on a line of positive evolution by which the democracy we have inherited might be
maintained. To do nothing in the face of challenges presented by change is to be thoroughly
negative, like section 6 of the Official Secrets Act itself, at a time when we are required to be
more alert and more positive in our efforts to preserve the political institutions and
arrangements we have inherited.

To the mover of the Address in Reply, the member for New Plymouth, I offer my
congratulations on a very well thought-out speech, as I do to the seconder, the member for
the southern tip of New Zealand, the member for Awarua. When I last spoke in this House I
was talking mainly about the economy, and probably baiting the Labour Opposition at that
time. Tonight I intend to devote myself more to the requirements of the Otago Central
electorate, taking into consideration the economic situation. First, I shall refer to some of
the successes of the Government during the past 12 months.
Mr Hunt: What about Scheme F?
Mr COOPER: I will deal with Scheme F and educate the member for New Lynn on it
shortly if he will only be patient and stop waving his tongue so much. When this Government
took office in 1975 it was confronted with the unrestricted growth in public sector employ-
ment, and certainly in public expenditure, that had occurred under the Labour Government.
The Prime Minister appointed the member who is now Minister of Energy Resources as
chairman of the Cabinet committee on expenditure to look into the tremendous escalation of
the Public Service work force. During the 1972-75 term, 22 000 extra staff had been
appointed. The committee looked at the resources of the country, with a population of only
3 000 000, and said, "Can we afford to have a rapidly increasing Public Service work force?"
The answer, of course, was "No". The principle applied was that of not filling as many
vacancies as would have been filled under the Labour Government. The idea was to fill five
positions for every six that became vacant, thus reducing the wage budget and the number of
departmental houses required. Some success has been achieved, with a 1.5 percent reduction
in the actual public sector work force and a consequent 1.25 percent reduction, or $50
million, in the wage bill met by the New Zealand taxpayer for this section of the community.
It is gratifying that not one person has been forced into unemployment by such action. When
a person retires, transfers, leaves on an overseas trip, or dies, he is not replaced. In other
words, there is less administration and more productivity.
Mr Hunt: What about Scheme F?
Mr COOPER: Well, with Scheme F, people will be employed in both the public and
private sectors. This successful and painless exercise kept unemployment at a low level and
kept people in productive work, and has been very much part of the economic resurgence
created by the National Government.
During my maiden speech last year I spent some time speaking about the very serious
results of the rapid increase in the number of people receiving the domestic purposes benefit,
and it was with some delight that I learned that the Government intended to set up the
Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee. I look forward with interest to its findings
and the Cabinet recommendations on them. The cost of the domestic purposes benefit for
27 000 recipients is a staggering $84 million. One problem associated with the benefit is that
it takes away one's initiative. A person eligible for the domestic purposes benefit has two
options: to go on the benefit or to remain in the public sector work force. Many people in my
electorate find that working 40 hours a week, paying for their transport and clothing, and
possibly for someone to look after the daily needs of their families they are at a disadvantage
compared to those on the domestic purposes benefit. In fact, those who remain in the work
force often find themselves no better off, and many of those who want to return to the work
force see that those who are receiving the benefit have far more leisure time and enjoy a
relatively higher standard of living.
There is a strong case for special recognition for those who wish to enter the work force,
providing their children are not placed at a disadvantage. New Zealand needs those people
in the work force and there should be some form of tax incentive to keep them and to help
them to make up their minds whether to accept the benefit or remain in the work force. If
that does not happen then the 27 000 people receiving the benefit will increase to 40 000
because there is a tendency to move towards a greater dependence on welfare. I want to
make it absolutely clear that I believe implicitly in a social security system that protects the
rights and needs of those who are in need. Opposition members who are trying to interject
are past masters at spending everybody else's money. That is why they are in Opposition.
People outside do not trust them and they have no ability to run the country.

acres can be brought forward through the development of irrigation in that area. What is the
difference between Scheme F and Scheme H? Scheme H flooded 8 orchards; Scheme F
floods about 16 orchards. We are talking about saving between $60 million and $80 million
over 10 to 15 years, and a loss of 8 orchards producing fruit from about 60 hectares. How are
we to do something for the orchardists involved? They have been told that they will have at
least 3 more years in their areas, and that they can come to the Government and, through the
generous compensation written into our policy with the amendments to the 1975 Act, will be
able to find another property or another way of developing in some other part of New
Zealand. I believe that many of them are reasonably happy to move off those orchards.
It is difficult, when land is being taken for a massive public work, to please everybody,
but there will be savings in capital cost, earlier bulk of power in the 4-year period, better
roading-$500,000 allocated last week for taking those vicious bends off the Lindis Pass road
and for reseal work—an investigation of irrigation, and new roading that will be of benefit to
the area and to the new project.
I believe that in our 1975 policy, which stated that compensation would be generous and
would take account of special circumstances when land was taken in the public interest, we
did what was required by a Government representing all the people. We know that we have
to do something positive. We feel that the aspects dealt with during the application for water
rights for irrigation will guarantee beyond any doubt that the recreational use, the irrigation
use, and the energy use will make the Clutha Valley a better place when the developers
move after, say, 20 years, to other areas of New Zealand. Finally, I should like to devote
some of my time to the problem of TV2 coverage in a sparsely populated urban electorate.
Mr SPEAKER: I am sorry to interrupt the honourable member, but his time has
expired.

Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): As the member will know, this
is a Budget matter and it would not be appropriate for me to comment on this question. I
might say that the decision was made last year in order to ensure that scarce resources were
used more effectively, and to induce some level of restraint where there was a high level of
importing.
Hon. W. W. Freer; As the Minister has said that this is a budgetary matter, can he

assurances in that direction.

Brucellosis Reactors
4. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Agriculture, How many brucellosis
reactors were identified last year, and how many is it expected will be identified during the
current year?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): The brucellosis testing season operates
from 1 September to 31 August. During the 1975-76 season, 35 000 reactors were identified.
For the current season, 1976-77, 17 000 reactors have been identified to date. The total for
the current season is not expected to exceed 20 000. The reduction for the current season in
relation to the previous year is as expected, and reflects progress being made with the bovine
brucellosis eradication scheme.
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is the Minister's estimation for this year's programme based on the
percentage of the number of cows tested and the number of reactors, and the programme to
the end of September?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No. The 17 000 reactors identified to date are those that have
actually been processed.
Mr Bruce Barclay: How was the 20 000 figure arrived at?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: One arrives at that figure by having a guestimate from what the
officers think they will be getting in.

Industrial Stoppages-Days Lost
7. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Labour, How many working days
were lost in 1976 due to strikes, and how does this figure compare with the previous 6 years?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): Working days lost in 1976
through strike activity were 488 165. The figures for the previous 6 years are as follows: 1975,
214 632; 1974, 183 688; 1973, 271 706; 1972, 134 505; 1971, 162 563; and 1970, 277 348.
Mr Marshall: As the days lost so far this year are running at about three times last year's
record figure-28 715 days lost to the end of February compared with 9919-does the
Minister expect an improvement this year?
Mr SPEAKER: That is a request for an opinion.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: It is indeed, Mr Speaker. It depends very much on the labour
movement in New Zealand. If the individual industrial parties will follow the constitutional
processes of the law provided by Parliament, there need be virtually no industrial loss; and if
members from both sides of the House, but particularly Opposition members because they
are associated with the labour movement, would urge the industrial parties to use the
constitutional processes, we need not have the rate of industrial loss that we had in the first 2
months of this year.
Mr Luxton: Can the Minister indicate the percentage of days lost in the freezing
industry?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I can do that only from table 18 in the Monthly Abstract of
Statistics. The total number of days lost in the first 2 months of this year were 28 715. In the
meat export works, which is the proper classification, 19 071 days were lost, or about two-
thirds of the total loss.
Mr Marshall: The Minister said that approximately 488 000 days were lost. Does that
figure include non-industrial stoppages, and if not, what would the figure then be?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Table 18 indicates that any stoppage which is the result of
disagreement by workers with measures taken or not taken by the Government or other
authorities as distinct from employers is excluded.

Hospitals for South Auckland
10. Mr DOWNIE (Pakuranga) asked the Minister of Health, Would he confirm that two
new hospitals are to be built in South Auckland, name the location of the sites, and say how
many beds each will have and when the hospitals are expected to be commissioned?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Health): The Government has approved the acquisition of
land for construction of general hospitals in the East Tamaki and Papakura areas, and has
approved the preparation of service and design briefs. The site at East Tamaki lies between
Botany Road and the Papatoetoe-Howick main highway. It is at present owned by the
Housing Corporation and can be made readily available to the hospital board. Land at
Papakura is privately owned, and a particular area has yet to be chosen. Current planning is
for ultimately up to 300 acute general beds, 128 geriatric beds, a 20-bed psychiatric unit, and
a 20 to 40-bed obstetric unit. The phasing of the development is such as to permit maximum
flexibility during the planning and construction period to permit changes in accordance with
varied needs or new technological advances. It is hoped to commission phase one of the first
hospital in 1980. Subsequent phases will be commissioned at intervals until complete
development is reached in 1986. The aim will be to develop the two hospitals simultaneously.
Mr Downie: How does this commissioning date compare with the date for the previous
proposition for the Wiri hospital?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Without notice I could not be sure, but the Wiri hospital was quite an
expensive and different proposition of a high-rise building where I would expect the
engineering problems, particularly the foundation problems on the lower levels, would have
been a big contract. To get something such as the Wiri hospital to a stage where you could
use it might well have taken until 1985 rather than 1980.
Mr Hunt: The Minister indicated that 1980 would be the earliest expected date for
completion of part of the hospitals. Can he indicate whether or not this would be 2 years
behind the proposals of the third Labour Government for the development of the facilities in
South Auckland?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I categorically deny the suggestion in that question. The site at Wiri
was bought by a previous National Government. When the present Government came to
power, no progress had been made. The member should know that it would not have being
possible to build an 800-bed hospital of that high-rise complexity in anywhere near this time.
This is not the complete health proposal. A health centre will be started this year in
Manukau City. There will be additional staff-more health assitants, more community
nurses, and more practice nurses. There is a great deal going on immediately, whereas
before the Labour Government did anything it would have sat and waited until white paper
legislation had been put in place.
Mr Wellington: Is the new concept of development of health services in South Auckland
in keeping with the wishes of most people in that area, ascertained as a result of the
Minister's many visits there; and can the Minister confirm that the nursing staff of the district
office in Wiri has been increased from 26 to 35?
Hon. T. F. GILL: I confirm the last figure, and also that we have on the estimates for
this year-authorised some months ago-a further $1.9 million to enable doctors to employ
hospital nurses in their surgeries, and to be available for domicillary care in the homes of
their patients. It is my understanding that the programme embarked upon is in accordance
with the wishes of the people, is in accordance with good, sound medical practice, and is in
accordance with the National Party policy on which it so resoundingly won the last election.
Mr Hunt: Notwithstanding the Minister's reply to my earlier question, will he now
answer the question I asked him—namely, is it not a fact that he has indicated a 2-year
further delay in the provision of facilities to patients in the South Auckland area?
Hon. T. F. GILL: The member's question contains a travesty of the facts. There is not a
2 years' delay. Authority has now been granted for the purchase of the land. We will get the

back to the National Water and Soil Authority, and appeal rights would still be available to
the people affected.

Catchment Board, which will also consider the multiple use of water for irrigation, power,
and possibly industrial purposes.

and can he give an assurance that in the interim no site preparation work will proceed?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG: My understanding is that the procedure to be carried out by the
Otago Catchment Board will take about 4 months. If the decision goes to appeal the period
could be as long as 12 months. In the meantime, an environmental assessment will be made
on any proposed work, and that applies to any extra work carried out at the proposed DG3
dam site as well as to the road deviation. The House should know that there has been a full
environmental report on the DG3 dam site in relation to scheme H, and therefore the fact
that there will be a dam there has been confirmed in all the schemes and has been covered by
the report, particularly as it relates to siting and site activity.

Hon. W. L. YOUNG: The honourable member can take it as he likes. The fact is that

can make up its mind and not dilly-dally when making a decision. Obviously Opposition
members do not care whether power planning goes awry and the people suffer power cuts,
but when scheme F goes ahead certain adjustments can be made. That is why we are
approaching the Otago Catchment Board—to ensure that the water rights, and particularly
those mentioned by the Labour spokesman on agriculture, are fully protected.

FREEDOM OF INFORMATION BILL
Mr PREBBLE (Auckland Central): I move, That leave be given to introduce the Freedom
of Information Bill. A hundred years ago, in promoting the first great Education Act, Foster
told the British House of Commons that Parliament, if it wished to protect democracy, must
educate its masters, the voters. Today, if we as a Parliament wish to promote democracy and
want democracy to be more than the latest television commercials, then we must ensure that
our masters, the voters, are kept informed. That is the objective of this Bill.
The objects are clearly set out in the preamble: "An Act to establish the public's right of
access to official information: Whereas the people of New Zealand have a political right to
be informed by their Government concerning the public business so that the people may
participate more fully in the democratic process; and whereas open government is necessary
for a strong democracy:" The key clause is clause 3, which reads, "... any person shall have
a right of access to official information." The Bill is divided into four parts. The first part
gives a right of information and obliges civil servants to keep information in such a way that


## p. 499 (#507) ############################################

9 June
499
Freedom of Information Bill
it is readily accessible to the public. Part II sets out the exemptions. Everyone concedes that
the Government has a right to keep some information confidential, and I have drafted these
exemptions on the side of caution because this Bill is the first step towards open government.
This is a serious Bill, and I hope the Government will seriously consider its adoption. The
exemptions are matters of New Zealand security, criminal investigations, personal records,
trading secrets, medical records, and Cabinet deliberations. They are self-explanatory.
Part III sets out the process of appeals, and states that the public's right to freedom of
information shall be enforceable by an application to the Administrative Division of the
Supreme Court, which I believe has the independence, integrity, and public support to be
the appropriate appeal authority. I gave consideration to a tribunal, but New Zealand
already has too many tribunals and the Supreme Court can best do the job of appeal
authority. Part IV states that the Act would be administered by the Department of Justice,
and has a key provision that the department must report every year to the House on the
progress of the legislation. The departments and bodies covered by the Act are set out in the
schedule. In clause 11 the Governor-General has power to add to the schedule, but no power
to delete a department from it. Members will notice that in the schedule that not only have I
covered departments of central government, but have also attempted to cover all the local
bodies and statutory bodies which at present have so much control over our lives. As a
precedent for this I have taken the New Zealand Ombudsman Act. I maintain that a person
has just as much right to information affecting him which may be in the Prime Minister's
Department as he has to information affecting him which may be held by his local pest
destruction board.
New Zealand is lagging behind the rest of the world in this field of freedom of
information. The United States, Scandinavian countries, and Holland are democracies with
working freedom of information legislation, and the United Kingdom, Canada, and
Australia are considering draft Bills. Members interested in this field will realise that I have
drawn upon all that legislation in drafting this Bill, but the overall shaping of the Bill is my
own work. While I do not pretend that all drafting problems have been resolved, I believe
this Bill is workable. A little later I will move that it be referred to the Statutes Revision
Committee so that evidence can be called and so that, with the combined wisdom of both
Opposition and Government members together with the services of the Department of
Justice, we can produce from this Bill a workable Act.
Many reasons have been advanced for the need for this type of legislation. Sir Guy
Powles has been a champion of the cause. Only this year he stated that New Zealand has
suffered too long under a closed-shop system of government. Numerous civil liberty groups
have called for freedom of information legislation, and the Commissioner for the Environ-
ment, as reported in the Evening Post this year, suggested that Government departments
could look at ways of making more information available to the public. Even the Young
Nationals in May this year called for the repeal of the Official Secrets Act and suggested it be
replaced with a freedom of information Act. One of the major recommendations in the
report of the Frank Holmes task force on economic and social planning called New Zealand
at the Turning Point is that more information be made available. The report points out that,
because of secrecy, quite often the right hand of Government does not know what the left
hand is doing.
The member for Hamilton West advanced as a reason for freedom of information
legislation the need to check the growth of Executive and Cabinet power. The Canadian
royal commission put the case very clearly when it said: "No democratic policy should rely
on the executive to police itself no matter how dedicated, well informed, honest, and hard
working its officers. If medical practitioners bury their mistakes, public officials hide theirs
under a cloak of secrecy." Secrecy should not be removed just to expose errors but because,
in a public process, errors are less likely to occur. The passing of this Bill would lead to not
only more efficient but better government. I noticed that in the United States, where there
has been some criticism of its freedom of information legislation, the customs department
found that by publishing its manuals the number of appeals was reduced from 50 000 to
11 000. In New Zealand, if the immigration section of the Department of Labour were to
publish the secret criteria by which it admits people into New Zealand, thousands of appeals
that clog that division would be greatly reduced. If the New Zealand Electricity Department
were to publish the criteria, which are at present secret, for its energy us proiections, we
could have an intelligent debate on whether or not New Zealand needs atomic power.
This Bill would have a dramatic effect on the news media. Members will recall that last
year the Prime Minister and his press secretary took the press to task for its alleged failings.


## p. 500 (#508) ############################################

500
9 June
Freedom of Information Bill
The Prime Minister in particular criticised what he said was a tendency to concentrate on
trivia; but the position is that the public and the media are not entitled to many of the facts
behind key issues facing Parliament and this country today. In some areas the Government
has a complete monopoly of information. Our media is not truly free when it is denied the
information it needs to keep its readers and viewers informed. This Bill would give us for the
first time a truly free news media, and if it became law I am sure the House and the country
would be agreeably surprised.
I was motivated to begin drafting this Bill by my anger that, as a properly elected
member of Parliament, I am unable to take part constructively in debates on issues facing the
people of Auckland Central because I do not know all the facts that lead the Government to
make many of its decisions. I believe that, on behalf of the people I represent, I should have
that information. We cannot have true democracy unless we have open government. In
moving this measure I acknowledge the pioneer work done by the member for Henderson,
who, as members know, at the time he was Minister set up a departmental committee to look
into this field. For this Bill to work the Government would need to introduce amendments to
the Official Secrets Act, and that line of action would have support from this side of the
House because for far too long that Act has needed amendment. My Bill is not a panacea,
but freedom of information, by involving citizens in their Government, and by informing the
voters, would help to restore the faith of the people in democracy, improve government, and
result in a better New Zealand.
Mr MINOGUE (Hamilton West): In raising this subject in my Address in Reply speech
I stressed the need for great care and responsibility in drafting any legislation dealing with
freedom of information for this country. I regret that I cannot look upon the document now
presented as being a responsible Bill. I shall go into the whys and wherefores of that opinion
in a moment. I appreciate and share the concern of the member for Auckland Central, but,
in sharing his concern, I cannot share his naive approach to the whole problem of freedom of
information. Indeed, I think it could be said that if there is anything I admire it is the
intellectual virginity of the member for Auckland Central. There is no lack of precedents for
freedom of information. I could table 50 in the House now, some fairly in line with what has
been drafted. Here is one from Nauru Island, probably just as simplistic; then there are
those from Sweden, the United States, the United Kingdom, Austria, France, Scandinavia,
the Canadian Bar Association, and Australia. The place is full of them; the world abounds
with them. The easiest thing any intellectual virgin could do would be drop a draft Bill in the
House, and say, "That is the answer to the freedom of information." Let us take a journey
around the world on the subject of freedom of information and look at some history.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Most of the Government members are doing that already.
Mr MINOGUE: The most naive gentleman of all is the one who is now interjecting. He
would not know the time in regard to freedom of information, and would see freedom of
information as freedom from information, the establishment of wonderful bureaucratic
forums and institutions such as his own Government had in mind when it was in power.
Good heavens, when we think of freedom of information we remember that if ever there was
a freedom-from-information Government it was the previous Labour Administration.
Having said that I record my respect for the personal endeavours of the member for
Henderson to achieve some progress in this field. Let us look at the traps which abound in
the freedom of information field. The United States has been quoted. I have made an
extensive study of the whole of the United States scene, including the hearings of the Senate
and committees which preceded the passing of decisions on the freedom of information. I
know that it took 10 years of study and such hearings before the first Act was passed, and
that, 6 years later, so unsatisfactory was the Act that it was amended. Some of the comments
made when it was amended include a letter from the United States Senate, Committee on
the Judiciary, Washington, D.C., and it is signed by Edward M. Kennedy. It states: "Last
week the freedom of information Act celebrated its sixth year of operation. During that
period of time the Act has brought about numerous changes in policies, as well as in
practices and procedures. . . While these changes have been beneficial, the expectation of
Congress that the doors of government would be opened to the public has not been fully
realised. Thus around 200 law suits have been instituted against the Government to require
disclosure of information, and this subcommittee is faced with the task of fashioning
legislation to clarify and strengthen the law." That took 10 years to pass. In fact, throughout
the American record there is clear indication that that first Act, painful though it was in its
origin, became in fact a freedom from information Act, and was cited as such.
In the United Kingdom the move towards an amendment to the Official Secrets Act,


## p. 501 (#509) ############################################

9 June
501
Freedom of Information Bill
which is the basis of this problem, began about 5 or 6 years ago following disclosures about
the British Government's involvement in the Biafran war. Mr Heath's Government was so
concerned that it set up the Franks Commission, which recommended certain changes. The
Labour Government in Britain became similarly committed, but not along the simplistic
lines suggested by the Franks Commission. Indeed, the lines to be followed have recently
been stated by the Home Secretary. I quote from a report which appeared in the
Christchurch Press of 26 February on the situation in the United Kingdom: "Five years after
an Old Bailey judge suggested that a section of Britain's Official Secrets Act-on which New
Zealand's is modelled should be pensioned off, the British Government had agreed to
reform. Section 2 of the Act that binds all unauthorised disclosure of Government informa-
tion is to be altered. . . But in announcing the proposed reforms, the Home Secretary, Mr
Mervyn Rees, said the changes would not get on to the statute book until at least 1978. Mr
Rees said section 2 would be replaced by a more liberal law and one which would be more
precise... British criticsm of the Act has mainly been directed against section 2 and there
has been little call for section 1—which deals with espionage. The New Zealand Act closely
follows the 1911 British Act, and is in places word for word. The beginning of the end for the
British section 2 came in 1971 when the Sunday Telegraph, its editor, Brian Roberts, and a
journalist, Jonathan Aitken—now a Conservative M. P.—were charged under it for disclo-
sures about Britain's role in the Biafran war. The defendants were acquitted and in his
judgment from the Old Bailey bench the judge said section 2 should be pensioned off. As a
result of the case the Conservative Government of the day ordered a committee of inquiry.
The committee recommended in 1972 that the bulk of the Government's business should no
longer be protected by an Official Secrets Act but that a new official information Act would
protect only the vital areas such as foreign affairs, defence, currency, and the reserves,
together with Cabinet discussion and decisions."
The draft Bill now before us would protect far more than that. Indeed, this Bill would
make non-disclosure more the rule than it is now for reasons that will become apparent later.
"Mr Rees said"—and here are some significant references-"that his proposed reform was
even more liberal than that proposed by the Franks Committee. A notable departure from
the report was the non-secrecy of some Cabinet papers." There is blanket exclusion in this
draft Bill of Cabinet papers while the British are in the process of working on it.
Mr Hunt: You could move an amendment to it. Don't destroy it.
Mr MINOGUE: The Bill is beyond amendment. A new Bill is required. The report
continues: "Mr Rees said that while the need to safeguard the collective responsibility of the
Cabinet remained fundamental the Government did not think that Cabinet papers deserved
the special protection of criminal sanctions. The reform will still include certain areas of
defence policy and strategy and of international relations, where unauthorised disclosure
would be prejudicial to British interests, to relations with a foreign Government or to the
safety of British citizens. Confidences of the citizen in matters like tax and social security
would also be maintained. Mr Rees summed the reform up by saying that it secures the
highest degree of protection for information, the disclosure of which might cause serious
harm to the interests of the nation."
The Bill I have circulated is a private member's Bill presented to the British House of
Commons, and the Government in the United Kingdom is expected to produce legislation in
1978 along the lines indicated by the Home Secretary. We can be assured that it is
thoroughly more liberal legislation than that suggested by the Franks Commission. I should
now like to turn to the Australian scene, where we have a most unfortunate situation, the
kind of situation in which the previous Government almost found itself. The Labour
Government of Mr Whitlam was committed to introducing a freedom of information Bill
along the lines of the United States legislation. For that purpose it established an inter-
departmental committee. Its report was dated September 1974, and covers between 30 and
40 pages. It took more than 2 years to produce, but it recommended a situation that closes
the door to more information than it would have disclosed. There is a bureaucratic
defensiveness or bureaucratic attitude to this matter which manifests itself, despite good
intentions, in the closing of more doors than it opens.
There is editorial comment on the inter-departmental report in the Sydney Bulletin of 14
August 1976 which summarises the essentials of the United States legislation from which I
shall give some brief excerpts. The essentials of the United States legislation can be briefly
stated: all Government departments and agencies must give a right of access to documents in
their files; any member of the public can exercise this right by specifying the document he
wishes to see; a department may not refuse to make a document available unless it falls

agencies.

6(j), quite apart from 6(b) and 6(c), he will find, "Information, the premature disclosure of

degree of protection-but no more than adequate protection-to that which is truly

Protection of that kind is secured in New Zealand by the Official Secrets Act, but I

at any rate before the Bill was introduced, the member for Hamilton West was saying out
loud and publicly that he agreed with that view, and shared my criticism of the Official
Secrets Act. As has been mentioned, I did set up an interdepartmental committee centred on
