Secrets Act if that were necessary and if the desired result could not be achieved by
appropriate provisions in the Crimes Act. I should be interested to know what progress was
made by that committee, and indeed whether it is still in being; I should also be interested to
know whether it is assisting the member for Hamilton West, or vice versa, to achieve the end
he is so anxious to attain and which the Government now proclaims is desirable of
attainment.
The present Bill has drawn on many precedents, and has, from my brief consideration of
it, incorporated the best features of all of them. As the member in charge of it has agreed, it
is by no means the last word, and he will be very ready to accept further improvements if
they can be suggested either by members of the House or by people giving evidence to the
Statutes Revision Committee. I for one welcome it. I believe it deserves full debate, to which
I enter one somewhat hesitant note at this stage.
It is a fact that what has been done in the United States has produced some spectacular
results, but the overall consequence has aroused some disappointment. The legislation has
resulted in a large and expensive set of administrative machinery, but has been very little
used in some states. There is no disputing the need for freer access to information of this
kind, and to public records generally. There is no disputing that those in charge of
information of this kind are far too prone to plaster it with a variety of rubber stamps ranging


## p. 506 (#514) ############################################

506
9 June
Freedom of Information Bill
from "confidential" to "top secret". There is, however, some feeling that the best way to
achieve this is not by legislative command but by administrative reform, or perhaps by a
combination of both. We are setting out on one path. It may be that to achieve the result it is
desirable to proceed along another path at the same time.
I have been struck by the activity that has been carried on in Australia through the
Attorney-General's department, and I was interested to read a report of an inquiry
embarked on by the Australians. The summary of conclusions runs to several paragraphs,
and I should like to cite two of them that are very much in point and relevant to the measure
before us. "The content of the freedom of information legislation requires an appropriate
balance to be made between the public interest and openess of access to information, and
public interest in maintaining the confidentiality of certain kinds of information." That is
what I believe this Bill sets out to do, and in my judgment it achieves it.
The other point is this: "The basic principle to be embodied in freedom of information
legislation should be that a person without the need to show any interest would have a legally
enforceable right of access to any identifiable document relating to public affairs in the
possession of a department unless that document is in a category of exempt documents to
which access may be denied." Whatever access may be available to the courts today to
enforce the production of documents of this kind depends entirely on the applicant being
able to show a special interest—a locus standi before the courts. Merely to say he is a
member of the public and as such is entitled to the information that has been collected at
expense to which he has contributed is not enough. He must show a special interest and,
generally speaking, the likelihood of a pecuniary loss if access to the document in question is
denied. That severely restricts any right of access that can be pursued through the courts;
and I think it negates any true freedom of information.
The object of this Bill is to open up that access, but not so widely, as the Acting Prime
Minister said, as to make an absurdity of it and to interfere with proper Government
consultations before a Government decision is reached. I have always believed that the
options should be open for a Government to change its mind before it had made up its mind;
and to require the Government to disclose its line of thinking could be prejudicial to
Government action. This Bill would not enforce anything of that kind. It would reserve the
right of a Government to close its doors during the time discussions are taking place, as it
should have the right to do. Once a decision is made, however, it ought to be in the public
domain. For the Government here, as Governments traditionally elsewhere have done, to
insist on overcautiousness and a greater right than is necessary to conceal from the public
that which is its entitlement to know is, I believe, wrong.

Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Before I call the next member perhaps I could make one or

be the motion put. The motion for leave to introduce a Bill, whether it be a Government Bill
or a private member's Bill, has traditionally been more misused, probably, than any other
that is debated in this Chamber. This is a private member's Bill. Traditionally, after the end
of such a debate-in which members are allowed to speak for 10 minutes each-provided the
main purpose of the Bill is not an appropriation and that an appropriation is only incidental,
such as in this case, the House has granted the private member the right to a second reading.
That debate is the normal type of second reading debate in which we discuss the principles of
the Bill. Normally also it is of limited duration in the number of speakers allowed.
I draw the attention of the House to the fact that we are having, in effect, two second
reading debates on the one question. That is highly irregular. Standing Orders are quite clear
that a question can be debated only once in each session, otherwise we just set about wasting
our time. That is quite inappropriate; we have better things to do. The custom has grown up
of having, in effect, two second reading debates on the introduction of a private member's
Bill one on the introduction and another on the second reading. I invite members to
consider this matter very carefully. Perhaps it could be appropriately brought up before a
meeting of the Standing Orders Committee, if one should be set up, but I do invite members
to consider it very carefully and at least to bring in occasional reference to the need for the
introduction of the Bill, and not simply debate what this Government did, what that
Government did, and what they could have done or should have done. That seems to be
hardly relevant to the main purpose of the motion-that this Bill be introduced.

I also point to two statutes operating at present that may in practice restrict the
availability of that information to us, but in law do not. The Bill will further restrict the
availability of that information. Exemptions are provided in sections 19 and 20 of the Oaths
and Declarations Act 1957. Clause 6(c) of the Bill states, "Any communication between
Ministers of the Crown including Parliamentary Under-Secretaries" shall be exempted and
kept secret. Sections 19 and 20 of the Oaths and Declarations Act 1957 provide that a
Parliamentary Under-Secretary makes no oath of secrecy. Section 23 (1) of that Act requires
the Executive councillor's oath to be taken as soon as he is appointed to the council. In
practice, this means that the oath is taken by Ministers of the Crown at the time of their

## p. 514 (#522) ############################################

514
9 June
Freedom of Information Bill
appointment, because successive Governments have observed the practice of appointing all
Ministers to the council. However, there is no legal requirement to this effect and it would be
possible, although unlikely, for a member of Parliament to be appointed as a Minister but
not as a councillor, in which case there would be no entitlement on him to take the oath of
secrecy.
In law, the effect of the oath is to protect the nature and content of advice tendered
formally to the Governor-General by Ministers acting as Cabinet or individually in the
Executive Council. In theory, it is open to a Minister, whether or not he or she as a member
of the council divulges what takes place in Cabinet, without any legal impediment and
without breaking the councillor's oath except in so far as the matters that are disclosed are
connected with material before the council. This Bill will close down that possible avenue of
information.
Has the member for Auckland Central considered an amendment to section 27(3) of the
Crown Proceedings Act 1950, which states, “. . . any rules made for the purposes of this
section shall be such as to secure that the existence of a document will not be disclosed if, in
the opinion of a Minister of the Crown, it would be injurious to the public interest to disclose
the existence thereof"? At first sight it would appear that the actual existence of a document
can be denied by a Minister if he considers it should not be produced in evidence. Until fairly
recently the impression would have been given that a court would accept such a denial as
conclusive without further inquiry, but that impression would no longer be tenable.
Developments in the law, particularly in England with the Crossman diaries case, suggest
that no discretion is absolute.
Notwithstanding the tenor of the statutory language conferring that discretion, evidence
will be sought as to the nature of the grounds upon which that decision is made. Perhaps the
most surprising aspect of this development is that at present Ministers are not immune from
a court's inquiry, and there are reported cases where a Minister's decision has been quashed.
That will be taken away by this Bill.
Because of constitutional convention and common law, Parliament has the right to insist
upon the production of documents, and I remind the member that an Act of Parliament
overrides the common law. Has the member for Auckland Central considered this issue?
What effect will this Bill have on the right of Parliament to insist on production of documents
and the answering of questions? Under the provisions of clause 6(c) what would happen if
the member for Tauranga, an Under-Secretary, wanted to ask the Prime Minister a
question? Would that be exempted because it would be a communication between a Minister
of the Crown and an Under-Secretary?
The appeal procedures set out in clause 8 are hopeless. If a person is declined
information, what we want is speed and an effective remedy. We should be able to go direct
to the court for an injunction. That would cut out the need for clause 9(1). Has the member
for Auckland Central considered whether we should go to the courts or to an Ombudsman?
In his introduction the member said with some satisfaction that the schedules were taken
directly from the Ombudsmen Act 1975. Then where is the name of the Legislative
Department in the schedule? Why has it vanished? Why is it in the Ombudsmen Act 1975
but not included in the schedule of the Freedom of Information Bill? Is it an oversight or a
deliberate omission? Where are the guards for sufficient staff to do all this work, for
sufficient time to deal with mischievous cases of persistent litigants? Where are the guards
against the holding of illegal records, the use of illegal information, or the use of disinforma-
tion?
As a member of the National Party I support open government. That means freedom of
information, not freedom from information, which the Bill is offering to us. It is offering to
close down avenues that at present are able to be used and legally are there for us to use.
This is a freedom from information Bill. The member for Auckland Central should have left

Freedom of Information Bill
The section of law dealing with Crown privilege-an important and complex section of
law evolved over centuries-is totally ignored. It is a section of law that cannot be ignored in
a Bill of this nature. Section 2 also refers to an "individual person". Presumably qualification
of the word "person" with the word “individual" means that information that cannot be
made available about individuals can be made available about clubs, societies, companies,
trade unions, and all other associations. The reasons for applying this to persons but not to
those associations is not made clear. These persons will simply not give the Government any
information that is detrimental to takeover bids and industrial negotiations, or any other
delicate issues. While that has been recognised in the personal front it has not been extended
to companies, trade unions, or societies.
Clause 4 requires that all information be indexed. When we seek what has to be indexed
we find this in the definition of "official information". It includes "material obtained or
compiled by, or provided for, an agency in the course of performing its functions and duties
which is held by, or is in the control of or under the supervision of that agency in any form";
also "any manual, instruction book, memorandum, or other document compiled by or issued
for the use of an agency's employees or agents", and the like. The suggestion is that these
documents have to be compiled by every one of the bodies mentioned in the first
schedule-about 2000 bodies. The reference to a "first schedule" is a little redundant,
because there is no other schedule. It is another example of the hard work and research that
went into drafting the Bill.
About 2000 bodies will have to employ persons, and it is expressly provided in clause 5
that persons are to be employed for the purpose, and they are to keep an index of every
document they possess. The index is to be kept up to date at all times. If that index is not
kept up to date any person in the country, whether or not he has an interest in the matter, or
whether acting on his own behalf or acting on behalf of anybody else, can bring an action in
the Supreme Court. That is in respect of any minor breach or any single document missing
among the many millions of documents held by these organisations. An action can be
brought in the Supreme Court by anybody, whether they have any locus standi, or any
special interest or not. The Supreme Court is enjoined by clause 9 to drop everything and
give first priority to determining the matter. If there are 2000 or 3000 applications in the first
week the Supreme Court will be out of commission for a year. What answer can the member
for Auckland Central give to that? As a practising lawyer he could not have failed to notice
that. This problem would have to be overcome before the Bill could become law, yet there is
no attempt to do so.
There is no evidence in support of the contention that the Bill represents the distillation
of the very best legislation found in other countries, brought together after many hours, even
months, of hard work by the member for Auckland Central. It exhibits none of the
symptoms of being such a measure. It flies in the face of the Public Bodies Meetings
Amendment Act 1975, passed by the Labour Government, which focuses on the question of
how much information should be made public. As a Government, the Labour Party's official
views were expressed in that Act, and section 4 provides that any local body may by
resolution exclude its proceedings from the public "if publicity would be prejudicial to the
public interest by reason of the confidential nature of the business to be transacted", or for
other special reasons. That view was put forward unanimously by members opposite who
were in Government in 1975.
Those views have not been included in the Bill introduced by the member for Auckland
Central, nor has it been suggested that those views should be included in the Bill. That was a
step implemented by local bodies throughout New Zealand-hospital boards, harbour
boards, catchment boards, and territorial local authorities. Having had that law since 1975,
and presumably accepting it as the official viewpoint of the Opposition, we are now told that
it wants to abandon that law and move to an entirely different situation where all
information must be made available.
The list extends to such trading organisations as licensing trusts. There is no explanation
from the member for Auckland Central as to how the Government Life Office, the State
Insurance Office, or licensing trusts, which are trading organisations, can be expected to
make available all information about their intentions. It is not contained within the
exemptions to clause 6, unless clause 6 is read very widely. If clause 6 is read very widely
then, as my colleague the member for Raglan has pointed out, the Bill merely opens up more
loopholes than it closes. If clause 6 is read narrowly then it does not allow a licensing trust or
the State Insurance Office, the Government Life Insurance Office, or the other trading
organisations to retain from public view information as to their intentions on financial or

ADDRESS IN REPLY
Adjourned debate on the question, That a respectful Address be presented to His
Excellency the Governor-General in reply to His Excellency's Speech.
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR (Timaru): With other members of the House, I extend my
congratulations to Sir Denis and Lady Blundell as they come to the end of their term of
office as the Governor-General and his lady. They have served New Zealand well. I join
other members in wishing them well in their retirement. I also join other members in
expressing pleasure at the visit to New Zealand this year of Her Majesty the Queen and the
Duke of Edinburgh, and the inclusion in the itinerary of the city of Timaru, which I have the
honour to represent in the House. This occasion brought great pleasure to many people from
Timaru and surrounding districts.
I congratulate the two members who made their maiden speeches in this Address in
Reply debate. I say to the member for Mangere that I have been 15 years in the House and
have never heard a more thoughtful, constructive maiden address. His feeling and concern
for his fellow New Zealanders came through loud and clear, and with an unmistakable ring
of sincerity that must have caused many members opposite to look hard at themselves and at
the direction of their policies. I congratulate the member for Pahiatua on his maiden
address, which was of a higher standard than any speech from the National benches I
listened to last year on a similar occasion. In fact, I noticed many expressions of concern on
his colleagues' faces, some of whom have been known to try on homburgs and tiger pants for
size in their fanatical desire to run over each other and Cabinet members to catch the eye of
their leader and Prime Minister, sole selector for their Cabinet. They saw within their own
ranks another rival to their ambitions.
This Address in Reply debate has been notable above all else for one reason: the
comparison between the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister. The Leader of
the Opposition, in opening the debate for this side of the House, gave one of the finest
addresses it has ever been my pleasure to listen to, and was followed by the Prime Minister
who, sensing he could not better it, fell completely flat, as flat as a pancake. In his address,
the Leader of the Opposition spoke at some length on democratic socialism, what it means to
the Labour Party, and what it means in New Zealand now. Had it not been for the discussion
at the recent Labour Party conference of its philosophy and objectives as a socialist party,
the National members would have had nothing to talk about when Parliament resumed.
Incorrectly thinking that this topic was embarrassing to the Labour Party, and so demon-
strating how completely out of touch National members and their speech writers are, many
members opposite referred to this issue in their first notices of motion. I notice that they
have smartly desisted after the thorough drubbing they had in the first two notices of motion
that were debated.
As the Leader of the Opposition reminded the House and the country, the Prime
Minister recently said that the two men he admires most in politics are Helmut Schmidt,
Chancellor of West Germany, and Lee Kuan Yew, Prime Minister of Singapore, both
leaders of democratic socialist parties. Before his recent overseas tour, the Prime Minister
might perhaps have nominated Mr Malcolm Fraser, Prime Minister of Australia, but, before
his gratuitous comments about President Carter of the United States of America, he had
come off second best in a confrontation with the Australian Prime Minister, and had got, for
his pains, a lecture on a number of topics from his Australian counterpart. They included
sporting contacts, international relations, and, thinly disguised but much needed, advice on
good manners. From our experience, this has probably fallen on deaf ears.
I have always believed that everyone should be able to have certain basic conditions in
his life, and that any New Zealand Government should ensure that they are protected. These
are: first, the right to work and receive a fair return for it; secondly, the right to be able to
house and provide for his family; thirdly, the right to an adequate health system-medical
and hospital treatment should be available when necessary, and as of right in cases of need;
and, fourthly, a society that emphasises the care of the aged, the young, the infirm, the sick,
and the needy. To me, this is democratic socialism; and these ideals are also included in the
objectives of the New Zealand Labour Party. The Labour Party has spelt out what
democratic socialism means in New Zealand in 1977, and members opposite do not like it.
National Party members-political opportunists, without objectives, without a philosophy,
and bereft of policy-have the hide to attack the Labour Party, a party with principle and
pride, that is prepared to restate, when its members are challenged, exactly where it stands.

The Government's attitude towards the Labour Party's discussing its philosophy reflects
the innermost fears of the land speculators and the building speculators. These men shake in
their slippers at the thought that they will not be permitted to live off the hard work and
struggles of other New Zealanders. The democratic socialist Labour Party will ensure that
the working farmer, the manufacturer, the small businessman, the housewife, and the wage
and salary worker have a fair share of this country's wealth, and that, as production
increases, all will share, not just the speculator and the profiteer. Democratic socialism
means developing this nation to the will of the people. I was interested to read that the
National Government has its internal problems. Mr Bob Jones has accused members
opposite of being socialists. I quote what he said in the Sunday Times on 3 April: "The
National Party when in office is a milder socialist version of the Labour Party."
Mr Bruce Barclay: Is it democratic though?
Hon. Sir BASIL ARTHUR: No, just socialist. Bruce Larsen, Chairman of the Auckland
Central Young Nationals, said that it was hard to distinguish where the policies of the
National Party began and the socialism of the Labour Party left off. Members opposite are
being accused by their own supporters of being socialists, yet they have the hide to get up in
the House and attack the Labour Opposition. However, we say that we are socialists and are
proud of it, and that this is what New Zealand requires to get out of its existing economic
problems. I refer members to another extract from the address made by the Leader of the
Opposition, who, when referring to the need for increased production and for industrial
relations—another topic I intend to mention-said: "We are determined to set this country
back on the road to industrial stability, and among other things we will create a climate in
which there is a real sense of job satisfaction, in which there is a fair reward for a fair effort,
and vice versa, by making it possible for people to be part of the enterprise for which they
work, not just raw material to be fed in one end and tipped out the other when they reach the
end of their useful life." That is the sort of message that Government members should have
been expounding to the House and the country.
What have we had during the Address in Reply debate? On 2 June the Associate
Minister of Finance was quoted in the New Zealand Herald as urging the nation to work its
way out of trouble. Fair enough, but this means co-operation between employer and
employee; it means a recognition of the role by the one for the other. It does not mean
standover tactics by the employer, it does not mean domineering tactics by the Government;
it means co-operation. The one is essential to the other.
We must increase production. The Associate Minister of Finance said we have to work
our way out of trouble, but he did not say how. He then went to Wanganui to address the
annual meeting of the savings bank. He told businessmen at an annual dinner at Wanganui
that his formula was a call for continued wage restraints, longer wage survey periods, and
limits on backdating of pay in a bid to combat inflation, which he said was unlikely to drop
below 10 percent this year. The next day he returned to Wellington, and said that New
Zealand's good employment and welfare system provided the Government with a basis for
an economics policy. It is always an economics policy, a policy of restraint on wage and
salary earners with no suggestion of control on costs and charges. However, the two go hand
in hand. As long as costs and charges increase, wage and salary earners are entitled to be
recompensed with a fair return for a fair day's work. But all we get are attacks on wage and
salary earners.
During the Address in Reply debate the member for Palmerston North referred to
greedy unionists who were not prepared to do a decent day's work. He did not refer to
employers who do not know a dashed thing about industrial relations. The member for
Tauranga talked in lofty terms about the need for increased production, but at the same time
talked about the bludgers in industry. What about some of those people on the other side of
the negotiating table, those employers who do not know what the term "industrial relations"
means? They do not know that it means an understanding that every man has his role.
During his speech in this debate the member for Tauranga made no reference to the
efforts being made by the Bay of Plenty Harbour Board to get container handling facilities.
When I was in Tauranga about 12 months ago, he said in bold terms that somebody had
made a terrible mistake and he would find out about it. He knew he was referring to his own
Minister, and was told so by the Bay of Plenty Harbour Board at a public meeting. I am
satisfied that the Bay of Plenty Harbour Board does need container handling facilities,
because in the future Auckland will be unable to handle adequately the containers that need
to be shifted through the northern part of the North Island. While on this matter, I should
like to return briefly to a little pamphlet published by the National Party in 1972, which

I turn now to the penal provisions introduced into the industrial legislation by this
Government, and remind members opposite that the Labour Government did not feel it
necessary to stand over New Zealand wage earners with penalty or lay-off provisions.
During the term of the Labour Government the strike figures were less than half what they
are at present. New Zealand wage earners deserve a democratic system of negotiation
through established channels of arbitration and conciliation. The sooner the provisions
imposed by this Government in the past 12 months are removed from statutes and
regulations, the sooner industrial relations will normalise. Unless this is done, we will not see
the industrial peace and understanding we all want to see.

The Government is placing emphasis on the family unit as the basis of our society.
People have left us in no doubt that they are concerned about what is happening. Too many
families are breaking up, too many children are unwanted except for the money they bring
into the family, too many children are unhappy and bored with life, and are getting into
trouble. In 1975, the people said, in no uncertain terms, "We want a National Government
that will act to protect the rights of our children, a Government that will protect our homes
and restore the good, strong, family life that existed before the Labour Government rot set
in." Early in 1976, the National Government responded by establishing a Cabinet committee
on family affairs. That committee has worked hard, and has done its homework. Reading the
statistics, we found that in today's world the welfare of children is at stake. In New Zealand,
in 1965, 1 in 12 marriages broke down; in 1975, 1 in 5 marriages broke down; and last year, 1
marriage in 3 broke down. At the same time, the marriage rate is dropping, the percentage
of extra-nuptial motherhood is increasing alarmingly, and more and more of the children

appearing before the children's courts are shown to be children of one-parent families.
Looking at the financial situation, the benefit or its equivalent in 1965 cost $900,000. Last
year, it cost well in excess of $80 million, and we recouped only $6 million from maintenance
payments. In other words, the deserting husbands and/or wives have not been accepting
their responsibilites to their children or to one another. I give fair warning that the National
Government will not allow this situation to continue. People can do what they like with their
own lives, but under a National Government they will not be able to shed their respon-
sibilities to their families and say that the taxpayer will provide.
The Domestic Purposes Benefit Review Committee gave the reasons it felt that the
family unit was disintegrating, marriages were breaking up at such an alarming rate, and
children were being neglected in too many cases. I can hear the member for Wigram trying
to interject. It is clear that he has not read the committee's report; otherwise he would not
have spoken in the House the way he did the other evening. The committee gave the reasons
for those problems as the generosity of the benefit, its ready availability, the rapidly
vanishing stigma attached to extra-nuptial births and marriage breakdowns, and the status
solo mothers are acquiring, which could in time place our two-parent family unit in jeopardy.
The committee also felt that in far too many cases the benefit rates are so high as to be a
positive disincentive to people entering or re-entering the work force where that seems
desirable. I must point out that at present a 15-year-old girl who has a child that she retains
for 15 years can automatically receive a benefit for life. I admit that many women go out to
work and do not accept the benefit, but the fact remains that a 15-year-old girl who has an
infant and maintains it for 15 years is entitled to a benefit for life. The committee also felt
that in many cases the benefit rates are so high as to facilitate the breakup of a marriage that
might otherwise have been saved. In making its recommendations, the review committee
also recognised that some women have endured for many years periodic assault, drunken-
ness, desertion, and so on, that no one could deny that in some of those circumstances it
would be far better for the women and their children to be free of the persons causing them
such misery, and that they should receive the domestic purposes benefit.
I shall summarise the recommendations made by the Domestic Purposes Benefit
Review Committee, which have been accepted by the Government. The existing domestic
purposes benefit will continue at the same rate until responsibility for the child has ceased.
Then, if the woman is under 50, she will be assisted to return to the work force. Although
emphasis will be placed on counselling for both married couples and single girls both before
and after their babies are born, before a benefit is granted the father of the child will be
interviewed, and a court officer will be empowered to make interim maintenance orders.
That will overcome the difficulty of the delay in hearing maintenance cases because of the
great pressure at present on the courts. For the payment of maintenance, de facto
relationships will carry the same responsibility as legal marriages, and we are going to step
up the collection of maintenance. Also, at first emergency benefits only will be payable, but
at all times—and I emphasise this-the Social Security Commission will ensure that hardship
does not result, particularly where children are concerned.

Mr SPEAKER: The position is somewhat complicated by the fact that I have not the
fullest detailed knowledge of the matter alluded to. It is, however, in the public interest that,
if a matter is not sub judice but involves questions of attitude to the courts, or attitude to the
law, it should be the subject of public discussion. We therefore need to look carefully at the
rules laid down. First I refer to Speaker's ruling 57/2, which says that Standing Order
186-which is the counterpart of the present Standing Order 183-precludes discussion of
matters pending adjudication, and is based on House of Commons principles and was laid
down to ensure that nothing said in debate should prejudice, however slightly, the decision
of any court. In the case in question, discussion of antecedent circumstances was disallowed
by Mr Speaker McKeen. The principle is well stated. The Standing Order that deals with the
matter is Standing Order 183, which reads: "(1) Subject always to the discretion of the Chair
and to the right of the House to legislate on any matter, matters awaiting or under
adjudication in any court of record shali not be referred to—(a) in any motion (including a
motion for leave to bring in a Bill), or (b) in any debate, or (c) in any question to a Minister,
including a supplementary question . . ." That applies from the time the case has been set
down for trial or otherwise brought before the court, if it appears to the Chair that there is a
real and substantial danger of prejudice to the trial of the case. The Order continues: “(2)
This Standing Order shall have effect-(a) in relation to a criminal case, from the moment
the law is set in motion by a charge being made; (b) in relation to cases other than criminal,
from the time when proceedings have been initiated by the filing of the appropriate
document in the registry office of the court. (3) This Standing Order shall cease to have any
effect in any case when the verdict and sentence have been announced or judgment given.
(4) In any case where notice of appeal is given, this Standing Order shall have effect from the
time when the notice is given until the appeal has been decided."
My knowledge of the exact position in this matter is inadequate, and I agree that the
onus is on the person raising the point to indicate the exact present position. But I
understand that a fine was inflicted, and was paid. I understand that costs were awarded
against a party, and there followed much discussion on whether those costs would be paid. It
is clear that the matter was spent in terms of Standing Order 183(3), which states, “This
Standing Order shall cease to have effect in any case when the verdict and sentence have
been announced or judgment given", because costs are not awarded and fines are not
inflicted until a matter is concluded. If, however, an appeal has been lodged, once again the
matter is sub judice, and I should not permit discussion. My impression, and I am subject
here to assistance from members of the House, is that no appeal has been lodged, but that
various organisations have discussed whether they will pay the costs. If that is the correct
position, the matter is not sub judice and the subject is not precluded. If an appeal has been
commenced, I will exclude discussion. Until I am informed to the contrary on confident
grounds, I must rule that the matter is not sub judice.

enforced against anyone else who breaks the law. When the day comes that unions are
beyond the law and are not punished for breaking it, we no longer have the rule of law in this
country.

I now deal with the work and responsibilities of the Forest Service. The member for
Timaru made some inquiries about the revised indigenous forest policy endorsed by this
Government last year. It is not an easy policy to implement, because we are dealing with ar
industry a hundred years old, and phasing it out over a period of about 10 years to a stage
where, instead of finding the greater part of its raw materials from our native forests, as it
has done in the past, it will be extracting no more indigenous logs from our forests than our
forests are producing. In the North Island, prior to the introduction of the indigenous forest
policy, most of the area to be logged, that is 3237 ha, would have been scheduled for
conversion into exotic species. However, consequent on the introduction of the policy,
1531 ha of this will, instead, be managed as indigenous forests. In the South Island the
situation is similar in that, of the 3725 ha scheduled for logging, 2693 ha—almost two
thirds-will be managed for sustained indigenous wood yield. Overall, considering the
relatively short time since the introduction of the indigenous forest policy and its acceptance
by the Government last year, substantial progress has been made in implementing the
policy.
A further step will be taken later this month. Planning for the Hokitika seminar on the
future of West Coast forests and forest industries is well advanced. The seminar is to be held
from 27 June to 1 July and at least 200 people will be participating. This will be the first time
the Forest Service has opened up fully to public discussion the options that are available
before any decisions are made on the utilisation of a forest resource as large as that of the
West Coast, the southern part of Westland, and indeed the Nelson-Marlborough areas as
well. The seminar aims to present a wide variety of information on forests of the West Coast,
information that has been gathered as a result of studies over the past several years. When
the principles of the revised indigenous policy were confirmed by the present Government,
its implementation had to take into account its effect on a long standing industry and those
engaged in it. This is undoubtedly true, and, despite the need to have regard for social
considerations and to introduce gradually those changes in forest management that are
required, substantial progress has been recorded. Clear felling of high quality indigenous
forest and conversion to exotic forests has been slowed, and indeed in some areas has been
terminated altogether, with selective logging and partial felling being substituted in order to
meet contractual commitments entered into many years ago. In the coming year, of the State
indigenous forest area to be logged in one way or another, 60 percent will be managed as
indigenous forest and 40 percent ultimately will be converted to exotic species. This
conversion programme is dominated by a lease arrangement entered into in the Bay of
Plenty about 9 years ago on the one hand, and on the other a need to provide substitute
wood on the West Coast of the South Island. The area of State forest logged in previous
years and planned for conversion is 1300 ha. The thrust of the new revised indigenous forest
policy is to maintain an indigenous forest structure, phase down an industry we have had for
100 years, and, eventually, to protect as large an area as possible of our remaining
indigenous resources.

In health, socialism means that the State-the elected representatives of the people-is
responsible for delivering an adequate health service to all people. We certainly do not have
that kind of health service at present. A socialist health system will remove from the people
the unpleasant choice that too many New Zealanders have to make today; to wait for up to 2

to health is one in which the Government realises that its task is to provide adequate health
care for everybody, and not to make sure, as successive National Governments have, that
our child care standards and our infant mortality rates are inferior to those of Puerto Rico
and Hong Kong. A socialist attitude to education is one that recognises, in those famous
words of Peter Fraser in the 1939 report of the Education Department, "that every person
has a right to a free education of the kind for which he is best fitted, and to the fullest extent
of his powers". A socialist attitude to education recognises that it is the State's responsibility
to cater adequately for everyone. That responsibility does not prevent people from choosing
a private education, but neither does it mean that $3.5 million is given to private schools
irrespective of need, and 4 months later several million dollars are taken out of the State

Government, the country is poised on the knife edge of economic recovery, and we have

In the 1870s, before provincial government was abolished, New Zealand was described as,
"a number of kingdoms without a common point of union between them". Such is the
divisive power of pressure groups in modern New Zealand that that description is equally apt
in 1977, and our small and intimate democracy must gain a new sense of national cohesion.
Too many of us quite improperly appreciate our role in society, and demonstrate it by the
frequent use of the words "our demands", and the very infrequent mention of the words
"our responsibilities". This is illustrated-by the member for Auckland Central, who is
trying to interject-too often by exploding claims on the State for assistance, especially in
welfare. State humanitarianism is based on the simple principle that the vulnerable
people-the aged, the handicapped, the sick, the disabled, and the deprived-have a clear
right to the things they need, such as medical treatment, income, and a life free from anxiety.
That is an acceptable philosophy, and there is not one Government member who does not
subscribe to it. I wonder if the member for Island Bay subscribes to that point of view.
However, there are two important qualifications. The first is that the way in which the
State has taken on one responsibility after another has tended to discourage self-reliance;
and the second is that, because the State has succeeded in sheltering New Zealanders from
discomfort for 40 years, the people are encouraged to think that the State will always be able
to do so. Events of recent years have proved that that is far from being the case. I remind the
House, and particularly members opposite, that over-expectation, or the stimulation of
expectation, is the historical and established enemy of democracy. We need to be careful and
watch the increasing inroads on Government expenditure made by the people-centred
votes-those for health, education, and social welfare. If we go back 40 years and trace the
impact of these votes on Government expenditure, we find an alarming trend. In 1937, the
State spent a quarter of its income on the people-centred votes. In 1947, the amount had
risen to 32 percent; in 1957, to 37 percent; in 1967, to 40 percent; and this year, it is
estimated that it will reach almost 42 percent. The conclusion is obvious.
We must be mindful of our priorities in these areas. The Cabinet committee on
expenditure and Ministers, in carrying out their departmental responsibilities, have forced
people inside and outside Parliament to think deeply about priorities and to determine anew
those things deserving of support. We should be warned of the dangers of yielding, as no
doubt Opposition members would, to the unreasonable demands of shrill pressure groups
who do not have a legitimate axe to grind. If we capitulate without just cause, we imperil the
security of those who have a legitimate need. Moreover, in times of financial stringency, if
New Zealanders want the best elements of State humanitarianism, there must be restraints
elsewhere. These are important matters, commanding a reasoned approach from all

Immigrants—Advice on Housing
1. Mr COOPER (Otago Central) asked the Minister of Immigration, What advice is
given to persons considering migration to New Zealand regarding availability of housing for
rental or purchase in New Zealand?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): Inquiries about settlement prospects in
New Zealand made to the Department of Labour by people within New Zealand and from
overseas are normally answered with a leaflet which sets out the relevant basic entry
requirements. The leaflet states: "There is a heavy demand for housing in New Zealand, and
all overseas applicants are required to show that they have long-term accommodation
prearranged." Applicants to overseas posts are similarly advised of the accommodation
requirement. They are also given information covering all aspects of the different types of
accommodation, availability, costs, and sources of finance where purchase of accommoda-
tion is concerned.

the House to examine?
Hon. T. F. GILL: Interested members, like any other New Zealander, can get one, and
I do not think they would want to use me as a post office. this pamphlet, L82, was originated
in 1975, and is under revision at the moment.
Mr Bell: Has this procedure been altered in any way since November 1975, when the
Government changed?
Hon. T. F. GILL: No. The pamphlet is currently under review. It has not altered in that
time.

the increasing number of immigrants from southern Africa, that housing in New Zealand is
not segregated according to race, and that, if they are not prepared to accept that fact, they
should not come to New Zealand?
Mr Wellington: A point of order, Mr Speaker. I would commend to your attention that

of questioning, should be asked to withdraw.

Hotel and Motel Occupancy in Auckland and Rotorua
2. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Tourism, In view of the report by the
Tourist and Publicity Department showing that Auckland and Rotorua reach maximum
hotel and motel room occupancy during holiday periods, what does he plan to do to alleviate
the crisis?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): There would be several areas in New
Zealand where hotels reach maximum occupancy levels at peak holiday periods, but this in
itself does not necessarily indicate a crisis situation. In considering the need for additional
accommodation, regard must be had for average occupancy over a full year's operations if
the viability of hotels is to be maintained.
Mr Kirk: How does the Minister relate the figures supplied by Tourist and Publicity
Department, that in March 1976 Auckland had a 98.6 percent room occupancy, to the
National Party's policy, which said that TADCO would be revitalised with representation
from the private sector to perform the very necessary and extremely useful function of
providing financial assistance for the expansion of tourist accommodation; and why has that
not been done?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: In 1975-76 the average room occupancy in leading hotels in
Auckland was 75.6 percent, and in Rotorua 69.3 percent. Hotels in several areas would
reach maximum occupancy levels at peak holiday periods but, as I said before, this does not
indicate a crisis level. However, there is a need for more hotel accommodation to be
developed in Auckland and Rotorua. The Tourist and Publicity Department is aware of
projects in varying stages of planning in both cities, and some applications are being
processed. I trust that the department will be able to meet the projects which come within its
critieria.
Mr Cooper: Would the Minister agree that if hotels and motels did not reach maximum
occupancy during holiday periods their business viability over the whole year would be very
suspect indeed? Would it be possible to make figures available to the Opposition spokesman
on tourism to further his education on this matter?
Mr SPEAKER: Order! The first part of the question was purely a request for an
opinion. The second part was, I think, needlessly working the House up. The Minister may
comment on the first part if he likes.
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: As in all business ventures there are more profitable and less
profitable periods. I do agree that if it was not for the good, the bad would look a jolly sight
worse.

considered in the overall context of possible developments, not only in health and education,
but for all Government spending in the present financial year. Our measures to counter
inflation require the spending of all Government departments to be controlled, and priorities
of proposed developments have to be carefully assessed.

ment departments in Wanganui I suggest that he submit another question.

State Services Tribunal Chairman
8. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Labour, What were the
"'ulterior motives" which prompted the Government not to continue the appointment of Mr
N. R. Taylor, S.M., as Chairman of the State Services Tribunal?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Acting Minister of Labour): The reasons for the Govern-
ment choosing not to recommend that Mr N. R. Taylor's term as Chairman of the State
Services Tribunal be extended have been made clear to both Mr Taylor and the Combined
State Service Organisations. It is the intention that the chairmanship will continue to be a
rolling one, with a change of chairman at appropriate intervals so long as the position
remains one of its current nature.
Mr Isbey: What consideration was given by the Government to the very strong feelings
of the CSSO for the retention of Mr Nigel Taylor?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Quite serious consideration. Throughout last month the
Minister of State Services was in consultation with the CSSO. On his departure overseas, I
continued the consultations and I put before Cabinet the CSSO's concern and recommenda-
tions before it finally made its decision that Mr Taylor should be replaced.
Mr Isbey: Is it not the essence of good industrial relations that the workers' side should
have a chairman in whom they have absolute confidence?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: No, that is a biased attitude. It is most important that the
chairman should be completely impartial and experienced. In those respects I have nothing
critical to say about Mr Taylor. I believe his successor, Mr Horn, will provide exactly the
same area of impartiality and judgment necessary in this post.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Would it not be fair to suggest to the Government that, if it is
proposing a rolling situation for this office, it should as a practice attempt to obtain the good
will of both sides in industrial relations in respect of anyone appointed to be their judicial
authority?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Yes, of course, if it is possible to get it, but very rarely can
one find a chairman who would be completely acceptable to both parties. It must be 20 years
since this post has been held for more than 3 years.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: As the Minister agrees with the view that such agreement should at
least be sought, why did the Government fail to do it on this occasion?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I made it very plain that the Government gave very serious
consideration to the concern of the CSSO and consulted with that organisation on more than
one occasion. Its views were put to Cabinet before we followed what the law requires: that
the Government, failing agreement, should make the appointment.

Price Control
10. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry,
Has he seen the statement made by his Under-Secretary and quoted in the New Zealand
Herald on 30 May 1977 that "In the longer term it is the Government's intention to reduce
direct price controls and to rely more on other legislation to further economic efficiency,
promote consumer interest, and encourage greater productivity", and, if so, what is the
legislation referred to, and, if it is not already on the statute book, when will it be introduced
into Parliament?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry): I have seen the
statement. The legislation referred to is the Commerce Act 1975 as amended.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: Could the Minister forecast when we are likely to see further
economic efficiency, consumer interest promoted, and productivity greatly increased, as a
result of the operation of the Commerce Act?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: These matters are the subject of continuing adminis-
trative policy. Regarding amendments to price control, we are currently working with trade
associations on possible changes to the regulations as they apply now. When we get the
economy on to an even keel and inflation properly under control, the long-term aim is to
return to a competitive system.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Would the Minister confirm that an early paper will be going to
caucus or Cabinet proposing amendments to the stabilisation regulations aimed at easing
profitability restrictions on companies?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: A number of trade associations have had discussions
with me and with officers of my department. We are reviewing the regulations as they stand
at present. I have informed these organisations that in current economic circumstances it is
necessary to operate price control. Any amendments that may be proposed by me will
certainly be going to Cabinet, but I cannot set a date at this time.
Mr Hunt: With further reference to the Minister's original answer and the statement by
the Under-Secretary that it is the Government's intention to reduce direct price control,
which section of the 1976 Commerce Act applies?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER: The Commerce Act provides for the Government to
take necessary control by means of legislation or regulations.

Oral Answers to Questions
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
CITIZENS AND ALIENS BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Citizens and Aliens
Bill be introduced. This is a Bill to consolidate and amend the law relating to New Zealand
citizenship and the registration of aliens, which is at present contained in two statutes, the
British Nationality and New Zealand Citizenship Act 1948 and the Aliens Act 1948. There
have been many changes in the nature of the British Commonwealth since 1948 which have
resulted in the countries of the Commonwealth placing increasing emphasis on their
individual citizenships. The Bill seeks to recognise that emphasis while at the same time it
does nothing to depart from due recognition of the common code of British subject or
Commonwealth subject status. The Bill does, however, also seek to put on a more common
footing aspirants for New Zealand citizenship who are on the one hand British subjects, and
on the other aliens-this term meaning any non-British subject.
Hitherto, British subjects have been required to have resided in New Zealand for 3
years—and this has been reducible to a minimum of 1 year in special circumstances, at the
Minister's discretion-before being eligible to apply for citizenship, whereas aliens have
been required to have lived here for a minimum of 5 years. It is proposed that henceforth
there will be a common period of 3 years minimum residence. In doing this the Government
is honouring a commitment made in its election manifesto. The reason for this is that
experience has shown that many immigrants from non-British countries are as well qualified
as British immigrants in character, knowledge of the English language, knowledge of the
responsibilities of citizenship, and general settlement into our community after 3 years
residence here. In very many cases a period of 3 years residence is sufficient for both British
immigrants and aliens alike to make up their minds on the important question of taking out
our citizenship and demonstrating their fitness for it. It is proposed, however, in recognition
of traditional ties with the lands of the great majority of our forebears, to retain the present
provision whereby citizenship may be granted to British subjects and Irish citizens at
ministerial discretion after 1 year's residence.
There was another distinction, too, between British subject applicants and aliens which
it is proposed to do away with. The legislation has referred to the registration of British
subjects as New Zealand citizens and to the naturalisation of aliens. For all practical
purposes, however, the distinction has been terminological only and the person who has
been naturalised has been, in the eyes of the law, as much a New Zealand citizen as the
person on whom citizenship has been conferred by the process known as registration. It is
proposed that the terms "registration" and "naturalisation" be replaced by the common
term "grant of citizenship".
The Bill seeks, too, to correct a situation which is regarded by many—and I think rightly
regarded as discriminating against the female. This, again, is honouring a promise made to
the electors. Under the present state of our law-and we are not alone in this; I am advised
that it is just the same with most other countries-it is not possible for citizenship by descent
to be conveyed through the female line. A married New Zealand father of a child born
overseas passes on his New Zealand citizenship to the child, but this is not at present the case
with the mother. The Bill proposes that citizenship by descent will be passed on equally
through the female line as with the male line to the first generation of children born
overseas, provided that such citizenship shall lapse if the birth is not registered in New
Zealand before the expiry of 12 months after attaining the age of majority. The Bill goes
even further, to the extent of enabling correction of what might be regarded as past injustice
against the female line of succession, by providing that the Minister may in his discretion
grant citizenship to any person born before 1 January 1978 if at the time of that person's birth
the mother was a New Zealand citizen otherwise than by descent; that is, if she were New
Zealand born or a naturalised citizen of this country.
As to the law affecting registration of aliens in this country, generally the Bill proposes
that this be re-enacted with little amendment. It is to be noted, however, that it is not
proposed to re-enact the present provisions relating to the deportation of aliens, usually for
criminal offences. The deportation of people who are not New Zealand citizens is a matter
for which responsibility is at present divided between the Minister of Immigration and the
Minister of Internal Affairs, the divisions being broadly that the Minister of Immigration is
responsible for British subjects under the Immigration Act, and the Minister of Internal


## p. 554 (#562) ############################################

554
10 June
Citizens and Aliens Bill
Affairs under the Aliens Act. Under both Acts the decision to deport is largely dependent on
any recommendation made by the court in which the offender has appeared. It is desirable
that one Minister and one department be responsible for all deportations, and it has been
agreed that it is appropriate that these be the Minister of Immigration and his department,
the Department of Labour.
Those are the main effects of the Bill on the present law. It is to be expected that there
will be widespread interest in this Bill and it is therefore desirable that it be referred to a
select committee. I intend to move at the appropriate time that the Bill be referred to the
Statutes Revision Committee.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): Right at the outset let me say that I unhesitat-
ingly approve of the removal of another area of discrimination affecting women and of their
being put on the same plane of equality as men in the power to transmit the inheritance of
nationality. This is a complex area of law. Although the problem is essentially simple, over
the years it has had the encrustation of judicial decisions, and a number of emotional
reactions. I think our earliest legislation was the British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act.
It was consolidated into the British Nationality and New Zealand Citizenship Act and is
being yet further consolidated; and from the Minister's summary I believe generally
speaking it is in the right direction. I certainly agree it is desirable to co-ordinate the
differences that have previously been in the law, such as the differing periods of residence
that must be served by aliens and British citizens, and bring them to the same level.
The retention of ministerial discretion, at least for those of British descent, is desirable,
but I would like to see ministerial discretion extended to the whole lot, right across the
board. No doubt that is a possibility that will be taken into account by the committee in its
consideration of the Bill. I am not sure of the substitution of the expression "grant of
citizenship" for the old process of naturalisation or registration. It is true that the word
"registered" citizen has not entered into our common language and I have yet to hear
anyone describe himself as a registered New Zealander. The phrase "naturalised New
Zealander" is a very common one and it might have been preferable to have consolidated
our use of the language in one familiar term rather than importing another somewhat
cumbersome phrase "grant of citizenship". Whether this will mean that a person availing
himself of that will be induced to call himself a granted citizen, or whatever, I do not know.
Generally speaking, I should like to make the point that this piece of legislation deals
essentially with people, their rights and obligations, including, as the Minister has
mentioned, the right of residence in New Zealand, and the likelihood of their having that
right of residence terminated by a deportation order made against them. It is desirable that a
right exercisable by the State should be concentrated in one authority whether it be the
Minister of Internal Affairs, the Minister of Immigration, or the Minister of Justice, but at
least it should be one authority rather than a duplication of approaches. The result is
differing rules of administration adopted by the various authorities. The hand of the State
can also bear heavily on the citizen, and it is imperative that ministerial discretion in the
exercise of these powers should be subject to proper scrutiny, and that there should be
appeal rights either to the constituted courts of law, or to some administrative tribunal.
I have not had time to study the Bill to see whether this detail is included, but I am
certain that there should be some avenue of appeal against the exercise of this discretion,
which could be capricious and oppressive. It is important to remember that we are dealing
with people, and often people who have been resident here for a long time but who have not
found it necessary to put into operation the machinery of the law that gives them full rights as
is the case of a New Zealand citizen, whether registered, naturalised, or by right of birth.
The committee will ho doubt study these points, but at first glance the Bill appears to be a
consolidation of existing legislation, and a simplification of an issue that has many complex-
ities, and which is confusing to people who are not as familiar with the English language as
might be a natural born New Zealander.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I thank the member for Henderson
for his helpful remarks, and agree that this is a complex area of law. I think the only point
requiring reply is his comment on deportation. As I mentioned earlier, this will be included
in the Immigration Bill, and I think that would be the appropriate time to take this matter
up.

member for Wellington Central about parents going overseas, adopting a child at 15½, and

This is a good question, and a delicate one. Clause 3, provides that for the purposes of the
Act a person shall, in the absence of evidence to the contrary, be presumed to be the father
of the child if he is or was married to the child's mother at the time of the child's conception

1969.
For members' information, the types of evidence are: the entry of the father's name in
the register of births as relating to the child concerned; an instrument signed by the mother
of the child and any person acknowledging that he is the father of the child; a paternity order
within the meaning of the Domestic Proceedings Act; and a declaration by the Supreme
Court as to paternity made under section 10 of the Status of Children Act. As well as these
types of evidence which in the first instance constitute prima facie evidence and in the fourth
instance conclusive proof of paternity, there is a fifth type of evidence—that an order made
in certain declared countries outside New Zealand declaring a person to be the father of a
child shall be prima facie evidence of paternity. For the purposes of this provision the Cook
Islands, Niue, and the Tokelau Islands are deemed to be countries outside New Zealand.
In reply to the member for St. Albans, an alien declined citizenship in the situation
mentioned by the member, can reapply at a later date when his application would be
reconsidered. Refusals or deferrals of citizenship are made without prejudice, therefore
allowing reapplication. I hope that has answered most of the questions raised by members.
Bill introduced and read a third time.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Internal Affairs): I move, That the Citizens and Aliens
Bill be referred to the Statutes Revision Committee, and that the proceedings of the committee
during the hearing of evidence be open to accredited representatives of the news media.
Motion agreed to.

I want now to deal with an address that I gave to the toastmasters' conference on 7 May.
There has been quite a lot of comment about it, and I want to clarify one or two things. This
is what I said: "While the methods of communication have become more diverse and faster
over the last century, this has served to confuse rather than improve communications for
leaders. Information is today's greatest non-diminishable resource and the average man is
bombarded from day to day with information of many sorts. The time when the politician
was assured of transmitting his message to the people by way of the news media, has gone.
The problem applies in reverse, too. With such a large number of divergent voices coming
through the news media it is difficult for the politican to assess just which opinion is
representative. Political leaders must now compete for media time with a multitude of so-
called experts, and when we do get an appearance on television or radio we are mindful that
often it is not what is said but how it is said that counts. Nearly everyone seems to have
become an expert on some subject but unfortunately knowledge does not always go hand in
hand with responsibility. The problem of competition for communication is common to the
whole free world. And not only has competition for time increased but the transmitter of
information, largely the news media, is getting into the act and fancying itself as a leader in
its own right." That is part of the speech I delivered at that conference.

Since we last met as a Parliament, the people of Taranaki have shared with the people of

In its promises to the people in 1975, the National Party said in its manifesto that a
National Government would continue its previous responsive and fruitful involvement in law
reform. Five standing committees are dealing with the reform of public and administrative
law, the law of torts, contracts and commercial law, criminal law, and property law and
equity. Each committee consists of experts drawn from the ranks of practising, academic,
and Government lawyers. I take this opportunity to express publicly the gratitude of the
Government and the nation for the very valuable and voluntary contributions made by those
members, both past and present, to the work of the various committees. It is imperative that
the laws of this country reflect prevailing social attitudes, a vital and unceasing task, but not
one that always grips the attention of the public.
In the legislative programme this session about 10 major bills of very great significance
will be considered, together with a number of minor ones. Because of the lack of political
interest in minor Bills, there is not a great deal of political mileage to be gained from
implementing the recommendations of the law reform committees; there is, regrettably, a
tendency to defer legislative action on their reports because of the other measures competing
for the time of the House. However, I take pleasure in the fact that the present Parliament
has already given effect to the criminal law reform committee's recommendations on
preliminary hearings in the Judicature Amendment Bill of September 1975. Both that Act
and the Insurance Law Reform Bill, at present before the Statutes Revision Committee,
resulted from the recommendations of two of the law reform committees. Last month I
introduced the Contractual Mistakes Bill, which is based on a committee report, and I expect
to introduce further Bills implementing committee reports on the law relating to the carriage
of goods, reported on in April 1968; four reports relating to the Evidence Act and dealing
with professional privilege in the law of evidence and on hearsay evidence, on which a report
was produced in 1967; on the ruling in Hollington v.Hewthorn on the admissibility of
convictions; on medical privilege, the report of which, completed in 1974, is being printed;
reports on wills and on the administration of estates; on fencing, the report on which was
produced in 1972; and on property and trusts. In all, the implementation of 13 reports is
contained in this programme of legislation. Two major reports remain unactioned, and I am
anxious that time be made available to give legislative effect to them. I refer to the credit
contracts report and the report on culpable homicide, which I have asked the Government
caucus justice committee to study.
The National Government has set about reshaping family law to meet present day needs
and realities, while recognising an obligation to reinforce, as far as the law can, the stable
family life that is essential to the well-being of our society. The Government's election policy
promised major reforms dealing with matrimonial property, divorce, and maintenance. I
acknowledge that these changes are a completion of the progress begun in the 1960s by the
late Mr Hanan, Minister of Justice in the second National Government. Last year we began
with the matrimonial property law, not merely because this was in an uncertain and
unsatisfactory state, but because there was already before Parliament a Bill, introduced by
my predecessor as Minister of Justice, the member for Henderson, which could be adapted
to give effect to the National Government's policy. Our aim was to produce a code for the
fair division of matrimonial property in the event of a marriage's breaking up, based on the
concept that marriage is an equal partnership of equal persons to which each contributes in
his or her own way. We wanted to combine certainty and justice of principle with flexibility
and fairness of application. Above all, we were concerned to recognise that the partner who
stays home to manage the house and bring up the children makes just as important a
contribution as the partner who goes out to earn the money. It is here, I believe, that the real
innovation of the new Act lies; it gets right away from the traditional notion that contribu-


## p. 572 (#580) ############################################

572
10 June
Address in Reply
tions in terms of money or property are more important than the less tangible ones. This is
not the occasion on which to expound the legislation in detail, but I do remind the House
that equal sharing does not mean that homes or businesses will have to be sold up when the
shares of the spouses are determined. The courts have wide powers to make orders that will
be just and sensible in the particular circumstances.
The Act deals only with situations that arise during the joint lifetimes of husband and
wife, and does not apply where the marriage lasts until death, as, happily, most marriages
still do. It would not be right simply to stop there, to recognise the share of the divorced or
separated spouses, but not that of the widow or widower. The next step, therefore, must be
to extend that Act's philosophy to the situation after a death. That poses quite formidable
practical problems, because the more discretion there is to deal with individual cases, the
greater the danger of having large numbers of estates litigated in the courts with the delay
and the expense necessarily involved. We are determined to devise a fair and workable
scheme, and I should like to be able to bring down a Bill before the end of this session.
It is important to keep our thinking straight on the emotive issue of what is referred to as
an easier divorce. There is little correlation between liberalisation of the grounds for divorce
and divorce rates; nor are the divorce rate and the marriage failure rate the same. We will
not promote sound family life, or preserve the realities of marriages, by forcing people to
remain together. We have undertaken to make an irreconcilable breakdown of marriage
after 2 years of living apart the sole ground of divorce. In giving effect to this, we have been
led to examine, not only the Matrimonial Proceedings Act, which deals with divorce proper,
but the separation provisions of the Domestic Proceedings Act and, not least, the provisions
for reconciliation. I am glad to say that we have received a very full and thought-provoking
report, commissioned from a former senior officer of the Department of Justice, now
retired, Miss Patricia Webb, to whom I am greatly indebted-and we are in the process of
examining it. The report also deals with maintenance law, on which it is almost impossible to
please or satisfy everyone. We must try as best we can to reconcile a man's-and it still
usually is the man's-responsibility to support a first family that has been broken up by
separation or divorce, and his responsibility towards the wife and children of a second
marriage. As long as we allow divorce and remarriage, we must be concerned with the
stability and well-being of both families. These and other conflicts make the promoting of a
just and realistic maintenance law difficult, but they do not excuse us from the need to act.
Looking further ahead, there is a real need to bring the adoption law up to date. This is
a large task in itself, and it may have to be left for the next Parliament to complete. We are
waiting also to see what the Royal Commission on the Courts will recommend on the subject
of special family courts, and, if the commission thinks them desirable and practical in New
Zealand, we will proceed to develop them as fully and speedily as our economic resources
allow. My goal, foreshadowed in our 1975 programme, is to have a single, consistent, and
coherent family law code for New Zealand, and I have outlined the steps we are taking
towards this.
The 1972 National Government set up the commercial affairs division of the Depart-
ment of Justice. We need to strengthen the administration of various Acts relating to the
commercial community; recent events have demonstrated the need to review that legisla-
tion. Regrettably, the resources of the division have been used more to put the ambulance at
the bottom of the cliff rather than to construct a safety barrier at the top. However, a start is
to be made this year, and a Bill will be introduced seeking to give greater protection to the
investing public. The investment of money is, of course, a calculated risk-and it will remain
so-although in some cases the risk is small indeed. But I do not regard the dissipation of an
investor's money by misapplication or mismanagement as a legitimate part of that risk.
Investment in a business or enterprise is one thing, reliance upon the honesty and responsi-
bility of management quite another. Many of the recent financial collapses, and the resulting
losses of investors' money, can be attributed to a lack of honesty and responsibility. Many of
those financial collapses occurred in areas where the law imposes no duty to issue a
prospectus, or to provide financial information. Accordingly, I propose to introduce a Bill
containing provisions that will apply to every commercial enterprise that asks the public for
money, whether or not it is for direct investment in itself. The Bill will make general the
application of the well-established and useful principles in, for example, the Companies Act
1955, relating to the issue of prospectuses, the appointment of auditors and trustees, and the
keeping and disclosure of financial information. The Bill will be based on the premise that
any commercial enterprise that asks the public for money ought to be subject to certain
duties and independent checks, to safeguard against the dissipation of investments by

mismanagement or misapplication.
