Mr DEPUTY SPEAKER: Two interesting points have been raised, and perhaps I could
deal first with the second one, made by the member for Roskill. It is fairly straightforward.
He took exception to the comment made by the Minister of Justice that a certain statement
was not true. Perhaps I could again consult the Concise Oxford Dictionary: "True: in
accordance with fact or reality; not false or erroneous". I remember sitting in the chair some
years ago and ruling out of order the use of the expression "It is not true" by no less a person
than the Rt. Hon. Sir John Marshall, when he was Minister of Justice, I think. On further
reflection I realised that my ruling at that time was not correct, because, in fact, what he had
said was that a certain statement was not true. Had he said that a member was not telling the
truth or was lying, that would have been a different matter. A statement can be said to be
incorrect, but the definition of "true" is "correct in accordance with the facts". We are
quibbling a little if we say that a member cannot say that a statement is untrue, because we
do not take exception to a member's saying that a statement is incorrect. It is quite out of
order for a member to suggest that another member has not been telling the truth or has
been telling lies. We cannot allow that, but we can allow a statement to be referred to as
untrue. I hope that the distinction is understood and that the honourable member does not
want me to repeat it.
The member for for Napier took exception to what he claimed to be the suggestion that
the Minister of Justice was accusing members of the Labour Party of being associated with
the Communist Party or the Socialist Unity Party. The Acting Prime Minister pointed
out-and this was later corroborated by the Minister of Justice-that the words used by the
latter were "playing into the hands of the Socialist Unity Party". Earlier this session, I ruled
that it would be quite out of order for members to accuse other members of being
communists or nazis or national socialists. These terms are considered by a great majority of
members on either side of the House to be offensive, and in those circumstances I have ruled
that they should not be used. If the Minister of Justice had said that members of the Labour
Party were members of the Socialist Unity Party, that would have been out of order; but he
suggested that, by certain actions, they were playing into the hands of such people. It is a
matter for debate to say whether or not members are playing into the hands of somebody
else. Were the Minister to have said that they were being dominated by the Socialist Unity
Party or unduly under the influence of that party, that would have been out of order, too.
One can say that they are influenced by them, but not that they are dominated by them. One
can suggest that they are playing into the hands of someone else, but not that they are
members of that party. I hope the honourable member for Napier can understand the
distinction I have drawn between what is parliamentary, and therefore a matter for
debate-suggesting that somebody is playing into the hands of somebody else—and what is
unparliamentary-suggesting that members are members of a prescribed political party.

other occupation. For a start, there is difficulty in establishing benchmarks for service pay
scales in comparison with other occupations. Defence can be an attractive occupation. I
certainly found it so for 26 years, and I am sure the Minister of Immigration found it an
attractive occupation for his 34 years or so. But a career in defence has many disadvantages.
It has a particular disadvantage for a serving member of the defence forces who is elected to
Parliament and is denied his end-of-service grant, as the Minister of Immigration and I know
only too well. I have not yet finished fighting that case. As an example of a particular


## p. 577 (#585) ############################################

10 June
577
Address in Reply
unattractiveness of defence life, I wonder how many people in other occupations would
enjoy having to move every 18 months or so, often without promotion. This means frequent
changes of school for children. My own children had to change schools 10 times, and that
would be typical of most families in a long-term service career. While frequent changes of
school might not be the traumatic experience for children that we adults think, parents have
to face the costs of buying new school uniforms. Often, defence bases are sited in the least
climatically hospitable areas. I wonder if anyone in another occupation would relish a winter
at Waiouru. I cannot really think that anybody would enjoy a couple of days at Waiouru
during the winter. In such areas there is no real urban community and no real shopping
centre, and there are no job opportunities for wives, or for teenagers and young adults.
New Zealand is facing extreme difficulty in retaining career servicemen, particularly in
the skilled areas such as the electronic and engineering trades. This affects the Navy more
than other branches of the service. It is encouraging to know that we are recruiting service
personnel. The service does not see the full advantage of training a recruit until 5 to 8 years,
when that person has become a master tradesman. I have been attracted by the advertising
for recruits by the three services, and it is encouraging to know that at least one New
Zealand advertising agency knows how to do a thorough and true job. Why do the services
have difficulty in retaining servicemen and servicewomen on a long-term basis? Remunera-
tion is an element. Most occupational groups in New Zealand have had a pay review in
recent times, but there has been no pay review for the armed services since 1965. I have had
more complaints about pay in the last 18 months than in the rest of my parliamentary career.
Some people claim that pay is not an important element of a service career, but the loss of
trained servicemen can be attributed in part to that. The frequency of postings is another
disincentive for career servicemen. The problem is not so much with the servicemen, but
with the wives, who jusifiably become sick and tired of moving every 18 months or so. There
are the attendant expenses of a transfer, the separation from home, and often the long wait
for housing. Servicemen and women have extended hours of work as duty drivers, duty
NCOs, orderly officers, and other duties not encountered in outside occupations, for no
additional pay.
I have particular pride in the man-management relations in the Army and Air Force,
and industrial management in New Zealand could look to the very good industrial relations
enjoyed by those two services. I shall be quite frank. I think the Navy has some way to go in
improving its man-management relations. Too often there is an almost Pepysian outlook at
man management in the Navy. It could be something to do with tradition, but I think the
Navy would well be advised to take an inward look at itself and bring its man-management
relations up to the excellent level in the Army and the Air Force.

NOTICE OF MOTION-ADMISSIBILITY
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): A point of order, Mr Speaker. Under Standing
Order 103, which deals with notices of motion, I desire to raise a point of order about notice
of motion No. 26. The reason I raise the matter so long after the giving of the notice of
motion is because the information it contained could, obviously, be checked out only after it
had been tabled. The motion accuses the Wellington Trades Council and a trade union of
intimidation tactics, the figure giving the number of people involved in the meeting is grossly
incorrect, and there seems an unsupported insinuation that the union had been a party to
intimidation. I see this as being unbecoming, and offensive under the terms of the Standing
Order.
Subsequent to the notice of motion, the Acting Minister of Labour saw the union and
has accepted its assurances on the matters used as a basis for the notice of motion, and at
that point accepts that the facts are incorrect. I further submit for your consideration that the
notice of motion anticipates an Order of the Day, which, of course, excludes it under
Standing Order 103 (c).
Mr SPEAKER: If I am to pursue the matter further I need more specific information. I
must have some guidance about which Order of the Day the notice of motion anticipates,
and also the insinuations alluded to. As the member will recognise that the notice of motion
is a fairly lengthy one, he might care to expand on what he said.
Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill): First, the Bill mentioned in the notice of motion is
the Shop Trading Hours Bill, which is No. 3 on the Order Paper. The insinuation is that the
union had been a party to intimidation. The union took the action it thought proper about
the insinuations, and met the Acting Minister of Labour at once. A press report states that
the union's assurance has been accepted by the Acting Minister, and at that point I think
must be accepted by the House. For those two reasons we seek that the notice of motion be
struck from the Order Paper.
Mr LITHGOW (Palmerston North): I should like to comment that the figure of 297,
quoted from the Manawatu Evening Standard, was also quoted in other newspapers. The
statement referring to the Shop Trading Hours Bill was: "further commends and assures full
support against any such reported intimidation . . . " If the House wants further information
I will be only too pleased to give the name of the newspaper that gave the facts of
intimidation following the Wellington strike.
Mr Hunt: Which paper?
Mr LITHGOW: The statement was made in the Dominion.
Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson): I suggest that it does not assist the honourable
member a great deal to quote an unnamed newspaper even though he does subsequently
give the name, somewhat hesitatingly. I accept, as of course the House must accept, the
assurance given my colleague the member for Roskill that the Acting Minister of Labour
accepted the inaccuracy of the language contained in the notice of motion. There is no room
left for argument-as to accuracy. We must accept the word of my colleague that he, in turn,
has the word of the Minister.
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing): The member for Roskill, who raised
the point of order, quoted Standing Order 103. Subsection (a) mentions, "words which
would not be permitted in debate”. There is not one word in the notice of motion that would
not be permitted in debate. The honourable gentleman himself would accept that much
harsher words have been used in debates. Subsection (b) states: “Contain any statement of
facts or name of any person unless they are strictly necessary to render the notice intelligible
and can be authenticated”. No person is named in the notice of motion, and the facts are
strictly necessary to render it intelligible. As the member for Palmerston North has said, they
can be authenticated as being a report from a local paper. Subsection (c) states: “Anticipate
discussion of an order of the day." The reference to the Shop Trading Hours Bill does not
anticipate discussion, it simply states what the notice of motion refers to, and refers to some
outside activity which had occurred as a result of the Bill being before Parliament.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Consumer Price Index-Percentage Increase
1. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Finance, What is the Treasury
estimate of the percentage increase in the consumer price index which will result from
increased prices of goods and services, due to Government action taking effect after 31
March 1977?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): Increases in the price of goods
and services since 31 March 1977 arising from Government action to meet increased costs
and maintenance in critical sectors of the economy are forecast to cause a rise of 1 percent in
the consumer price index during this year.
Mr O'Brien: I presume that the 1 percent includes the retail electricity charge figure,
plus the increase in petrol costs and the increase in motor registration fees. In view of the fact
that electricity charges, petrol price increases, and motor registration fees enter the
production costs of most goods produced in the New Zealand economy, does the Treasury
prepare an estimate of the secondary effect-that is, the indirect effect-on prices when
those increases are being considered; and, if so, could the Minister state that figure?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: This figure is based on the use of electricity bulk rates and
the motor spirits taxation. At short notice I cannot give the member the sort of figure that he
asks. This is a complex field—the CPI is a difficult field—and I must have advice in time to
provide anything as detailed as that.
Mr Hunt: In his original answer the Minister gave an estimate, but he did not indicate
whether or not it was the Treasury estimate. Was the answer he gave to the first question
asked by the member for Island Bay the Treasury estimate?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: The figures I have are based on the figures provided by my
department, and if the member would like to have them I had perhaps better give them to
the House. The itemised breakdown of the figure is, for the electricity bulk rate from 1 April
a total effect of 0.86-the direct effect 0.4, the indirect effect 0.46; motor spirits tax from 1
April, direct 0.14, indirect 0.06, total 0.20; giving a total of 1.06.
Mr Hunt: When the Minister used the words "my department", was he referring to
Treasury, or to another one of the portfolios he holds?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: These answers are prepared by the department—the
Treasury.
Mr O'Brien: As they are Treasury figures, could the Minister convert the percentage
figure into a dollar and cents figure faced by the average family as a consequence of this
increase?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: As usual, I would not wish to mislead the House. It is
imperative that, in matters of statistics, we get detailed professional advice.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.

Social Welfare-Disability Allowances
2. RICHARD WALLS (Dunedin North), on behalf of Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East),

introduced until 10 October 1975. Statistics are compiled for financial years, and in the
period 10 October 1975 to 31 March 1976, 532 applications for disability allowance were
received, of which 374 were processed before the end of the financial year. In the year ended

calculated that if 1c were to be added to the price of every packet of 20 cigarettes, and every
glass of beer sold in hotels, the consumer price index would rise by 1.03 points. If a 1c per
glass increase is applied proportionately to the price of a jug of beer, the resulting increase of

price index for the March quarter 1977 stood at 1373. A rise of 1c in the price of 20 cigarettes
and a glass of beer would result in an index of 1374 which represents a rise of 0.07 percent. If
a proportionate increase in the price of a jug of beer is included, the index would be 1375,

Immigrants-Categories
5. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Immigration, What was the number of
categories of immigrants, both subsidised and non-assisted, acceptable to New Zealand in
October 1972, what changes to this number have occurred between October 1972 and the
present day, and on what dates did these changes occur?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration): There were three commonly used methods
of emigration to New Zealand. Under the first, the subsidy scheme, limits were first
introduced on the number of acceptable occupations in April 1974. The 35 acceptable
ocupations at that time were reduced to 8 occupations in April 1975. The second was an
assisted passage scheme under which the New Zealand Government paid the full fare. In
October 1972 approximately 125 occupations were approved under the assisted passage
scheme, which was abolished in April 1975. The third scheme attracted no subsidy. In April
1974, when entry controls were introduced over the previously unrestricted British, an
occupational list dividing occupations into three categories based on demand was developed.
In its final form in December 1974 this list covered 113 occupations. In December 1975 the
list was reduced to 35 occupations. It was raised in September 1976 to 120 occupations and
raised again in May 1977, to 243 occupations.

packing houses. Up till fairly recently no separate figures were kept for ordinary goats

"Yes, I have read the article in the New Zealand Herald of 13 May on tuna fishing referred

fish in New Zealand waters, including the Japanese, and the New Zealand Government as

School Certificate Fees
14. Mr MARSHALL (Wanganui) asked the Minister of Education, Can he explain why

raised to a maximum of $14.50 in 1976?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR (Minister of Education): The 1976 increase in School Certificate
fees provided further revenue to cover a higher proportion of the cost of running the
examination that year. For example, the increases in fees paid to examiners, markers, and
supervisors was increased last year by 45 percent. The additional revenue gained this year
will help to offset these increased costs.
Mr Marshall: Does the Minister have any idea how much extra money will result from
the total collection?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: The revenue last year was $975,000. It is expected that the
revenue this year will be $1,240,000. Last year the deficit in the examination account was
$217,000, and even with this increase it is expected that there will be a deficit of about
$87,000 this year.
Mr Wellington: Is the prime purpose of the increase to meet the increased salaries and
fees payable to the assessors of the School Certificate examination-in other words, the
teachers themselves?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: That is correct. The increase that was made last year would not
of itself have covered the cost, but with another 45 percent increase in the fees for markers
and supervisors and examiners there was a very substantial loss, which will be nearly
recovered by this increase.
Mr Hunt: As the increase from $14.50 to $18 represents a 25 percent increase at least, is
it now the Minister's philosophy that the user-pays principle should be applied to the School
Certificate examination, resulting in those who can least afford it paying the most, as a
percentage of their income, for their children to sit the examination?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: I have already said that the fees do not completely cover the cost
of the examination, and I suspect that the deficit this year will be about the same as the
deficit when the Labour Government was in power.
Mr Courtenay: What was the fee in 1975-the last year of the third Labour
Government-and what will it be in the second year of the fourth National Government?
Hon. L. W. GANDAR: Frankly, I cannot quite remember what it was in 1975.
[Interruption.] I do not think members should regard this as a subject for laughter. There is a
tremendous number of details that I cannot carry in my head. It would be foolish of me to
give an answer without knowing the exact figure. There was not an increase in 1975, but
there was an increase in 1976 to cover expenses. There has since been a 45 percent increase
in costs, and therefore we are making some effort to recover them by an increase of 50c per
paper this year.

## p. 587 (#595) ############################################

Urgent Question-Admissibility
should be interested to know in what circumstances the Chair is prepared to allow such
urgent questions to be asked.
Mr SPEAKER: I do not think we should spend a lot of time in any lengthy discussion of
this matter, but some guidance might perhaps be very briefly given. I have felt there is a
danger of an accumulation of urgent questions in the same way as we have, I think, far too
many notices of motion for the good health of the running of the House. I have no guidance
in the second direction. In the first I have, and it is a Standing Order that permits urgent
questions to be asked when there is urgency in the public interest. A classic circumstance in
which I regard urgency in the public interest as existing is one in which some irrevocable
course of events is about to happen—for instance, if a building is about to be demolished. It
could not be "de-demolished" and put back again if, on consideration, the Minister thinks
there is a good case. That is the reason I allowed the urgent question that went in today. As
to whether or not traffic officers should go about their duty in pairs at certain times and in
certain places; I felt that was an administrative decision-probably a departmental matter,
but a matter that will no doubt be looked at from time to time and will not cause something
irrevocable to happen by tomorrow morning. This is not, I should say, a matter for
ministerial intervention but rather of administration at departmental level. Those are the
broad reasons I allowed one question and not the other.

ADDRESS IN REPLY
Adjourned debate on the question, That a respectful Address be presented to His
Excellency the Governor-General in reply to His Excellency's Speech.
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): The Address in Reply debate gives
each Minister an opportunity to explain the responsibilities he handles on behalf of the
Government and the country. It is also an opportunity to review progress made. When I
spoke in the imprest supply debate earlier this year, comment was made by Opposition
speakers that I had failed to mention energy. I shall devote my entire address to the subject
of energy. The Government believes that it is not advisable to impose the long-term
consequences of an energy policy on people without their prior knowledge, or, if possible
consultation with them. On becoming the Minister of Energy Resources one of my tasks was
to chart the next steps in developing an energy policy that the country has been looking
forward to. Members will appreciate that there are many variables involved, and some of the
factors raise questions that cannot be answered for some time.
In consultation with my caucus colleagues and my advisers in the departments I
developed a proposal, which I explained in some detail at the recent energy conference in
Wellington, to produce a document called "Goals and Guidelines towards an Energy Policy
for New Zealand, First Public Draft." It is intended to produce the document later this year,
and it should set out, as its title suggests, the goals of the Government's energy policies, and
the guidelines that should be followed to reach those goals. It is intended that the document

months after its production a consensus on the reactions will evolve to enable the Govern-

would encompass not only the Government's thinking, but also the Government's thinking
suitably modified by the best responses coming forward from the people.
This approach does not suggest a Government that is unsure of itself, but a Government
that realises that the future energy needs of the country and how they might best be met are
subjects of first importance, not just in Government administration, but also in the
development of New Zealand's society. Therefore, it is not only appropriate, but it is very
fitting, that this document should be discussed publicly. While Minister of Energy Resources
I shall endeavour to tell the people what the Government is proposing, and why, and
whenever possible the people will have the opportunity to contribute to the policy. Members
appreciate that from time to time there are decisions that must be made by the Government,
and the Government will stand by those decisions. There are undoubtedly many alternative
approaches available, but when it is possible to involve the community in consultation that
policy should be adopted. Public comment is healthy, and will be an interesting indication of
the importance the public attaches to the subject.
In the time available I cannot touch on all matters concerning the energy scene, but I
shall dwell on a few of them. The first is nuclear energy. Within the last few weeks the fact
finding group on nuclear power chaired by Sir Malcolm Burns has reported, and its report is
now a public document. The report tended to confirm my earlier estimation that we have
some breathing, thinking, and planning time before a decision about nuclear power must be
made. In its 1975 manifesto the Government made it clear that it would make no decisions
on nuclear power generation until it had received the findings and recommendations of the
royal commission it was to set up. The royal commission has been set up, and is sitting, and
later this year it will investigate nuclear energy in North America and Europe. The royal
commission, chaired by Sir Thaddeus McCarthy, is expected to report to the Government
early next year. The Government will await the findings of the royal commission before it
announces future decisions and plans.
There are several other observations in the report of the fact finding group on nuclear
power that are worth noting. The report suggests that the evidence before the committee
showed that it would be possible to postpone the decision on nuclear power, but it "must be
faced ultimately, and can only become more difficult with the passage of time." This is
expanded on later when the committee makes the point that if we think in terms of using
alternative sources of energy before we face up to this decision we may very well be creating
environmental problems that we would not wish to create, and it would mean that the
comparison was no longer between a nuclear programme and possible alternatives, but
between a nuclear programme and total commitment to all the alternatives. The report
states, "In terms of resource utilisation such a plan would close an alarming number of
options for succeeding generations." It is obvious that this report and the report of the royal
commission are documents which must be available to the Government for close and careful
scrutiny before it can form a firm and long-term energy policy. This is another good reason
why the goals and guidelines approach is most suitable.
One particularly vexatious area that I should like to refer to is the industrial dispute that
has bedevilled the Marsden B power station project for some time. As at 9 June, out of a
possible 355 working days 211 have been lost due to industrial disputes on that project. The
cost of supervisory overhead expenses, hire of plant, and so on, is between $13,000 and
$15,000 a day, giving a total of between $2,743,000 and $3,165,000 for the 211 days lost. That
is a cost to the Electricity Department. With regard to lost wages, this can be argued in
various ways, and after a comment I made on television recently some of the union officials
saw fit to argue with me, but I have here a pretty conservative analysis of the position. The
basic facts are these: The average gross wage, including allowances, is $158 a week. Average
take-home pay is $110 a week, and the number of men involved, including subcontractors, is
265. Using those figures, and assuming a full number of men for the period, the gross wages
amount to $1.8 million, and the take-home pay amounts to $1.25 million. If every dollar
turned over four times-and this is an interesting comment made in the same television
programme by a Whangarei retailer-it represents the loss of about $100,000 of spending to
the city of Whangarei each week. In addition, the Government has spent $300,000 on extra
storage, and has $25 million worth of plant waiting at the site to be installed.
All this could have been avoided—and it still could be stopped-if those involved would
see fit to bury their difficulties and return to work. I still hope that good sense will prevail.
The problem has dragged on, and it is a very poor commentary on our industrial relations. It
is a particularly distressing commentary on the sense of community concern-or lack of
it-of the people directly responsible. There have been talks as recently as the weekend, and


## p. 589 (#597) ############################################

589

this morning. I still hope good sense will prevail, but the public is entitled to know that in a
very close vote on a return to work only a week or two ago the vote was lost on the strength
of a small number of proxy votes sent from boilermakers in the Wellington area. Work at
Huntly is proceeding. It is now at a critical stage, with many key jobs being worked on. The
deadline for the first commercial power production is 1 April 1979, and if all goes well and
everyone co-operates this deadline should be met.
Members will be interested to know that New Plymouth is completed, with all machines
working. Stratford has been producing a good amount of power during the year, and has
been performing well. Whirinaki is an interesting new development; three machines are
ready for service. We are waiting there for the oil supply pipeline to be completed, and it
should be completed within the next 3 or 4 months. Work is being done in the Upper
Waitaki. The commissioning programme for the Tekapo canals and Tekapo B station is
being carried out. The full production of power from Tekapo B is expected about the third
week in August. Work on Ohau A and Ohau B is proceeding according to programme.
I should like to say a word about Auckland Thermal No. 1. As members will know, the
Electricity Department had proposals for a substantial thermal station at Waiau Pa. This
project ran into a certain amount of criticism in hearings before the Franklin County
Council. The Electricity Department has no wish to do other than serve the interests of New
Zealand well and faithfully. At present, it is undertaking concurrently studies of such things
as combined cycle alternatives, and the availability of sites. The work is being done in co-
operation with the Auckland Regional Authority and the Ministry of Works. A study is also
being made of the combined cycle type of power generation used by overseas operators, and
the experience that has been gleaned from this. Two senior engineers have been abroad
making personal studies. Consultants on behalf of the department have been involved in
discussions with manufacturers of this sort of equipment and with prospective suppliers, and
a number of design studies have been completed. We hope, as a result of the investigations
now being carried out, to be able to make a recommendation to the Government by
September, or shortly afterwards, on the practicability of accepting a combined cycle
alternative to the more traditional and more orthodox thermal proposal for Waiau Pa.
Members will appreciate that there are several advantages in the combined cycle
proposals. I have not time to detail them, but the plants use gas more efficiently; by perhaps
7 percent or 8 percent. They are smaller and can therefore be located closer to industrial sites
or to the centre of a city. It is also possible to build them in stages, and it may very well be
possible to space such projects in different parts of Auckland, thereby minimising the cost
and reducing the physical problems of reticulating the power through the Auckland area.
May I say a word or two about coal? For several years the coal industry was considered
to be on the way down, and on the way out. This is not now the case, and the coal industry
has made a considerable recovery since about 1971. I have not time to read the figures I have
here, but I am sure members will accept my assurance that the increase in coal production
has been healthy and has been achieved with an absolute minimum in staff increases by the
Department of Mines. There are some problems that should be referred to. There is a
shortage of skilled staff at all levels, but particularly there is a shortage of trained,
experienced management for underground mining, and quite frankly it will take some years
to rectify this problem. It is also worth noting the need to develop new underground mining
techniques, and so improve the present extraction rate from 37 percent to, we hope, more
than 70 percent. This problem is being actively tackled, but a solution is not expected before
the mid-1980s. If we can raise the extraction rate of recoverable coal to 70 percent, the
reserves will increase by about 50 percent. In energy terms this would be worth one or two
oil or gas fields the size of Maui. Members will therefore realise the importance of our
making progress in this new form of technology in mining coal.
There are other aspects of energy responsibilities that I should like to discuss, and one is
particularly relevant to today's circumstances. The Government proposes to merge the three
energy portfolios of Energy Resources, Mines, and Electricity into one new, stronger, top-
level Ministry of Energy. This proposal will be carried out this year-in fact, I hope to
introduce legislation to make it possible within a few weeks. It is interesting to note that the
Labour Party's 1972 manifesto stated: "Labour will expand and strengthen the Ministry of
Energy Resources to become wholly responsible for the co-ordination and development of
the country's fuel and energy resources." In other words, the administrative change that the
Government is introducing this year was proposed by the Labour Party in its 1972 policy, but
the Labour Government, in its 3 years in office, failed to make the change. It moved away
from a strong Ministry of Energy, because it spread the responsibilities this Government is

giving to one ministry among three ministers. That was an administrative move of the worst
kind. The Labour Party in its manifesto said that the Ministry of Energy Resources would
administer and operate the State coal mines. It did no such thing. It also said that the
Ministry of Energy Resources would administer and operate the New Zealand Electricity
Department. The Labour Government did not carry out that proposal, but kept two
separate ministries. The 1972 Election Manifesto of the Labour Party stated that the

previous Labour Government. It is an interesting commentary on the way in which, despite
being in office for 3 years, Labour members never really came to grips with the task of being
the Government and directing the economy.

Mr SPEAKER: I thank honourable members for their assistance. The problem is a little
complicated, but not, I think, too difficult. In the first place, the point raised by the member
for Henderson, although a sound one, does not necessarily cover the position completely.
He said that Standing Order 413 is designed to avoid a waste of time and undue expansion of
debate, or words to that effect, and I think that is entirely correct. The aim was to eliminate
the number of debates on reports recommending petitions to the Government for considera-
tion, favourable consideration, or most favourable consideration. Those are now substan-
tially precluded except where there is a rider, though a brief expression of thanks may in any
case be made by one person to the committee for having dealt with the petition.
I think the matter is covered by the point raised by the Acting Prime Minister. The most
relevant Standing Order, it seems to me, is 173, which states: "No member shall allude to
any debate of the same session . . ." but that does not preclude him from alluding to the
subject. What is precluded is reference back to speeches and things that happened in the
debate. If there is a debate on, say, atomic energy, then it is quite out of order to say, in the
same session, “The honourable member for Waikikamukau said so-and-so, and I do not
agree, and those are my reasons." But the subject of atomic energy is certainly not excluded
from the House for the whole of the session.
So the position, as I see it, is that allusion to the handling, or proper manner of
handling, of any type of petition-whether it should go to the House or elsewhere-is not
out of order, but any reference whatever to anything said in the House when the committee's
report was before the House previously this session would be out of order. On the question
of saving time, we should bear in mind that the member has 20 minutes to speak, whether or
not he devotes some minutes to this, or the same number of minutes to something else.
Finally, on the overall subject, I shall read from page 423 of Erskine May, 19th edition,
where we find this: “Reference to prior debates of the current session, whether in the House
or in the Committee of the Whole House, which would tend to reopen matters already
decided has been discouraged, even if such reference is not irrelevant. This rule has not
always been strictly enforced: particular circumstances may seem to justify a member in
alluding to speeches made in past debates, and the Speaker will judge, in each case, how far
the rule may properly be relaxed. The rule does not, in any case, apply to debates on
different stages of the Bill"-where there may be reference to speeches at earlier stages. I do
not propose to relax the rule but I do say this, that any reference at all to what was said in the
House on this subject previously in this session is forbidden, but that reference to the subject
itself is not.

One issue of importance in Otago has been freight subsidies. The Government is acutely
aware of the problems associated with high transport costs. Though most severe in regional
development areas, it is a national problem affecting all aspects of the economy. For this
reason questions of transport costs and efficiency need to be approached in the context of
long-term planning and a co-operative effort to streamline transport so that users can plan in
the knowledge that an efficient and realistically priced service is available. Freight subsidies
are and have always been seen to be at best a short-term palliative for firms facing the
general problem of rising costs. The cure can be found only in the control of rising costs, the
control of inflation-a priority the Government has attended to with some success-in
making the best possible use of transport resources, and in encouraging regions to do those
things with which they can identify and do best. The aim of the revised freight subsidy
scheme announced in the 1976 Budget was to phase out this form of assistance. A flexible

Address in Reply
In spite of our best efforts, and in spite of some successes, the fact remains that each year the
carnage continues, and will continue until either we somehow change our attitudes towards
its causes, or we are prepared to follow the example of France or the lead of the legislators in
South Australia.
A study of the role of alcohol in fatal road accidents in New Zealand in 1970 showed
that at least 31 percent, perhaps up to 61 percent, of fatal accidents involved alcohol. That
year, New Zealanders aged 15 years and over each drank an average of 8.26 litres of absolute
alcohol, equivalent to well over 30 gallons of beer. By 1974, that figure had increased to
11.36 litres, equivalent to about 50 gallons of beer. We must remember that 2 percent of the
drinkers consume 20 percent of the alcohol. The trends in New Zealand are similar to those
in France up to about 1970. By that time, Frenchmen aged 15 years and over consumed an
average of 28 litres of absolute alcohol. By about that time, the use of half the number of
hospital beds in France and 40 percent of the public health cost were attributed to alcohol-
related disease, injury, or accident. Clearly, we are heading in the same direction. Twelve
years ago the French Government initiated an education programme aimed at teaching the
young, in particular, how to drink safely. It has taken more than 10 years for this programme
to show any tangible result, but France is now the only Western country where the
consumption of alcohol, the road toll, and alcoholism are all showing a decline; all the rest
are showing an increase.
In South Australia, the society, the consumption of alcohol, and the road toll are all
similar to those in New Zealand. The State Government, however, has taken positive action
to bring about a change for the better. Recent research into drinking drivers in South
Australia identified them as, on average, male, young to middle aged, married or, if single,
living with their family, employed as skilled or semi-skilled workers, and convivial drinkers
who prefer to be with company rather than alone. They do not drink to drown their sorrows,
but to enjoy themselves with their friends. They are ordinary people like you and me. Two
distinct groups have been identified among the drinking drivers: first, the non-addicted
drinking driver, usually a casual drinker, and a one-time offender; secondly, the alcohol-
dependent driver. Research work in South Australia showed that more than 50 percent of
drunken drivers are alcoholics, and that driving under the influence of alcohol is often an
early sign of alcoholism. Indeed, recognition of this important early sign may lead to the
rapid and reliable diagnosis of the condition of alcoholism before it has progressed to the
stage commonly known as classical alcoholism, the skid-row type that a blind man would be
able to recognise, and which, unfortunately, is often beyond cure.
The report in the Otago Daily Times of 23 May this year on the Dunedin course for
impaired drivers indicates that the work done by Miss Mary Anderson shows similar results
to those found in South Australia. In Dunedin, it was found that most of the people
repeatedly convicted of drinking and driving offences could be alcoholics, without realising
it. Seventy-eight percent of a random sample of Dunedin drivers convicted of a drinking and
driving offence have an alcohol problem. While the non-alcoholic driver tends to be
frightened back to his senses by his first offence and court appearance, the alcoholic is likely
to continue to drive under the influence of alcohol in spite of his previous arrests. Some of
these people have been apprehended as often as five times and, when one remembers that
the odds against being picked up are something like 2000:1, one can feel appalled at how
often that fellow has been at large, creating a hazard to other road users. Moreover, he is
likely to have a blood alcohol level of more than 180, which would put most non-alcoholic
drinkers on their ear, but leaves him, as an alcoholic, still able to function, in a fashion.
Seventy percent of the alcoholic drivers under study in South Australia were in the early
stages of alcoholism, which is usually unrecognised or ignored by doctors, and yet at this
stage alcoholism can be treated successfully. For too long we have focussed our attention on
the skid-row person as the alcoholic, and neglected the majority of alcoholics, who are like
most of us in appearance and in ways. They are employed, they own houses and cars, they
live with their families, and they drive on the roads. Drunken driving is often a symptom of
the early stage of alcoholism, when the prognosis is still good, and when many people can be
cured. It is now acknowledged that legal sanctions are of little value in controlling the
increasing incidence of driving offences. This is not really surprising, because drunken
driving is, in many cases, simply an early sign of alcoholism. In such cases, enforcing the laws
and imposing stringent penalties will not solve the problem, unless consideration is given to
treating the individuals concerned.
It is well known that, the longer the duration of excessive drinking, the greater the
likelihood of developing an addiction to alcohol, with all its consequences. Time and

quantity are the causes of alcoholism; nothing else. One research worker found that it takes
an average of 12 years of regular heavy drinking to develop the unmistakable symptoms and
signs of alcoholism. A fair measure of what can be defined as heavy drinking is three jugs of
beer a day. For some people, particularly the very young, alcohol is a much more sudden
poison, and they can become addicted in a very short time indeed. Although 50 percent of
the alcoholic drivers under consideration in South Australia admitted being in strife with
alcohol, hardly any of them were spotted by their family doctors. Many who consulted their
doctors about gastric complaints were given prescriptions for various medicaments, but only
one driver was advised to cut down on his drinking. Obviously, doctors are reluctant, for
various reasons, to ask their patients about drinking habits. Alcoholism, it appears, is the
only diagnosis avoided in medicine. There could be no simpler explanation of excessive
drinking than to regard it as a result of some underlying psychological problem. Alcoholics,
in fact, come from a cross section of society in respect to physical, mental, and social health.
The misleading idea that people are driven to drink by their personal problems largely arises
from the effects of alcohol on the personality of the person. Many alcoholic drivers were
emotionally normal before becoming addicted, but their problems developed as their
dependence on alcohol increased. We are looking at the results, not the causes.

Mr HARRISON: When we adjourned, I was discussing the associated problems of
alcoholism and road safety, and describing some of the steps taken by the State Government
in South Australia to deal with them. No doubt the war against alcoholism should be fought
simultaneously on all fronts, but recent experience in France shows that education of the
young is one effective weapon. The other system of dealing with the problem of alcoholism,
which shows promise, is that adopted in South Australia, where early identification of many
alcoholics is possible through the apprehension of drinking drivers, who have to receive
treatment at an early stage when there is a good chance of recovery. To sum up, drinking
drivers are not dissimilar from the ordinary citizen. Many drinkers were successful and
adequate people before the addiction developed. Moreover, it has been shown that when the
addiction is broken, those people can return to their previous normal condition. Drinking
drivers fall into two distinct groups: first, the non-addicted; and, secondly, the alcohol-
dependent. More than 50 percent of drinking drivers are alcoholics. About 70 percent are in
the early stages of alcoholism, when there is a very good chance of successful recovery after
proper treatment.
On 16 December last the Governor of South Australia assented to Act No. 103, which
amended the Road Traffic Act 1961 to 1976, and the penalties for offences such as driving
under the influence of alcohol or drugs, driving with a prescribed level of alcohol in the
blood, and failure to comply with alcotests, breath tests, and blood tests-all of which
provisions are similar to those in New Zealand. In the 1976 legislation, penalties were fixed
for the first, second, and subsequent offences. For every offence, a disqualification from
driving for varying periods, ranging from 6 months to more than 3 years, was stipulated. In
addition, for the first and second offences, penalties included fines and/or prison sentences.
For subsequent offences, in all cases fines were dispensed with and a prison sentence became
obligatory. This certainly makes tough reading, but the amending Act also provides that,
where a person offends again within 3 years of his previous conviction, the court, before
imposing any penalty, shall order him to attend an assessment clinic to determine whether he
suffers from alcoholism or drug addiction. The superintendent of the clinic has to report to
the court and to the offender, and, after giving him an opportunity to give evidence on the
report, the court shall, on being satisfied that the offender does suffer from alcoholism or
drug addiction, disqualify him from holding a driving licence until further notice. For his
second offence, then, he shall also be disqualified until further notice, but after an
appropriate lapse of time the offender may apply for a revocation of the disqualification
order. Before the court can allow this, he must attend the assessment clinic, and the court
must be satisfied from the superintendent's report that the offender no longer suffers from
alcoholism or drug addiction. Compulsion, then, is virtually an essential element in the
South Australian scheme. The alternative for the individual on his second drunken driving
offence is either disqualification and treatment, or disqualification and imprisonment or a
substantial fine.
However, compulsion in this way is no different from the compulsion in the breath and
blood tests we have in New Zealand. Indeed, while these are a means whereby the offender
helps condemn himself of an offence, the compulsion applied in South Australia is likely to
be beneficial to him. Voluntary attendance at a driving course has obviously failed. The

statements we have to answer on this, which is perhaps the most explosive possible subject,
should be based on distortions of fact. We can do nothing about the ready audiences

I want now to say a few words about the role of private foreign investment in this
country. There is no way that this country can generate from domestic sources the capital
formation required to satisfy more than a fraction of our developmental needs in the
foreseeable future. We can, of course, turn to such institutions as the World Bank to help fill
the gap, particularly for infrastructure development, but the private foreign investor, too, has
an important role to play and, in my view, could play an even greater role in the future.
There are still many people in the country, particularly those on the left of the political
spectrum, who have an attitude of jingoistic hostility towards private foreign investment in
this country. The more extreme of them conjure up paranoiac visions of faceless forces bent
on as much acquisition and exploitation as they can get away with. We all know that there
have to be safeguards for private foreign investments, and we all know that a country like
New Zealand does not have unlimited capacity to absorb foreign capital, particularly at a
time such as this. Those who would deny private foreign investment an important role in our
country's future are out of touch with reality.
As an example of the benefits to New Zealand that can be derived from this source of
investment, I cite a project with which I am reasonably familiar through my recent
involvement in relevant negotiations. This is a development package involving a milk
recombination plant at Dubai in the Arabian Gulf, and a vegetable oil refinery at Helensville
in my electorate. In both cases, the Kaipara Dairy Co. provides the expertise and the key
role and the financial backing comes from an overseas investor, Dr S. Oskar, a Paraguayan
national with highly placed financial contacts in the United Arab Emirates. In our contacts
with the Arab world, two of the many interesting points to emerge are, first, their interest in
recycling oil earnings into investment in 'politically stable countries and, second, their
personal way of doing business. That is why the contacts such as Dr Oskar has made in
Dubai are so important. Many foreigners have come away from the Arabian Gulf area
without making the contacts that count, because they do not have personal contacts who are
known and trusted by the Arabs. This Government has itself been conspicuously successful
in making contacts that count in Saudi Arabia and Bahrain. Help is now coming from the
private sector, with a breakthrough in another part of the Gulf. The benefits the new
package project will bring New Zealand are impressive by any standards. First of all, the
milk plant will create a new market. It will also consolidate New Zealand's presence in the
Arabian Gulf and complement the market development that has already been started. It has
also stimulated further interest to invest on the part of the Arabs. I know for a fact that they
are interested in the meat field, and within the next few weeks there will be further visits
from this area to discuss the possibility of a new meat deal.
The milk plant is a new and unique project, involving a dairy company making its own
raw material and converting this to consumer products at the market-place. It points the way
to a new role for private enterprise in this field and, incidentally, a $750,000 export order for
the Dubai plant has been made with an Auckland company. The vegetable oil plant means
substantial overseas savings, through a conservatively estimated saving of $1 million in
added value. It will mean cheaper products for the consumer, because of bulk order
discounts, charter shipping freight rates, and fewer middleman charges because of Dr
Oskar's personal contacts with growers overseas. It also means regional development, and a
possible revival of interest in a domestic vegetable-oil industry in the north. The financial
structure of these projects is also interesting. The Kaipara Dairy Co. and Dr Oskar will have
10 percent each of the shareholding in the Dubai plant, the remainder being Arab. In the
case of the oil refinery, there is a 60 percent New Zealand equity with no less than 50 percent
which can be taken up in employee shares. These projects represent an impressive new
development by any standards, and the Kaipara Dairy Co. is to be congratulated on the very
innovative approach it has shown recently. I am sure that everybody in the House wishes it
very well indeed with its new venture.
I now turn to one aspect of the portfolio of Attorney-General that has preoccupied me a
great deal over the last year. I refer to the judiciary, which is facing an exceptionally heavy
period of pressure; work is mounting up, particularly in the Auckland area, but this is
certainly not due to any lack of quality or of application on the part of the judiciary. The

mounting wave of litigation has caused bottlenecks, which are always detrimental to our
system of justice. To that extent, I must agree with recent comments that there has been a
slow down in the efficiency of the court process. What people have not stressed, however, is
the practical difficulties involved in expeditiously dealing with this problem. At a time when
every aspect of Government expenditure has had to run the gauntlet of an expenditure
committee, which has performed its work with formidable efficiency, it has taken a great
deal of persuasive argument to secure the new judicial appointments so far secured. Since I
took office, there have been three new permanent Supreme Court appointments; virtually a
new Court of Appeal, with a new president and a new member; and one true temporary
judicial replacement. One further permanent Supreme Court appointment is to come, one
additional member is to be appointed to the Court of Appeal, and there will be an additional
true temporary judge.
People who are intimate with the legal system will know that for some time there has
been considerable controversy over temporary judicial appointments as against permanent
appointments. In fact, there are two kinds of temporary appointment. Probationary appoint-
ments are made when a judge is, for an interim period, appointed on a temporary basis prior
to his appointment being subsequently made permanent. I believe we should not have such
appointments, and while I am Attorney-General such appointments will be made only for
very short periods, if at all. However, I cannot accede to the Law Society's request that I
commit myself to no further true temporary appointments—that is, appointments made for a
specified period on a temporary basis. The report of the historic Royal Commission on the
Courts will not be available for at least a year, and it would be unrealistic to assume that
there will be immediate action on its recommendations; at the very least there will be a time
gap before the House resumes the following year to effect any statutory changes needed. As
Attorney-General I must, therefore, have as much room for manoeuvre as possible. I must
be able to appoint another true temporary judge if necessary. I do not want to do this, and if
it is possible to make additional permanent appointments I will do so.
I turn now to my new portfolio of Postmaster-General and I should like first to say a
word of personal appreciation to Mr Sewell, who recently retired from the post of Director-
General of the Post Office. Mr Sewell was a man of great loyalty and integrity, and his
regard for his staff was apparent in all sections of the Post Office. He presided over a very
difficult period in its history, but a period also of considerable achievement. I should like
also to congratulate the new director-general, Mr George Peters. He and I have already
found considerable personal affinity, which augurs well for our future joint efforts. I have
taken over the administration of this portfolio at a very difficult time. The Post Office is the
largest trading organisation in the country, employing 38 000 people and with assets valued
at more than $600 million. It has also been one of the most efficient trading organisations
and, consequently, the public has always assumed that its services are available on demand.
Unfortunately, over the last 2 or 3 years economic conditions have put pressure on
resources; waiting lists for telephones have tended to get longer and projects have been
deferred.
When the National Government took office, it was very shocked to see the consequ-
ences of the previous Government's policy on the Post Office. In 1973, the loss incurred by
the Post Office was $2 million, but by 1976 that had risen to $39 million. This meant not only
that the Post Office was facing a greater loss than it had ever faced, it also meant that the
demand for Post Office services was artificially inflated, which aggravated an already
difficult situation. Post Office finances are back in the black, and the Government is
determined to continue this viability on the basis that the Post Office should be a successful
paying trading department. The Government is devising a plan; some decisions have already
been made, while others have yet to be taken. I undertake that while I am Postmaster-
General I will do all I can to meet the inherited backlogs with a minimum of delay. A major
problem is the very high import content of much of the equipment used by the Post Office,
so even when the money is available there is still the problem of the amount of imports we
can afford. The Government's aim is to bring the services back to a level of such high
efficiency that the public once again takes them for granted. When economic conditions
force a slow down of the massive investment flow required, it is important that the public
should understand why the Government cannot promise that services will always be
available on demand, and why it cannot promise that the position will be righted quickly. I
am very proud to be associated with this giant organisation. The Post Office is planning a
publicity campaign, which, it is hoped, will reach a very wide audience and draw attention to

When the National Government took office, the Prime Minister asked me to chair the
Pacific Islands Industrial Development Committee, and I want to speak for a few minutes
about this scheme. W hen in Opposition, I was spokesman for Island Affairs. The National
Opposition's policy recognised the importance of economic development to social progress
and better standards of living for the people of the South Pacific, and listed five areas where
it saw economic development as necessary. One of those was to facilitate increased
employment opportunities in the Islands by encouraging New Zealand manufacturers,
through special taxation or depreciation allowances, to consider Pacific Island ventures and,
where EEC agreements are in force, to take advantage of wider export possibilities. The
National Government set up the Pacific Islands industrial development scheme. The
committee of which I am chairman comprises two representatives from the Federation of
Labour, two manufacturers representatives, and one officer from each of the Ministry of
Foreign Affairs, Treasury, and the Department of Trade and Industry. The committee met
several times early in 1976 and agreed that New Zealand industry should be encouraged to
move to the Pacific Islands. We reported to the Minister of Trade and Industry, who in turn
put the scheme before Cabinet. After that I led the Pacific Islands parliamentary group,
comprising members of Parliament and representatives of the Pacific Islands Industrial
Development Committee, which discussed the general terms of the scheme
New Zealand has a very close association with the Islands, and the number of Pacific
Islanders now living in this country is increasing; between 1971 and 1976 there was a 50
percent increase in the number of Polynesian people living in New Zealand. During our visit
to the Islands we were given figures showing that for the 18 months to June 1976 more than
16 000 people from Western Samoa, Tonga, and Fiji came to New Zealand. Although most
came as visitors, a few came under work schemes and some for other reasons. Many of those


## p. 616 (#624) ############################################

616
14 June
Address in Reply
people became overstayers, thus creating a problem. We must have a fair amount of
sympathy for the Island countries. In 1974, copra was selling at US$700 a tonne on the world
market, but by December 1975 that had dropped to US$200 a tonne. For countries such as
Western Samoa and Tonga, copra is a very important means of earning overseas exchange.
The scheme announced will initially cover Fiji, Tonga, Western Samoa, the Cook
Islands, and Niue, and has been designed to assist the provision of incentives to encourage
New Zealand firms to develop manufacturing enterprises in the Pacific Islands, to provide
assistance to those countries to enable them to develop export markets for their products,
and to provide special access to the New Zealand market for ventures established under the
scheme. We looked at various critieria: the value of the venture to the Island economy, the
local resources, the foreign exchange benefits, the employment opportunities likely to result,
and the extent to which the venture needs assistance and incentives from New Zealand. W e
believe that the ventures should be commercially viable and should not require on-going
assistance. We studied the desirability of attracting ventures to a particular Island location,
and considered the need to maintain rational industrial development within the Islands.
There is no doubt that co-operation is needed among the Island countries about the type of
industrial development to take place on any Island. We considered the provision of special
access to the New Zealand market, and studied the need to prevent undue disruption to
production and employment in New Zealand.
The incentive we suggested was suspensory loans, which in our opinion are very
generous; we are prepared to help with staff training costs, transfer costs for staff, and plant
and feasibility studies; and we are prepared to give indirect assistance through loan finance.
The Development Finance Corporation is willing to consider applications for commercial
loan finance. The New Zealand Government is prepared to make grants to assist with local
equity, because it is thought that some of the ventures should have a local equity. Where
necessary the provision of special access to the New Zealand market will be the subject of
consultation with interested parties-the Federation of Labour and the Manufacturers
Federation. Both the federations have indicated they will view access to the New Zealand
market favourably. One of the first questions asked by those making inquiries is whether the
New Zealand market is open to them. We have assurances from the Federation of Labour
and the manufacturers that they will treat each application generously. I believe that there is
a desire in New Zealand to have a certain movement of goods back to New Zealand, and I
am sure we will have co-operation from the manufacturers and the Federation of Labour.
There are opportunities under the Lomé agreement for New Zealand firms to go into the
Pacific Islands and, provided there is a 50 percent content from the EEC as well as from the
Pacific Islands, there is access to the EEC market which is not available from New Zealand.
Tonga has a population of 100 000, and Western Samoa of between 160 000 and 170 000,

population of 8000. It is necessary that we do everything in our power to create job
opportunities in the Islands. It is not in New Zealand's interests to have as many as 8000
people coming to New Zealand annually, but that is the type of increase we face. Agriculture
will remain the base for Pacific Island countries, but we can do quite a lot for them. The
Pacific Islands Industrial Development Committee has had about 80 inquiries, about 10 of
which look to be fairly serious. Some of them will provide for the local market, so they are
small ventures; others will provide for the local market, the New Zealand market, and Third
World countries.

$805 a hectare, an increase of 9 percent on the previous year. In 1972 the increase was 19.5

massive hike with an increase of 45.7 percent bringing the value up to $1,402 a hectare. In
1975, still under the Labour Government, there was again an increase of 21.3 percent, or a
value per hectare of $1,702. Listen to the 1976 figure. It was $1,809 a hectare, or an increase
of 6.2 percent. We did not have those massive hikes of 45 percent, 21 percent, and 19 percent
which we had under the Labour Government. For fattening farms the story is somewhat
similar. In 1972 there was an increase of 9.5 percent; in 1973 it was 15.3 percent; in 1974 the
increase was 23.8 percent; in 1975 it was 32 percent; and in 1976 we did not have those
double figures because the increase was 5 percent.

Oral Answers to Questions
WEDNESDAY, 15 JUNE 1977
Mr Speaker took the chair at 2.30 p.m.
Prayers.
ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Venison Exports
1. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru) asked the Minister of Agriculture, What was the volume
and value of venison exports last year, and what are the projected figures for the present
year?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): During the year ended 30 June 1976,
New Zealand exported a provisionally estimated 2652 tonnes of venison, which had an f.o.b
value of $8,171,000. During the year ended 30 June 1977, exports of about 2750 tonnes, with
an f.o.b value of $11.5 million, are likely.
Mr Elworthy: Is it a fact that in the last 2 years the volume of venison exports has
increased more rapidly than any other form of meat exports?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No, the peak year was 1972, and since then the total exports
have fallen to an extent, because more rigorous hygiene regulations have been brought in.
But superimposed on top of that, there is the rapidly growing domestically reared deer
industry.
Mr Bell: What proportion of the 1976 exports came from domestically farmed deer, as
compared to wild venison?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No, I do not have those figures with me, but I can find out for the
member if he wishes.
Mr Wetere: To what countries is venison being exported?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: Germany is the largest market, and there are some peripheral
countries in Europe. It is hoped that once domestically reared deer are brought in, with
post- and ante-mortem inspection, the American and Australian markets will open up.
Mr W. R. Austin: Does the Minister have the venison export figures on a provincial
basis, and, if so, how important nationally is the Southland venison exporting industry?
Hon. D. MacINTYRE: No, I do not have the figures by provinces, and I do not know if
they are kept by the department. Normally, we would be able to find out from the export
houses and areas from which they come.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
Magistrates' Court Cases in Christchurch
2. Mrs BATCHELOR (Avon) asked the Minister of Justice, How many full-time
magistrates are at present working in Christchurch, are there any delays in the hearing of
cases, and what is the number of cases awaiting a hearing?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice): The approved establishment of magis-
trates for Christchurch is seven. The present complement is six, one of whom is on sabbatical
leave. There are some delays in the hearing of cases, and at present there is a total of 318
domestic and 379 civil cases awaiting hearing. Although not specifically asked for, I think,
the honourable member would like to know what I am doing about the delay. In an effort to
overcome these arrears, relief arrangements have been made, including appointing a retiring
magistrate to relieve from August. My department is actively seeking suitable appointees for
the seventh position. In addition, last month I instructed my department to undertake a
comprehensive review of the magisterial work load in Christchurch in comparison with other
districts, to ascertain whether or not an eighth position should be established.
Mrs Batchelor: I thank the Minister for answering the question before I asked it. Do the
318 domestic cases tend to be the type of case of most concern to women; for example,
custody and maintenance cases?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I expect so, but that is not to say that the civil cases would
not also be of interest to women. I do not have a breakdown of the cases on the ground of
sex.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: What is the best estimate the Minister can give of the time


## p. 628 (#636) ############################################

628
15 June
Oral Answers to Questions
needed to dispose of these arrears and at the same time keep up with current work?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: Inevitably it will depend on my success in obtaining agree-
ment from practitioners to accept appointment and also on whether the result of inquiries
leads to the establishment of an eighth position. At present, the judgment of the department
is that present arrears represent about one magistrate's sitting time for a full year, so that the
position is very serious and is tending to worsen. The delay in obtaining a hearing can vary
considerably depending on the nature of the case, as the member would know. For example,
an uncomplicated civil case could be given a hearing as early as mid-July and a similar
domestic proceedings case in mid-August. For the more complex cases the delay would be
longer and would depend on the availability of a sufficiently uninterrupted period of sitting
time. At present the average delay is about 3 months, and my assessment of one magistrate's
total work for 1 year is about the closest I can come to answering the member's question
asking how long it would take to get everything up to date.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: When the Minister gives his estimate of the work load for one
magistrate for 1 year, that implies that the magistrate would be playing no part in the current
throughput of work.
Hon. DAVID THOMSON: I agree.
Question transferred to Supplementary Order Paper.
National Superannuitants
3. Dr SHEARER (Hamilton East) asked the Minister of Social Welfare, What is the total
number of national superannuitants aged 70 years and over, and, of these, what number
would have an annual income of over $5,000?
Hon. H. J. WALKER (Minister of Social Welfare): At 31 March 1977 there were
163,894 national superannuitants aged 70 years and over. This group represented approxi-
mately 44 percent of all national superannuitants. National súperannuation is payable to

press ahead with the exploration programme. The honourable member will appreciate that
the holes in fact are drilled at very widely spaced intervals and each hole represents a
different geological structure.
Hon. W. W. Freer: Are they encouraging or not?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: If they had been really encouraging we would have been drilling

endeavour to obtain an answer for him. From my general knowledge of the subject I can tell

hydrocarbons are to be found. Among the more important are the geological dome-like
structures. Until such time as these dome-like structures are established there is, of course,
no need to start drilling at all. When a dome-like structure is established, and seismic surveys
can help greatly to define these, there is still no guarantee that the nature and the porosity of
the rock in the structures are such as to be suitable points for the accumulation and gathering
of hydrocarbon substances. In the final analysis these can only be proved by drilling.

Secretary of Energy
6. Hon. A. J. FAULKNER (Roskill) asked the Minister of State Services, Is he aware

will be to amend the third schedule of the State Services Act 1962 to include the new

acted to invite interested people to apply for the position of permanent head. The
commission is well aware that an appointment cannot be made until the legislation is passed.

against the appointment.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Does the wording of the advertisement assume that the position will
be established in the form now conceived by the Executive, or is there any allowance for
possible amendment to the legislation in its passage through Parliament?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The wording of the advertisement is open. It is possible there
may be change, although it is highly unlikely having regard to the nature of the proposal.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Do I take it from the Minister's answers that Cabinet does not see
this use of Executive power without the approval of Parliament as an excess of use of
Executive power?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The answer is definitely no. It is preparedness for a position that
is all-important to this country. Those who listened yesterday to the Minister of Energy
Resources will appreciate that the urgent need is to get on with the job. Once this ministry is
created we want the right man who might be interested to be available at relatively short

Executive power on the basis of urgency when in fact urgency should have applied in the first
instance to the legislative authority?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I think the member is trying to make a mountain out of a
molehill. The Government has made a decision that it will put a legislative proposition to this
House. When the legislation is passed-and the Minister has indicated it is a matter of
priority-the Government wants to be in a position to act upon it.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Surely the Minister and his colleagues in Cabinet will have
considered that many people in the three departments concerned will be disturbed by this
move in regard to a top position carrying a salary of at least $28,000, particularly when the
action is being taken without legislative authority? Surely Cabinet should have given urgency
to the passing of the legislation first?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: I must refute the assertion. While that might apply in one or two
other instances, full consultation took place between the Cabinet committee and the State
Services and the heads of the various sectors which could be affected by the move before any
proposition was put to Cabinet and to the Government.
Hon. A J. Faulkner: Parliament is being ignored.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Parliament has not been ignored. Appropriate legislation will
come before Parliament, and I give the member an assurance that no appointment will be
made until Parliament grants the authority to make it.
