Economic and Financial Restraints
8. Hon. R. J. TIZARD (Deputy Leader of the Opposition) asked the Minister of
Finance, Why, when he has constantly preached the need for restraint in economic and
financial matters, has he permitted the very considerable increase in the money supply
during the calendar year 1976 referred to on page 18 of the recent report of the New Zealand
Monetary and Economic Council?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Energy Resources): I reply on behalf of the Acting
Minister of Finance. There are two definitions of money supply in New Zealand: first, the
money supply generally known as M1, comprising currency and trading bank demand
deposits; secondly, the money supply and selected liquid assets generally known as M3,
comprising the factors in M1 plus trading bank term deposits, and the total deposits of
savings banks, finance houses, stock firms, and money market dealers. There is always area
for argument on this subject both here and abroad as to the correct level of money supply
growth and which indicator of the money supply is the most important in any particular
circumstance. The Monetary and Economic Council has focused attention on trends in M3.
An equally valid approach would be to note the sharp downward trend in M1, which has
decelerated consistently quarter by quarter from 19.8 percent annual growth in the March
1976 quarter to 6.3 percent in the March 1977 quarter. The growth rates of M3 have been
substantially affected by the March 1976 monetary measures which greatly increased the
deposit effectiveness of banks, finance companies, and to a lesser extent savings banks. The
Holmes task force was very critical of the massive money supply fluctuations consequent
upon Labour policies. For instance, M1 moved from a 30 percent September 1973 quarter to
a 1 percent December 1974 quarter to a 19.8 percent March 1976 quarter, which, although
the Government had changed by that time, was the effect of the previous Government's


## p. 632 (#640) ############################################

632
15 June
Oral Answers to Questions
policies. There was a similar wild fluctuation in M3 under the Labour Government. Two
factors emerge since March 1976 which indicate the improving health of the monetary scene.
First, growth in M1 has fallen steadily, and, secondly, there has been a less sharp downward
movement in M3, but an encouraging lack of wild variation from quarter to quarter. Our
money supply growth is on a par with OECD comparisons.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Could I cut through that mass of verbiage and refer the Minister to
page 21 of the report, which shows that the total change in the year to December 1975 was
$213 million, but the total change in the year to June 1976 was $399 million? Does this
indicate that the National Government did nothing for 6 months after taking office?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: The member has obviously been unable to understand the answer
given. I would draw to his attention the important difference between M1 and M3, and
remind him that although the Monetary and Economic Council's table is based on M3, that is
not the basis for international comparisons. I should like to read from the London Economist
of 28 May, and remind the honourable member that the M1 money supply in New Zealand
for the March 1977 quarter was 6.3 percent increase. In Australia the figure was 8 percent; in
Canada, 7 percent; in France, 8.5 percent; and in West Germany 8.5 percent. The figure for
Holland was 6 percent, and Holland is the only country with a better record of controlling
money supply under M1 than we have.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Put your money where your mouth is.
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I do not think it is edifying to have a senior member of the
House calling out, "Put your money where your mouth is."
Hon. G. F. GAIR: It is quite all right. We are used to such comments from that
honourable member. In Italy, the money supply has risen on an annual rate in that quarter
by over 20 percent; in Japan it was 11 percent; in Sweden, 11 percent; in the United States,
6.5 percent; and in Britain it was 10 percent. The New Zealand figure is a clear indication
that the monetary policies introduced by this Government in March 1976 are working, and
are producing a number of healthy trends in the market, which were denied by the policies of
the Labour Government. It is very interesting to see the wild fluctuation in money supplies
quarter by quarter from March 1973 to March 1977-
Mr SPEAKER: Order! I really feel that this is moving towards a lengthy speech, instead
of being an answer to the question.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Could I ask the Minister to come back to New Zealand, and explain
why the figures on page 21 show that the increase in the money supply in New Zealand was
at almost twice the rate in the first 6 months of the National Government than it had been
during the 3 years of the Labour Government?
Hon. G. F. GAIR: Whether one used the M1 formula or the M3 formula, there is still an
improvement from March 1976 up to the present. We are talking about the last five quarters,
and in the case of M3 these are the annual rates of increase at quarterly rests. The M3 figures
fell from 16.7 percent to 15.3 percent. The M1 figure, which is the best international
comparison and the best indication of progress, has fallen from 19.8 percent to 6.3 percent.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: I would simply ask the Minister to make a New Zealand comparison
between what the National Government said it would achieve and did achieve and what it
criticised the Labour Government for achieving to December 1975.
Hon. G. F. GAIR: I shall be delighted to do that. In 1973, when the Labour
Government came to office, the money supply under the M3 formula moved in this
fashion-and these are annual increase rates at quarterly rests, forgetting the decimal points
and giving the main percentage movement: 25 percent, 26 percent, 27 percent, 21 percent.
Those are the figures for the first year of the Labour Government. The figures for the first
year of the National Government were: 16 percent, 19 percent, 16 percent, 17 percent, 15
percent. That is the worse of the two situations. The better of the two situations and the
more significant-and we were better than Labour under the M3 formula-under the M1
formula is, in the first year of the Labour Government, with the same relative figures: 25
percent, 29 percent, 29 percent, and 22 percent; and in the first year of the National
Government: 19 percent, 16 percent, 10 percent, 13 percent, and 6 percent. In each case the
facts prove that the contention of the Deputy Leader of the Opposition was wrong.

Militant Unions
Mr N. P. H. JONES (Invercargill): I move, That this House notes with deep concern the
findings of the Commission of Inquiry into the Heavy Engineering Industry and its conclusion
that the closure of nine companies with boilermaking components was "due primarily to the
disruptive tactics and restrictive practices imposed upon them by certain sections of the
Auckland and Wellington Boilermakers Unions", and that the Government and in particular
the Minister of Labour be applauded for pursuing a firm but fair approach towards responsible
unionism but now serves notice to irresponsible unionists that it will not tolerate the disruptive
tactics of militant unions using such methods to extort and demand with threats of strikes the
satisfying of their own selfish ends at the expense of the people's interests.
I draw the attention of the House to the commission's report. It is quite apparent that
the findings of this inquiry substantiate as fact what the country has known for some time;
that we have a militant group of mainly imported Tyneside and Liverpool mafia inside the
boilermakers' union who are working in concert with, and in league with, the Socialist Unity
Party to sabotage and wreck certain essential industries within the heavy engineering
industry. The report spells out in chapter and verse the reasons why nine engineering
companies have had to close down workshops, or part of their operations, over the past 7
years. Those companies, together with another 18, were intimidated by the wreckers in the
boilermakers' union, who throughout the past 7 years have deliberately and continuously
used excuses in four major demarcation areas on a number of occasions.
The report also states that the union has deliberately breached six major areas of the
Industrial Relations Act on numerous occasions, and has deliberately resorted to 24
different types of the most blatantly restrictive trade union practices the country has ever
seen. The union is still carrying out those practices at the Bank of New Zealand site. The
union representatives are probably meeting the Minister of Labour right now, but the union
members could not even stay at work, they went out on strike.
Hon. F. M. Colman: What happened to deregistration?
Mr N. P. H. JONES: I am just getting on to that. The National Government has made
some pretty hard and unpopular decisions about the country's economy to rectify what it
inherited from the Labour Government. I should say that most people, including many
responsible trade unionists, would like to see the Government making just as hard and
unpopular decisions against the wreckers and the union mafioso who, supported by the
Socialist Unity Party, are wrecking the trade union movement and sabotaging industry.
These sort of tactics, which the report brings to light, have no place in New Zealand, or in
the trade unions, and notice should be given along the lines of this motion to the
boilermakers in particular, and any other hard core militant unionists in essential industries,
that such tactics will no longer be tolerated by the Government.
I think we would all have the greatest respect and admiration for the firm and fair
manner in which the Minister of Labour is trying to administer his portfolio. In my view, and
that of most reasonable and fair minded people, the Minister is doing a very good job under
terrific handicaps being imposed upon him by militants who are politically motivated to
wreck certain essential industries named in this report. It is no coincidence that the industries
selected by the boilermakers are the very essence of our economy-the pulp and paper
making industry, the hydro industry, and so on. The commission's findings about the tactics
of the boilermakers' union, as well as the Socialist Unity Party, and its practices of extortion
and intimidation, should be published by every newspaper. If this report was in a paperback
it could well become a best seller, and would prove conclusively to every fair-minded and
right thinking New Zealander that what we have been claiming for years is in fact going on.
We hear the same story from Labour members about the reds under the bed. They are
not under the bed now. At its last conference the Labour Party refound its soul and
reaffirmed its ultimate socialist policy, so the reds are practically in the Labour bed. Let us
look at some of the tactics resorted to by the union and mentioned in the report. One
company was singled out for attack by militant members of the boilermakers union because
of the importance of its work-steel work for hydro generators. It was believed that a small
group of militants was set up in the plant to disrupt production. Because the manager of the
firm had occasion to speak to one of the men for persistent idleness, the boilermakers
stopped work immediately and asked for the manager to be removed. They refused to work
shifts, or overtime after 12 o'clock, unless they got paid until 8 a.m. Groups of workers then
took turns at walking off the job immediately after midnight, refusing to fill in worksheets,
refusing to punch timeclocks, and just starting work when it suited them.
The union nominated those to work overtime, and selected men for jobs with the

company. The boilermakers frequently demanded mates to work with them on jobs that did

Dr WALL (Porirua): On behalf of the member for New Lynn I move, That this House
notes with grave concern the premature decision taken by the Agricultural Chemicals Board to
remove warning labels from packs of the weedkiller 2,4,5-T before the Department of Health's
investigation has been completed, and recalls that the reactionary and subjective approach of
the Agricultural Chemicals Board resulted in New Zealand being one of the last developed
countries to ban the use of DDT, and resolves that the conflict of interest demonstrated by this
latest decision of the Agricultural Chemicals Board demonstrates the need for appropriate
adjustments to the Agricultural Chemicals Act.
This is a complex and difficult problem. The House will recall that this is not the first
time that the problem of the agricultural chemical, and particularly the problem associated
with its possible teratogenic effects, has been raised here. Each time the matter has been
raised because of the unusual incidence of spina bifida in areas where the weedkiller has
been used extensively. No one would pretend that there is absolute proof of association, but
if we are going to wait until then before we issue such a simple thing as a warning then a great
many grossly deformed children will, sooner or later, be born. Our concern is that a warning
was on the label that did not in any way restrict the use of the chemical, but it did warn that
there was a possibility, and that possibility—no matter what the Minister may say about his
best technical advice-still exists, that children in utero may be damaged by it. Quite rightly
the warning said the weedkiller should be kept away from women of child bearing age.
Because of the nature of the effects of spina bifida, whatever damage is done is caused,
probably, within the first 14 to 16 days during the closure of the ural tubes. Then it is a bit
late to put on a warning; the warning was that it should be kept away from pregnant women.
Probably by the time a woman was satisfied that she was pregnant the danger to the foetus, if
there is a danger, was past. Quite properly the warning was to women of child bearing age.
What concerns me is that because no association has yet been proved in the case of
humans, the warning has been removed. We know that one of the chemicals involved in the
weedkiller Dioxin has very definite teratogenically destructive effects in experimental
animals. It is banned above a certain concentration in weedkilling mixtures and it is banned
in even lower concentrations for use under conditions in which human beings would be in
close proximity to it. It concerns me that, because it is unattractive to the manufacturers
and marketers of this chemical the Minister has apparently decided it need not carry a
warning that could discourage its use on farms where there are young married couples, and
the Minister has allowed his departmental officers to permit the removal of this very wise
warning. It may be unnecessary but at least it is wise.
Hon. D. MacINTYRE (Minister of Agriculture): This debate is taking place because of
what is said to be a premature decision on the part of the Agricultural Chemicals Board,
which removed the warning that used to appear on labels of containers of the weedkiller
2,4,5-T. Women were being warned that there might be a threat from the weedkiller. In
Canada, a similar warning was removed about 8 years ago. The Agricultural Chemicals
Board was set up in 1959 under the Labour Government. It came into force in 1960 and it
was given statutory powers as a statutory board. To my knowledge no Minister has ever
interfered with those statutory powers. It was to be an independent body and was originally
to give recommendations on the use of DDT. Since then its functions have increased.
The membership of the board includes a representative of the Department of Health,
who was a party to the decision. Before the decision was made, I published a letter from the
Minister of Health. The letter appears also in the New Zealand Medical Journal of 25 May
1977. It states: "The Department of Health has advised the Hon. D. MacIntyre, Minister of


## p. 643 (#651) ############################################

15 June
643
Discussion of Motions
Agriculture, of its current views about spina bifida and 2,4,5-T. Abnormalities such as spina
bifida have long preceded the introduction and use of 2,4,5-T. The research in England
shows that the incidence of spina bifida increased for 100 years up to 1942 when it reached a
peak of 2.1 deaths per 1000 live babies. It then fell rapidly for 5 years, rose temporarily after
the war and then fell progressively until the end of the 1960s." In other words the
Agricultural Chemicals Board, including a representative of the Department of Health,
decided that the board could be at risk if the warning was left on packages when it had
evidence from the Department of Health and from the medical journal that there was no
risk.
The decision was delayed for some time while the Department of Health was carrying
out an independent review. Finally, as was its right, the board decided that, in view of the
evidence it had, it could hold the matter up no longer. It had searched the world and had
gone in to the subject in great depth. At that stage it could be argued that the board made a
mistake in that it knew that the Department of Health's report would be received. However,
the board acted within its statutory authority and I have given the reasons for its decision.
Also, I remind the member for Porirua that part of the motion deals with the use of
DDT. As I have already said, the Agricultural Chemicals Board was set up by the Labour
Government in 1959, and legislation was implemented in 1960 specifically to deal with the
problems caused by the use of DDT. The first regulations about the use of DDT were
introduced in 1961. The statement in the motion that New Zealand fell well behind the rest
of the world in banning that chemical is not accurate. New Zealand followed the rest of the
world very closely. It followed the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, and
Europe. The use of DDT was banned because it was a threat to human life; because the
chemical was ingested into the animal chain and finally finished up in humans.
The time allowed for discussion of the motion having expired, the motion lapsed.

WRITTEN QUESTIONS
Transferred on dates shown
Police Diplomatic Protection Squad
1. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Police, Will he inform the House what
specific incident, if any, led to the announcement made by Commissioner Burnside on 24
March that henceforth a special squad of armed police patrols would be set up to protect
diplomats and VIPs, and in what way will they operate?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied, There was no specific incident
which led to the formation and introduction of a police diplomatic protection squad on 21
March this year. The police are the Government agency responsible for the protection of
diplomats, and previously these duties were carried out as part of normal police routine.
However, the commissioner considered that in view of international developments in
terrorism it would have been imprudent to continue to rely on this method. The Government
fully supports the formation of this squad. Our obligation as host Government to provide a
reasonable degree of protection will not be taken lightly. For obvious reasons I am not going
to detail the manner in which the squad will carry out its duties, except to say that it is
numerically small, will normally perform its duties in uniform, and, to ensure an effective
response is possible, one member of each patrol will be armed. The fact that a squad
member has immediate access to a firearm does not alter the traditional police policy that
police in this country do not carry firearms as a matter of routine. The Government
recognises the futility of providing added surveillance without a capacity to respond
immediately.

Borrowing Companies-Government Responsibility
8. Mr ALLEN (Tauranga) asked the Minister of Justice, In view of the recent failures of
certain borrowing companies and the personal loss suffered by many individual citizens, is
there any way in which lenders of money can be restrained from lending on bad risks and is it
the business of this Government to direct people how to lend money?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, The Government has no
responsibility to direct people where to invest their money and it would be contrary to good
sense to do so. Still less, of course, should it indemnify or in any way appear to offer an
indemnity to lenders for losses they incur. What the Government has a responsibility to do is
to establish proper rules requiring those who borrow from the public to disclose adequately
the true nature of their proposal. As well, it should as far as practicable see that the funds
thus obtained are used properly in the way represented by the borrower and that the
borrower reasonably administers his commercial undertaking. I intend advertising legisla-
tion to be introduced this year to attain the goal of adequate disclosure and to empower
proper investigation of those who borrow from the public. Nevertheless, the principle of
caveat emptor must still apply to the actual decision made by the investor. Those who seek
higher returns must take greater risks. The Government should assure only that proper
information is available to the intending investor so that he can make an informed decision,
and that the borrower uses the money as he has undertaken to do.

Common Fund Negotiating Conference
10. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, Was
New Zealand represented at the Common Fund negotiating conference which opened at
Geneva on 7 March, and, if so by whom, and, whether personally represented or not, has the
Government taken any steps to express its views to the conference, and will it join with other
primary-producing countries in giving all possible support to the implementation of the
Common Fund concept as originated at the UNCTAD 4 conference in Nairobi, designed to
protect developing countries from the market fluctuations to which their single-commodity
economies are so vulnerable?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied, New Zealand
was represented at the Common Fund negotiating conference by the permanent representa-
tive to the Office of the United Nations in Geneva. The resolution passed by consensus at
Nairobi established a date for a conference on a Common Fund at which the detailed
structure of a fund could properly be negotiated. A possible framework for the Common
Fund was later established by the UNCTAD secretariat, and this has received support from
the Group of 77. New Zealand, along with most Group B countries, is unable to support all
aspects of this concept. At the negotiating conference in Geneva New Zealand mentioned its
past support for efforts to achieve greater stability in international trade and its willingness to
discuss the practical issues of commodity stabilisation. We suggested that more detailed
study was, however, required on various options before any generally acceptable solution to
commodity instability could be found. The Government remains of the view that the
practical course is for agreement to be negotiated on a commodity-by-commodity basis, but
this does not preclude a common financing mechanism. Negotiation of elements of an
appropriate Common Fund will continue in November at a reconvened session, and we
would hope that more progress can be made at that time. New Zealand will attend that
conference, and in the meantime will continue to support efforts to find a practicable
solution to the problems addressed by the Common Fund concept.

Vietnam and Chile-Refugees
12. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Immigration, In view of the Govern-
ment's statements that it is prepared to take refugees from Rhodesia and Northern Ireland,
what consideration is he giving to the request by the representative of the United Nations
High Commissioner for Refugees (Mr Olaf Volfing), as reported in the Christchurch Press
on 5 May, that New Zealand should admit refugees from Vietnam and Chile?
Hon. T. F. GILL (Minister of Immigration) replied, Current immigration policy places
high priority on humanitarian factors, and New Zealand continues, as in the past, to accept
refugees and displaced persons from a number of sources. At the request of the United
Nations High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), the resettlement of Chilean refugees
has been given priority in recent times and three quotas of approximately 70 Chilean families
(each with an average of 4 members) have been admitted for permanent settlement since
1974. A further quota of 30 families was agreed to in October 1976, even though the third.
quota had not been filled, because of the particular urgency accorded to the situation of
refugees from Chile by the UNHCR. At the time of the crisis in Vietnam, New Zealand
mounted a special exercise for Vietnamese humanitarian cases, most of them involving
people who had links with New Zealand (e.g., through relatives or because they had studied
here.) Forty-seven families comprising 135 persons were accepted under this programme.
Refugee schemes are normally considered by the Government following consultation with
the Inter-Church Commission on Immigration (ICCI)—a voluntary agency set up 6 years
ago at the instigation of the National Council of Churches and the Catholic Church, and
having as part of its function the sponsorship of refugees. Financial support has been
provided to the ICCI by the Government in the setting up of this function. The number of
refugees who can be accepted at any one time is dependent on the availability of satisfactory
long-term resettlement resources in New Zealand. Group programmes of assistance on
arrival, and support extending sometimes over long periods, are set up by the ICCI on a co-
operative basis with Government agencies. The Government at present has under considera-
tion an appeal from the UNHCR to accept refugees from Indo-China. Consultations are
under way with the ICCI on the ability of New Zealand to offer worth-while resettlement
assistance to these people in the light of the ICCI's already heavy commitment to assist those
Chileans, Vietnamese, and other refugees already residing in this country.

Clutha River—Declaration as Water of National Importance
21. Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt) asked the Minister of Works and Development, Can he
confirm the statement of the Clutha Action Committee that the Cabinet is considering
declaring the Clutha River a "water of national importance"; what are the consequences of
such a declaration upon environmental considerations and upon the utilisation of the waters
of the river for public purposes such as electrical generation, irrigation, recreation, and other
public water usage; what are the rights of the people to express their attitude on any
declaration that this river be declared a water of national importance; and what rights do
they have to object or question any scheme for use and development of the river when such a
declaration is made?
Hon. W. L. YOUNG (Minister of Works and Development) replied, Cabinet is not
considering declaring the Clutha River a water of national importance. The grant of a water
right for a Government work is made by the National Water and Soil Conservation
Authority. In considering an application for a grant, the authority first obtains a report from
the appropriate regional water board. The board invites public submissions about the
application, and includes these in the report and recommendation to the authority. The
grant when made includes those conditions which the national authority considers necessary.
The decision of the national authority can be appealed against by affected persons on
matters of fact. For a water of national importance the same investigative process is
followed. The National Water and Soil Conservation Authority does not grant the water
right itself, but makes recommendations concerning it to the Government. The grant is then
made by the Governor-General by an Order in Council. There are no rights of appeal
against such a decision.

of maintenance. At 31 March 1977 some 36 300 maintenance orders and registered mainte-
nance agreements were in force, and these had a nominal annual value of $30.5 million.
These are provisional figures only at this stage; the final figures will be published in my
department's annual report.

Kerikeri Airport
27. Hon. M. RATA (Northern Maori) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and
Meteorological Services, Would he indicate: (a) what the lease period is for Kerikeri Airport
with Mt. Cook Airlines Ltd.; (b) what the costs of the runway construction will be; (c) what
the costs to the Government will be for providing safety services; (d) what the costs are for
night lighting; and (e) what the annual costs will be for the Government in manning and
maintaining the services provided?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services)
replied, (a) Mt. Cook Airlines has a 20-year lease for Kerikeri Airport; (b) Mt. Cook
Airlines was responsible for the construction of the runway, and I understand that the cost
involved is between $250,000 and $300,000; (c) the estimated cost to the Government for
providing safety services has yet to be finalised, but an estimated cost is $40,000; (d) again
the costs for night lighting are not yet available, although the estimated cost is $20,000; and
(e) annual maintenance costs which are to be borne by the Government are expected to be
between $2,000 and $5,000. Mt. Cook Airlines and the Government have agreed that there
will be no Ministry of Transport staff based at the airport. The airline will operate the
communications equipment and will man the crash-rescue appliance.
(3/6/77)

Underground Mines-Development
29. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines, What new underground
mines other than those at present under construction are being planned for development,
what is the commencing date for these mines, and what is the additional estimated annual
production?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, Three underground mines are at present
being planned by the Mines Department: (1) a replacement for the Linton mine at Ohai.
Planned production is 44 000 tonnes a year from early 1979; (2) a new mine in the No. 2
seam at Ohai to be located below the present Morley mine. Planned production is 300 000
tonnes a year from late 1980; and (3) Strongman West to replace the present Strongman
mine. Planned production is 120 000 tonnes a year from 1981.
(3/6/77)
Mining-Development Complexities
30. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines, What are the "develop-
mental complexities and costs" referred to by the Secretary of Mines in the autumn issue of
New Zealand Coal?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, The developmental complexities referred to
by Mr Dick are the complexities of recovering up to 70 percent of the coal in a seam 50 ft
thick when present methods of underground mining will permit the extraction of less than
half of this amount. If a way can be found to do this then it will undoubtedly increase the unit
cost of coal production. This will ultimately require a decision to be made on how much we
are prepared to pay to increase the extent of our recoverable coal reserves.
(3/6/77)
Police Protection-Foreign Diplomats
31. Mr CHRISTIE (Napier) asked the Minister of Police, In view of the setting up recently
of a special squad of police to protect diplomats, would he say what the grounds are for the
allocation of armed patrols to foreign diplomats and whether each of the 30-odd overseas
countries with representation in New Zealand automatically has a patrol assigned to it or has
to make special application?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied, The grounds for supplying
surveillance and protection to foreign diplomats are constantly under review and are dictated
by the nature of information received from various sources, overseas trends, and the wishes
of the individual head of mission. To divulge the level of security afforded to each mission
would negate to a great extent the very purpose of establishing such a squad. I am somewhat
surprised—although perhaps I should not be—that the member did not perceive this when
he drafted his question. Obviously, this type of information should not be released, and it
will not be.
(3/6/77)

Air New Zealand-Freight Capacity
35. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorolog-
ical Services, What plans are being made by Air New Zealand to increase the freight capacity
from New Zealand to Australia, particularly from Wellington?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Civil Aviation and Meteorological Services)
replied, Air New Zealand is at present investigating all alternatives of providing additional
freight capacity from New Zealand to Australia, including the leasing of aircraft, the
modification of a DC8 aircraft, and the provision of ad hoc charters. The task has been
compounded by the fact that there is comparatively little air freight moving eastbound across
the Tasman, creating a situation in which aircraft with high operating costs would be
required to fly empty on the return journey to New Zealand. Air New Zealand is in the final
stages of its investigations, but at the same time a reduction in demand for capacity is now
occurring with the result that space is available on aircraft out of Wellington while at
Auckland and Christchurch export freight is being cleared with minimum delays.
(3/6/77)
Coal Drilling
36. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Mines, Can he list the areas

years; and give some indication of the possible results?
Hon. G. F. GAIR (Minister of Mines) replied, In addition to production drilling and
drilling to add further to coal reserves in existing mines, the Mines Department, assisted by
the Department of Scientific and Industrial Research, is carrying out two major exploration
programmes as well as several smaller ones. The major programmes are in the Huntly area,
where 12 rigs are at present operating, and in the Eastern Southland lignite field, where
there are 6 rigs. The smaller exploration programmes are on the West Coast. The number of
holes drilled in each of the last 3 years and those drilled so far this year are:

In addition to the exploration drilling at Huntly, production drilling has for successive
years been: 1974, 191; 1975, 57; 1976, 35; and 1977, 0. The exploration drilling in the Huntly
area since 1974 has added very substantially to the reserves of coal. Drilling has been carried
out in more than 14 different localities. One area, for example, is Huntly West, where the
total in-ground reserves are now 293 000 000 tonnes. Having proved the existence of a
substantial tonnage of coal, increasing attention is now being paid to defining areas which
are most suited for mining in the medium term. The present programme in Eastern
Southland is the commencement of an evaluation of the whole field. It is too early yet to say
what the results might be. Investigations on the West Coast include three localities at
Denniston, in one of which, the Sullivan mine, an additional 800 000 tonnes of coal have
been located. There are also programmes in the Millerton fire area, where 41 holes have
been drilled since 1974, and at Charleston, where 5 holes were drilled last year in a
continuing programme. The Millerton programme has shown the existence of 9 000 000
tonnes of coal within opencast limits, and at Charleston the reserves have been approxi-
mately doubled.

ment, What has been the average price of sections in Auckland during 1972, 1973, 1974,

Woodville Post Office
42. Mr ROGERS (Onehunga) asked the Postmaster-General, Would he confirm that the
Woodville Post Office is an earthquake risk and structurally unsound, and, if so, when will
the post office building be replaced?
Hon. P. I. WILKINSON (Postmaster-General) replied, The building was erected in 1903
and is reaching the end of its economic life. All older masonry buildings constitute a risk in
severe earthquakes such as might be expected once in 100 years. There are hundreds of
buildings in New Zealand that are comparative or worse risks. The Post Office has a
systematic system of replacing its buildings, taking into consideration all relevant factors
such as earthquake risks, economic life, etc. For obvious economic reasons, such a
replacement programme must extend over many years. A timing for the provisions of the
new building cannot be given at this stage.

Auckland-Land Development
44. Hon. Dr A. M. FINLAY (Henderson) asked the Minister of Finance, Is it correct, as
reported in the New Zealand Herald of 18 May, that urban and industrial developments in
Auckland are likely to face delays of 1 or 2 years because of the Auckland Regional
Authority's lack of servicing finance, and that the first of these likely to be affected is a large
scheme for housing and industry around Sturges Road, Henderson?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance) replied, It is a matter for the
Auckland Regional Authority itself to determine the priority of the works it undertakes
within the bounds of the finance available to it. The problem that has faced the authority
over the years is one that has faced every local authority in New Zealand-a general
shortage of finance on the loan market. The Government has taken a number of steps to
attract more loan moneys to finance local authority capital works, and indications are that
these have been effective. We are watching the position and are at present obtaining from
local authorities information on their capital works and loan requirements to enable a
further assessment to be made. In recent years the Auckland Regional Authority has relied
heavily on the National Provident Fund for its loan finances, and indeed in the 1976–77
financial year the fund provided almost $16m, or nearly 80 percent of the amount raised by
the authority. No assurances can be given that more Government help will be forthcoming in
the present year, but it is pleasing to note that, with the appointment of Sir Peter Tait, a
consultant experienced in the field of local authority loan raising, the authority is taking
positive steps to help itself.
(27/5/77)

Communist States-Reciprocal Trade
53. Mr SCHULTZ (Coromandel) asked the Minister of Overseas Trade, Has he seen the
report in the Dominion of 12 May that "Walding urges reciprocal trade", with particular
reference to communist States, and can he state what reciprocal trade took place with
communist States during 1974 and 1975 and what was the total trade during 1976-77?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Overseas Trade) replied, I have seen the report. I
am not aware of any reciprocal linked trade deals between New Zealand and the socialist
countries in Eastern Europe in 1974-75. In the year ended 30 June 1975 the total value of
New Zealand's exports to the USSR and the socialist countries in Eastern Europe was
NZ$65.8 million. In the same period the total value of imports from these countries was
NZ$9.6 million. The value of New Zealand's exports to the People's Republic of China
amounted to NZ$10.1 million, and imports NZ$13.7 million. The trade figures for the
1976-77 period will not be available until after 30 June, but the total value of New Zealand's
exports to the USSR and Eastern Europe in the year ended 30 June 1976 was NZ$109.8
million, and imports NZ$7 million. During this period the value of exports to the People's
Republic of China was NZ$25.3 million, and imports NZ$10.8 million. The policy of the
Government is to expand trade both ways with these and all other countries, and we will
always be prepared to consider any proposals leading to this end so long as New Zealand's
long term interests are met.

recommendations, my present feeling is that adequate finance and assistance are available
for sheep farmers to upgrade or replace obsolete woolsheds.

Plural Voting
63. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Justice, What protection exists to
ensure an elector whose vote may have been usurped in a plural vote by another person has
his actual vote recorded and not invalidated?


## p. 662 (#670) ############################################

662
15 June
Questions and Replies
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, When a returning officer, during
the scrutiny of the rolls, finds what appears to be a plural vote by one person (that is, a name
is ruled off on two separate booth rolls) the practice is for the returning officer to contact the
voter and ask if he voted and where. If the returning officer is satisfied from those inquiries
that the elector did in fact cast only one vote, that vote is recorded and the other ballot paper
removed, unless it appears that the wrong name was ruled out. Sometimes a name has been
ruled out in error, and, upon being satisfied that this is so, no further steps would be taken by
the returning officer. However, if the returning officer is satisfied that some person has voted
twice, both ballot papers are removed from the count.
(27/5/77)
Electoral Roll-Checks on Enrolment
64. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Justice, On what basis do electoral
officers ensure that persons claiming enrolment on the electoral roll are bona fide persons?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, An electorate officer must accept
an electoral enrolment card at face value provided it is correctly completed. It is seldom that
an elector completes an electoral enrolment card by personal application to an electorate
officer. All applications for enrolment are acknowledged by sending to the elector an
acknowledgment card. Should an acknowledgment card be returned by the Post Office with
a notation suggesting that the address is incorrect the electorate officer can take further steps
to check.
(27/5/77)
Electoral Roll-Checks on Voting
65. Mr O'BRIEN (Island Bay) asked the Minister of Justice, What safeguards exist to
ensure that the person who casts a vote at a general election is in fact the person claiming to
be the one whose name appears on the electoral roll?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, The electoral system in New
Zealand is based on trust. A person seeking to vote in a polling booth gives his or her name,
address, and occupation to the poll clerk, who then checks the roll to ensure that the same
information is recorded and rules out the entry. The deputy returning officer issues the ballot
paper. The Chief Electoral Officer knows of only one case in all his experience in which a
person has voted in the name of some other person. In some electoral systems, electors are
required to produce an identification card before being permitted to vote. A New Zealand
elector could be required to produce the acknowledgment card sent after the application for
enrolment was received, but this has never been suggested.

Armed Robbery Prosecutions
69. Mr BRILL (Kapiti) asked the Minister of Justice, How many prosecutions for armed
robbery were launched, and how many convictions followed, during 1976 and 1977 respec-
tively; and during those 2 years what was the average sentence imposed following convic-
tion?
Hon. DAVID THOMSON (Minister of Justice) replied, There is no separate offence of
armed robbery. Prosecutions are brought under section 235 of the Crimes Act 1961, which
relates to aggravated robbery. I am unable to supply statistics for the years referred to: the
figures for 1976 have not yet been collected and the statistics for the first 5 months of this
year are not available. Statistics for the years 1973, 1974, and 1975 show the totals of persons
sentenced in the Supreme Court as being 41, 30, and 55 respectively. These figures include
persons committed for sentence to the Supreme Court after pleading guilty following a
preliminary hearing in the magistrate's court. The statistics for these 3 years do not specify
the actual length of sentence imposed, but from the available figures, and using the mid-
point in each classification of sentence as the mean, the average length of sentence for each
of the 3 years is as follows: 1973, 3 years 7 months; 1974, 4 years 1 month; 1975, 3 years 9
months.

UNCTAD-Establishment of Common Fund
70. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, In view of
his statement at the Nairobi UNCTAD talks that it was premature to consider the
establishment of a Common Fund to aid the third world, and the fact that a similar attitude
was adopted at Geneva in March, when would he consider it expedient to support such a
fund?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied, I did not
make any statement at Nairobi that in any way implied that it was premature to consider the
establishment of a Common Fund. In fact, my statement welcomed the decision of
UNCTAD IV to concentrate attention on commodity problems. I also expressed the hope
that it would be possible to start work on this area quickly, and that it would be possible to
reach a sufficient measure of agreement to enable significant progress to be made. I also
suggested that all possible solutions be examined, and that both producer and consumer
interests be considered. That remains the New Zealand position, and was the position taken
by the New Zealand delegation at Geneva recently. We are fully aware of the problems of
commodity trade, particularly as they affect developing countries, and we have in the past
supported specific agreements aimed at resolving these difficulties in particular
commodities. We will continue to follow these policies, and we will continue to work
towards practical and realisable solutions to the overall commodity problems that concern
UNCTAD.

DA Diesel-electric Locomotives
72. Hon. F. M. COLMAN (Petone) asked the Minister of Railways, To what extent was
local capacity assessed in either the railway workshops or New Zealand heavy engineering
firms before a decision was made to rebuild 35 Da railway diesel-electric locomotives in
Australia?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Railways), replied, The Railways Department's
workshops are fully committed on locomotive repairs and the building and maintenance of
other railway rolling stock. This was taken into account when considering the rebuilding of
the DA locomotives, as if this work was done in the department's workshops it would have
been at the expense of practically every other item of locomotive repairs or maintenance.
Major items have to be supplied from the original manufacturers in any case, and major
refurbishing of electrical equipment to the standard required can be performed only in
Australia or the United States. New Zealand heavy industry could perform some of the
work, but would require considerable capital investment to purchase specialised machines to
do all the work. When tenders were called for the rebuilding of the locomotives two New
Zealand firms did collect the tender documents, but replied that because of the specialised
nature of the work they were unable to assist the department.

88. Hon. W. W. FREER (Mt. Albert) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, How

garment quota have been assisted as a result of official discussions, and what is the extent of
the help in monetary or quantitative terms?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied, A delegation
went to Canberra early last month and gave the Australian authorities details of firm orders
prepared by the Textile and Garment Manufacturers' Federation that were not expected to

large any residual problem may be. As a result of the discussions held in Canberra the
Australian Government is fully aware of the impact of its actions on New Zealand exporters,
but I do not believe it would be helpful to their cause to discuss publicly the approaches open
to the Australian Government in dealing with individual import applications.

Policewomen, South Auckland
97. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Police, (1) How many
policewomen are attached to youth aid sections or J teams in the South Auckland police
districts as at 1 June 1977; (2) are schools and other social agencies served by the Otahuhu
Police Station able to have immediate access to policewomen when the need arises; and (3) is
the Minister aware of the immense respect in which local Otara Community Liaison Police
Officer Constable M. Anderson is held, and does he have plans for extending the hours of
this office?
Hon. ALLAN MCCREADY (Minister of Police) replied, (1) No policewomen are at
present attached to the Youth Aid Section or J teams within the southern division of the
Auckland district. Vacancies in these sections are advertised nationally, and the most
suitable applicant selected. The fact that any applicant is a policewoman does not alone
ensure selection for such posts. Other factors such as age, experience, and maturity are much
more important in ensuring that the most suitable person is appointed. The police do not, of
course, discriminate between male and female personnel. (2) Currently there are eight
policewomen stationed at Otahuhu. One is on leave without pay, one is employed on general
inquiries, and six provide 24-hour-coverage, 7 days a week. Under normal circumstances
schools and social agencies have access to a policewomen on duty, if in fact this proves to be
necessary. (3) I am well aware of the fine work being performed by Constable Anderson, the
Community Liaison Officer, at Otara. He has earned the respect of the community by his
efforts. The commissioner has no plans to extend the hours at the Otara office as this would
mean a second constable being appointed there whilst other deserving areas without a liaison
officer were denied such services. The accommodation at present being used by the police at
Otara is required by another Government Department, and any assistance the honourable
member can give to locate suitable alternative premises would be appreciated.

Hikurangi Swamp Scheme
103. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister of Works and Development, Can he give an assurance that, when the last pumping
station is completed as part of the Hikurangi swamp major scheme, the whole scheme will be

Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied on behalf of the Minister of Works
and Development, "At this stage there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that

protection throughout the scheme area. I have visited the area and am aware of the
problems. Possibly the works originally proposed may not achieve the desired standard of
protection throughout the scheme area. If so, other measures will be considered when the
scheme has reached a stage where flows can be measured accurately. I understand these
investigations will be carried out next year."

Housing-Effect of Immigration Policy
105. Mr TALBOT (South Canterbury) asked the Minister of Housing, What effect has the
implementation of the Government's immigration policy had on the availability of houses
during the past 12 months?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied, Under the Labour Government,
New Zealand was getting a net permanent migration gain of approximately 30 000 a year,
absorbing about one-third of all houses being built. In other words, we needed an additional
9000-odd houses each year for this reason alone. This situation has now been reversed, and
the outflow potentially frees nearly 4000 houses. The effect has been to relieve the pressure
on the building industry and to make a significant contribution in easing the housing
shortage. The relief accorded is already being reflected in the waiting list for State rental
houses, which stood at 12 420 on 31 March 1977 compared with 14 899 12 months
previously.

Housing Policies-National Party Manifesto
107. Mr MALCOLM (Eden) asked the Minister of Housing, Can he advise the House
which housing policies included in the 1975 National Party manifesto have been
implemented so far?
Hon. E. S. F. HOLLAND (Minister of Housing) replied, The Government's priority
objectives in the housing field have been to restore the role of the private sector as the
principal source of house mortgage finance and to give a greater choice to and make home
ownership possible for all of those willing to earn and save for it. In pursuit of these aims the
Government has made two major adjustments of public sector security ratios, implemented
a revised mortgage guarantee scheme, extended the benefits available under the home
ownership scheme, made second mortgages available to eligible home ownership account
depositors, extended the availability of loans for secondhand houses through the Housing
Corporation, widened the availability of low income supplements for those on low incomes,
and introduced a pilot scheme of the Home Guidance Bureau. In addition, corporation
rental housing policies have been changed to provide for limited tenancies and the tenancy
savings scheme, and the sale of rental houses has been reactivated. Other policies soon to be
implemented include the building performance guarantee scheme, the legislation for which
is currently before a select committee. In addition, a review of the unit titles legislation is
being implemented.

Container Terminal-Marsden Point
110. Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru), on behalf of Mr ELLIOTT (Whangarei), asked the
Minister of Transport, Does he acknowledge that the situation at the Auckland and
Wellington container terminals, particularly the congestion and projected congestion as
container demand grows, makes the Marsden Point case for an international container
terminal very much stronger?
Hon. C. C. A. McLACHLAN (Minister of Transport) replied, The problem of fluctuating
congestion at the North Island container terminals would not be solved by the provision of a
third container port at Marsden Point. The problems of congestion are short term, and
current development at the two North Island terminals is expected to cope with all projected
container traffic from 1979 to the late 1980s. If container facilities at Marsden Point were to
be developed, the port would not be ready for container traffic until the early 1980s, at which
time the problems of congestion at Auckland and Wellington would have been alleviated.

Waitemata City Council
113. Mr HUNT (New Lynn) asked the Minister of Local Government, Has he yet received
any information which would justify his setting up a commission to take over the Waitemata

view of the many specific comments that have been made about this council's activities over
the past few months?
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government) replied, The answer to the first part
of the question is no. The only section of the Municipal Corporations Act under which a
commission or commissioner could be appointed is section 411, which requires as a
prerequisite that a council must wilfully or substantially refuse to perform the duties and
powers vested in it by or under that Act. I have not received any information that would
justify action under that section.

Public Companies-Return on Shareholders' Funds
122. Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau) asked the Minister of Trade and Industry, What
return on shareholders' funds does his department consider reasonable for public com-
panies, and does the department accept shareholders' funds as being the amount shown in
the accounts of a particular company or does it have some other measure?
Hon. L. R. ADAMS-SCHNEIDER (Minister of Trade and Industry) replied, In matters of
price control the Secretary of Trade and Industry exercises an independent statutory
discretion. However, in determining the prices of goods and services pursuant to the
Commerce Act 1975 the secretary does not employ a uniform rate of return on shareholders'
funds but sets a rate in each case which he considers appropriate having regard to the
considerations required by section 98 of the Act to be observed by him. The rate will
normally bear some relationship to the previous earning rate of the company and the return
of any other public companies engaged in similar activities. The quantum of shareholders'
funds shown in the accounts is subject to reduction on account of circumstances such as the
revaluation of assets, assets employed outside the company, and assets not attributable to
goods and services subject to price control under the Act.

Deficit Before Borrowing
125. Mr LUXTON (Piako) asked the Minister of Finance, Can he inform the House what
the deficit before borrowing was when expressed as a percentage of the net Government
expenditure for the 1972-73 financial year, the 1975-76 financial year, and the 1976-77
financial year?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Associate Minister of Finance) replied on behalf of the
Minister of Finance. In 1972-73 the net Government expenditure was $2,219 million, and
revenue was $2,013 million, leaving a deficit of $206 million, or 9.3 percent. In 1975-76 the
net expenditure was $4,385.9 million, and revenue was $3,384.2 million, leaving a deficit of
$1,001.7 million, or 22.8 percent. In 1976-77 the net expenditure was $4,506 million and
revenue was $3.999.9 million, leaving a deficit of $506.1 million, or 11.2 percent. In short,
the deficit before borrowing expressed as a percentage of net Government expenditure for
1972-73 was 9.3 percent, in 1975-76, 22.8 percent, and for 1976–77, 11.2 percent.

Computers-Filing Systems Benefit
134. Mr ALLEN (Tauranga) asked the Prime Minister, Has any evidence been presented
to him tending to show that information filed with a computer is any more liable to illegal
access than information in other filing systems, and what are the benefits of computer
filings?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister) replied, I have had no evidence that
information filed within the computer is any more liable to illegal access than information in
other filing systems. On the contrary, the security built into computer systems, and the
restrictions placed on access to information on the computer, are far more stringent than
ordinarily apply to manual systems. Some of the benefits of computer filing are of course
quicker access to more accurate up-to-date information; specific data can be extracted
quickly; and statistical and management information, which would not normally be readily
available, can be provided.

support the recommendations made in the report both orally at that conference and by
action elsewhere?
Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Minister of Foreign Affairs) replied, The report referred to

nations. The Government accepts the conclusion, and I can assure the member that the

DISCUSSION OF QUESTIONS—ADJOURNMENT
[Note The questions and the replies referred to in this discussion appear on the
preceding pages, and are numbered consecutively from 1 to 170.]
Miss DEWE (Lyttelton): For the purpose of discussing Ministers' replies to questions, I
move, That the House do now adjourn. I refer to question 83, which was addressed to the
Minister of Social Welfare and dealt with the domestic purposes benefit. This matter has
given me great concern, and I think I speak for many people in the community who have
fears about the repercussions of the payment of this benefit to solo parents. In 1971, $4
million of the taxpayers' money was spent on this benefit, and in 6 years the figure has risen
to about $84 million. It is that increase, and its implications for society, that worry me. At
present, 50 000 children are being looked after by solo parents who are receiving the
domestic purposes benefit. I believe society will face tremendous problems with these
children, who have no stable roots. The money is of concern, but it is the implications of this
instability and insecurity that disturb me even more.
The numbers of people who qualify for, and are claiming, the benefit are even more
frightening; in 1973 there were 9000 beneficiaries, and 4 years later the figure has risen to
28 000. I am also concerned with parental responsibility. The Minister of Social Welfare has
spoken recently about fathers being responsible for their children, whether those children
are born in or out of wedlock. I believe that the public is beginning to demand that fathers
accept their responsibility, or be accountable to the taxpayer. The care of 28 000 women and
50 000 children is a tremendous burden on the taxpayer. The State does have some
responsibility, but the greatest responsibility lies with the mother and the father jointly. The
generous benefit available to these women causes concern, and the committee that reviewed
the benefit was concerned that women might be encouraged to take the easy way out by
applying for the benefit, and would not make an effort to provide for their families. The
problem is large, and it will be even larger in the future if steps are not taken now to remedy
it. I believe that a lot of the money presently being paid to beneficiaries could be channelled
into research to establish why this change in our society has occurred.

In question 141 I asked the Minister of Finance, "What is the Government's estimate of

standard of living if there is a 15 percent inflation of consumer prices, and what further

time wage was not $109.75. He chose to refer to the male wage, which is higher, but the

Mr Brill: It was the male wage.
Mr LANGE: The question was based on the average ordinary-time weekly wage of
$109.75, and an answer was not given on that for the perfectly good reason that it would have
disclosed an appalling situation. The Minister's calculations show that on his basic premise a
man requires an increase of 29.2 percent in his gross wages to keep up with inflation. In other
words, an increase of $33,40 in the gross wage, or 30 percent, is needed to keep pace with
last year's inflation. The other significant point about the answer given by the Acting
Minister of Finance was that it did not take account of family benefit. I do not know whether
that is an indication of the Government's intentions about the family benefit-whether it is
proposed to take it out of the calculations of the income of a family man- but in my
calculations the family benefit is included at the rate of $3 a week, and one is entitled to
assume that that benefit can be used by a family to support itself.
The significance of the figures is that for every 1 percent of inflation an increase of more
than 2 percent in gross wages is needed to keep pace. The Government's argument that
increased wages cause inflation is nonsense. Wage increases have to be double the rate of
inflation to maintain the family man's ability to buy essential commodities. It is even more
difficult for people on lower incomes to increase their standard of living. To achieve a 5
percent improvement the family man needs a gross wage increase of $43.41 a week to take
him from $109.75 to $153 a week. That is one of the fundamental wrongs in the way the
Government is managing the economy. It is not that the Government does not want people
to earn more, but that it prohibits them from doing so with a tax on the ordinary-time
earnings of ordinary people such that it hits them at the rate of more than 50c in the dollar
earned.
We cannot look at inflation without regard for the level of the ordinary average income.
The Government is the greatest creator of inflation, and this Government more so than any
other. The revenue attracted by taxation is even more than this Government dreamed of,
but with a surplus on its hands it has not given relief to the people who need it.

ADDRESS IN REPLY
Adjourned debate on the question, That a respectful Address be presented to His

Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I regret that on this occasion I cannot join
with other members in complimenting the mover and the seconder of the motion, because I
was not here to hear them. However, I do join with many other members in congratulating
Her Majesty on the Silver Jubilee of her accession to the Throne, and the Address in Reply
to the Speech from the Throne is the appropriate occasion for extending New Zealand's
greetings to Her Majesty on this notable event.
It is pure coincidence that exactly one week ago, to the minute, I was privileged to be
asked to represent New Zealand at a thanksgiving service held in the 800-year-old St.
Pierre's Cathedral in Geneva. The cathedral was about to be closed for renovation, but
special permission was granted for the attendance of about 1400 people to pay tribute on the
occasion of the Queen's Silver Jubilee. It is fitting to note that New Zealand was given the
honoured position of being second in the ceremonial parade leaving the church. That honour
was granted to New Zealand, but any pride I may have had in acceding to that request, with
my wife, was somewhat tarnished when I found I had been sitting on a sticky gooby that a
tourist had left just before the church closed. I had difficulty in rising from my seat.
Hon. Dr A. M. Finlay: By gum!
Hon. J. B. GORDON: None the less, the honour given to New Zealand was tangible
recognition of the place it holds in the Commonwealth; there were 133 nations gathered for
the ILO conference.
I want to allude to some of New Zealand's industrial relations problems and, in
particular, to elucidate a little on some of the comments that have been passed since I
returned. A comment was made on this this afternoon, but was ruled out of order; I will not
allude to that, because if I did I think I would be offending against Standing Orders. In trying
to summarise the many points of interest as between the ILO conference, industrial relations
overseas, and New Zealand's present problems, I must plead that I am suffering a little from
jet lag. I have other problems on my mind, and my notes are necessarily abbreviated. My
speech must be taken with errors and omissions excepted.
The question has been raised as to why, since my return, I have not referred to the
American and Canadian contract systems of wage negotiation. That is merely an oversight
on the part of the press, which saw fit to take one extract from an interview in London. Sir
Thomas Skinner commented this week that I had failed to comment, and highlighted it as
something that I had overlooked. I think that in the longer term the system could have quite
useful application in New Zealand, and we could move towards it. In the American and
Canadian contract systems there is a built-in consumer price and wage index. In most of the
north-western States of the United States a 3 percent movement in the consumer price index
would give a wage movement equivalent to 1c an hour. In Canada, on the other hand, a


## p. 698 (#706) ############################################

698
15 June
Address in Reply
movement of 0.4 percent in the consumer price index would give 1c an hour in wages. In one
or two odd contracts the movement is 1:1-if the consumer price index moved by 3 percent,
wages would move by 3 percent. That is a rarer type of contract.
The contract system has one very great virtue that is often overlooked by people who
suggest that there are no penalties or ties on unions in other parts of the free Western World.
Both Canada and the United States qualify within that definition. Under the contract system
there are literally no strikes. Both parties know that if there is a lockout or a strike either
party is in for a very heavy penalty. In some cases, particularly in Canada where they have an
industrial relations board, penalties can be awarded as from the union to the employer, or
vice versa, and one party virtually pays the equivalent of damages. This provision was
included in our legislation last year, and some exception was taken to it by the Opposition.
That is conveniently overlooked by many people, who say that there are no penalties or
inhibitions on unions in other countries. In the very brief time I was in the United States I
met one of the negotiators in a metal workers' contract for a single group of workers of 45
000 men and women-but mostly men. The conciliation leading up to the renegotiation of
the contract was expected to take less than 3 weeks-and it is legal to take strike action
during the renewal of a contract. It was expected that the contract would proceed by mutual
agreement in smooth conciliation, and that that would be the end of it. I made a brief visit to
British Columbia, a State of Canada with a population similar to that of New Zealand, with
similar industries and topography, and a similar climate. Probably if I had to choose where in
the world to live other than New Zealand, it would be British Columbia. It has a Human
Rights Commission working inside the Labour Department. The legislation was passed only
2 years ago, and priority has been given to the establishment of the Industrial Relations
Board, which was set up as an independent arbitrator and divorced from politics. I envy the

did not yet have the law. I concede that in Canada they do have industrial unrest; they have
strikes. The member for Roskill pointed this out in response to a necessarily abbreviated
press review.
In Ontario I met probably the most unusual Minister of Labour that one could find-Dr
Bette Stevenson, aged 53 or thereabouts, the mother of 6, and an ex-president of the
Canadian Medical Association, who had been only 3 weeks in Parliament when her Prime
Minister chose her for Minister of Labour-presumably on the assumption that she knew
something of the psychology of human relations which, after all, are the mainspring of
industrial relations; and, secondly, that she had been able to control the Canadian Medical
Association, and therefore would have the ability to run a Ministry of Labour. I commend
his choice. I thought she was a fantastic woman. On the day she entertained me to lunch she
had already walked 24 miles electioneering in the local State elections.
Hon. M. Rata: Not on water?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Not on water, no. To be fair, at that stage, the unemployment
ratio had moved from 7.5 percent to 9 percent. Ontario is the most rapidly growing State of
Canada. It tends, as Auckland does, to generate the problems of the growing community.
Rivalry between Montreal and Toronto has now swung definitely in Toronto's favour, since I
understand its population is now 500 000 greater than that of Montreal. In the middle of an
election campaign, with all her problems, she made a statement that I would not dare make
nor would I absolutely endorse. It was reported a day after I had left her that she considered
that the optimum out-turn to keep balance and discipline in the work force, and full
employment, was for 3.5 percent of the work force to be unemployed. She made that
statement when she had a 9 percent unemployment rate. I do not endorse that 3.5 percent
for New Zealand, but the message and moral came through very clearly in many countries,
particularly in Europe. That very notable Minister of Labour-in a climate and atmosphere

A vexed question, and an interesting one-it certainly was one I considered worthy of
looking at in New Zealand, and my comment from London was that we might consider
it was the question of appointment of trustees for misbehaving, malcontent unions in
preference-and I repeat those words "in preference"-to deregistration. That seemed to
strike some people in New Zealand on a tender nerve, possibly because it was the major
point taken out by the subeditor from a fairly lengthy interview I gave in London. I stand by
what I said then: I still think it is worthy of study in New Zealand.
This afternoon I faced one of the most touchy and delicate industrial
problems deregistration of the boilermakers in Wellington, deregistration being the ulti-
mate weapon and one no Minister likes to use. This afternoon a previous Minister of Labour
referred to the history of that particular union and the number of times it had been warned
about deregistration before it was finally deregistered. I suggest that if there is any
intermediary course short of deregistration we should at least explore it. In Canada they put
trustees, under a judge, in charge of the seamen's union for a period. The union recovered
and went on in a perfectly normal way without any loss of funds. There was no deregistra-
tion. I merely repeat that I thought it was an item worthy of closer study, be it by policy, by
our party, or by anyone else, as an alternative to the very unpleasant and unpalatable
deregistration provision on which a Minister of Labour in New Zealand can call. Yes, it is
worthy of study.
In Canada I found many people whom I would have liked to bring back to New Zealand
to help us here. This week Sir Tom Skinner suggested that rather than talking about
trusteeship I should have talked to the British union leaders. I say to the House and to Sir
Tom that I spent a very pleasant one and a half hours with Jack Jones, leader of the Trade
Union Council, who is about to retire in, of all places, what I guess the Opposition would
term the holy of holies-the red-clothed table in Labour Party headquarters in London.
Sitting at the top of the table I looked across at Ernie Bevin's balehooks in a glass case.
When I said to Jack Jones, "We still use those in New Zealand", he found it hard to believe,
but we do, and I was impressed that they were there. Today, Britain's problems are not
dissimilar to those of New Zealand, with one notable exception; it has strikes and a high
unemployment rate as well. If I have time, I will later allude to a strike that was running
while I was there.
Now I shall pass quickly over the scene in Britain, because I do not think there was
anything of advantage there for New Zealand. London was getting ready to celebrate the
Queen's Silver Jubilee and I thought the British people were in a state of euphoria. When we
talked to the politicians I found it difficult to get anything of a positive policy from either
party. I met the Minister of Labour and other Ministers, and the shadow Minister of Labour.
In fact, I met 24 members of Parliament in Great Britain. Jack Jones and some other
politicians made it clear that they could not expect voluntary wage control to continue with
the Government's inflation rate running, as it was while I was there, at almost 17 percent-
later it did reach 17 percent. It was not a happy picture. The Port Talbot steel strike was on,
and from that and other strikes we have little to learn from Britain.
I shall now refer to a couple of items from the Continent that are of interest and may
have some bearing on the New Zealand industrial scene. When I reached Sweden, the
Swedish Parliament was debating co-determination. Naturally, the new Government was a
little uneasy, having taken over after 40 years of socialism. Sweden has a totally different life
style and structure. Incidentally, the House had electronic voting. With the Beehive so far
away from this Chamber, some of our legislators may later like to study that possibility. One
could not pick up the worker participation or the co-determination of Sweden and plonk
them down in New Zealand society. That just is not on, but Germany was an object lesson to
all. I, like the recent parliamentary party from New Zealand that toured later, visited DGB
headquarters in Dusseldorf, and I could not help but admire the three-storey research
building built by an enormously wealthy trade union movement, all on a voluntary basis. In
fact, trade union membership ranged from 35 percent to a maximum of about 90 percent, the
latter being mainly in the construction or motor assembly industry.
In Germany the key thing that made workers' councils tick-and I met workers'
councils-and made their industrial relations so much better was, first, the limited number of
unions-about 16-but, more than that, the absolute discipline of members; and we must
remember that these unions are voluntary. Unions, generally, take 1 percent of net wages by
