Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS (Manukau): I believe that New Zealand is at a crisis point in its
development. We are faced with a rocketing inflation rate, a serious decline in productivity,
and a taxation system that crushes any incentive or hope for the average person of building a
better way of life for himself and his family. At the moment there is a dog-eat-dog mentality
in New Zealand with certain powerful groups in the community openly using rip-off tactics
and saying, "To hell with everyone else." We all know this to be correct. The speculators are
sucking like leeches on the victims of inflation, and rent-racketeers, and the few businessmen
who through extra mark-ups can do it, are allowed to get away with exploitation. The
Government is leading the flood of price increases by totally irresponsible increases in its
own charges. To break out of this, we have to start accepting the basic truth that if we are to
have long-term prosperity and a stable economy there has to be something in it for everyone
and not just for the greedy few who happen to be on top at the moment. The Government
ignores the problems, or, at best, potters around with the frills.
On the other hand, members of the Labour Party are concerned about the other society
that the National Government ignores by turning its eyes to the wall in the hope that it will
go away. Let us look at that other society for a moment. At least one family in three in New
Zealand is living in what I can only describe as a poverty trap-a poverty trap not in the
sense that the family is starving in the streets, but in the sense that it is being forced to live in
conditions of hardship and is being denied the normal quality of life that many of us take for
granted. These families are trapped in the sense that they are locked into their situation by
Government policies.
The late Norman Kirk used to describe the welfare State as an adventure that opened
the door to new opportunities. In 1977 that door is firmly shut for at least one family in three.
No matter how hard those people work or try to save or to get ahead they are being squashed
down into a life of hardship and want; and there is nothing as helpless as the man who wants
a better life for his family and is unable to achieve it. Let us consider why one family in three


## p. 701 (#709) ############################################

15 June
701
Address in Reply
is trapped against its will in an unacceptable standard of life. There are many reasons, and
three in particular. The first is the taxation structure, which is making the average income
earner pay up to 60c in the dollar on any increase in wages he receives. Then there is the
housing problem, with high rates of mortgage interest, rent racketeering, and impossible
refinancing terms. Finally, but not least, the huge increases in many basic costs of living
items are not matched by similar increases in take-home pay.
Let us consider the relative net income position of selected families on the average
ordinary-time weekly wage. In 1966, the net income of a married man with two children was
6 percent above his gross income, with the family benefit added to his wage less taxation. His
marginal rate of taxation was 20c in the dollar. Today the marginal rate of taxation of that
man on the average ordinary-time weekly wage is not 20c in the dollar but 40c in the dollar,
and his net income, instead of being 6 percent above his gross income, is now 12 percent
below it. In other words, the man on the average ordinary-time weekly wage is now 18
percent worse off relatively than he was 10 years ago. The man on the average income is
being actively penalised for daring to strive to better himself and his family. We are placing
such people in a poverty trap and ensuring that they stay there. Then we wonder why a man
in that situation reacts in despair.
It is the same with housing. The Prime Minister has said that concern about housing is
against the facts, but for many it is the No. 1 problem. Housing finance has never been in
such a disastrous situation-and it is becoming worse every week-with old and reputable
sources of finance moving out and leaving the field open to fringe finance groups, which are
making a killing. I shall return to that later.
Let us consider for a moment what it means to try to scrape together money for a house
today. First, the Government has cut the amount of funds available from the Housing
Corporation by at least one-third. Housing costs have rocketed, and there is an all-time gap
between the corporation loan, if you can get one, and the real cost. The figure is between
$13,000 and $14,000. In its manifesto the National Party said that it would bring in the
private sector. What private sector? The Government has allowed open slather with
mortgage rates and with its ludicrous monetary policies so that interest rates are now running
at record levels. The cost of financing the purchase of a home has risen faster than almost
any other cost in the last year, and that is saying something. First mortgage rates from
private sources are about 12 percent and can rise as high as 18 percent.
Hon. E. S. F. Holland: That's not correct.
Hon. R. O. DOUGLAS: I will prove it is correct later on. Second mortgage funds are
virtually unobtainable through conventional sources. Most law firms have pulled out and the
major finance companies have moved in to fill the gap, charging real interest rates of up to 23
percent. This means that many families are paying up to $70 a week without touching the
principal, and that is crippling their lives. Young couples are being asked to put off having
children for at least 5 years. Those who, because of circumstances, are forced to live on one
income have to provide for their families on about $30 a week left over after mortgage
payments. People are being forced to take second and third jobs to try to keep up. Those are
the facts of housing today and that is what the Prime Minister is running away from when he
says, "Concern about housing is not in accordance with the facts."
The position is so bad that many people are desperate enough to get themselves into
quite untenable positions. They are desperate enough to take a chance and, having done so,
fall into the clutches of the fringe finance companies. They take on short-term mortgages at
exorbitant interest rates, and can afford to pay only the interest. At the end of 2 or 3 years
they have no equity, and at present no hope of refinancing their mortgage. These people
end up on the street with nothing to show for their efforts; and hundreds of families are
facing these difficulties now. At least one forced sale a day occurs in Auckland, and a similar
pattern exists throughout the country. That is only the tip of the iceberg, because most
people sell voluntarily before the courts move in. It is a tragedy and a waste, and of all the
ways in which the Government has conned the people and failed to honour its promises this
would be the worst.
On 6 April the Minister of Housing was quoted in the New Zealand Herald as saying
that "he assured home owners facing mortgage refinancing problems that the Government
would not allow massive forced sales of houses to occur". That assurance is not worth the
paper it is written on. The deputy manager of the Housing Corporation was quoted in the
same paper a few days later as saying that "he gathered that the corporation would take over
from the Public Trustee as a lender of last resort, but he did not know when". Of course he
did not know, because the Minister himself does not know, and does not know because he

I shall give an illustration of what has happened to Wattie's products in recent times. My

10.6 percent, from 37c to 41c. From January 1973 to December 1975, during the Labour
Government's term in office, the product increased from 25c to 37c, an increase of 48

for making a profit, and the implication is that it will make less profit in the future. In 1973 a
can of Watties' pears was 29c, but in 1975 it was 46c, an increase of 17c, or 59 percent.

would do better. It did not do better, and the rate continued to increase. It increased for the

measures that are bringing inflation under control. Inflation for the September quarter was
3.2 percent, for the December quarter 2.8 percent, and for the March quarter 2.6
percent-less than 12 percent on an annual basis. Inflation is coming down under the
National Government's policies and measures introduced in the interests of the consumer.

production, distribution, and exchange, so in effect it would mean the nationalisation of
every factory, company, and farm-they are the producers-every freight company, private

I have been a member of the House for 18 months now, and during that time I have
become more and more concerned at many facets of our society and the trends manifesting
themselves therein. I believe I am not alone in this concern, particularly about the social
problems in our midst, because many members have alluded to these problems during this
debate-social problems such as alcoholism, drug addiction, marriage breakdown, and the
solo mother situation. All of these will have far-reaching effects on New Zealand in the years
ahead but, in addition to these social problems one problem tends to haunt me like a
nightmare-the problem of the cost of government. It terrifies me that education, health,
and social welfare are consuming 66c in every dollar that the Government collects in
taxation from the New Zealand taxpayer, leaving only 33½c in every dollar for all the other
services that the New Zealand public expects the Government to provide. These include
local body finance, subsidies for the arts, recreation, and sport, roading-because not all of
it is funds from the National Roads Board taxation-the courts and legal aid system, the
probationary service, the police—and we know a lot about the police-the advisory services
in agriculture and other areas, trade promotion, transport, and defence—and those are just a
few. We must not forget the new 200-mile economic zone, which is about to come into
operation, and our having to police it to protect our own territorial waters. All of these have
to be provided out of the remaining 33½c in every dollar collected by the Government after
we have paid for education, health services, and social welfare.
Throughout all New Zealand we hear clamourings for more and more spending by the
Government. As recently as last Sunday I heard on Radio New Zealand a remark made by
Keith Ovenden, a lecturer at Victoria University, to the effect that it is accepted in New
Zealand that it is the Government's job to take care of everybody. I want to disabuse the
public of New Zealand of that notion, if that is what it believes. It is not the Government's
job to take care of everybody. It is the job of the Government to provide for the care of
those who are sick, handicapped, or in need, but it is not to provide for everybody. The
Government, or, to be more precise, the taxpayer, cannot afford to provide for everybody.
If the public expects its Government to provide for everybody, it has to be prepared to foot
the bill and to pay more in taxation, for that is the only way that provision for each and every
one can be made. A Government's job is to provide the economic climate and the incentives
for people to provide for themselves and to ensure their own future by diligence, enterprise,
and productivity. The New Zealand taxpayer is an unusual animal. He is enthusiastic and
eager to receive much from the Government in the way of benefits, subsidies, and services,

preferably for nothing, but he is reluctant to appreciate that he, as the taxpayer, has to pay

New Zealand is bedevilled by inflation, but not as bedevilled now as it was under the
last Labour Government. Inflation affects us all and is causing anguish to many. To vanquish
this devil, the public must learn to accept some unpalatable facts. The first is that every
dollar the Government spends in excess of its income feeds the inflationary spiral. The
second is that the sure way to overcome inflation more quickly is to increase productivity. In
simple layman's terms, we have to work harder and produce more at the factory bench, in
the office, or on the farm-wherever we may be, including this House. The third is that,
unless the first two facts can be realised, to survive as a trading nation we must ultimately
expect a fall in our accustomed standards of living and affluence. Earlier this year, I had the
privilege of participating in a joint parliamentary tour of Japan with the member for New
Lynn and the member for Auckland Central from the Opposition side, and the member for
Franklin and the member for Kapiti from the Government side. We saw much and we
learned more, but one lasting impression remains with me-the industry of the Japanese
people. Couple that industry with the efficiency and industriousness of the Japanese
industries themselves, and we would see the answer to our problems, if we cared to look. My
concern is that New Zealanders may have progressed too far along the road of assuming that
comfort and easy living will continue, and accepting that "the Government will provide".
We may have progressed too far for the public to stop itself on this self-propelled destructive
course, a course which will lead to the destruction of our democracy, our way of life, and our
welfare State. I can only hope and pray that New Zealand as a nation will shoulder its own
burdens and responsibilities before it is too late.

I am also very concerned at the decision of the New Zealand Ports Authority to allocate

how the New Zealand Ports Authority can justify its present attitude. I received a copy of

The third matter to which I should like to refer is the need for a cardio-thoracic unit at

consistent and persistent nagging to ensure that the unit goes ahead at full speed, and with no
undue delay.

Parliament has been treated by this Government with contempt, and the law courts with

will do no harm to air it again tonight. The annual exercise which determines well in advance
the rate at which power stations should be built is called energy forecasting. The initial
decisions affect the lives of hundreds, if not thousands, of people. It is the responsibility of
the Committee to Review Power Requirements to assess the power and energy needs for the
future. It is on the basis of that committee's forecasts that another committee, called the
Planning Committee on Electric Power Development in New Zealand, recommends to the
House, by way of an annual paper in a report, what power stations should be built-their
type and location, and the rate at which they should be built. That recommendation is made
to Parliament annually, and is normally taken up by the Government. Both those commit-
tees are able to influence power planning, which has a very great effect on the future of the
country. I believe that the shortcomings of both committees are serious, in that they
comprise members who are principally interested in only one of the many energy
sectors—that is, in electricity. That is a serious shortcoming in power planning. Dwell for a
moment on the fact that the resources these power stations use are not connected with
electricity. The stations produce electricity, but the primary fuels which drive them are as
diverse as natural gas, geothermal energy, coal, water, and oil. But the interests of those

who represent the primary fuel sectors are not represented on the committees responsible

Rt. Hon. B. E. TALBOYS (Acting Prime Minister): Earlier this evening, my colleague

prepared for me, and it makes an extraordinary interesting story. He bought those shares,
and held them until 10 June this year. He paid for 500 shares at $1.97 each—a total of $985.
In the time he held those shares, he had two bonus issues, two cash issues, and a convertible
debenture issue; but he had to sell his rights in order to pay for those issues. Therefore, he
ended up with 819 shares and 17 convertible debenture issues. When he sold those shares at
99c each on 10 June this year he had not 500 shares to sell, he had 819; and he received not
$985 but $829 instead. Therefore, he registered a loss of over $155. What was his income
over the period? The dividends he earned from his investment in that company amounted to
$413. That income, as a return on the capital, works out at 3.97 percent, but if one considers
the loss he made his return amounts to 2.6 percent. So, that individual, who was condemned
by the honourable member for Manukau, would have been better off if he had put his money
into the Post Office Savings Bank.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS
Tourists from Australia and Pacific Islands
1. Mr KIRK (Sydenham) asked the Minister of Tourism, As the March statistics show
that there is a net reduction of 3608, or 15.5 percent, in visitors from Australia and a net
reduction of 646, or 27.3 percent, in visitors from the Pacific Islands, compared with the
month of March 1976, what is the Minister doing actively to encourage more tourists from
these areas?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD (Minister of Tourism): I note that the honourable member has
directed his question only to the month of March. The year to March 1977 shows a much
lower downturn of 3.7 percent from Australia while other influences will have contributed to
the fall of 5660 visitors from the Pacific Islands. The latest statistics of total Australian
departures for all destinations including New Zealand show a levelling off at December
1976. The honourable member makes no reference to the growth in other areas-USA up
5.7 percent, Canada up 2.5 percent, Western Europe up 16.1 percent, and other countries up
32 percent. The Tourist and Publicity Department is increasing its already successful
advertising and promotion in Australia.
Mr Kirk: Is it not true that National Party policy statement No. 12 on tourism contains a
statement by the present Minister that due to the valuable contribution of tourism to the
country's overseas earnings New Zealand will be promoted more vigorously overseas; and, if
so, why has there been a decline in the number of Australian tourists visiting New Zealand?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: It is elementary. Obviously fewer people are coming to New
Zealand, although the revenue from tourism is up on last year. In 1972 we had 109 788
visitors from Australia. In 1976 the figure was 231 358, a considerable increase.
Mr Talbot: Surely in the long term the number of tourists coming to New Zealand from
Australia would depend on the downturn in the economy in Australia and not to any lack of
activity in promotion by the Minister and his department in New Zealand?
Hon. H. R. LAPWOOD: Surveys done by the department show that the greatest falloff
in business from Australia is in the 18 to 25 year age bracket, which would show that some of
the falloff is due to economic conditions in that country.

4. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Finance, Can he confirm that
the interest on the official overseas debt has now risen to over 5 percent of commodity export
receipts?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON (Acting Minister of Finance): The latest period for which
figures for interest on official overseas debt is available is the year ended 31 March 1977.
Official overseas interest payments for that period were $157.8 million. Total export receipts
on an OET basis for the same period were $3,120.9 million. The ratio of interest on official
overseas debt to export receipts is, therefore, 5.1 percent.
Mr Lambert: Is the Minister aware that in March 1974 the ratio was only 2 percent of
commodity export receipts, and would he attribute the grave position that has developed
directly to the borrow-and-hope policies of the Labour Government?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: Since 1974, New Zealand has borrowed overseas at a high
level to sustain the economy, and certainly the proportion of borrowing to export receipts
has risen from about 2 percent at the end of 1974 to just over 5 percent now. This is a matter
of economic adjustment, and it is a matter for political controversy as to the cause.
Borrowing is an essential element at present, but the Government will try to restrict it as
much as possible.
Hon. R. J. Tizard: Could the Minister explain to the member for Western Hutt why, if
this is a matter of grave concern, the National Government does not stop borrowing
overseas?
Hon. H. C. TEMPLETON: As a matter of economic policy we indicated that, following

Immigration Policy-Effect on Full Employment
6. Mr LAMBERT (Western Hutt) asked the Minister of Labour, Has the net loss of
migrants in 1976, brought about by the National Government's immigration policy, had any
effect on the maintenance of full employment in this country?
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): The Government's immigration policy has
helped to promote full employment. This has been achieved by a carefully selective policy,
which has admitted to New Zealand those persons whose skills have been required to
maintain economic growth. As the situation has changed, so the degree of selection has been
changed. However, this policy has not been implemented in isolation, but has been linked to
the Government's employment policy.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: Since there has been a net outflow of people between the ages of
20 and 30 years, who are in the employment bracket, will the policy of exporting the
unemployed continue in order to maintain full employment?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The situation will not vary markedly from when 13000 New
Zealanders left the country in one year under the Labour Government.
Mr T. J. Young: As the Minister has confirmed that the net immigration loss was caused
by the National Government's policies, can he say what the unemployment situation would
have been without that policy?
Mr SPEAKER: That is a purely hypothetical question.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It is not only hypothetical, but a question of emigration not
immigration.
Mr Luxton: Can the Minister confirm that the increase in employment opportunity was
0.9 percent for the year ended October 1975, and also 0.9 percent for the year ended
October 1976?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It would be unfair of me to confirm that as I do not have the
figures in front of me. I think the member's assessment is accurate.
Mr Isbey: Is it not a fact that the migration of skilled tradesmen overseas will have a
most adverse effect on New Zealand's productive capacity, and that that will be as serious as
rising unemployment?
Hon. J. B. GORDON: The answer is definitely in the negative. The most recent report
indicates that the largest classification of people leaving New Zealand is in the unskilled
capacity. Under the immigration policy administered by the Minister of Immigration, the
Government is allowing for the skilled tradesmen that are in the shortest supply and greatest
demand to enter the country. A recent advertisement in a London newspaper produced 3000
replies.

Mr FRIEDLANDER (New Plymouth): I thank all members who participated in the

enjoyed listening to it. I could offer one observation-he will require all his ability as a
speaker if he is to make the Labour policy sound credible. I also congratulate the member

fact that he showed us what an excellent mind and an excellent brain he has. I welcome both
these members to the House, and I am sure we will hear more from them. I look forward to
their contribution in future debates.
In moving this debate, I drew attention to many aspects of the economy. I drew
attention to the reduced rate of inflation as shown by the consumer price index. That subject
was further discussed by many of my colleagues on this side of the House. We drew attention
to the improved current account deficit, the reduced deficit before borrowing in the Budget,
and the halt to the increase in unemployment seen under the last Labour Government.
These are areas in which we have seen significant and most encouraging improvements, and
Opposition members were not able to refute those points during the debate. Members on
this side of the House also drew attention to a most important part of our economy; the
sector related to exports; the sector that will be responsible for dragging us out of our present
economic problems-problems that the Labour Government failed to face up to. In
agriculture, which Labour members did not look at too closely when they were in power, we
can show a significant improvement. Forestry, manufacturing, and fishing also show
improvement.
The Deputy Leader of the Opposition, who is trying to intervene, endeavoured to talk
about the economy, but the facts he put forward were remarkably thin. In fact, I do not
believe any facts were there at all. He has, in recent weeks, made one announcement that

retirement. Opposition members were unable to challenge the facts about the economy
presented from this side of the House. Virtually no Opposition speaker dealt in any detail

something emotive that we can lift up. Let us talk about the cost to the average man." I

curious arguments they have put forward in this debate. Labour members failed to mention

UPPER HUTT CITY (REPRESENTATION AND FINANCIAL UNIFICATION) BILL
Hon. R. L. BAILEY (Heretaunga): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time.
This Bill has come about because the Upper Hutt City Council wants to streamline the
council structure and the number of councillors to enable it to work more smoothly in the
interests of the community. I am bound to say that the original proposal which I was required
to bring to the House was one that I could not support wholeheartedly. Initially the Upper
Hutt City was enlarged with the joining of what was then known as the Rimutaka riding,
which came about because of a suggestion made by the Local Government Commission in
1972. The Order in Council was signed on 15 January 1973, enabling the Rimutaka riding to
become a portion of the city of Upper Hutt. Because of that amalgamation, the city of Upper
Hutt is the second largest in New Zealand in land area.
The people of the Rimutaka riding were happy to join with the city of Upper Hutt then,
on the basis that there would be proportional representation on a ward system. The
suggestion was that the system would operate for 10 years, but after only one election the
Upper Hutt City fathers decided to bring forward a Bill which I was required, as the local
member of Parliament, to present to this House, asking for a modification of that scheme.
As I said earlier, this is the modification which I could not support wholeheartedly. The
Local Bills Committee spent a considerable time on this issue and I am pleased that it
listened attentively to the representations made. The Rimutaka Ratepayers Association
made its views very strongly known as did other individuals, and I am pleased to inform
members that the modifications that have come forward retain the ward system, for a period
anyway. That is what this Bill is all about.
From the next local body elections the number of Upper Hutt City Council representa-
tives will fall from 17 councillors to 12. Of course, the mayor is on top of all that, and it will


## p. 735 (#743) ############################################

mean that the people in the Rimutaka area will still have their proportional representation
although the number of their representatives has been dropped from four to three. It is
desirable that this situation continues for a little longer, or until such time as the people in
the area feel they can be fully absorbed. Clause 3 provides for the financial modifications. At
present the rate for the Rimutaka riding is struck separately from that for the city of Upper
Hutt. It will now be incorporated. That also is desirable. I am happy to support this measure
as it now stands since it has been so drastically modified by the Local Bills Committee. It is a
much more acceptable piece of legislation than initially came forward.
Mr COMBER (Wellington Central): I support the local member who has moved the
second reading of the Bill. It is appropriate to point out that the work that was done on the
Local Bills Committee is indicative of all that is good in our parliamentary system. We heard
the representations, we listened to the arguments, and discussed the issues as well as the
differences of opinion in a bipartisan spirit. We liaised with the sponsor, the member for
Heretaunga, and as a result of all that made substantial changes to the Bill. As the member
for Heretaunga has pointed out, we certainly came up with a far better Bill than was
introduced into the House.
I can appreciate the reasons for the Upper Hutt City Council's seeking a change to the
Order in Council of 15 January 1973, which alters the boundaries of the Hutt County and the
city of Upper Hutt by excluding the Rimutaka riding from the then Hutt County; but looking
beyond that we had to weigh up that argument against the better interests of the people who
would be affected by that change, and especially the people in the Rimutaka riding. The
select committee, I believe, properly decided on the change. It is a fact—and this observa-
tion was made during the hearings that many people, no doubt in good faith, did not object
to the scheme promulgated by the Local Government Commission because they were
assured that the position spelt out in the scheme and codified finally by the Order in Council
provided for the arrangement to stand for 10 years. Obviously as a Parliament we cannot be
seen to be breaching that good faith.
The main operative clause was clause 3. Originally it was to merge the two urban wards
into one, thereby reducing the number of wards from three to two, or in other words leaving
a rural ward and a city ward. As the member for Heretaunga has pointed out this was
opposed by the local ratepayers association and that was one very good reason advanced for
the change we now have in the Bill. I should like to read from the report of the Department
of Internal Affairs; one of the key factors that influenced the thinking of the select
committee. The report says; "There is objection to the provisions of the Bill, which unites
into one urban ward the two presently exisiting urban wards. The principal grounds for
objection were that this set aside a determination of the Local Government Commission that
the three wards should exist for 10 years, which was arrived at after considering objections to
the provisional scheme. It was suggested to the committee that the inclusion of this provision
in the scheme, and its application for 10 years, were virtually the conditions under which the
'contract' uniting the operations of Hutt County with the Borough of Upper Hutt was
allowed to proceed without a poll. It is true that the commission inserted these provisions
only to satisfy objections to the provisional scheme. By so doing a poll on the scheme may
have been averted." I think that is self-evident. It is also true that the commission had doubts
on continuing two wards for 10 years when it referred to the fact that "by 1977 it will be time
to redraw the ward boundaries of the city". After hearing the arguments advanced by the
ratepayers association, the committee felt that it could not go along with the original
suggestions.
The power to reduce or increase the number of councillors lies with the local authority,
but it is also a fact that the Order in Council of January 1973 effectively took that right away
from the Upper Hutt City Council for the reasons already advanced. The committee also felt
that was another compelling reason, but I think it is fair to say that a satisfactory compromise
was reached. While not accepting the main arguments advanced by the Upper Hutt City
Council, the committee has been able to satisfy the council on one point-the reduction in
the number of councillors. As I have said, the council did have this power under section 23 of
the Municipal Corporations Act, but for the Order in Council. Local government must not
only be viable, but must also be independent and free to make that type of decision for
itself-but overriding all this is the Order in Council to which I have already referred.
An argument was advanced that ratepayers in the rural ward should also be entitled to
vote in the combined city ward, which would have introduced the right to a dual vote, and
the Local Bills Committee quite properly rejected that argument. The principle of one-man-
one-vote is embodied in local government elections as well as central government elections. I

LOWER HUTT CITY (FREE AMBULANCE SITE) BILL
Mr T. J. YOUNG (Hutt): I move, That this Bill be now read a second time. This Bill was
introduced during the recess, and under Standing Order 266 the first reading was deemed to
have taken place, and the Bill was referred to the Local Bills Committee. The Bill seeks to
validate a deed entered into by the Wellington Free Ambulance, the Lower Hutt City
Corporation, the city of Lower Hutt, the city of Upper Hutt, the borough of Petone, the
borough of Eastbourne, the Hutt County, and the New Zealand Red Cross Society. This
deed was signed on 30 June 1976, and sought to transfer land in Lower Hutt at present
owned by the Wellington Free Ambulance to the New Zealand Red Cross Society. The Bill
is a local Bill, because the Wellington Free Ambulance is deemed to be a local body with
representation from the local authorities throughout the region.
The Bill also seeks to repeal the Free Ambulance Bill brought down in 1954, under
which an arrangement was made by deed with the Lower Hutt City Council for the
Wellington Free Ambulance to be established in Lower Hutt on another site. That deed
provided that the land should be used for the free ambulance service, and for no other
purpose. When an approach was made by the New Zealand Red Cross Society, it was
necessary for the local bodies concerned to agree to the transfer of this parcel of 21 perches. I
am pleased to say that there was no resistance whatsoever to this. The Red Cross Society has
long been established in Lower Hutt. There is a very healthy Hutt Valley centre, and a
Lower Hutt subcentre. For some years there was a Red Cross Society building in Market
Grove, Lower Hutt, but it had to be pulled down and an arrangement has been made with
the Wellington Free Ambulance service for the Red Cross Society to use another parcel of
land, again in Market Grove, adjoining the free ambulance service land.
The Bill also provides for the transfer of a small parcel of land now owned by the
Wellington Free Ambulance service to the Lower Hutt City Council for street-widening
purposes. I think the amount involved is about 5.96 perches, and the Lower Hutt City
Council will give alternative access from W oburn Road to the free ambulance service as a
quid pro quo. The Bill, therefore, has these two provisions: the transfer of 21 perches of land
to the Red Cross Society, and the transfer of another 5.96 perches to the Lower Hutt City for
street-widening purposes, the free ambulance service to get new access to the land it
occupies at present. The area of land that has been occupied by the free ambulance service is
2 roods 6.39 perches. I have asked the free ambulance service whether it has any need for
further land for expansion, and as far as it can see it has enough room for expansion. The
transfer of land is quite satisfactory to the free ambulance service. It has had no need for the
land in the past, and does not envisage any need in the future.
Mr ELWORTHY (Oamaru): I support the second reading of the Bill. It came before the
Local Bills Committee yesterday, and the degree of consensus was such that the committee
heard submissions on the Bill and deliberated, all within 20 minutes, which was a refreshing
change from some of the hours spent recently by that committee. The ground has been well
covered by the member for Hutt, but perhaps I can summarise the objectives of the Bill. The
first objective is that the Free Ambulance (Lower Hutt Site) Act 1954 will be repealed, and
the deed set out in the schedule to the Bill will be validated and declared to have been
executed lawfully by the parties. The land subject to the transfers will be deemed not to be
rateable property for the purposes of the Rating Act 1967.
A portion of the land now held by the free ambulance service and surplus to its present
and envisaged needs will be transferred to the Red Cross Society, without consideration, for
the erection at the expense of the Red Cross Society of a building for the purposes of its

constitution. Another part of the land at present held by the free ambulance service will be
transferred, without consideration, to the Lower Hutt City for street purposes, and the

The Red Cross Society will construct its premises in such a manner as to cause no

LOCAL ELECTIONS AND POLLS AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. When introducing this Bill I indicated that clauses 2 and 3 were of
significance to the local authority general elections on 8 October. Clause 2 sets out to make it
clear that any elections or polls held in conjunction with a territorial authority's election or
poll are to be conducted by the method of voting decided upon by the territorial authority.
The principal Act authorises a number of voting methods that local authorities generally may
use for their elections or polls; postal voting, spread voting, that is voting over not more than
11 consecutive days; the use of mobile polling booths; and the orthodox 1-day poll.
In the case of postal or spread voting, the Act makes it clear that when a territorial
authority has decided on one of those systems for its elections, all elections and polls to be
held by its returning officer at the same time as the authority's election will be conducted by
that system. The same applies to the use of mobile polling booths. The purpose of this was to
avoid the administrative difficulties and voter confusion that would arise if a number of
elections or polls conducted at the same time by the same returning officer were to use
different voting methods. By a quite unintentional omission in last year's consolidation of
the Local Elections and Polls Act this principle was overlooked in relation to the orthodox 1-
day poll. Clause 2 rectifies this omission, and concentrates into one provision the controls
already existing in the Act in respect of postal and spread voting, and the use of mobile
polling booths.
The clause also provides a solution to the situation in which two or more ad hoc
authority elections or polls are to be conducted together and different voting methods are
proposed. It is provided that the authorities themselves should decide on the system to be
used, and, if they cannot reach agreement, the returning officer, who in almost every case is
the returning officer of the territorial authority, will use the system last used by his territorial
authority. In the case of a single election or poll the effect of the clause will be to allow the
local authority concerned to determine which of the options will be used.
Clause 3 is simply a consequential amendment. It removes redundant words from the
style of the nomination forms prescribed in the schedule to the principal Act, thus removing
a possible source of confusion for returning officers in their preparations for the elections.
Clause 4 also makes a consequential amendment that was overlooked last year. It simply
lines up the period for lodging a petition for an inquiry into the conduct of a loan poll under
the Local Authorities Act 1956 with the period specified in the Local Elections and Polls
Act. Loan polls are conducted in accordance with the Local Elections and Polls Act, which
prescribes a period of 21 days for lodging these petitions. These amendments are necessary,
and are fully supported by the municipal and counties associations.

LOCAL GOVERNMENT AMENDMENT BILL
Hon. D. A. HIGHET (Minister of Local Government): I move, That this Bill be now
read a second time. When introducing the Bill, I mentioned that clause 2 was really a
consequential amendment and that clause 3 restored an electoral right removed by the Local
Government Act 1974.
Mr Hunt: It helps the absentee landlords and the rich.
Hon. D. A. HIGHET: We are well aware of the political philosophy of the member for
New Lynn. Democratic socialism it is called. As I was about to say, the need for the
amendment made by clause 2 arises from changes made by last year's Local Elections and
Polls Act. The whole purpose of the amendment is to enable a returning officer conducting a
poll on a Local Government Commission scheme to give the amount of notice of the poll
required by the Local Elections and Polls Act 1976. The Local Government Act requires the
returning officer to conduct a poll in not less than 35, nor more than 42, days after he has
received the request for the poll; whereas the Local Elections and Polls Act requires 42 clear
days' notice to be given of the date on which the poll is to be held. The provisions are in
conflict to the extent that the returning officer cannot give 42 clear days' notice of the poll
even if he delays the poll until the forty-second day, which is the last day on which he must
conduct the poll. The amendment proposed in the Bill extends the period within which the
poll is to be held to not more than 49 days after the returning officer receives the request. For
the benefit of members opposite, I shall repeat that. The amendment proposed in the Bill
extends the period within which the poll is to be held to not more than 49 days after the
returning officer receives the request. This will allow the 42 clear days' notice of the date of
the poll to be given, as required by the Local Elections and Polls Act. The purpose of
extending the period of notice under the Local Elections and Polls Act was basically to
provide more time for clerks of local authorities to prepare and check the rolls to be used,
and for returning officers to finalise their arrangements for conducting the poll. These are
very important considerations, having in mind the increasing populations of some local
authority districts and the need for accurate rolls. This was amply demonstrated recently in
Waikouaiti. I was not prepared to change the required period of notice to overcome the
conflict I outlined.
Clause 3 contains the significant amendment made by the Bill. Section 168 of the
principal Act at present restricts the right to vote in the election of members of community or
district community councils to those electors possessing a residential qualification in respect
of an address within the community. Section 169 restricts the right of candidacy to the same
class of elector. A ratepayer residing within the community is deemed to have a residential
qualification and can take a full part in the elections. The result of this is that non-resident
ratepayers, notwithstanding an interest in common at least with resident ratepayers of a
community, are disenfranchised. The member for New Lynn seems to disagree with this.
They are therefore prevented from offering themselves as candidates for elections to those
bodies. Clause 3 simply removes these restrictions. More significantly, however, clause 3
removes a real anomaly in the present law, which discriminates between non-resident
ratepayers of a community under the jurisdiction of a district community council and those
of a community under the jurisdiction of a community council. The effect of the current law
is that non-resident ratepayers of a community council can take part in the election of county
councillors to represent the riding in which their community is situated, but non-resident
ratepayers of a district community council are prevented from doing so.
The forthcoming elections on 8 October would have seen the first full application of
these provisions. Preparations for elections necessarily include a thorough study of all
relevant law, and in the course of preparing for the forthcoming elections the curious
distinctions I have mentioned came to light. The amendment proposed in clause 3 has been
sought by many county councils, which are the class of territorial authority most concerned
with district community councils and community councils, as well as by private citizens.
During the first reading of the Bill, it was asked whether any of those citizens who supported
the amendment in clause 3 would be candidates for election. The many letters I received did
not provide the specific answer to that question. However, a number of the county councils
who wrote to me expressed concern that valuable members of county town committees and

county borough councils, the bodies supplanted in the present law by community and district
community councils, were prevented by the present law from seeking re-election.
The amendments proposed in this Bill are necessary. No objection to them has been
made known to me. In fact, when the Bill was introduced, the Opposition spokesman on
local government said he believed his side had no opposition to the Bill. If however, he
thinks differently on reflection, we shall of course accept that. Certainly, no objections have

Dr WALL (Porirua): First, I wish to make it quite clear that the Minister was not correct
when he said that the Opposition had no objection to this legislation. He will recall that in
the introductory debate we asked that the Bill be referred to a select committee for study,
because some of the principles are somewhat involved and required more than the few
seconds' study available to this side of the House on the introduction of the Bill. In the
course of our study it has become apparent that our request to the Minister was not only wise
but necessary, and I urge him to take that step now, because this legislation is not quite as
simple as the Minister would have us believe.
Two principles are involved. The whole idea behind the formation of community
councils and district community councils was that they should promote a sense of commun-
ity, that they should be the organisation of expression of community interest and community
feeling about all matters concerning local body administration that would affect them most
strongly. The essential point was that they should have a community of interest and be
concerned about local matters. If we enlarge the franchise, we enable people who may not
have any community of interest whatsoever to vote for members of those county councils
and district councils. Therefore, after the passage of this legislation, the whole question must
arise of whether or not those local bodies are correctly named. It is possible that the councils
could represent people who have no association whatsoever with the community.
The other principle involved, which the Minister mentioned in concluding his remarks,
is whether the ratepayers in the area should have any voting rights at all in this. The
imposition of rates and the responsibility to the payers of those rates does not affect
community councils at all, so the non-resident ratepayer cannot justifiably claim in equity or
justice any right to representation on ordinary community councils. Any claim to representa-
tion must be based on the financial contribution he makes. He will possibly have the right to
representation through the people on the council who decide what his financial contribution
will be, but that does not in any way apply to community councils. I am waiting to hear from
the Minister if there is any justification for enabling non-residents, whether ratepayers or
non-ratepayers-non-residents with voting rights-to be elected to community councils.
This also applies to district community councils, because those members elected to district
community councils have no direct rating responsibility, although they do indirectly in that
they have the right to appoint members to the rating authority- which would be the county
council or the local body-in whose area they form part of a riding.
As the legislation now stands, only those who are non-resident ratepayers have lost the
right to indirect representation—not direct representation on the body that imposes the
rates. Against that, we introduce a very real threat of loss of character to the community
councils and district community councils. In areas such as Wainuiomata, where there are
many people in the local community and few absentee ratepayers, the issue is not in doubt
and the principle is of no importance. To introduce into this debate the problems associated
with these would be to distort the picture, as the Bill affects very much the smaller areas and
those in which the community council and the emphasis on community interest are very
much stronger. In the course of this debate, members who represent areas that will be
affected will speak on this matter, but at this stage I want to draw the attention of the House
to the numerous places that have many non-residential ratepayers who have either bought
up property to hold on speculation-and there is a significant number of those in New
Zealand-or whose residence in the community is just for brief holiday periods. These
people are ratepayers, but in no way could they be said to have a community of interest with
the real residents. The real community of interest for these non-residential ratepayers lies in
their permanent place of residence. I am not exaggerating when I say that there many places
in New Zealand that have a preponderance of absentee ratepayers who will be given a
representation and will be able to stand for election to a body that is supposed, and was
obviously designed, to reflect a community of interest. These people have no community of
interest whatsoever with the local people.
I realise that difficult problems are involved here. If the Minister had realised what was

The communities that will be affected by this measure are predominantly holiday
communities, and Great Barrier Island may or may not qualify for that description. Many
other parts of New Zealand—particularly the Auckland area, the Coromandel Peninsula,
and various areas of the East Coast and Northland-experience an influx of people at
holiday times-not just holidaymakers, but property owners as well. In considering
community of interest, in this context we must remember that the typical structure of these
areas is a very small permanent community and a huge influx of holidaymakers, a substantial
number of whom own property in the area. I would have thought that community of interest
consisted of devising ways in which these people and the interest they represent could
usefully be brought together. There is no more useful way than through the district


## p. 747 (#755) ############################################

16 June
747
Local Government Amendment Bill
community councils, or the community councils, which can be aptly defined as nothing more
than statutory ratepayers' associations. The councils have power to make representations to
the parent body and, on a fair reading of the Bill, they are statutory ratepayers' associations.
It is essential, in areas such as Coromandel, Northland, and the East Coast, that they
function as such; it would be a serious matter if other ratepayers and the local residents were
at loggerheads.
The common interest of ratepayers in a ratepayers' association is making representa-
tions to the parent council about the money that needs to be expended in the area and the
amenities that need to be provided. I know a typical case, in which representations have
been made by property owners and local residents for the establishment of a community hall.
There is no suggestion that there is any fundamental conflict or cleavage. The interest is
recognised as common, because many of the holidaymakers, who often have a modest
income and young families, help to create an amenity that will be used by the local
community in the off-season, when the hall will be used for playing bowls and other
pastimes. In many of these areas, there is a definite identity of interest in establishing the
basic facilities provided by the parent council. It is on the basis of joint representation that
these amenities will be established.
Much has been said about Great Barrier Island. I am at a loss to understand why the
member for Auckland Central said that the Local Government Amendment Bill takes away
the right of that small community to decide its future, and that the island will lose its local
council. I have never heard such negative and defeatist nonsense in my life. Nothing in the
Bill will take away the identity of the local council or cause it to cease to exist. The only
reasons it could cease to exist are indifference on the part of the community and, above all,
its inability to finance essential activities. As a member of the Roads Board, I am aware of
the difficulties that the council experiences in roading and the heavy subsidies that we
poured into roading facilities on the island. It is absolute nonsense to suggest that that
council will be legislated out of existence. It will either continue or cease to exist, depending
on the ratepayers' wishes and whether it is a viable economic undertaking. Those are the
only criteria in that situation. The people who have argued that there is a conflict in the
community of interest have failed to understand that there will be a merging of interests and
that the ratepayers and residents will be more effective in a ratepayers' association, because
that, in effect, is what a community council or a district community council is.
Having said these things, I can see little point in labouring the real meaning of clause 3.
The short title and clause 2 not being in dispute, the only issue is the one I have just
discussed. Much of the discussion we have heard proceeds on the rather tortuous and strange
assumption that there is a cleavage and division between the local ratepayer and the non-
resident ratepayer, whereas in my experience it is necessary that they come together and
realise they have common interests. I repeat, the definition of a statutory ratepayers'
association and that of the interest of residents and ratepayers is the same. They are all
ratepayers if they own property, so it would be ludicrous if one set of ratepayers was
excluded from the right to representation on such an association. It is imperative that their
interests be merged and married, so that there is a co-operative effort to better these local
communities. If we accorded with the ideas advanced by the Opposition in this debate, we
would be deliberately perpetuating the myths that have been propounded. We would be
saying that absentee landlords are fundamentally evil. Absentee landlords have nothing to
do with this issue. They are ratepayers who should be brought together with residents, who
are also ratepayers, to make ratepayer representations to a local authority for the purpose of
bettering the community. Much of the distinction that has been made is highly emotive,
highly irrelevant, and quite ill conceived. I see no reason for the Bill to be referred to a select
committee.

The Bill takes another major step towards dismantling the concept of community
created by the 1974 Act. The community councils instituted by the 1974 Act were meant to
reflect the ideas, ideals, and feelings of the people in communities of up to 2000, 3000, and
4000 or even fewer, if necessary. They were meant to get active democracy, real democ-
racy, at grass roots. The moment that the right to vote for those community councils is taken
away from the community itself, as this Bill proposes, and given to the bricks and mortar, to
the Queen Street farmers, another knife is put into the corpse of the community councils and
that great concept that Henry May initiated in 1974 is destroyed. This is the second time the
Government has done it. The 1974 Act provided that the community councils would be
effective and would have statutory powers of community participation. Those powers were
stripped from the communities in the first amendment to this Act, which was introduced by
the Minister of Local Government last year. The second step now seeks to destroy what is
left of community councils, which, in the Government's view, are simply committees of the
territorial local authorities, not the voice of the people, as envisaged by Henry May. The Bill
sticks another knife into the other ribs of the community, and tells them, "People who don't
live in your community will have a say in what little voice you have." They are being given
the power to vote, to speak on behalf of the community, even though they do not live there.

SHOP TRADING HOURS BILL
Hon. J. B. GORDON (Minister of Labour): I move, That this Bill be now read a second
time. Since its introduction late last year, and as promised, this Bill has been studied
carefully by the Labour Committee. Fifty-seven separate submissions were received and the
committee heard 30 of these in person. I made it clear from the beginning that the
Government was prepared to listen to constructive comments on the Bill. Indeed, the
committee has borne out this contention by making many important and very useful
amendments, most of which have resulted directly from evidence presented to it. I thank the
members of that committee for the efforts they have put into revising the Bill. I also thank
those people who made submissions for their assistance. Nevertheless, this Bill has not been
an easy one for the committee to deal with. A small Supplementary Order Paper will be
made available as soon as it is printed, and it implements two or three small changes
requested this week by the shop assistants union.
Criticism from some quarters has not been helpful. Erroneous assertions as to the
supposed detrimental effect of the Bill have been, at best, misleading and, at worst,
downright disruptive. I refer, of course, to the personal interpretations placed on the Bill by
union officials and members on the other side of the House which have been given much
prominence by the media. I ask here why statements by myself and the Acting Minister were
not given similar prominence. Likewise, unions and pundits, and even editors- and some
Opposition members as well-have forgotten or been too lazy to reread the Hansard
speeches from when the Bill first came into the House. I refer in particular to one of
yesterday's editorials that suggested that a press statement I had made indicated there was
something erroneous in the drafting of the Bill, and suggested that if that was so it should be
put into the Bill right away.
Much of the misunderstanding arises from the fact that people either become bush
lawyers, or consult lawyers who consider themselves better equipped in drafting legislation
than the Parliamentary Counsel, whom we all rely on for sound legal advice. The Bill does
not depart from the concept originally set out in the introduction. Many shop assistants in
certain parts of the country have gone on strike in protest against the Bill. Many have voted
today not to go on strike, and I commend them for that. They have taken this action because
they have been told by union officials what this Bill will supposedly do to their working lives.
I sometimes wonder if these prophets of doom are talking about the same legislation we have
before us tonight. I know that some strike action was decided on before the Bill was reported
back from the select committee. How any reasonable person could decide on such action
before knowing what changes the committee proposed is beyond my understanding. An
editorial in the National Business Review suggested that the Government had produced a
wan, wishy-washy piece of legislation. I suggest to that editor that he has not read the
original Hansard of the time the Bill was introduced.
Mr Malcolm: Scaremongery!
Hon. J. B. GORDON: It is scaremongery. I also know that strike action was mainly
engineered on a foundation of false claims and misconceptions. Such a situation in New
Zealand is to be deplored. False claims about the Bill's effect have varied. Some claim that
shop assistants would have to work 14 hours a day Monday to Friday, and also on weekends,
for no extra pay. How silly can some people get? There is absolutely no basis for these
suggestions. The major awards relating to shop assistants prescribe a 40-hour week to be
worked Monday to Friday, with not more than 8 hours at ordinary rates. Any time worked
after 6 p.m. at the latest is to be paid at penal rates. The one late night a week is an exception
to this under the arrangement inside the award in the Act.


## p. 757 (#765) ############################################

16 June
757
Shop Trading Hours Bill
Unfortunately, these wild claims have been accepted without question, or if questioned
given the wrong answers, by some workers and also by other members of the public. What
does the Bill do to award provisions? I concede the Bill does override the closing hour
provisions in awards and collective agreements, but it does not in any way affect the working
hour provisions. They are covered by, and can be renegotiated under, the Industrial
Relations Act, and the workers are adequately protected. In the awards and collective
agreements covering shop assistants there are two distinct types of clauses. On the one hand
there are the closing hour provisions, which dictate when a retailer may open his shop. These
are the provisions affected by the Bill. On the other hand, there are the working hour
provisions, which provide for the actual hours of work of shop assistants, and their rates of
pay. These provisions are not affected in any way by the Bill. I trust those words can be
recorded and remembered.
In so far as wages, hours of work, overtime, penal payments, and general conditions of
work are concerned, the unions will continue to negotiate with the employers. Workers are
not losing any protection they already have. Opponents of the Bill also claim that wide-
spread weekend trading will result. That is nothing but wild speculation that is not supported
by any reasonable interpretation of the Bill, and certainly not by the amended criteria set out
by the committee. The right to trade on weekends is strictly governed by the Bill. It was in
this area that the committee made substantial amendments that are intended to prevent a
proliferation of weekend trading. It is clear from the specific provisions of the Bill that the
amount of weekend trading will be and can be limited.
The existing legislation relating to trading hours—the Shops and Offices Act 1955-has
been in force for 22 years. It presents the Department of Labour with formidable enforce-
ment problems, and indeed on many occasions the shop assistants union has lodged
complaints about the manner in which the present Act is being enforced or policed. Now it is
suggested that we go back to the status quo. What we are trying to do is legalise what is
happening at present, or stop the practices the union has complained about to the Minister of
Labour. Breaches of the Act are numerous, but because of the legal complexities involved
they are difficult to prove. On top of this, the courts have tended to impose only very small
fines, and many shop occupiers tend to treat these as licences to operate illegally. This is
clearly an unsatisfactory situation; it is not good legislation. Any responsible Government,
and any honest Government, has a duty to ensure that the law is capable of proper
enforcement. The provisions of the Bill will be capable of enforcement by officers of the
Department of Labour.
Shop trading hours at present are determined by the trading hour provisions in the
various awards and collective agreements, and consequently vary for different types of
shops. Indeed, some shops close within the hours set down, and I had evidence that one
butcher's shop closed at 3 p.m. on Fridays. There is nothing in the law to stop the owner
doing that, nor is there anything in the new law. The Shops and Offices Act makes such
provisions binding on shops. It is permissive, and they can do what they like inside those
hours. This Bill removes the fixing of trading hours from the scope of the awards. To that
extent I concede that some of the shop assistants may have been worried, but they are
adequately protected. This Bill sets down the trading hour limits for all shops. Those hours
are to be from 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday to Friday. Those are merely outer limits. It does not
mean that shops must remain open for that span of hours. The opening period within that
span is left to the individual occupier, and we have seen this system in hotels, and in the glide
time within the State services.
The Government is satisfied that suitable and orderly patterns of weekend trading will
soon be established, or confirmed as established, particularly some of the existing practices,
legal or illegal. This Bill merely provides a framework for more flexible hours within the
tight parameter set out in the revised Bill. Since the law was last reviewed, living and social
patterns have changed drastically. This Bill moves with the times, I hope. A shop wishing to
trade outside the specified span of hours-that is, on weekends or late at night-has two
options. As at present, it can open to sell and display only approved goods, formerly called
exempted goods. Alternatively, it can apply for an authority to open. This is also the
situation under the existing law. The main difference is that shops within a particular area
will now be able to make a joint application only on a majority.
The body hearing the applications has been strengthened by the committee at the
suggestion of some witnesses. Instead of comprising a full-time commissioner with a part-
time associate, which was proposed to replace the existing tribunal, the new Shop Trading
Hours Commission will consist of three people. The commissioner will be a barrister or


## p. 758 (#766) ############################################

758
16 June
Shop Trading Hours Bill
solicitor with at least 7 years' experience, which is the basic criterion for the appointment of a
magistrate. We may even see fit to appoint a magistrate. May I interpolate here that I gave
assurances, as I did to the retailers and to the shop assistants union this week, that there will
be adequate consultation on this with both parties before any such appointments are made.
When hearing individual applications the commissioner alone will grant or refuse the
application. For area applications the three members will sit together. The increase in the
size of the commission reflects the importance of the task it must undertake and the care it
must exercise in an area application.
Certain criteria are listed for the commission to take into account when hearing an
application. In this respect the Bill as introduced has been greatly added to to try to give
some protection. Some of those making submissions feared a proliferation of weekend
trading unless the criteria were tightened up. The committee was cognisant of this argument,
and has injected a greater element of social responsibility into the criteria. The original Bill
required the commission merely to look at four things: public demand; the nature of the area
in which the shop is situated, and whether it is a tourist or holiday area; the interests of the
occupier of any other shop; and the public interest generally, including the interests of
persons living in the vicinity of the shop concerned.
The Bill before the House tonight expands this list of criteria considerably, and largely
in the light of requests made to the committee by the various interested parties. First, the
commission can grant an application to the extent only that it is satisfied that it is in the best
interests of the public generally. In satisfying itself of this, the commission must then look at
eight things: public demand; the effect on retail prices; the effect on family and other social
patterns in the area; the nature of the area, including whether it is a tourist or holiday area,
and the class of patron to be served; the stability, and orderly and economic planning and
development, of any wider area, and of the transport and other services in any wider area;
the interests of the occupiers of other shops; the need to minimise the amount of commercial
activity taking place on Sundays-with the exception, of course, of the routine ones we have
at present, such as railway terminals and airports where travellers find they need some of the
necessities of life; and the application of the principle of the 40-hour week and any
derogation from that principle-that is added as a basic criterion.
I think we have moved extensively to meet the opposition voiced at the committee to
the limited criteria set by the commission. These provisions relating to the opening of shops
for extended hours can by no stretch of anyone's imagination be seen to clear the way for so-
called, and often accused, open slather on the weekends. That is not the Government's wish.
We have no desire to see a widespread extension, even on Saturday mornings.
Hon. H. R. Lapwood: The Opposition was misleading the people.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: Not only the Opposition-also some private lawyers, if they had
lawyers, but certainly some unionists. The right to trade on the weekend has been clearly
circumscribed. We do not envisage nor do we want widespread downtown Saturday opening.
We do not want to create in New Zealand a replica of Detroit or Los Angeles. Nothing is
further from our desires, and that is why we wrote in the criterion involving regional
planning. You cannot open if it will have a detrimental effect on the downtown area. The
Shop Trading Hours Commission will have one additional function under the Bill. Any
changes made must be recommended by the commission. Under the present Act, the
Minister must set up a special review committee for this purpose. One of the key points in
the initiation of the Bill was the fact that a former Minister had a review committee and did
not see fit to adopt all the decisions it handed to him.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: They were split decisions.
Hon. J. B. GORDON: There were some minority decisions, but the Minister did not see
fit to accept even all the majority decisions. Numerous other small amendments have been
made to the Bill by the select committee. These rectify anomalies that were highlighted by
many of the submissions. The Government, having taken all the relevant criticism into
account, has made the necessary concessions and adjustments sought.
I now deal with the Bill, clause by clause, and itemise where it has been changed. Clause
1 is perfectly simple: the short title and commencement date. In that there will be a separate
date for the creation of the central registered roll, that will be in the Supplementary Order
Paper, and will be 1 January, a realistic date for the department to prepare a roll of some
6000 shops that are already on the exempted list. There is no proposal to delete them. Clause
2 is an interpretation clause. Clause 4 makes special provision for markets. Every stall within
a market is deemed to be a shop. The clause also provides for a method of identification of
market stalls, and that is a tightening up on the existing law, and enables policing of any


## p. 759 (#767) ############################################

16 June
759
Shop Trading Hours Bill
extended hours of markets that are illegally open.
Clause 4A establishes a Shop Trading Hours Commission. This consists of a commis-
sioner, who is to be a barrister or solicitor of at least 7 years' experience, and two other
members. Clause 4B provides that every decision of the commission is to be a majority
decision, except that the commissioner alone may hear and decide on applications from
individual shops for extended hours. Clause 4C provides for the remuneration of the
members of the commission. Clause 4D requires the Department of Labour to provide the
commission with administrative and secretarial services. Clause 4E requires the commission
to make an annual report to the Minister, for tabling in the House. Clause 5, as amended by
the select committee, provides for two classes of goods: approved and special goods. The
commission is to hear representations and make recommendations on a review of these
classes of goods. Parliament or the Minister will not establish a review committee, as we
have had in the past. By clause 5A, when the commission wishes to recommend that
individual items be declared approved goods, it may advertise its intention to do so. I intend,
during the Committee stage, to introduce an amendment that will make it mandatory for the
commission to advertise its intention. The commission cannot make any recommendation
until it has considered all objections it receives.
Clause 6 provides that, subject to the other provisions of the Act, all shops must be
closed outside the hours of 7 a.m. to 9 p.m. Monday to Friday, and on certain public
holidays. However, a shop can remain open as long as it is selling or displaying only
approved goods. Clause 6A provides for the transferral of certain holidays when they fall on
Saturdays or Sundays; that is another provision, incidentally, that protects staff. Clause 7
allows pharmacies to open at any time to sell urgently required medicines and surgical
appliances, a common practice today. In addition, the Secretary of Labour may grant special
authority for pharmacies to open at other times. Clause 8 allows shops where postal business
is carried on to open especially for that purpose. By clause 9, the Secretary of Labour may
authorise bookstalls at public passenger transport terminals to open; that is the existing law.
Clause 10 exempts bazaars and other like charitable sales from the operation of the Act,
while clause 11 exempts bona fide commercial travellers.
Clause 17 allows occupiers of individual shops, or the occupiers of the majority of shops
in an area, to apply to the commission for authority to open outside normal hours. Under the
present Act, only individual shops can get exemptions. Originally, we proposed that local
authorities could apply. That has now been deleted from the revised Bill as reported back.
Clause 18 sets out the procedure for making an application to the commission for extended
opening. Clause 19 contains the rules governing applications and the decisions of the
commission. It sets out those persons who may appear before the commission. The
commission may refuse or grant the application either unconditionally or subject to
conditions. It may be a condition of an order that the shop or shops close at some specified
time, and unless there are special circumstances that time is to be such as to enable the
worker to have two consecutive days off. That was in the original Bill, is still there, and we
still intend to make it work. The commission is to grant an application to the extent only that
it is satisfied that its granting is in the best interests of the public generally. In satisfying itself
of this, the commission is to have regard to those eight criteria I mentioned earlier. Orders of
the commission may be amended or revoked by the commission.
Clause 20 deals with the powers of inspectors to enter and inspect shops. An inspector
may examine any person he finds in charge of a shop, and require him to give his name and
address, and to sign a statutory declaration of the matters in respect of which he is examined.
That is to enable us to police the new law once it is introduced. Clause 21 is the offence
clause. Included in this is the offence of obstructing an inspector, a practice that has grown
up of late. The maximum fine for all offences is raised substantially, and will be $500. Clause
22 is a procedural section. Clause 23 states the effect that the Act has on awards and
collective agreements. That is cardinal to the claim of the Government that it has protected,
and will protect, the rights of the worker. Clause 24 charges the Department of Labour with
the administration of the Act. Clause 25 is a savings clause, and clause 26 provides for
consequential amendments and repeals.

Bill is a genuine attempt to meet what has been a proven public demand, operating illegally.

what the commission decides on the evidence should take place. It is designed to protect the
shop worker and all those involved in the essential industry of distribution. It is not aimed at
disrupting our way of life. Those who suggest that should closely examine the speeches made
when the Bill was introduced.
