Speaking in support of the second reading, I want to set out exactly where we have come
from and where we are going. At present, we have a 2-day weekend, which in broad terms
most New Zealanders, and, I am sure, most Government members support. Over the last 2
years, however, a series of problems and pressures in specific areas has developed, caused by
all sorts of reasons-changing social patterns, pressures of life in urban areas, and growing
numbers of women working in the community. In many areas there has been de facto
Saturday shopping as a result of those pressures. There were loopholes you could drive a
truck through, and some retailers were driving trucks through the loopholes.
Inspectors of the Department of Labour were being openly and physically obstructed in
Auckland. Other retailers were advertising on television the fact that they were illegally


## p. 764 (#772) ############################################

764
16 June
Shop Trading Hours Bill
open on Saturday mornings. There were signs of community pressure. There were petitions
from Parnell, from the Wellington hardware retailers, and from private petitioners-one
petition from Auckland having more than 21 000 signatures. There was a growing pattern of
opinion polls, from the 1971 Heylen poll, to a Victoria University poll in 1972, to a 1976
Heylen poll, which demonstrated that public opinion was changing and putting pressure on
the present system. Up and down the country there was editorial support for change.
What was holding the line and protecting us against a flood of Saturday trading? It was
an Act dated 1955-22 years ago. In fact, the 1955 Act was based on a 1920s Act, which was
itself an amendment of a 1908 Act, which was an amendment of an Act from the 1800s. Even
if one concedes that there were reasonable changes in the Act of the early 1920s, the
legislation that was trying to hold the line against the community pressures of 1977 was
basically over 50 years old. When the Act was originally drawn up in the 1920s, New Zealand
hardly had the motorcar, and retail trading patterns and pressures were entirely different.
The public was not mobile, and the female work force was not mobilised. The only criteria in
support of Saturday trading were to be found in section 10B(3) of the old Act, which said
that three things should be borne in mind, the first of which was public interest-if you can
define public interest, and many lawyers and courts have tried for a long time.
Mr Courtney: I bet you couldn't.
Mr MALCOLM: No, I find it very hard to define public interest, and that is exactly the
point I want to make to the member for Nelson. In the old legislation, public interest- a
term almost incapable of being defined-was the only thing holding the line against
widespread Saturday trading. Two other criteria were offered-interests of occupiers of
other shops, and the desirability of providing service to the public at all reasonable times.
The old Act said there was a need to obey the precedent of desirability of service to the
public at all reasonable times. I submit that that provision, plus the public interest
provision-which the member for Nelson agrees cannot be defined-constituted a very thin
line indeed against the pressures of the 1970s.
And who had to interpret section 10? It was a Shops and Offices Tribunal that consisted
of one man. At times he had an associate who worked in the South Island, but he himself
worked as one man while his associate worked independently. As a retired magistrate with
no specialised knowledge of retail trading, and no expertise in commerce or industrial
relations, he was dependent on case law to define nebulous abstractions like public interest.
All that was needed was that this one-man Shops and Offices Tribunal should allow a couple
of situations to develop that gave a case-law precedent for trading on Saturdays, and then the
flood gates would have opened and there would have been no legal way to close them.
This Bill provides for a three-man commission, called the Shop Trading Hours Commis-
sion, and gives the members specific functions for protecting the public interest. I shall
review these functions and compare them. Whereas the concept of public interest was
formerly ill-defined, the Bill now lays down the criteria. The public interest now includes
issues such as public demand, the effect on retail prices, the effect on family and other social
patterns, the nature of the area in which the shop or shops concerned are situated and the
class of patrons to be served thereby, the stability and orderly economic planning and
development of any wider area, transport and other services in any wider area in which the
shop or shops concerned are situated, and the interests of other shops. With the exception of
the last mentioned, these considerations were previously ignored.
The need to minimise the amount of commercial activity taking place on Sundays, is
also provided for and, contrary to what the member for Avon would have us believe, for the
first time in legislation affecting shop workers there is the application of the principle of the
40-hour week. This has quietened Opposition members, and when the shop assistants union
officials hear the truth spoken in the House tonight they will be quietened also. More
importantly, when the tens of thousands of shop assistants and union members, who have
been herded like sheep by the sheep dogs of the union executive yapping at their heels, hear
the truth they will quieten down.
The working hours of shop assistants result from negotiations between the union and
management, and are then incorporated in the award. The working hours cannot be changed
without the consent of the union unless an arbitrator makes a decision against the union,
which is very unlikely, but is a risk that currently exists. The Bill does not in any way restrict
the union's right to negotiate the actual working hours. Does that not run contrary to what
the public and the shop assistants union have been told?

Summarising, the Bill does not in fact do the terrible things that certain opponents of
the Bill claim it does. It provides a better balance to the issue of retail trading hours. It
provides more protection in the circumstances of the 1970s, when there are new pressures on
the retailing community that were not there back in the 1920s, when the Bill was first
drafted, and in the 1950s, when it was amended. It provides for Saturday shopping in specific
areas, for specific reasons, on a rational basis, without extensive Saturday trading occurring,
because a good set of balanced criteria is given. It does not encourage a flood gate of
Saturday shopping, but allows for rationality. It is simple, logical, and unemotive legislation,
which the people, once they hear the truth in this second reading debate, will appreciate and
thank the National Government for.

passage to which the Minister of Energy Resources took offence, "What is in it for the
advertising agents?" implying that in some way there is a link between the Government, this
Bill, and what advertising agents might expect from it. Any suggestion that the
Government-or, for that matter, the Opposition-is acting under the influence of any
group outside the House is clearly out of order. I suggest it should be ruled out of order on
that basis as well.
Mr Malcolm: I do not find the statement that I am an advertising agency person at all
offensive. I suggest it should also be pointed out that I worked as a social worker for many
years. I should prefer an accurate description of my background. However, I resent deeply
the imputation by the member for Nelson that I may in some way be supporting the Bill
because I am getting something out of it.
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: All members who have been in the House for some time
discourage these remarks, but that is about the most tasteful way I have ever heard it put. I,
too, have been the victim of such an attack.
Hon. T. F. Gill: You call that tasteful?
Hon. A. J. Faulkner: It is the most tasteful I have heard for a long time. I have been the
victim of similar remarks on several occasions. I have tended to take it. As the member for
Eden suggests, I have seen remarks reported inaccurately in the paper. It seems to me to be

16 June
767
Shop Trading Hours Bill
a matter of taste and context, and often, of course, it adds to the stature of Parliament and
the person concerned. To rule it out is foolish, but it might be a good idea if members had a
little self-control about other members' private affairs, and avoided some of the problems we
have had to face since this Government took office. It ought to be a matter of self-control,
rather than control from the Chair.
Mr COURTNEY: Speaking to the point of order, I do not wish to complain, but I should
like to make you aware, if you are not already, that I have received a continuous barrage of
interjections about my private interests, and I have taken it in good fun, and shall continue
to do so. If I am taking it I am entitled to give it as well, and that is what I was attempting to
do, in rebuttal, to the member for Eden.
Mr SPEAKER: I am unaware of the details of any little private feuds in the back row.
Whether or not the member who had the floor was the one who referred, I think ineptly, to
the occupation of another member in the back row, I do not know. Standing Order 184 is
relevant, and states: "All imputations of improper motives, or unbecoming reference to a
member's private affairs, and all personal reflections, shall be deemed highly disorderly."
do not think the references to the occupation of a co-member of that portion of the Chamber
reached the level of contravening that Standing Order; they were therefore not "highly
disorderly".
However, references to other members' occupations in any sort of disparaging way are
unfortunate, and, in the interests of good order in the Chamber and good taste, they should
be omitted. There was not any grave departure from propriety in what the honourable
member said, but I think he did say it was interesting that an advertising agent had been
asked to support the motion, and that perhaps he was about the only member who could be
found to speak for it. It was suggested that it was also said "What is in it for him?", although
that has been denied. At all events, that sort of thing is sailing closer to the wind than
members of the House, including the member who has the floor, would think is desirable,
and I suggest that the debate should not proceed in that way.
Mr COURTNEY: It will be obvious that we on this side of the House are violently
opposed to this legislation, because we see it destroying not only New Zealand and the New
Zealand people but also the 40-hour week, established by a Labour Government in years
gone by, but never supported by this irrational National Government. This is the thin edge
of the wedge. Members opposite are trying to get their foot in the door to destroy and take
away from the people the 40-hour week that was worked towards for so long. Do we live to
work or work to live? What is the philosophy of these people? Is it big money that is dictating
to the Government? I suspect it is. Have the Prime Minister's men sown the seeds in the
minds of the people? This is what the Holmes task force said: "The consequences of
diversification have been gross under-use of existing shopping facilities, restricted service
outside normal shopping hours, and a decline in the average sales per store, with obvious
consequences for store profitability." I suspect that that is being fed into the heads-not the
minds of this irrational National Government. Members opposite are being led by the nose
by this group that has slotted itself in below the Prime Minister, or is being slotted in by the
Prime Minister below him.
The Government is completely inconsistent. On introducing the second reading the
Minister said that there had been very few changes, but the member for Eden, running off at
the mouth, said there had been about 19 changes, so what notice can we take when we get
this sort of inconsistency? We are told that the country wants this legislation. Who wants it?
The big developers?
Debate interrupted.
The House adjourned at 10.30 p.m.
